News.title: Wes Streeting urges Brits to stockpile water and tinned goods: 'be alert but not alarmed'
News.content:
Wes Streeting urges Brits to stockpile water and tinned goods: 'be alert but not alarmed'

Labour's defence secretary Wes Streeting has urged households to prepare for winter and stockpile water and tins in the event of an emergency - but the BBC Question Time audience branded it scaremongering

View 3 Images Wes went on to explain the Government want people "to be alert but not alarmed". (Image: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Wes Streeting has urged Brits to stockpile items like water and tinned foods ahead of winter as part of the party's 'Be Ready' campaign, but the BBC Question Time audience laughed and argued it was 'scaremongering'.

‌



‌



The first question to be discussed on this week's Question Time held in Scunthorpe was "Are we already in a proxy world war?"

‌



On the panel this week we saw: Labour's defence secretary Wes Streeting, the Conservatives’ shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat, the Green Party's Ellie Chowns, economist and journalist Stephanie Flanders, and comedian Geoff Norcott.

‌



View 3 Images Wes went on to explain the Government want people "to be alert but not alarmed". (Image: BBC)

British troops to join major NATO exercises in Poland amid Ukraine war READ MORE :

Fiona said: "Wes, tell us about this, because the government has launched this campaign for national resilience... what are we supposed to be doing in terms of tins and water?"

Wes Streeting responded: "So, today the Government launched a 'Be Ready' campaign. And what we had in mind when the campaign was being prepared was about some of the everyday threats we face, we've seen the wildfires this summer, we'll be thinking ahead worried about flooding this winter and what happens if the water pipes burst in the freezing cold, as can happen.

‌



"It's about saying to households that you can be ready by having three litres of bottled water per person per day to last you three days. Have some tinned goods that will last you a few days that might not require the microwave or the stove to heat up. Have you got first aid kits? Do you have a battery powered torch? Do you have a portable charging pack for your mobile phone? Just really practical things that I think all of us could do with."

He added: "We want to get the country ready, there's not a specific thing we've got in mind when we put this out but of course those things I've just listed that might help you through some powercuts or it might also help you through if your local shop is subject to a cyber attack and your card isn't working at the till."

‌



View 3 Images Tom Tugendhat disagreed with the lady in the audience (Image: BBC)

An audience member questioned Wes, saying: "Don't you think that's just scaremongering? Because people then go and panic buy which then affects us again."

‌



Tom Tugendhat stepped in and said: "Having some personal resilience is something that many people do already. Forgive me madam, I don't agree with you, I think the British people that by and large are pretty sensible."

To which the audience laughed and Fiona interjected: "Who can forget how many loo rolls we bought under the pandemic?" Tom responded: "I don't think it's a big ask to ask people to have a couple of days of supply."

Article continues below

Wes went on to explain the Government want people "to be alert but not alarmed".

BBC Question Time returns in Warwick next week.

News.title: Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton for Earthshot Prize countdown
News.content:
Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton for Earthshot Prize countdown

The Earthshot Prize looks to recognise and reward issues and ideas to help save the planet. It has been staged in London, Singapore, Cape Town, Boston and Rio de Janeiro.

View 3 Images Prince William appeared on The Graham Norton Show (Image: Matt Crossick/The Press Association/PA)

Prince William made a surprise appearance on an Earthshot Prize edition of The Graham Norton Show. The episode will air on BBC One on Friday, October 23.

‌



‌



He was joined by Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham. The Price of Wales sat down to gasps from the audience to speak about the environmental award, which connects all four guests.

‌



The Earthshot Prize will take place in Mumbai in November. Here, William will meet Bollywood stars as he learns about India's film industry, play with cricketing royalty and preside over the ceremony awarding £5 million in prize money.

‌



View 3 Images Prince William was joined by Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham (Image: Matt Crossick/Press Association)

Alongside the global finalists, children across India were encouraged to tackle environmental issues this year under the "I can Earthshot Challenge".

‌



The project is halfway through its decades-long cycle to recognise and reward issues and ideas to help save the planet. So far, the event has been staged in London, Singapore, Cape Town, Boston and Rio de Janeiro since its launch in 2021.

It has attracted a host of stars, including the other members of the Norton sofa on Thursday: Blanchett is an Earthshot Prize council member, Irwin is a global ambassador for the prize and Waddingham hosted the 2023 Earthshot awards in Singapore.

‌



View 3 Images The Prince and Princess of Wales at the 2022 Earthshot Prize Awards in Boston (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

William, who is first in line for the British throne, spoke about the origins of the prize and its role in identifying and supporting innovators around the world.

Article continues below

Blanchett described the Prize as a "tapestry of solutions", while Irwin spoke about the role the prize has played in building a new generation of environmental advocates.

The Earthshot Prize edition of The Graham Norton Show will air on Friday evening at 22.40 on BBC One as part of the countdown to the awards next month.

News.title: Woman, 27, charged after police officer shot in foot in Nottingham city centre
News.content:
Woman, 27, charged after police officer shot in foot in Nottingham city centre

Nottinghamshire Police have charged a 27-year-old woman after an officer was shot in the foot in Nottingham city centre.

View Image Forensic officers at the scene after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre. (Image: Joe Giddens/the Press Association)

A 27-year-old woman has been charged after a police officer was shot in the foot in Nottingham city centre.

Aisha Zaman, 27, of Collison Street, Hyson Green, was charged by police with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence.

Nottinghamshire Police also said that she had been remanded into custody and is due to appear before Nottingham Magistrates' Court on Friday.

In an update tonight the force said that the officer is still in hospital receiving treatment after he was shot in the foot in the early hours of Sunday morning.

"The officer approached two people acting suspiciously and received a gunshot wound to the foot," the statement said.

Several other people have also been arrested in connection with the incident, according to police, including two men, aged 24 and 30, and two women, aged 25 and 21, who have been arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

A 35-year-old man and a 33-year-old woman have also been arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and assisting an offender. Both remain in police custody.

Detective Chief Superintendent Rich Bull, who is leading the investigation, said: "We would just like to take this moment to thank the public. The outpouring of support for the injured officer has been greatly appreciated.

"We continue to support him as he undergoes further treatment in hospital and are keeping him and his family fully informed of the developments in this investigation.

"He has asked for privacy during this incredibly difficult time.

"We have now charged a 27-year-old woman in connection with this incident.

"We hope this offers the public some reassurance.

Article continues below

"Our investigation team are still following a number of lines of inquiry to ensure those responsible are arrested, charged, and put before the courts."

Anyone with new information that could help our inquiry are being urged to call 101 quoting incident 106 of 18 October 2026 or Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: 'Alarm bells are ringing in the NHS — as gran faced 30-hour wait in A&E'
News.content:
'Alarm bells are ringing in the NHS — as gran faced 30-hour wait in A&E'

Shocking cases like Joan Jones’s lay bare the human cost of the pressures facing the health service after years of Tory mismanagement, as extreme heat in the summer adds to strain

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Watching a loved one wait hours in agony in A&E is the stuff of nightmares.

‌



‌



Alarm bells should be blaring in the NHS over the appalling case of 86-year-old Joan Jones, who was left “rolling over in pain” in 30 hours she spent waiting to be admitted at the Royal Albert Edward Infirmary in Wigan.

‌



NHS waiting times are presented as figures on a spreadsheet but behind every number is a person, who is in pain and often terrified as they wait for treatment. Shocking cases like Joan’s lay bare the human cost of the pressures facing the health service after years of Tory mismanagement.

‌



Squeezed funding, staff shortages and decades of failure to fix social care have put the NHS under intolerable strain. Demand is now rocketing in the summer as well as winter due to extreme heat, giving the NHS no respite.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper made a welcome commitment of £140million for urgent care at the weekend but she acknowledged that this winter will be even more challenging than normal after such a heavy summer. Andy Burnham appears to be ready to grip the intractable issue of social care reform — which will free up beds.

But patients like Joan can’t afford to wait.

‌



Calling time on fire and rehire

Ministers are finally calling time on bad bosses firing and rehiring workers on worse terms.

Whether the final aim of employers is to cut pay or slash holiday entitlement, the abysmal practice sounds like it belongs in the Victorian-era not the 21st century.

‌



Unions have long battled for the change and Labour promised the move in the 2024 election.

In March next year — albeit with a short delay confirmed on Thursday — "unscrupulous" fire and rehire practices will be restricted.

‌



It is just one measure contained in the landmark Employment Rights Act brought in by this Labour government to boost workers' rights. It is one The Mirror champions.

Cash in the attic

It was an extraordinary case of cash in the attic for one Pokémon fan.

Article continues below

The anonymous collector became an overnight millionaire after his haul of mint condition cards sold for a staggering £1.56million at auction.

The collection had been gathering dust after his son lost interest in the game. Bet he's glad his dad held onto them.

News.title: Covid-bereaved families demand Matt Hancock is stripped of Privy Council role after damning care home report
News.content:
Covid-bereaved families demand Matt Hancock is stripped of Privy Council role after damning care home report

Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK says the actions of former Tory health secretary Matt Hancock 'led to thousands of avoidable deaths' in care homes

View 4 Images Matt Hancock arrives at the Covid inquiry (Image: Getty Images)

Families who lost loved ones in the Covid pandemic have blasted Matt Hancock for abandoning care homes and lying to the public during the pandemic.

‌



‌



They are urging the Prime Minister to strip the former Tory of his life-long appointment to the Privy Council – a body of senior advisers to the Monarch, which is given access to top secret information. Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK, a group representing 7,000 people, has set up a petition.

‌



A spokesman said “It is indefensible that Matt Hancock remains a member of the Privy Council. We will pursue every available route to accountability. This is just the start. We urge the Prime Minister to take this important step.”

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror just click on the link here to find them at the top of your feed.

View 4 Images Matt Hancock giving evidence to the Covid-19 Inquiry (Image: PA)

The former Health Secretary was criticised this week in a damning Covid-19 Inquiry report about how untested hospital patients were discharged into care homes where tens of thousands of residents died.

‌



The disgraced Tory had claimed to have thrown a protective ring around care homes but inquiry chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, concluded: “Quite the opposite was true.”

A spokesperson for the families group said: “The inquiry found Hancock knew how vulnerable the care sector was to a pandemic. He had been warned years before, yet did nothing to prepare for it.

‌



“He then decided to discharge untested patients into the care homes he had left unprotected. His actions led to thousands of avoidable deaths.

“He abandoned care homes and lied to families about their loved ones’ safety. His ‘protective ring’ claim was a lie. Bereaved families live with the consequences of that callous incompetence every day.

‌



“His removal would publicly acknowledge his responsibility for those deaths.”

View 4 Images A group of people comfort each other during a service at the National Covid Memorial Wall in London (Image: PA)

‌



All Cabinet ministers are appointed to the Privy Council, which dates back to the 13th century. They are given the lifelong title: “The Right Honourable”.

Members take a binding, historic oath of secrecy which allows the government to brief them on highly sensitive, classified state intelligence or national security matters – under “Privy Council terms”.

‌



This mechanism ensures that even senior opposition politicians or former ministers can be brought into the loop in national emergencies.

Though there are more than 700 current Privy Counsellors, the vast majority play no part in its daily business.

‌



As Health Secretary, Matt Hancock attended meetings to get the monarch’s approval on Covid-related legislation. Now no longer an MP, his membership is largely an honorary status.

A member is only removed if they choose to resign – usually in disgrace – or if the Prime Minister recommends that the King expel them.

‌



New Labour minister Elliot Morley was expelled in 2011 after being convicted of offences relating to the MPs’ expenses scandal. He was the first expulsion since Edgar Speyer in 1921 for trading with the enemy during the First World War.

View 4 Images Matt Hancock claimed the Tories threw 'a protective ring' around care homes (Image: PA)

‌



Earlier this year, former PM Keir Starmer brought about the expulsion of Lord Mandelson over his financial ties and relationship with the US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The Covid-19 Inquiry’s sixth report on the care sector this week told how 43,000 people died with the virus in care homes during the pandemic.

‌



It concluded failures such as lack of Covid tests and PPE were the result of a lack of pandemic planning. It said a pandemic preparedness exercise conducted in 2016, Exercise Cygnus, recommended developing social care surge capacity but it was not carried out.

The report said: “Decision makers faced an unenviable choice. They could keep patients in hospital pending tests becoming available and risk of running out of hospital beds for Covid-19 patients and increasing the risk to vulnerable patients fit for discharge.

‌



“Alternatively, to free up capacity, they could discharge patients who were potentially Covid-19-positive and run the risk of Covid-19 being introduced to vulnerable residents in care homes.”

Mr Hancock told the inquiry it “was a question of what is the least worst solution”. He resigned as Health Secretary in June 2021 after being found to have broken social distancing restrictions while having an affair with aide Gina Coladangelo.

Article continues below

The Mirror contacted Mr Hancock for comment.

News.title: Gran, 86, subject to nightmare 30-hour wait in A&E while 'rolling over in pain'
News.content:
Gran, 86, subject to nightmare 30-hour wait in A&E while 'rolling over in pain'

Barry Jones told how he watched in shock as police brought alleged criminals to the Albert Edward Infirmary in Wigan, Greater Manchester who he said received care before his elderly mum

View 5 Images Joan Jones was left in a hospital trolley as she waited to be admitted (Image: Family Handout)

An 86-year-old gran was left "rolling over in pain" during a nightmare 30-hour A&E wait, her family has said.

‌



‌



Joan Jones was rushed to the Albert Edward Infirmary in Wigan, Greater Manchester, by ambulance in the early hours of October 18 after she suffered a collapsed gallbladder. The gran was sent to A&E, where she was subject to the mammoth wait after it is alleged she was told by a nurse she wasn't a priority.

‌



During those 30 hours waiting at the hospital, her son Barry Jones, 62, from Ashton-in-Makerfield, Greater Manchester, said he watched in despair as criminals were admitted for treatment immediately as they arrived with police.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Andy Burnham welcomes world-first dementia drug trial after dad Roy dies from the disease READ MORE :

View 5 Images Barry Jones said his mother faced an 'agonising' wait (Image: Family Handout)

'The whole system is upside down'

Mr Jones said: "The situation was unbelievable. Mum was so tired and weak. Even other people in the waiting room were saying, 'what's she doing in here?'. "Police were bringing [alleged] criminals in and they were going straight in to get treatment. The whole system is upside down. It's wrong that those people are getting seen first."

‌



Furious Mr Jones said his mum was eventually given a pillow and put on a trolley bed in the hospital corridor, but only after repeatedly repeatedly asking nursing staff for help.

Angela, Joan's daughter, said her mother had been put through a "traumatic experience" at the hospital, adding elderly patients were being "let down" despite having paid into the system that should be supporting them their whole lives. Her experience came after the infirmary was found to be among the worst in the country for wait times.

‌



View 5 Images Joan only received a trolley after her family repeatedly asked nurses (Image: Family Handout)

Watchdog had downgraded hospital's urgent and emergency care

A Care Quality Commission (CQC) report from September downgraded urgent and emergency care at the Royal Albert Edward Infirmary from "good" to "requires improvement" after patient concerns were raised.

‌



The report stated that the trust was "among the worst in England" for people spending upwards of 12 hours in its emergency department, with more than 900 people saying they faced such stays in the month prior to the inspection. The report called for "rapid improvements", and after it was delivered the trust said it was "working hard" to make them.

While severe, the infirmary is not the exception to the rule in the UK, with 12-hour waits for a hospital bed having surged in recent years, reports the BBC.

‌



View 5 Images Yvette Cooper has promised to tackle hospital waiting times (Image: Getty Images)

NHS corridor care crisis deepens

According to NHS England data, the number of people waiting more than 12 hours following a decision to admit - also known as a trolley or corridor wait - has increased exponentially per quarter. The quarter ending March 2015 reported that just under 1,000 people were subject to these waits at the time, while the amount exploded to more than 155,000 in the quarter ending March 2025.

‌



The latest data from September 2026 shows that 129,199 people were left waiting four hours before admission, roughly 4,307 per day. The same data showed 50,582 more than 12-hour waits that month alone - 1,686 per day. This was up from 44,951 in August.

The figures also showed that an average of 3,310 patients in England received corridor care each day in the month of September, split between 2,549 in A&E departments and 761 in other hospital areas. Ending corridor care has become a key priority of Health Secretary Yvette Cooper, who said on October 18 that she had asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending the practice for children.

‌



That came after the case of Finlay Roberts, two, who spent hours in a busy A&E corridor shortly before he died. Finlay’s mum Liz Roberts, from north London, said: “I think it's very difficult to assess how unwell somebody is when you're sitting in a corridor with everything going on around you. The reality was he was the sickest person there, that evening. Just a few hours later, he’d be back there and they'd be saying that he had died.”

View 5 Images Medics did not identify that Finlay was seriously ill (Image: Supplied)

‌



'Alarm bells are sounding'

Ms Cooper said there would be new standards for caring for children in English A&Es, and that figures on corridor care by age would be released for the first time.

Age UK estimates that older Brits are disproportionately impacted by corridor care, however, with one in 10 people aged between 50 and 59 waiting 12 hours or more. The number rises to one third, the charity estimates, when the hospital waits of people aged 90 and older are considered.

‌



Health and Social Care Secretary Yvette Cooper told The Mirror: “For Joan and her family to have to go through this is just awful, and incredibly distressing. Nobody should be treated on a trolley or in a corridor, or have to endure this kind of wait in our A&Es. We cannot accept this standard of care, particularly when people are at their most vulnerable.

“We have a major turnaround programme underway across the NHS, after years in which it was neglected, but there is a lot of essential work to do, especially for hospitals to turnaround A&E, and I have made clear that tackling corridor care must be a priority.

‌



“On Sunday, we announced £140million for 14 more urgent care schemes, on top of the 25 due to open in time for this winter, to boost NHS capacity, free up hospital beds and help tackle the unacceptable corridor care and waits so patients like Joan are treated quickly and in an appropriate space.”

Layla Moran, chair of the health and social care committee, said: "Joan's agonising experience should shock us all. Whilst this happened at a hospital known to be underperforming, alarm bells are sounding across this country's A&Es that waiting times and corridor care are likely to ramp up as winter approaches.

‌



"The Health and Social Care Committee has requested an evidence session with ministers on how the government is preparing the health service for winter pressures so that what should be extreme cases like this can hopefully be kept to a minimum."

Mary Fleming, the CEO of the Wrightington, Wigan and Leigh Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (WWL) said in a statement that she was sorry to hear about the family's concerns.

‌



She said: "We welcome the opportunity to speak with her family directly, understand their concerns and provide any additional support we can. Because of increased demand across our urgent and emergency care services and delays in discharge, some patients are experiencing longer waits than we would ever want.

"We understand how worrying and stressful it can be when someone you love needs urgent care." Ms Fleming added that the hospital is trying to reduce wait times following "unprecedented demand" for its services.

Article continues below

She added: "We're working hard to develop alternatives to Emergency Department but while we do experience periods of unprecedented demand, we will continue to treat patients in order of clinical priority and to ensure people receive the right care, in the right place, at the right time."

News.title: Storm Austen: Brits face 19 flood alerts as 80mm of rain to batter country tonight - see full list
News.content:
Storm Austen: Brits face 19 flood alerts as 80mm of rain to batter country tonight - see full list

With Storm Austen sweeping in within hours, the threat of floods is growing as the the Environment Agency pinpoints the areas most at risk in the next 48 hours

View 3 Images The flooding in Herefordshire last year caused lasting damage (Image: PA)

Brits are not only readying themselves for intense winds and heavy rain as Storm Austen sweeps in — but the prospect of flooding too.

‌



‌



Already, people in 19 areas have been told to be prepared with flood alerts issued on Thursday. The warnings come with the storm set to make landfall in the early hours, with the Met Office urging people living in some parts of the UK to consider preparing an “emergency” kit ahead of its arrival.

‌



The far Southwest of England could see wind speeds reaching as high as 90mph, while coastal areas covered by yellow warnings may see gusts of 70mph. Heavy rain is expected to be a major hazard too. As well as sounding a caution for rain and wind, flooding is feared in the next 48 hours.

‌



The Environment Agency has particular concern for the South Devon coast at Beesands, Torcross, Slapton and Dawlish. You can follow the storm on various webcams right here.

Storm Austen watch live: Webcams from around UK to show horror 90mph winds smash Britain READ MORE :

View 3 Images Many of England's alerts are in Devon and Dorset (Image: Check for Flooding)

In England there are eight, with the Met Office warning of road, rail, air and ferry services being affected, with longer journey times and cancellations possible. Power cuts may occur, they say, with the potential to affect other services, such as mobile phone coverage.

‌



There are almost a dozen alerts in Scotland, with Aberdeen, Dundee and Edinburgh among the cities covered in the alert. Up to 80mm of rain is expected to hit - the equivalent of one month-worth of rainfall for the capital.

‌



Elsewhere, an Amber Wind Warning covers Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly, Plymouth, and parts of west Devon from 1:00am to 10:00am on Friday. Yellow Wind and Rain Warnings are valid for swathes of southern England, south Wales, the English Channel coast, and parts of Scotland. A rare Red Warning has been issued the Channel Islands, with schools closed there on Friday.

View 3 Images Aberdeen, Dundee and Edinburgh are some of the 11 areas in Scotland covered (Image: sepa)

‌



The relentless low-pressure system is heading to UK shores later tonight with Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season, is expected to affect south-west England in the early hours of Friday.

The Met Office urges people living under the yellow rain warning to consider preparing a “flood plan and an emergency flood kit”. It has published advice regarding what to include in an emergency kit.

‌



Met Office Deputy Chief Forecaster Chris Bulmer said: "Storm Austen is expected to bring a spell of impactful weather to parts of the UK from Thursday night and through Friday.

"While there remains some uncertainty in the exact track of the storm, there is increasing confidence in the potential for disruptive winds across parts of southwest England, which is why an Amber warning has been issued.

‌



"Winds gusts could potentially reach 60-70 mph for a time, and these strong winds will be combined with spells of heavy rain. People in affected areas should keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings as the event develops."

But that's not it - over the weekend, Storm Boelo will affect Northern Ireland, Scotland and parts of northern England with what the Met Office described as "impactful winds".

‌



Where flood alerts are issued

England

South Devon coast at Beesands, Torcross, Slapton and Dawlish

South Devon coast from Start Point to Dawlish Warren

West coast of Dorset

East coast of Dorset

Christchurch Harbour

River Churnet and River Tean

Lower River Soar in Leicestershire

News.title: Man charged with murder after ‘stabbed’ mum dies following Bridgend crash
News.content:
Man charged with murder after ‘stabbed’ mum dies following Bridgend crash

Clifford Foster, 61, of Bridgend, has been charged with murder after after housing association worker Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died after her car crashed into a wall, having sustained 'puncture wounds'

View 2 Images Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after her car crashed into a wall on Coity Road in Bridgend (Image: South Wales Police)

A man has been charged with murder after a housing association worker died following a car crash in South Wales, having sustained “puncture wounds”.

Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after her car crashed into a wall on Coity Road in Bridgend on Monday afternoon.

Clifford Foster, 61, of Bridgend, has been charged with murder in connection with her death, which is not being investigated as a “domestic incident”.

He is due to appear at Newport Magistrates’ Court on Friday.

South Wales Police previously said Ms Barnfield had suffered “puncture wounds” which were not sustained in the collision.

View 2 Images Police at the scene of the incident near Brook street, Bridgend (Image: Media Wales)

Senior Investigating Officer Claire Lamerton, of South Wales Police, said: “My thoughts remain with Eleanor’s loved ones at such a devastating time, and they continue to be supported by specialist officers.

“This is not being investigated as a domestic incident, and I encourage the public to not speculate about the circumstances as court proceedings are now active.”

In a tribute issued through police on Wednesday, Ms Barnfield’s family said: “Mum was the kindest, most loving bravest person in the world.

“She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends. She was our rock.”

The murder charge follows a “significant policing operation” around Ger-y-Nant, which is managed by the Valleys to Coast housing association, where Ms Barnfield worked.

Ger-y-Nant, a sheltered housing and retirement complex of 13 flats, has non-resident management staff and accepts new residents aged 60 or over, according to an online profile of the facility.

Valleys to Coast housing association chief executive, Jo Oak, said previously: “We are devastated by the tragic death of our colleague, Eleanor Barnfield.

“Eleanor was a much-valued member of the Valleys to Coast team, and her loss has been deeply felt by everyone who knew and worked alongside her.

“She made an important contribution to our organisation and to the communities we serve, and she will be remembered with great warmth and affection by her colleagues.

“Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Eleanor’s family and friends at this unimaginably difficult time.

‌



“We are doing everything we can to support those affected by her loss.

“We continue to co-operate fully with South Wales Police and, out of respect for Eleanor’s family and the ongoing investigation, we will not be commenting further on the circumstances of her death at this time.”

‌



A Welsh Ambulance Service spokesperson said previously: “We were called on Monday (October 19) at approximately 12.44pm, to reports of a road traffic collision on Coity Road, Bridgend.

“A Cymru High Acuity Response Unit arrived on scene seven minutes after the initial call at 12:51pm, with two emergency ambulances arriving to provide additional support at 1.07pm and 1.13pm.

‌



“Advanced critical care support was delivered by the Emergency Medical Retrieval and Transfer Service who arrived in a Wales Air Ambulance charity helicopter.

“The patient was conveyed by road to hospital.

‌



“We are aware that contradictory and misleading rumours regarding a delayed ambulance response have been circulating on social media.

“These are factually untrue and we would encourage members of the public not to speculate.”

News.title: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns public
News.content:
Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber-attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, the defence secretary has said.

Wes Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.

He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies.

Streeting also said that cyber incidents - like the recently discovered critical security flaw in the programming language which powers much of the internet - will happen "more and more".

Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that the UK is facing a greater threat to the country, "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime".

Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford earlier on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households.

He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and the flooding that is expected this winter.

Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".

The defence secretary referenced the critical security flaw in the PHP programming language which has left organisations around the world scrambling to update their systems.

In the UK, 32 government services were offline while the potential cyber-security issues were addressed.

"It's not just from foreign states engaged in espionage or sabotage; it's also organised criminals," Streeting told Question Time.

"In this world of AI that we live in... it does also present threats if people are innovating and pushing against conventional [cyber] defences."

News.title: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope
News.content:
Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.

A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the Â£25,000 prize.

"I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry."

It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994.

Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Raye said she'd "poured everything I had" into the record, which features the global hit song Where Is My Husband?

"I made this album not focusing on commercial [success], not focusing on making things cookie-cutter," said the 28-year-old.

"Some of these songs are seven minutes. They're indulgent. They're maximalist."

Across 17 tracks and 73 minutes, the record tells a cinematic story about a relationship that ends in tears on the rainy streets of Paris, then follows our plucky heroine as she dusts off the debris and emerges stronger and more resilient.

Along the way, it features both of her grandparents, the soul legend Al Green, four separate orchestras and more than 100 musicians.

News.title: Amber warning in place as Storm Austen hits parts of UK
News.content:
An amber weather warning has come into force in parts of the UK as Storm Austen brings a swathe of powerful winds and heavy rain on Friday.

South West England is forecast to be worst hit by the storm which the Met Office warns could bring travel disruption, power cuts and a possible danger to life.

Wind gusts of 60-70mph, with 80mph in exposed locations, are forecast across Cornwall and parts of Devon, where the Met Office warning is in force until 10:00 BST.

Wind gust of 45-60mph are forecast more widely across most of England and Wales, where two less severe yellow warnings will be in force throughout Friday. A separate yellow warning will also cover part of Scotland, including Glasgow and Edinburgh, from 06:00 BST.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over while buildings could also potentially be damaged, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm.

A number of schools are closed in the impacted areas with many others opening later than usual to avoid the strongest winds.

Train cancellations and speed restrictions are possible because of the increased danger of branches and trees blocking railways.

A number of ferry sailings have also been cancelled, including crossings between Pembrokeshire and Ireland.

Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places.

As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre.

That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph.

The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph.

All schools in Jersey have been told to close on Friday because of the high winds predicted to be caused by Storm Austen.

Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors - paranoia deepens as traitor behaviour splits opinion
News.content:
Once the croissant crumbs had been cleared, it was time for a mission that threw the cat among the pigeons - not least because the traitor's lair it took place in "smelled like a litter tray", according to Jerry.

Miranda felt there were more complex olfactory notes at play: "A mix of salmon, cheap cologne and crotch." Delightful.

The mission involved each player having to build a shield on a plinth in front of them out of 3D jigsaw-type pieces which were buried in troughs in sawdust. Think Krypton Factor meets lucky dip.

At three intervals, a bell would ring, and the players all had to stop and put on blindfolds for a few minutes. The traitors could then remove theirs and go about sabotaging the handiwork of anyone they fancied.

And while James A revealed he was "starting to have more fun" after murdering poor Ross, if there was a prize for the worst traitor of all time, he would still smash it.

He was too scared to take off his blindfold and remove any shield pieces from the faithfuls, leaving the dirty work - and all the risk - to fellow traitors Maya Jama and King Kenny. Suffice to say, they were not impressed.

"He didn't even lift the blindfold off - I'm speechless," said Maya.

James A knew he was in trouble: "I'm aware I'll get a dressing down in the turret but I am the one who killed Grant Mitchell."

He wasn't wrong about the telling off. And the fact he completed his own puzzle, earning himself a shield, must have really riled his co-conspirators.

To be fair, you could argue he's playing a blinder - there's been very little suspicion of him so far.

Three other celebrities also managed to complete their shield puzzles - James B, Joanne McNall and Michael Sheen - but no money was banked after Maya and Kenny panicked and didn't remove any pieces at their last opportunity.

But the task at least threw up another bunch of mad theories for the faithfuls to chew over, as they tried to unsuccessfully guess where the floorboard creaking was coming from as two of the traitors tried to creep around the room.

It was good news for Romesh at least, whose hay fever saved the day - Sharon Rooney could hear him sniffing constantly next to her so knew he couldn't have been a traitor.

Maybe the tickly moustache isn't helping his allergies - and combing it won't make much difference.

News.title: Grid operator says lights will stay on this winter after concerns
News.content:
The body in charge of Britain's electricity network has given assurances that the lights will stay on this winter after concerns were raised by some of its engineers.

The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months.

However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation.

NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days".

It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine.

"While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO.

In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables.

News.title: Give more people weight-loss jabs on the NHS, say MPs
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands more people should be given access to the weight-loss injection Mounjaro on the NHS in England, a cross-party group of MPs says.

The Health Committee said the current plan for 220,000 people to have this jab for free on prescription in 2028 was a "woefully small number" and "unambitious".

This represents only around 6% of eligible people and is a key reason why more than a million have been paying privately for weight-loss injections, including Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The committee says a two-tier system is emerging in which only the wealthy can get good access to the medication that curbs appetite.

News.title: Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show
News.content:
The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.

During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.

As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa.

They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet".

The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films.

William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives Â£1m.

The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November.

Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro.

The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability.

At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible".

The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday.

News.title: Items recovered in search for missing fishing boat and crew
News.content:
Items belonging to a fishing boat that vanished off the north coast of the Isle of Lewis last week have been recovered as the search for the vessel and two missing crew members continues.

Norman "Tam" Murray, 40 and Murdo Morrison, 23, were on board the Kilda when it disappeared on 13 October.

The body of crewmate Douglas Craigie, 49, was recovered from the sea in the early hours of the following morning by rescuers.

On Thursday, police confirmed that items belonging to the vessel had been recovered from what was described as "an area of interest" off the coast near Port of Ness.

The search was carried out by Police Scotland's marine and dive unit and partners.

A Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) exclusion zone has been in place for divers and vessels in an area between the Butt of Lewis and Port of Ness, but this will be lifted from 23:59 on Thursday.

Insp Neil Taylor, local area inspector for the Western Isles, said the search was a "complex operation" and asked for officers to be given "time and space" to carry out inquiries.

He said: "Efforts are continuing to work with partners and we are doing everything we can to get answers.

"While the Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) exclusion zone will be lifted tonight, we would urge people not to put themselves at any risk.

"Please do not attempt to carry out searches in areas which put you at risk of harm."

A GoFundMe for the families affected by the event has raised more than Â£148,000, against a target of Â£110,000.

News.title: Private care home investors a risk to public sector, regulator says
News.content:
Private companies buying up care homes for older people in England could undermine the government's ambition to create a universal care service, the regulator says.

The Care Quality Commission's annual report, external highlights how an increasing share of the care home market is owned by large firms - the five biggest have increased their share of the market by 26% in the last two years, driven by interest from US property investors. Between them they own around one in seven homes.

While there could be benefits, there are concerns the trend can lead to higher prices and a reduction in the quality of care - something the CQC says needs to be monitored.

Meanwhile, home care, providing support to help people wash and dress in their own home, has become more fragmented, with a greater number of smaller providers.

The CQC says this could create inefficiencies - nearly a third of these services are providing care to four or fewer people.

In contrast, there are few smaller care homes judged important for providing specialist and personalised care.

Small care homes have always represented a tiny proportion of the care home market, but over the last 14 years the numbers have fallen significantly, particularly those that combine care with nursing support, which are down by a quarter.

News.title: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".

The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show.

Statements from the woman's parents were also heard in court, saying their daughter had told them about the alleged attack, and that she had been "very worried about HIV".

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

The witness said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre, and that he then sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead.

She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after", she said she "was just crying - really upset".

The witness said Brand had forced her into having anal sex at the end of an encounter that started off consensually.

"He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her.

"He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt".

The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started.

News.title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
News.content:
Barclays is cutting around 5,000 staff as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.

The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce.

The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall.

Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy.

Although not all of the cuts are due to AI, their scale will prompt further concern over the impact of the new technology.

Company spending on AI is increasing along with claims new tools can replace some of the basic tasks currently done by staff such as administrative and programming work.

HSBC, Standard Chartered and Danske Bank have also flagged AI-related job cuts this year.

"It is a hot button topic," said AJ Bell investment analyst, Russ Mould.

However, banks had not yet made big moves towards the widespread introduction of AI and they would be considering the implications for security and customer service before implementing AI technology to make financial savings, he said.

"Any company at any time needs to keep on top of its cost base," he said.

"It will be intriguing to see what other banks say in their results in the coming weeks.

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union that represents banking sector workers said the company was "using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce".

"Employers should be focussed on upgrading employees' skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach," she said.

Barclays is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected.

AJ Bell's Russ Mould said despite "reaching for the AI lever" Barclays had failed to match expectations with its financial results.

Barclays also revealed it made Â£2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast.

Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business.

"AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future.

"We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake.

"Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."

Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers.

Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years".

"Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said.

Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further Â£1.1bn of savings in 2027.

News.title: Tommy Robinson hired detectives to find journalists, court told
News.content:
Political activist Tommy Robinson has told a court he hired private detectives to track down and photograph two reporters to "put pressure" on them.

The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, told Southwark Crown Court he was "shocked and scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".

He has denied two charges of harassment causing fear of violence to reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber after the 2024 Southport attacks.

Robinson is accused of writing posts on X, sending direct messages and making phone calls that made the two journalists fear the risk of vigilante attacks.

He denied wanting to expose the journalists to threats of violence, and said he felt his actions were "totally reasonable... under the circumstances".

News.title: Lockerbie bombing accused loses bid to have case thrown out
News.content:
She referred to a longstanding American legal doctrine, which stipulates that a court's right to hold a trial is not impaired if the suspect has been the subject of a forceful abduction.

"This rule rests on the principle that due process of law is satisfied when one present in court is convicted of a crime after a fair trial and in accordance with constitutional procedural safeguards," said the judge.

"Put differently, there's nothing in the Constitution that requires a court to permit a guilty person rightfully convicted to escape justice because he was brought to trial against his will."

In her ruling, the judge said there were two exceptions to that doctrine.

One would apply if Marimi had been brought before the court through the US government's "deliberate, unnecessary and unreasonable invasion" of his constitutional rights.

For that exception to be triggered, the challenged conduct had to be carried out by, or at the direction of, US officials.

The judge said Marimi's allegations "at best suggest that US government officials exerted pressure on Libyan officials to facilitate a rendition, not that US government officials directed or controlled the challenged conduct."

The second exception to the doctrine would apply if the US government had violated an extradition agreement which was the only way a suspect could be transferred between the two countries.

The judge said the US government had invoked two conventions to secure Marimi's appearance in a US court.

News.title: Map thief leads 'merry dance' with return promises
News.content:
Defence barrister Jessica Flain said West had partly paid a man to restore the map, but he would not hand it back until the full fee was settled. She asked for sentencing to be adjourned for seven days so a friend could pay the balance and West could take the map to Charing Cross Police Station.

Judge Charlotte Welsh refused, saying she did "not believe a word of it".

She said West had told the court in June that he could return the map within seven days, and in August that it was with a friend and he would retrieve it once he had recovered from heart surgery.

"Again, that appears to have been a lie," she said. "You were charged in February. You have had eight months to return the map."

The judge said she believed West had a buyer in mind and had stolen the map "to order".

The court heard he had 27 convictions for 107 offences in the UK and abroad, mostly for dishonesty and including 41 thefts. They included a burglary conviction in Hungary in 2011 and a theft conviction in France in 2013, and he had also been convicted under various identities.

Flain said West, a father of two, was "ashamed and embarrassed" and had been in debt and unable to meet basic living costs. She described the offence as "a short-term, pressured decision by an elderly man living in difficult circumstances".

Judge Welsh said the map was of "international cultural significance" and the damage had "permanently diminished what can be learned from it". The court was told the two digital copies of the atlas are incomplete.

West was jailed for three years for criminal damage, with concurrent sentences of 16 months for theft and six months for possessing a bladed article. The judge refused to suspend the sentence, saying immediate custody was needed "to deter other people from doing precisely what you have".

News.title: Police should not be scared to wade in to stop wrongdoing, says Badenoch
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised punishments for people who intervene to "do the right thing" in a speech at the Police Federation conference.

Telling delegates she was "not scared to wade in", she called for more support for members of the public as well as police officers who step in to stop wrongdoing.

Badenoch also criticised Labour for failing to send a minister to the conference for two years in a row.

The prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman rejected the claims, stating the police have the government's "full backing" and are benefitting from investment. The BBC has contacted the Home Office for comment on ministerial attendance at the police conference.

In a speech at the conference, Badenoch said: "Too often these days, we fail to recognise sacrifice and service.

"Whether it's hounding brave and elderly veterans through the courts, hounding police officers who try to do the right thing, or even ordinary members of the public who step in to help only to find that they're in trouble themselves.

"It's no wonder the people in this country are becoming too scared to wade in, too scared to do the right thing. Well, I am different. I am not scared to wade in, and I am not scared to back the police."

The Conservative leader listed police officers who have been killed in the line of duty, such as PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough who died in the Cleveland A66 crash, and PC Andrew Harper, killed investigating a quad bike theft.

She also attacked police being investigated following controversial cases, including the case of 24-year-old Chris Kaba, who was shot by Sgt Matthew Blake in 2022 after he tried to ram his way past police cars.

The police officer was put on trial for murder before being cleared, with Badenoch saying his "job was made harder because he didn't get the backing he deserved".

Badenoch also attacked Labour, saying: "I think it is telling that for two years in a row, the Labour Government has not sent anyone to address this conference â not the policing minister, not the Home Secretary.

"You are the ones who enforce the law. You are the ones who ensure there are consequences for bad behaviour. That's why, if we want law and order back in our country, back on our streets, we need to back the police."

Responding, the prime minister's official deputy spokeswoman said: "I would reject those claims.

"The police have the government's full backing and as you will have seen from various reports this morning, we are continuing to invest in our police and we are bringing forward reforms following the Bernard Hogan Howe report in due course."

The Home Office has been contacted for comment about ministerial attendance at the conference and whether the government is still planning to recruit 13,000 police officers.

News.title: Fahnbulleh says she backs home secretary on migration after comments to journalists
News.content:
The energy minister has insisted she backs Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's immigration reforms after she made what she described as a "light-hearted remark".

Miatta Fahnbulleh was repeatedly asked in an interview on Wednesday whether she supported the government's plans to increase the time it takes for migrants to gain permanent UK residency, but refused to.

Referring to that exchange, she joked to reporters on Thursday that she did not explicitly answer the question because she had told herself she would "never lie".

In a later statement, she said: "Today I made what was meant to be a light-hearted self-deprecating remark. I didn't get it right and it hasn't come off as I intended."

She added: "I fully support our home secretary and the government's position on migration reform."

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

The government wants to double the time it takes most migrant workers to qualify for permanent residence from five years to 10 years, while in the case of refugees it could take 20 years.

Mahmood told Labour Party conference in September the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country".

But a significant number of Labour MPs and trade unions want her to water down the proposed policy.

Downing Street has repeatedly insisted that Mahmood is considering responses to a consultation exercise before finalising the reforms.

On Wednesday, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to make sure we get this right."

Asked earlier on the same day on Sky News, whether she backed the proposed reforms, Fahnbulleh said: "We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution."

She was pressed several more times on the issue, saying the government was consulting on the proposals and would "will come out with the measures that we take forward".

At a lunch with political reporters on Thursday, Fahnbulleh said: "I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge [on Sky] yesterday, but nevermind."

In her later statement, she said this was a joke and suggested it was not intended to show she did not support Mahmood's reforms.

"As I said earlier this week, it's absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship," Fahnbulleh said.

It comes after another Cabinet minister, Angela Rayner, criticised the proposed changes ahead of Labour's conference in Liverpool.

Rayner warned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules.

She later denied there was a split within the heart of government over the issue.

News.title: Models in wheelchairs take center stage at Romanian fashion show, in photos
News.content:
