In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Aussie boxing legend Jeff Fenech hospitalised as he faces fresh new health battle: 'He's always a fighter'
Sports.content:
Aussie boxing legend Jeff Fenech hospitalised as he faces fresh new health battle: 'He's always a fighter'

Australian boxing legend Jeff Fenech has been hospitalised with heart problems, with his NRL star son-in-law Bradman Best revealing the family’s concern ahead of his Kangaroos debut.

The four-weight world champion, 62, was admitted to Strathfield Private Hospital around 10 days ago after suffering severe fatigue, breathing difficulties and feeling unwell.

Fenech has since had a blood clot removed from his wrist and undergone tests to investigate whether a potentially life-threatening staph infection has returned.

A recurrence has not been confirmed.

Best, who has a baby daughter with Fenech’s daughter Kayla, disclosed the hospital stay while discussing the boxing great’s influence on his career.

The Newcastle centre is preparing to make his Australian Test debut against Fiji on Sunday, but took time to acknowledge Fenech’s health battle.

Jeff Fenech, 62, has been hospitalised after suffering heart problems, fatigue and breathing difficulties

Bradman Best paid tribute to his father-in-law ahead of his Australian Test debut

Fenech has reportedly had a blood clot removed from his wrist and undergone tests for a possible recurrence of a serious infection

‘Jeff has been massive for me, I just want to give a quick shout-out to him,’ Best said.

‘He’s actually in hospital at the moment.

‘I’m thinking of him. He’s tough, he’s always a fighter.’

Best said Fenech had become an invaluable source of advice as he worked towards representing Australia.

‘Jeff has done a lot for me in my career,’ he said.

‘I was visiting him last week and he’s always giving me tips on what to do and how to be better.

‘It’s special having a father-in-law like that who’s a four-time world champion.

‘He’s an icon in Australia and it’s special having a bond like that with him.’

Tim Tszyu’s preparations for his world-title clash with Erislandy Lara have been disrupted by his trainer’s hospitalisation

Fenech became one of Australia’s greatest boxers, winning world titles across four weight divisions during a career that earned him the nickname ‘The Marrickville Mauler’

Asked whether Fenech’s condition was serious, Best remained hopeful.

‘Yeah, he will be right. He’s always a fighter. He’s been in there with a few heart problems and stuff, but he’ll be good.’

The hospitalisation has also interrupted Tim Tszyu’s preparations for his planned WBA middleweight world-title clash with Erislandy Lara.

Fenech became Tszyu’s head trainer in July, helping guide him to a unanimous decision victory over American star Errol Spence Jr.

Tszyu credited the veteran trainer with helping inspire that result, which set up his pursuit of a world championship in a second weight division.

With Fenech sidelined, fellow trainer Basil Nassis has taken charge of Tszyu’s work in the gym.

The Lara bout is expected to take place in Australia in November or December, according to the reports.

Fenech hopes to recover in time to be involved, although the Telegraph reported he is unlikely to perform padwork during the build-up.

The latest scare follows two major heart operations.

In October 2019, Fenech underwent emergency open-heart surgery in Thailand while preparing Jack Brubaker for a fight against Tszyu.

He needed another six-hour open-heart operation in 2024 during a serious infection.

Sports.title: British boxing has a world beater in the ascendancy. Daniel Dubois is starting to look like a monster - and he's ready for Oleksandr Usyk, Anthony Joshua, Tyson Fury or anyone else, writes JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
'Bring him on,' roared Daniel Dubois when asked if he would like a third fight against the greatest boxer of his generation who has beaten him twice.

Oleksandr Usyk, who is in a state of limbo somewhere between vacating all the heavyweight tiles and semi-retirement, is a genius so may not fall readily into the trap baited on the banks of the Thames in the dark hours of this Sunday morning.

Ukraine's war hero will have watched Dubois annihilate the gallant Fabio Wardley and recognised that Dynamite Daniel is no longer the callow youth he wiped the canvas with a couple of times during his reign as the undisputed world champion.

Promoter Frank Warren is not given to understatement but when he said 'Daniel has matured now' he was only scratching the surface of the transformation.

It may be a stretch to compare Dubois with the once terrifying Sonny Liston but to those rivals wearing the other belts he needs if he is to become undisputed then he is starting to look like a monster.

'I want them all,' said WBO champion Dubois. He was referring to the winner between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua in December, who will thereby hold a WBA title, as well as IBF and WBC champions Filip Hrgovic and Ajit Kabayel.

Daniel Dubois knocks down Fabio Wardley during his annihilation on Saturday night

Dubois has declared himself ready to fight anyone in the heavyweight division

Their availability, especially that of AJ or the Gypsy King, will be determined no doubt by there being many more millions in the Aladdin's Cave from which Saudi Arabia has helped finance the welcome flux of mega-fights of late.

If so then Warren is promising a 2027 bursting with monthly heavyweight spectaculars as lustily anticipated as Dubois' second demolition of Wardley . At the rapid conclusion of which another packed O2 crowd was switching its allegiance from a love affair with Fabio's romanticised emergence from white collar boxing to realisation that Britain has a world beater in the ascendancy.

One who may be growing, also, into more of a box office star than the monosyllabic Liston ever was. If his accurate bravura prediction of a 'bash and smash' slaughter of Wardley and his most jovial media conference yet which followed are anything to go by.

Having nursed his confidence in the Dubois family cocoon Daniel now has a mansion of his own to live in and a selection of race cars to drive. No more Mister Shy Guy but none the less likeable for that.

The transition to full manhood was rounded off over the two fights with Wardley. This included recovery from two early knockdowns in the first Fight Of The Year battle to a brutal 11th round stoppage victory.

And now the onslaught triggered by a staggering right hand blow only 17 seconds after the first bell which imposed an eight count on the ropes. Followed by an overwhelming TKO in round two. Wham, bam and thank you man. No criticism this time of a delay in calling it off. In flew the white towel, in jumped referee Steve Gray.

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua fight each other in December - and Dubois wants the winner

There has been some nagging at the edge of Dubois' triumph. Suggestions that Wardley came back too soon after the second-half beating in May. But if five-and-a-half months is not sufficient time to recover then how long would be? The immortal Joe Louis used to fight once a month, for heaven's sake.

Wardley, honest man that he is, blamed himself. Having lived to fight another day he vows to do better enough to launch a comeback campaign for another world title. Meanwhile Dubois, at 29 last month, heads for the stratosphere as champion of the next generation of heavyweight boxing.

As the new monster of the prize-ring? It took The Greatest Of All Time to stop the Liston beast In his awesome tracks. Might Usyk be the Muhammad Ali in waiting for Dubois? Maybe. Perhaps not since he is the older legend now. It would be fascinating finding out.

The tombstone on Sonny Liston's grave in Las Vegas describes him simply as A MAN. Frank Warren is right about Dubois becoming exactly that.

Sports.title: Former heavyweight world title contender boxer dies 'suddenly' aged 40: Denis Boytsov, once set to fight Tyson Fury, was unable to speak for 11 years after mysterious 'attack'
Sports.content:
A former world No 2 heavyweight boxer once primed to fight Tyson Fury has died aged just 40, after 11 years of care following an 'attack' in which the perpetrators were never found.

Russian Denis Boytsov pulled out of a fight with Fury in December 2012 and was considered the world's second-best heavyweight behind Wladimir Klitschko. He had a 36-1 record when his career was cut short in 2015.

Boytsov suffered serious head injuries in a Berlin subway tunnel and had to be placed into a medically induced coma because of swelling on the brain.

A statement on the boxer's website suggested he was the victim of an attack linked to his boxing career. 'It is possible that this attack was linked to the boxer's sporting activity,' the statement said. 'Around two years ago, Boytsov was receiving threats constantly.'

His wife Olga Litvinova was left deeply upset and suggested Boytsov may have been the victim of an attempted 'assassination' after that series of threats.

Now, 11 years on, Boytsov's family have revealed he died 'suddenly' this week after many years in care. His father says the cause of death was a detached blood clot.

Russian boxer Denis Boytsov died this week from a detached blood clot at home

Boystov is pictured in his boxing gear in hospital after the 'attack' on him in 2015

'A blood clot broke off,' Nikolai Boytsov told Russian news agency TASS. 'There was nothing they could do; it was instant death. Three minutes and that was it.

'This happened at home. His wife fed him and started turning him to the side. He suddenly broke down, started shaking, turned blue. And his whole life was over.'

Brother Maxim Boytsov revealed Denis had been unable to speak in the 11 years following the Berlin incident. Boytsov underwent extensive treatment in Germany and then back in his homeland.

'No, we didn't communicate. He just nodded yes and no. But he understood everything. I courted him for ten years. But it didn't work out,' said Maxim.

Boytsov's funeral is set for today in the Russian region of Oryol.

British former heavyweight boxer David Price - who once beat Fury in 2005 - revealed Boytsov's punching power was much stronger than that of Anthony Joshua, having trained with both.

Boytsov's wife Olga was by his side as he died in Russia this week

Boytsov was due to fight Tyson Fury in 2012 and was considered a top heavyweight fighter

'I sparred a Russian called Denis Boytsov in Germany once. He only hit the top of my head, but he was a powerful puncher,' Price told the Daily Star.

'I think he got his career cut short, he got absolutely battered and left for dead, he couldn't fight again. But I remember him being a really powerful puncher.'

Sports.title: Britain's only female boxing referee faces backlash as she REFUSES to accept fighter's towel being thrown in twice - moments before technical knockout by a brutal headshot at the O2 Arena
Sports.content:
Britain's only female boxing referee faces backlash as she REFUSES to accept fighter's towel being thrown in twice - moments before technical knockout by a brutal headshot at the O2 Arena

It is the best-known sign of submission in sport - but a boxing referee at the O2 Arena on Saturday night twice refused to accept a heavyweight fighter 'throwing in the towel' before he was brutally beaten.

Heavyweights Adam Olaniyan and Dan Garber were fighting in London on the undercard of Daniel Dubois' victory over Fabio Wardley - with Bradford fighter Garber, 41, beaten by technical knockout (TKO) in the second round.

But focus after the fight has instead been on referee Amy Pu, after she allowed Garber to undergo more punishing headshots even after his team had tried to stop the fight. Pu, the UK's first and only female professional boxing referee, kicked a towel thrown by Garber's team out of the ring to allow the fight to continue.

Garber had been dismayed by his team's attempts to submit and Pu elected to continue on with the fight. Seconds later, Olaniyan, 20, unleashed a flurry of further punches which sent Garber to the canvas to end the contest. Garber's team had thrown in another towel but that was also ignored before Pu stopped the punishment.

Garber could be seen receiving oxygen ringside after the fight.

It is rare for referees to overrule the decision of the boxer's corner to end a bout but is allowed within the sport's rules. British Boxing Board of Control (BBBofC) regulations state that the towel does not automatically end a fight and referees are left with the authority on when to do so.

Referee Amy Pu finally steps in to end Adam Olaniyan's fight against Dan Garber on Saturday

Garber's team twice tried to throw in the towel to stop the fight but Pu refused the submission

But fans were unimpressed by Pu's decision-making, with footage of her kicking the white towel out of the ring going viral after being posted by broadcasters DAZN.

'Ref nearly got dan garber killed. Kicking the towel out idiot,' one viewer wrote on X.

Another fan said: 'Dan Garber receiving oxygen after referee Amy Pu inexplicably refuses the corner's towel and allows Olaniyan to pile more damage in. Rules should be changed to make the towel coming in an automatic fight ended. Refs don't know what's been happening in the gym.'

And another picked apart Pu's record, writing: 'Bbbofc referee Amy Pu has been mostly terrible all night, two stoppages called earlier than they needed to be, kicking the towel out to let Dan Garber take more punishment, this is not new for her.'

Originally from Taiwan, Pu took up boxing in her 30s in London and later became a professional referee in 2024. She has spoken about isolated issues of suffering from racism and sexism in the male-dominated world of boxing.

'On the professional side, I have to say the reaction has mostly been really positive,' Pu told the BBC earlier this year. 'During the amateur days, there were some odd comments and stuff. I think one of the hesitations I had before turning professional was also for that reason.

'People have just been so supportive, knock on wood, I haven't really had any criticism directed at me because of my sex or because of my race.

'I'm really grateful and I hope that it continues, that people should see me as a referee. They can give me stick as a referee, not as a female Asian referee.'

Rising star Olaniyan's record now stands at 5-0 in his short professional career, while Garber has 14 victories to 10 defeats.

Garber, for his part, did not appear disappointed with Pu's decision-making. Writing after the fight on Facebook - instead focusing on the money he had made and being able to 'buy a third house'.

He said: 'What an experience, took the fight last week and we knew what we was up against but no excuses.

'Maybe this is the end now for me, time waits for no-one. Bought 2 houses out of boxing and tonight gets me a 3rd, it’s been a massive part of my life. If it is the end then what a way to go out in front of 20,000.'

Sports.title: Stunned inside 17 SECONDS and over in two rounds: Brutal Daniel Dubois was explosive in deciding his Fabio Wardley rematch and is now the undisputed champion-elect, writes JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
To hell with the romance. Stuff the slow starts. Never mind most of the O2 shouting against him.

Daniel Dynamite Dubois exploded into the ring with such power and brutality that he might have sent a tsunami along the Thames.

What he did beyond doubt last night, and what cannot be contested by Fabio Wardley or the three other world heavyweight belt wearers, was announce himself as the undisputed champion-elect.

White-collar Wardley was disabused of any notion he might regain the WBO title he lost to Dubois five months ago.

He was stunned in 17 seconds by Dubois's first booming right-hander of a red-hot night. And so the pain continued unabated.

'Fabio is a great boy, coming in for the second time, but it was my time, and my era,' said Dubois. 'I had my intentions, bad intentions, from the beginning.'

Daniel Dubois brutalised Fabio Wardley in their rematch as he wrapped things up in two rounds

This time there was no delay in Wardley's corner throwing in the towel. No point in the referee delaying the inevitable.

Dubois's sledgehammer blows rained down like missiles, with none travelling in the opposite direction.

One of the rival world champions was here to see the ferocity in person. Filip Hrgovic, who had disposed of Moses Itauma recently, sounded somewhat shell-shocked.

Agit Kabayel may be in no rush to meet Dubois. Nor, perhaps, will the winner of December's WBA clash between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.

This was an enormous statement by a man whose courage had been questioned but who will now be favourite to hunt them all down in his quest for the succession to Oleksandr Usyk as the undisputed champion.

'I'm the champion now, and I want to get some big fights in,' said Dubois. 'At this stage in my career, big money, big fights.'

The next generation of heavyweights has arrived.

So the irresistible force and the immovable object came to blows again at the O2. Dubois had risen from the canvas twice in the spring to claim his second world heavyweight title. Wardley, who neglected to finish him off, paid such a bloodied price that he left us wondering how he had stayed on his feet.

After being dropped in the opening seconds in their first fight, Dubois delivered revenge this time around

Their mutual hammering in Manchester had left us greedily wanting more at the O2.

Both pledged to put the savagery on after-burner second time around. Forget the concerns for their health.

In the parlance of the first promotion, Don't Blink was the warning to all those in attendance. These two had spent their careers knocking people out for fun or sometimes being stopped themselves.

No one expected this fight to go the distance. Not the fighters themselves. 'Me early,' predicted Dubois. 'Me earlier,' said Wardley.

'Twelve rounds?' opined promoter Frank Warren. 'No chance.'

The majority of the crowd were with the underdog, roaring Wardley into the ring. Partly from their feeling for romance, with a white-collar boxer breaking into the highest echelons of the heavyweights.

Dynamite Daniel's reception was more subdued. Even a hint hostile. Wardley hoped for a first-round knockdown, but that went to Dubois.

The first right of the night had Fabio reeling on the ropes for an eight count. More hell followed.

Dubois may have found greatness and is the undisputed champion-elect in the next generation of heavyweights

It was all over in round two. Wardley was brave as always, but his corner could not let him keep taking sledgehammer blows without reply.

'I just came in and I didn't execute the game plan properly,' Wardley admitted. 'I hold my hands up to that; that is entirely down to me.'

'A little white-collar boy like me could never have dreamed like this,' he added, reflecting on a sold-out O2 despite defeat.

Dubois may have found greatness with this mammoth performance.

Sports.title: Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon.

Not, at least, according to those who watched him endure 11 gruelling rounds against Daniel Dubois in Manchester in May. Not according to those who questioned whether his corner should have pulled him out earlier, as his face became increasingly battered and his right eye swelled shut. And certainly not according to those who believe the punishment he absorbed makes a rematch a risk too far.

But Wardley has never been one to follow the script.

When the 31-year-old first faced Dubois, 29, he did so as the WBO heavyweight champion. He dropped his opponent twice in the opening three rounds, threatening to produce one of the biggest victories of his career before Dubois fought his way back into the contest and eventually stopped him in the 11th.

Now, with the WBO title back on the line, Wardley finds himself in more familiar territory in one respect: he is the challenger, the underdog and the man many expect to lose again.

And, as he explains when we sit down ahead of the rematch, he rather likes it that way.

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon but he's never one to follow the script

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

'It's been the staple of my career for as long as I can remember, well, since I started. It has been the main focal point. After the first five or six fights, when I started to step up the level, even incrementally, even slightly, people were saying I was going to lose, that it was a step too far, and all the rest of it. It's all the stuff everyone's heard before,' he says.

'It's a side of the coin I'm very much used to, and the pressure's off. I'm the challenger here. I'm expected to lose and expected to go even quicker, and Daniel's supposed to put on a better performance, and all the rest of it. So there's no pressure on me. There's nothing on my shoulders.'

It is a strikingly relaxed assessment from a fighter preparing to walk back into the ring with the man who inflicted the first defeat of his professional career.

Wardley, however, insists that defeat has done little to change him. He is not pretending that losing a world title is enjoyable, but nor does he regard it as a defining moment in his life.

'Not a lot has changed. I'm not that different. Don't get me wrong, a loss is never fun. It's never nice, it's never enjoyable. But for me, at least, it wasn't soul-crushing or devastating, and it hasn't had any effect on me as a person, my character or anything else.

'The job’s the job, the game’s the game. From the very beginning, I’ve accepted that getting through heavyweight boxing unscathed isn’t guaranteed, especially given the way I compete at the highest level and my desire to take on the biggest challengers out there.

'I think people forget that the first time around, I picked Daniel. I asked for that fight because I looked at the crop of heavyweights and thought, "That's the best one to challenge myself against."

'Knowing that about myself, and knowing that's my angle, was I ever going to get through this undefeated like Floyd Mayweather? Probably not. So, look, it comes how it comes. But as long as I'm happy with myself in terms of the performances, that I've given my all and all the rest of it, I can sleep at night.'

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

Wardley took a lot of punishment in the latter rounds of their first encounter in May (above)

It is that willingness to put himself in the firing line which has made Wardley such a compelling heavyweight. His fights are rarely short on drama, and the first meeting with Dubois was no exception. He started at a blistering pace, dropping DDD in the opening 10 seconds, only for the momentum to swing as the punishment began to accumulate.

By the later rounds, Wardley was absorbing heavy shots and fighting through considerable damage. His condition between rounds prompted questions about whether the contest should have been stopped sooner, with particular scrutiny falling on his corner for allowing him out ahead of the 10th.

Wardley disagrees with the suggestion that his team failed him. He regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

He is equally dismissive of the noise surrounding the timing of the rematch, arguing that those watching from the outside cannot know the full picture of his recovery. His position is that he and his team are best placed to judge the damage he sustained and whether he is ready to fight again.

For Wardley, the prospect of another brutal encounter is not something he has brushed aside or refused to think about. It is a reality he has had to confront with himself, knowing that by stepping back into the ring with Dubois, he is willingly putting himself in a position where he could once again withstand a frightening amount of punishment.

It is a remarkable thought process: to acknowledge the possibility of enduring the same damage all over again, to ask himself whether he is prepared to go through it, and then to make peace with the answer before he has even thrown a punch.

'It's a level of early acceptance. The second I triggered the rematch clause, even before that, I had to have a conversation with myself and ask, "This could go the exact same way. Are you ready for that? Are you OK with that?"

'As long as the answer is yes from me to me, then cool, let's go. But by now, it's nowhere near my brain as a question mark or something I'm having to deal with, battle with or anything else. It's already been ticked off, boxed and put away. It is what it is.'

Wardley was checked by the doctor and spoken to by the referee multiple times in the fight

As a result, Dubois became a two-time heavyweight champion and will now defend his belt

There is little melodrama in his delivery. When the possibility of going through the same ordeal again is put to him, Wardley does not attempt to dress it up as fearlessness or pretend that the risks do not exist.

'It's an acceptance of the game and the sport we got into, and especially the way I fight as well,' he says.

That approach is perhaps best illustrated by what goes through his mind when he is taking punishment in the ring. Wardley is not a heavyweight who is inclined to retreat quietly after being caught cleanly. His instinct is to make sure his opponent knows there will be a response.

'Especially in those moments, it's about getting back at them. All right, you took one… let your hands go. Don't just let them get away with it for free. At least let them know. Let them have it in their brain that if they get off a few shots, I'm not just going to take them, run away and roll over.'

It is a mindset that makes for spectacular viewing, but one which also places enormous demands on a fighter's corner.

Wardley describes those 60 seconds between rounds as almost too precious to waste on anything other than the information he needs to continue. With the clock ticking and another round approaching, he wants tactical instruction rather than an emotional check-in.

'No, I think it's 90 per cent tactical, 10 per cent everything else, because in those moments, compassion doesn't need to come into it. That's not where the compassion needs to be.

'Those 60 seconds are so precious, such a small moment. It feels like a click. It feels like nothing. It feels like it's done and gone so quickly that you're on your stool, you're off your stool and the next round has started.

'In that time, you need to get the information. It's not time for, "Oh, a little rub on the shoulder. Are you doing OK, Fab? Is everything alright? Are you going to be alright, mate? Do you want me to dab your face a bit?" No. Let me know what I need to know. Let's get this going again.'

Wardley knows that the rematch will be gruelling. He knows his durability will continue to be questioned. But he also knows why he wanted the first fight in the first place.

For Wardley, the pursuit of the biggest challenges has always mattered more than protecting an unbeaten record. Defeat by Dubois has not changed that. He is back because in his mind, the possibility of the same ending has already been accepted and because it’s a risk worth taking.

Sports.title: Daniel Dubois' second clash with Fabio Wardley promises to be even MORE brutal than their first, writes JEFF POWELL MBE - as May's champion vows to 'bash and smash' his rival
Sports.content:
Daniel Dubois' second clash with Fabio Wardley promises to be even MORE brutal than their first, writes JEFF POWELL MBE - as May's champion vows to 'bash and smash' his rival

Even the most hardened boxing fans can be taken aback by the depths of brutality which two men are capable of inflicting on each other. Especially the heavyweights.

So it was on the Saturday night this May when Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley battered hell's bells out of each other in Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena. Wardley dropped his world title challenger twice in the first three rounds. Just 28 seconds into the 11th, Dubois had to be pulled off the champion he had reduced to a bleeding and battered but still-standing wreck.

We mere mortals can only ask: How on earth do they do it? ‘We’re fighters,’ says Dubois. ‘Honoured to share a ring with him.’

‘Born to do it,’ says Wardley, who found out that truth of himself when he tried white collar boxing. ‘Love being in with such a great fighter.’

What in heaven goes through their minds at the prospect of doing it again, as they are on Saturday night at the O2? Do they not realise the danger this sledgehammer head-banging presents to their health?

Prepare yourselves, dear gentle readers, for this stunning answer from Dubois: ‘Dementia? If you’re talking about dementia, no point worrying. We’ve probably got it already.’

Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley have both spoken of their love for stepping into the ring with one another ahead of their rematch on Saturday

But as brutal as their meeting in May was, tomorrow night's clash at the O2 has been teased as even bloodier

A chilling insight, this, into the mentality of men who fight not only for a living but for the lust for glory, the thrill of battle, the roar of the crowd, the smell of the greasepaint, the glare of the lights and not least their manly pride.

And on nights like this, for a world championship. This time the WBO belt which Dubois ripped from Wardley’s fairy-tale grasp five months ago.

What, no nerves? ‘I live with the chaos,’ says Dubois. ‘Chaos all day every day and specially on the night. I love the fear. It gives me the power. I hold the chaos in until it’s at its peak when the first bell goes. Then it explodes as I let it out. Which brings power and clarity.’

Wardley comes not only from his different background in commerce but also with an opposite mindset. He says: ‘No one wants to lose a world title but if it has to be, then what really matters is how it happens.

‘I feel more relaxed and confident having proved I can engage a top-level fighter in a great fight, which everyone expected me to lose easily. Calm makes me better.’

That and the lessons he learned in the five months since his gladiatorial — and only — defeat thus far. ‘We’ve studied every critical moment of the first fight,’ he says. ‘And I’ve adapted where necessary. Had to because I have more to work on than Daniel with all his experience.

‘But we’ve not only looked at me. We’ve looked at him. He’s not as adaptable as me. He’s not suddenly going to become light-footed and free moving. I’ll give him something different.’

To which Dubois says: ‘I’ll give him another beating. Bash him up. Smash him worse than before. And quicker. We didn’t know quite what he might do in the first fight. Now I know what to expect.

‘I also know that he’s not good enough to adapt. I’m his daddy now.’ That is clarity, Dubois style. He also discounts those two knock-downs. As a man who has been a slow starter at times — although not when he demolished Anthony Joshua from the get-go — he says: ‘Things happen in boxing. You can get caught. But I also know now that he doesn’t have the power. No real power.’

Wardley, for his part, denies that he was as badly hurt as it appeared in fight one. Their respective trainers have disagreed about the 11th-hour stoppage. Dubois’ coach Don Charles says the towel should have been thrown in earlier.

Wardley supports his man Ben Davison’s assertion that he was still in the fight throwing punches, saying: ‘The optics looked bad, what with the blood and the bruising and the punches. But I trust my team to take care of me. Trust them with my life.

‘A lot of the punches were glancing and in the 10th round I shook him with an uppercut. If the big right that followed had connected cleanly we might have had a different ending.’

This man who escaped office drudgery to chase his dream hopes to go on to meet the December winner of Joshua v Tyson Fury. Dubois fancies some of that big money but is also looking beyond, to unifying all the other world titles vacated by Oleksandr Usyk.

Will the ending on Saturday be different from Wardley v Dubois One? Probably not. Dynamite Dan likely added the more valuable knowledge to his wider experience and has never looked this bullish before a fight.

What we do know for sure is that this pair will give us another thriller.

Sports.title: How Antonelli will manage the pressure as F1 coronation looms
Sports.content:
Fighting for a maiden Formula 1 world championship can be an excruciating experience. The history books are rife with nerve-wracking title deciders, from Lewis Hamilton's last lap pass on Timo Glock in Brazil 2008 to Fernando Alonso being lured into a strategic trap in Abu Dhabi 2010. Little more needs to be said about Abu Dhabi 2021.

Kimi Antonelli won't need to go through any of that as he gets his first of six match points to become F1's youngest-ever world champion at the age of only 20. And he has earned that luxury with his staggering consistency, backing up his season-leading eight grand prix wins that have netted him a comfortable 102-point cushion on Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

All Antonelli needs to do in Austin is to hold serve, avoid calamity, and then take a more straightforward opportunity over the remainder of the American triple-header in Mexico or Brazil.

But as his first mathematical chance arrives this very weekend, it's only normal the young Italian was peppered with questions over what could be, and what it would all mean, as F1 set up shop at Austin's Circuit of the Americas.

"We had a meeting with Bono [race engineer Peter Bonnington] this morning and we said to just have fun and always have the same mindset as I had all year," Antonelli said. "One race at a time and just try to do the best I can every race weekend and then we'll see. But of course, if I do things well, then the result will come.

"We'll try to finish the job properly and then we can enjoy the rest. But for sure, it will be an incredible achievement."

Kimi Antonelli, Peter Bonnington Photo by: Reginald Mathalone / NurPhoto via Getty Images

What's been so remarkable about Antonelli's title campaign isn't that he was capable of it, as that's the reason why Mercedes put its faith in the Bologna native as Hamilton's long-term heir.

The real shock is both the speed at which he has completed that trajectory, and the massive turnaround from a deeply troubled maiden campaign in 2025, when he struggled for consistency, which then affected his confidence as his year spiralled out of control.

The first glimpses that the 2026 version of Antonelli was a different beast than last season’s more frail iteration came at the very first race. In Melbourne, Antonelli brushed off a 25G crash in final practice to claim second on the grid, finishing there in the race behind Russell.

Overcoming that crash showed Antonelli was a much more mature and even-keeled person than the one who neared a breaking point over the 2025 Belgian Grand Prix, and received tough love from team principal Toto Wolff for an underwhelming spell that continued after the summer break.

"If something like that would have happened to me last year, like in Melbourne, probably the rest of the weekend would have been very compromised," Antonelli acknowledged. "When you get one full year of experience in F1, then you come back the next year and you just feel better. Things happen a bit easier, because you're not forcing them to happen as much.

"This year, I took a step back and just tried to focus on the important things and to enjoy it as much as possible as well. Not only the driving, but also the process. Mentally I've been in a much happier place this year compared to last season. [You learn] how to move on together as a team from difficult situations."

"He's had a perfect season" - Charles Leclerc

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Jayce Illman / Getty Images

That night and day difference between freshman and sophomore Antonelli has also taken aback his rivals. When asked by Autosport what has surprised him the most about Antonelli's 2026 campaign, Charles Leclerc singled it out.

"What has surprised me is the first year to the second year," said the Ferrari star. "Already from the very first laps with this car, we could see that he was very strong, and in the first qualifying of the year, first race of the year, he was very strong.

"I think you could tell that these kinds of cars were just fitting him much better, and the hard work that he had done between the seasons paid off. It was very clear after two, three races that he would be a big contender.

"It's been near perfect. There was one mistake two or three races ago, but that's probably the only one. He's had a perfect season."

That newfound unshakeability makes it easy to forget about Antonelli's tender age as he's set to break Sebastian Vettel's record by three years. And there was something inadvertently amusing about Antonelli saying it would be "something I've dreamt of since I was little", which in his case isn't a particularly long period of time.

But as Antonelli pinches himself to be in such a luxurious position, there's no reason to deviate from the mindset that got him this far. Just for a few more races.

"To find myself in such a position is incredible," he said. "But at the same time, I need to keep going, keep pushing. It's not over yet."

Read Also: Formula 1 The maths behind when Mercedes could become F1 world champions in 2026

Sports.title: Verstappen warns COTA bumps are “unacceptable” and “out of control”
Sports.content:
When the United States Grand Prix came up during the Formula 1 press conference in Singapore, Max Verstappen immediately joked that he would have to order a new spine. The four-time world champion had followed the World Endurance Championship round in Texas – The Lone Star Le Mans, held over the weekend of 6 September – and said he was shocked by the condition of the circuit.

Although Verstappen was still able to laugh about it with Kimi Antonelli at the time, he made it clear during the media day in Austin that he is genuinely concerned about the “unacceptable” track conditions.

“From what I saw in WEC, it was extremely badly bumpy. I'm not really looking forward to that, to be honest, for your spine,” said Verstappen. “I was joking about that in the last race, but it's not really a joke to be honest. We mentioned this already for years, that it's actually getting a bit out of control.”

The problem stems from the ground beneath the circuit. Built on Texas’ infamous high-plasticity clay, the track suffers from a severe shrink-swell effect as weather conditions change. This constant shifting leaves the circuit extremely bumpy, particularly in the heavy braking zones where the asphalt is subjected to the greatest stress.

Ahead of the 2026 race, certain sections have been resurfaced again, including the stretch between Turns 9 and 11. In addition, repair work was carried out to address the bumps between Turns 12 and 19. Two years ago, ahead of the 2024 United States Grand Prix, the entire track was resurfaced.

When Autosport asked Verstappen whether he believes more needs to be done, the four-time world champion stressed that the location itself should not be used by the organisers as an excuse.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

“It's very bad. Of course, you can use the excuse that the soil is the problem, but then you should have known that and you need to make sure that you reinforce it more,” the Dutchman said.

“I mean, I love this track, I love this place. It's one of the best layouts ever and it's one of the, I would say, best venues and best cities to be at. But for me, the bumps that we have are unacceptable.

“Over time, they've been grinding a little bit here and there, but you're putting a plaster on the big problem and that's just what's underneath. That's what you actually need to tackle in the first place.”

According to Verstappen, far-reaching measures are needed, with attention being paid not only to the tarmac itself, but also to the soil beneath it.

“But that, of course, means you need to really fully open up the track,” he added. “That costs a lot of money and time, but honestly, that's the only way to get rid of it. Because yeah, these bumps are not natural and they are out of control.”

Why F1's 2026 cars could make things even worse for drivers

At first glance, it might seem like a blessing in disguise that F1 no longer uses the ground-effect cars of recent years. After all, those cars had to be run particularly low and stiff, but when asked by Autosport, Verstappen made it clear that the 2026 machinery could actually make things even more painful.

Race start Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

“It's probably worse because we have very low ride heights while cornering,” said Verstappen. “On the straights you have the SM mode, so you go up. But in most places under the braking especially, you actually bottom out more than before. And most of the bumps are under braking or in the corner, not on the actual straight.

“Under braking, it's like actually a very stressful moment – especially when there are these kind of awkward bumps, not just bumps from the track getting older, but bumps from the surface underneath, the soil just moving up and down. Sometimes it's very hard to know what to expect, or if you’re a tiny bit offline, you don't know what is there because no one really drives there. So, yeah, it's really not nice.”

All of this means that drivers' backs take a considerable beating. Verstappen says he has already experienced this at COTA in previous years.

“Last year, for example, you pull around 5-6G in a corner, but I had some impacts, the vertical load, which was like over 9G on my spine,” he said. “I can tell you that it’s really not fun and especially the older you get, you think about that more and more. That's not what you want.”

Verstappen added that his spine is already not in the best possible condition after more than 11 seasons in F1: “I think sometimes people don't really understand that. I can tell you from the checks that I've done from my spine, the bottom end of the spine doesn't look that great.

“I know that's part of racing and I know that can be part of sport, but it's of course also further damage from the cars that we had the last few years. And now if we continue finding this acceptable to drive on, then you are going to suffer from that much more.

“People can say, yeah, but there are worse sports out there for damage to parts of your body. For sure, but that's why I'm not doing them. So, yeah, it's not nice.”

Sports.title: Why Colapinto spoke out against abuse targeting his own F1 team
Sports.content:
It has become a recurring topic during Franco Colapinto's media sessions throughout the 2026 Formula 1 season: the Argentine feeling the need to speak out against abuse on social media.

Colapinto discussed the issue at length during an exclusive interview with Autosport in Monaco, as well as during many of the race weekends that have followed since.

After the Singapore Grand Prix last time out, however, the Alpine driver felt the urgency to go a step further and address his fanbase directly in a video message. Among other things, he said he appreciated all the support from his fans, but added that directing hate towards others does nothing to help his own F1 career.

“First of all, I've always been very grateful for all the fans supporting me,” said Colapinto, when asked by Autosport about his statement ahead of this weekend’s United States Grand Prix.

“But I think in every sport and fan base, it's got a bad side as well, the hate side of people putting bad comments and not helping athletes perform at their best. To me, it crossed a few lines lately.

“I think it was probably the last thing I could do, to put out a statement of me talking in a video like that. It was always going to be positive, so I was keen to do it.”

Franco Colapinto, Alpine Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Explaining what he meant when he said that certain lines had recently been crossed, Colapinto revealed that even members of his own team had been targeted on social media. Colapinto found that unacceptable, prompting him to speak out once again.

“Especially my mechanics got a lot of hate,” revealed the 23-year-old. “My engineers as well, people from my team that want me to do well and that help me to perform. I'm working with them daily and seeing them getting these kind of messages, it just hurts me in general.”

Asked whether these were comments on the team's official Instagram account or personal messages sent to team members, Colapinto replied: “I don’t have their phones, but from what I understand, they receive messages and comments. Again, it just crossed the line for me.”

In practice, this includes mechanics who work on Colapinto's car and make adjustments to, for example, the front wing from one qualifying segment to the next.

They are then wrongly held responsible for a difficult session and subsequently receive hateful messages on their accounts, although Autosport understands that Alpine has taken measures to minimise the impact.

Team members are advised to keep their personal social media accounts private and not show any team logos, in order to minimise the risk of receiving unwanted messages.

Franco Colapinto, Alpine Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Nevertheless, that does not address the actual problem at its root, which is precisely why Colapinto has once again made an urgent appeal to fans. He also stressed that the problem is not limited to F1, but affects society as a whole.

“I've been talking about this for the last 10 races probably,” he said. “I do my best, but I think it kept crossing some lines. So this was the last thing I could do, making a video, and I think it helped.

“You saw it with Max as well. He also made a statement about it. It's happening a lot around us. It's an issue that we’ve got in sports nowadays, in sports and in many different areas of life. Artists, actors, it's everywhere.

“Personally, it doesn’t hurt me too much. I don't look at those comments too much, I don't put too much attention. But for some it does [affect them]. And that’s why we need to put attention on it. We need to improve it and hopefully this video does improve it slightly.”

Sports.title: Sainz yet to be "convinced" that F1 2026 will finish in the Middle East
Sports.content:
Carlos Sainz has admitted that it's "difficult" to be convinced by Formula 1's chiefs that its final rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi can go ahead as planned despite the ongoing Middle Eastern conflict.

Both F1 management and governing body the FIA have maintained the position that the final two rounds of 2026 in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, scheduled back-to-back at the end of November and first weekend of December, can go ahead as planned.

With no resolution in sight for the ongoing conflict between the US and its ally Israel, and Iran, and new strikes on Saudi Arabia by the Houthi rebels, the situation in the Middle East remains extremely volatile.

The outlook is also likely to be influenced by the US midterm elections on 3 November, with several outlets reporting the US and Israel are preparing for fresh attacks on Iran afterwards.

F1 has been working on a contingency plan with an alternative season finale in Imola, on the weekend of the planned Abu Dhabi race, but all indications from series chiefs are that they are very keen to press ahead with the Middle Eastern double-header based on the current information and assurances they have received from various stakeholders.

But Sainz, who acts as director of the F1 drivers association GPDA, feels it is "difficult" and "premature" to envisage a finish in the region based on the current news cycle.

Abu Dhabi GP 2025 Photo by: Nicolas Economou / NurPhoto via Getty Images

"They seem very convinced that it's going to go ahead," Sainz said on Thursday ahead of this weekend's United States Grand Prix in Austin. "I think on my personal side, and not speaking as a GPDA, it's very difficult to be convinced right now because there's still plenty of things happening in the Middle East.

"And also there is obviously an election that is going to happen in the US and things that are going to happen in the political side of the world that could affect the next month and a half very suddenly. So, I think it's relatively premature to be so convinced."

But Sainz also felt that the drivers have little choice but to put their faith in what series executives decide, as they have more information on what is happening on the ground.

"As it stands, we would go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi and if the FIA and Formula 1 decide that's still safe and a good scenario, I think we as drivers have to go with whatever they say," the Spaniard added.

"It's not like we don't have as much inside information as they have, so we need to follow their lead and trust in their decision making.

"But only as it stands, I think the world can change a lot in the next month and a half. So we need to be [reactive] to whatever happens and not just go because we want to go right now."

Sports.title: When Cadillac will open its F1 engine factory
Sports.content:
Cadillac has revealed its Formula 1 engine factory will open on 18 December.

General Motors was approved by the FIA in 2025 as a power unit supplier from the 2029 season onwards, hence the construction of new F1 engine facilities at the manufacturer’s base in Charlotte, North Carolina.

“We're opening our whole engine factory, if you will, in Charlotte, North Carolina on 18 December,” General Motors president Mark Reuss announced in a conference at Autosport Business Exchange in New York. “So that's coming really well.”

General Motors now has another couple of years to design its own power unit, though the timing may be suboptimal – FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has committed to F1 switching back to V8 engines – potentially running on sustainable fuel with a smaller share of electric power – by 2031. In that case, GM’s powertrain would get two seasons in action at best, potentially just one if the switch is brought forward to 2030.

In the meantime, Cadillac is running customer Ferrari power units, and the team’s maiden season has been tricky thus far. It is the only outfit yet to score a point in 2026, and the MAC-26 has qualified slowest of all at the last four rounds.

General Motors president Mark Reuss presents Cadillac's one-off shakedown F1 livery for Barcelona Photo by: Cadillac Communications

“You know, we’re not here to finish last, so we’ve got to follow through and build this team, build the powertrain and build the car, like we did in GTP,” Reuss said. “That takes a little more time here, because this is a place where we've never raced. You’ve got to get the right people with the right engineers and the right drivers, and we’ve got to get that process really going, and it's logarithmic, it's not linear.”

Veterans Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas have been bringing invaluable experience in that context, but they have also been recording their worst career results.

“You can't win every race – no one can win every race – so when it happens, when they have a day that is unfortunate, or mistakes were made, they move on from that race and perfect their craft – whether it's with the car or themselves, or their physicality, or whatever that is – and they drive for that perfection,” Reuss said.

“Both of these gentlemen in the race for us do that, and they really understand what it takes and the process. I'm very, very happy that they're patient with us, to be honest; that takes a special person.”

Sports.title: Slater set for F1 practice debut with Audi in Mexico
Sports.content:
Audi junior Freddie Slater will make his debut at the wheel of a Formula 1 car with a couple of Free Practice 1 outings in Mexico City and Sao Paulo.

Audi took over the Sauber team ahead of 2026 for the German brand’s maiden F1 season, incidentally launching a new driver academy, which has largely rested on Slater’s shoulders.

Previously an Italian F4 and Formula Regional European champion, Slater has lived up to expectations by taking second place in Formula 3 behind Ugo Ugochukwu – the 18-year-old Briton was the highest-placed rookie in the standings.

Ahead of his step up to Formula 2 with Invicta – following in the footsteps of fellow Trident F3 racers Gabriel Bortoleto, Leonardo Fornaroli and Rafael Camara – Slater will be in action in FP1 at the Mexican and Brazilian grands prix, helping Audi fulfil the rules’ young-driver requirements.

Alpine reserve Paul Aron was loaned to Audi on two occasions earlier this season for free practice sessions, and Slater is getting the team’s last two mandatory rookie outings, replacing Nico Hulkenberg and Bortoleto once each.

“Getting behind the wheel of a Formula 1 car at a grand prix weekend is a big moment for me and something I’ve been dreaming of since I was a kid,” Slater said. “I’ve learned a lot this year, and these free practice outings with Audi will be another opportunity to keep gaining on-track experience.

Freddie Slater, TRIDENT Photo by: Dom Gibbons - Formula 1 via Getty Images

“Being part of the Audi Driver Development Programme has already given me some incredible opportunities, and I am grateful for their trust and support. I’m really looking forward to getting out on track: my focus will be on doing the best job I can, helping the team with its programme and taking as many learnings as possible from both sessions.”

Audi racing director Allan McNish added: “We have seen Freddie making great progress throughout recent years, both on and off the track; it is the right time for Freddie to step up.

“These appearances in Mexico and Brazil will give him valuable experience of a Formula 1 race weekend, and another chance to continue his development before he steps up to Formula 2 next season.

"We are looking forward to seeing him in the R26 and supporting him through these two important FP1 sessions.”

Colton Herta in at COTA

Earlier, Cadillac test and development driver Colton Herta will be in action at this weekend's United States Grand Prix, driving Sergio Perez’s car. Austin will mark the Californian’s fourth FP1 session of the year, though his latest, in Monza, was cut short by a suspected hydraulic issue.

“Driving the MAC-26 in front of the American fans at COTA is going to be special,” Herta said. “I have great memories at this track – winning my first IndyCar race here back in 2019 was a huge moment in my career, so stepping into an F1 car on this layout feels like coming full circle.

Colton Herta, Cadillac Racing Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“I’ve built up a good rhythm with the team through my previous FP1 runs in Barcelona, Budapest, and Monza, so my goal for Friday morning is straightforward: execute the test programme cleanly, help the engineers gather good data on the set-up, and hand the car back to Checo with some useful feedback to support the team for the rest of the weekend.”

Team principal Marcin Budkowski added: “The high-speed sweeping section in sector one [at COTA] and the tight, low-speed turns at the end of the lap are a tricky for car set-up, and the bumps always add an extra dimension.

“We are looking forward to having Colton back in the car for FP1 on Friday, and we also plan to bring some small floor and cooling upgrades for evaluation.

"Colton knows this circuit very well from his IndyCar career, so his feedback will be valuable as we establish our baseline for the weekend.”

Currently a lowly 19th in the F2 standings, Herta told Autosport he was still aiming at F1 by 2028, while his plans for next year remain unclear.

Sports.title: MotoGP "can’t just copy" F1’s Drive to Survive success – Chase Carey
Sports.content:
Liberty Media director Chase Carey believes MotoGP “can’t just copy” Netflix’s Formula 1 docuseries Drive to Survive to gain widespread recognition.

Liberty acquired F1 in January 2017, and one of the major events under the American company was the release of the Netflix show’s opening season two years later, which substantially contributed to the world championship’s increased popularity.

Liberty then bought 84% of Dorna Sports (now known as MotoGP Sports Entertainment Group) in July 2025. The group is seeking to make motorcycle grands prix more diverse – 11 of the top 12 riders in the 2026 MotoGP championship are Spanish or Italian – while increasing its presence in the United States.

“Certainly there are elements of what teams need to do in MotoGP that will have similarities to Formula 1,” Carey said in a conference at Autosport Business Exchange in New York. “Obviously, it is a global franchise.

“In some ways, MotoGP is even crazier. When you look at these guys, they look like they're lying on the pavement riding the motorcycles around. But it is a sport that also has its unique characteristics. And I think you can't just cookie-cutter [the approach].

“It's early days. They're working on it, developing the strategies, the opportunities of how you take that sport and grow it in the way we've tried to with Formula 1.”

Drive to Survive has been credited with introducing F1 to a brand-new audience, boosted by the COVID-19 pandemic’s lockdowns, which first occurred a couple of weeks after season two was released.

“Drive to Survive is probably the most obvious example,” Carey acknowledged. “We recognised we needed to have the personalities that make up the sport, give them a bigger platform and let fans engage.

“The digital world today is a 24/7 world. The premium experience is still that live race, but at the end of the day people are connecting with the race, following the race and clips of the race, clips of what people are doing, things going on behind the scenes.

“They're following that 24/7. So we need to continue to find ways to feed that appetite and that desire to connect with their sport, provide the vehicles that enable fans to connect with the sport in that way.

Liz Claman and Chase Carey Photo by: Bryan Bedder / Getty Images

“Right now the US is the biggest YouTube market for our sport. So it tells you about the connection we're having through [those] vehicles.

“Drive to Survive has become a centerpiece in the digital efforts. A lot of efforts are going on with digital, but that certainly is the centerpiece. It has been an incredibly important, valuable franchise for us.”

Many competitions, in motorsport and beyond, have attempted to emulate this success, but Carey doesn’t believe that would be right for MotoGP.

“You should look for opportunities,” the American insisted. “Realistically, everybody saw Drive to Survive and then everybody tried to do it. Golf tried to do their Full Swing, tennis tried to do Break Point – everybody.

“Usually, you can't just copy something. I think we learned that at Fox with American Idol. American Idol sort of captured the world's imagination, and there were shows that came behind and did well, but there was only one American Idol that really did that.

“I think generally you can't go out and do the same thing. You've got to find ways to use opportunities, use personalities, use digital platforms, develop great partners.

“A partner in Formula 1 like Apple, I think this is where Apple has brought a whole new perspective to how you broadcast and connect with fans. So I think that type of opportunity, you've got to then see what you can do with it, how you develop it.

“They have to follow their own path and find their own opportunities. The Formula 1 movie was a great opportunity for that, but you can't just go out and do a MotoGP movie. That may not be the right opportunity.

“But there may be something else – there will be something else. It's probably not just doing the same things you did, it's finding those opportunities, finding those personalities.”

Sports.title: Horner reveals Red Bull call to thank him for F1 engine project after maiden win
Sports.content:
Christian Horner has revealed Red Bull shareholders called him on the back of the Red Bull Ford Powertrains engine’s maiden Formula 1 victory in Malaysia.

Horner joined the Milton Keynes-based squad as its team principal when the brand acquired the Jaguar outfit ahead of the 2005 season, but was sacked and replaced by Laurent Mekies in July 2025.

Across two decades at the helm of the team, Horner not only led it to eight drivers’ and six constructors’ titles but also oversaw its transition from an engine customer into a power unit manufacturer, following Honda’s exit from F1 at the end of the 2021 season.

Red Bull was able to keep using the Japanese powertrains until last year; its own power unit, designed in collaboration with Ford, debuted in 2026.

The Red Bull engine clinched its first victory at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, courtesy of Max Verstappen, with the Dutchman making it back-to-back wins one week later in Singapore.

“We managed to do it on the chassis side and then the challenge came, could we do it on the engine side?” Horner related in a conference at Autosport Business Exchange in New York.

“You know, we needed to have an engine after Honda announced their withdrawal in 2020. So we created this start-up company, Red Bull Powertrains, with the same philosophy of attracting the talent, giving people a chance, giving people the opportunity, and then empowering them and encouraging them to push the boundaries.

“I've been super proud to see how that engine has developed and delivered this year.”

Christian Horner Photo by: Autosport

Horner’s contribution was acknowledged by the brand itself, as he received the aforementioned phone call from its leaders.

“It was an appreciated gesture, seeing that engine and knowing what went into it, you know, the sweat and tears along the way,” the Briton continued.

“For all the men and women involved, it was an incredible, incredible achievement. And their 16th attempt to win a grand prix, which is very hard at the best of times.

“I was very grateful to both the shareholders who reached out, and [Red Bull CEO] Oliver Mintzlaff who reached out to thank me as well. It was quite a different call than I had from him 15 months earlier.”

Horner is referring to the phone call that led to his dismissal, as his position had become increasingly precarious following Red Bull cofounder Dietrich Mateschitz’s death.

Errol Barnett and Christian Horner Photo by: Bryan Bedder / Getty Images

Horner did not have the Verstappen camp on his side and was losing the support of the Yoovidhya family – Chalerm Yoovidhya is a majority owner of the company – but still describes the news as “pretty abrupt and quite brutal”.

“I felt that things were changing,” he added. “Nothing stays the same forever, and after the founder, Dietrich Mateschitz, sadly passed at the end of ‘22, it was always going to be the case that the company was going to evolve and was going to change.

“Dietrich, he was Red Bull, he was the power behind it, he made all the big decisions. And suddenly, obviously, trying to replace somebody like that is impossible.

“Inevitably, as the group evolved and took on that challenge, it was just different. There was a drive to bring more control back into the head office, and that sat differently from the autonomy that we'd enjoyed at Red Bull Racing and in Milton Keynes.

“It was a different path that essentially what we were on, and you could feel that that was changing. It wasn't that it was right or wrong, it was just different. And I didn't feel, certainly, that it was what had allowed us to achieve so much success over the years.

“So, inevitably, it came to an end.”

Sports.title: Spotlight: Hamilton to race until he’s 45? ‘I’m forced to stay longer to race in Africa’ | Briefs
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has already extended his Formula 1 career longer than he originally indicated he would: the 41-year-old famously said earlier in his career he wouldn’t still be racing in his forties.

How much longer is he prepared to go? Will he carry on as far as Fernando Alonso , whose new contract will keep him in the cockpit beyond his 46th birthday?

Hamilton suggested as much today when discussing F1’s forthcoming new race in Rwanda. “I’m now forced to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa, and that’s been my dream, to be able to race in Africa,” he said.

F1 has not confirmed exactly when its first race in Rwanda will take place. It stated the race will join the calendar some time in the “early 2030s”.

Hamilton will turn 45 on January 7th, 2030. If he’s going to be on the grid for F1’s long-awaited return to Africa, he’ll be in his mid-forties.

Sports.title: “Difficult to be convinced” F1’s Qatar and Abu Dhabi rounds will happen – Sainz | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Carlos Sainz Jnr has doubts whether the final two rounds of the Formula 1 season in the Middle East will go ahead as planned.

The November and December rounds in Losail, Qatar and Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates have been in doubts for months due to the ongoing war between the US and Iran. The war previously led to the cancellation of the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian grands prix in April (the former took place earlier this month, in name only, after being relocated 6,000 kilometres away to Malaysia).

The series’ CEO Stefano Domenicali previously indicated a decision was needed by mid-September. However no final announcement has yet been made. While FOM and the FIA has repeatedly stated the races will go ahead, they have made arrangements for Imola in Italy to take over as the venue for the finale if needed.

Sainz acknowledged F1’s governing body and commercial rights holder “seem very convinced that it’s going to go ahead.” But the Grand Prix Drivers’ Association director said he personally has doubts due to the political situation, including the potentially significant midterm elections in the USA which are less than two weeks away.

“On my personal side and not speaking as a GPDA [director], it’s very difficult to be convinced right now, because there are still things happening, plenty of things happening in the Middle East, and also there is obviously an election that is going to happen in the US, and things that are going to happen in the political side of the world that could affect the next month, month and a half, very suddenly.

“So I think it’s relatively premature to be so convinced, but as it stands, we will go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi. If the FIA and Formula 1 decide that it’s still safe and a good scenario, I think we, as drivers, have to go with whatever they say.

“We don’t have as much political information, as much inside information as they have, for sure, so we need to follow their lead and trust in their decision-making, but only as it stands.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“The world can change a lot in the next month, month and a half, and we need to stay diligent and reactive to whatever happens, and not just go because we want to go right now.”

The Losail International Circuit issued a press release yesterday drawing attention to its two major events next month: the F1 grand prix and the rescheduled round of the Moto GP championship which was originally due to take place in April.

Sainz said the GPDA is prepared to follow the FIA’s guidance.

“The GPDA, as united as we are, we don’t have half of the information that Formula 1 and FIA have with all the political battles that are happening in the world,” he said.

“I think the GPDA can help a lot to understand the sport, or make the FIA and F1 understand the sport, what makes racing better, what makes a race track better, what needs to be changed in order to get more safety. But about political matters, realistically none of us have the information and the contacts that F1 and FIA have.

“So, similar to [the media], you need to trust in a way the decision that F1 and FIA take about that matter, but as I said before, we need to stay reactive and see how situations change, I think they will do that and they will take the right decision when it comes.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Oscar Piastri agreed the drivers were prepared to put “our trust in the FIA and F1.”

“There have been difficult situations in the past through conflicts and all kinds of things,” he said. “So we’ll put our trust in F1 and the FIA and listen to their advice.”

“We might have to get some snowploughs out if we race in Imola,” he added. “But I think I’ll leave it to F1. I think Imola has just been touted as the replacement, then hopefully it’s above zero. That’s all I ask for.”

Update: Williams has issued a further statement from Sainz regarding his comments on the Qatar and Abu Dhabi grands prix:

“Following some reporting of my comments in the press conference earlier today about ending the season in the Middle East, I want to be clear that I know the FIA and Formula 1 will put safety first and completely trust them to make the right decision. We look forward to racing in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.”

Sports.title: “Free Congo!”: Hamilton welcomes F1’s return to Africa, with reservations over Rwanda | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton indicated he has mixed feelings over Formula 1’s choice of Rwanda as the venue for its first grand prix in Africa since 1993.

The seven-times world champion has repeatedly called for the series to return to the continent and lobbied F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali on the matter. However he acknowledged the criticism F1 has faced for choosing to race in Rwanda.

“I’ve been advocating for a race in Africa for many, many, many years,” he said, describing his “countless meetings with the stakeholders, so many meetings with Stefano at his office in London, but also race weekends.”

“Countless calls. ‘What’s happening?’, ‘where are we going?’, ‘who are you meeting with?’. Many meetings with different presidents from different countries, lots of phone calls with different presidents in different countries within Africa.

“For me it’s a place that deserves to have a grand prix. It’s [about] more than just one country, it is about the continent in itself and there’s so many beautiful countries within it and the people are so lovely.

“The culture is so rich and I think it’s important that we get to show that to the world and we get to do that with our sport. We get to go to all these different countries and people see some of these countries they didn’t really know too much about and all of a sudden it’s on the screen and kids are talking about it. They go to school talking about. So I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix.”

However the Rwandan government has been accused of backing a rebel militia in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo. Amnesty International claims the M23 group has committed human rights abuses which “may amount to war crimes”.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Therese Kayikwamba Wagner, the DR Congo’s minister of foreign affairs, said she told Domenicali last year it would be “morally indefensible” for F1 to hold a race in Rwanda. She called for F1 to guarantee its race will not be paid for using wealth Rwanda has taken from DR Congo.

Hamilton, who has previously spoken out against human rights abuses in and by other countries F1 visits, indicated he is aware of the concerns over visiting Rwanda and said the series should not overlook them.

“Of course I don’t get to choose where we go and naturally there’s problems all over the world today,” he said. “I’ve seen many of the stories, but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. Growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum: a lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism and the west intervening.

“But if you see the people, you see so many designs that are out there today, top brands come from Africa and it’s got all the richest resources.

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Of course, going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there. So hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more about what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation.

“I guess I’ll finish it off with: I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”

Sports.title: Verstappen would have won Singapore GP in a Ferrari, says Hadjar: ‘It was the fastest car’ | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen’s Singapore Grand Prix victory would have been even more dominant if he had been driving for Ferrari, according to his team mate.

“I don’t think we have the fastest car,” said Isack Hadjar ahead of this weekend’s race in Austin.

His team mate Verstappen has won the last two grands prix in a row. He beat Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc by seven seconds in Singapore.

However Hadjar believes his team mate is getting more from his car than Ferrari’s drivers are from theirs.

“The car is still very hard to drive,” he explained. “In Malaysia it was dominant but I don’t think in Singapore it was the fastest car. That’s what I believe.

“I think if you put Max in the Ferrari he would have won the race with more margin so that’s my opinion. In Singapore I think [the Ferrari] was the fastest car.”

Verstappen beat Charles Leclerc to pole position by five hundredths of a second. Lewis Hamilton, who was quickest in Q1 and Q2, was another seven hundredths of a second behind in the other Ferrari.

Hadjar finished 10th in Singapore after starting from the pit lane due to a penalty for replacing a failed power unit. He is eager to have a more competitive weekend in Austin.

“It was one of those weekends where you get a failure in each session, so you learn from it and we just move on,” he said. “I’m happy to be here in Texas. I like that track and the car’s been, performance-wise, working really well the last couple of weekends.

“We’re confident as a team, but of course we are aware of the upgrades in the other garages so we’re still down to earth. We still know our weaknesses on the car, we’re still working on it.

“So I just want to go out there and have another clean one because the last two weekends have been very frustrating considering the car I have been given.”

Sports.title: FIA’s new Formula 1 Race Operations Centre opens at FOM’s Biggin Hill base | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The FIA is using Formula 1’s base at Biggin Hill in the UK as the site of its new Race Operations Centre.

Biggin Hill is the home of F1’s broadcasting operations, where raw footage from the hundreds of camera operators which cover every session are combined into the video feeds seen by millions of viewers worldwide.

The governing body of motorsport announced the opening of the new facility which will allow its officials to manage events around the world without being present in person.

A key part of the facility’s functions will involve providing support to race control and stewards on decisions during sessions. It will assist in detecting when drivers have jumped the start or lined up incorrectly on the grid, exceeded track limits or committed offences in the pit lane.

The ROC will also use new artificial intelligence systems to automate processes and detect incidents.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem and Formula 1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali were among those who attended the formal inauguration of the new facility.

“As the championship grows globally, it is vital that we continue to invest in the people, technology and infrastructure that underpin world-class race operations,” said Ben Sulayen. “This state-of-the-art facility will strengthen our ability to support accurate, consistent and efficient decision-making, ensuring that our sport continues to operate at the highest possible standards.”
