The Aare Ona Kakanfo of Yorubaland, Iba Gani Adams, has described the late leader of the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere, Pa Reuben Fasoranti, as a symbol of integrity, discipline and selfless service to the Yoruba nation and Nigeria.

Adams, who expressed sorrow over Fasoranti’s death on Tuesday at the age of 100, said his passing marked the end of an era in Yoruba leadership and Nigeria’s socio-political history.

In a tribute, Adams said Nigeria had lost a leader whose wisdom and principled positions on justice, true federalism and good governance had guided generations.

“We have lost a leader whose wisdom and principled stance on issues of justice, true federalism, and good governance had been a guiding light for generations,” he said.

He described Fasoranti’s contributions to Yorubaland as immense and multifaceted, noting that, as Afenifere leader, he championed Yoruba unity and cultural pride while advocating the protection of Yoruba interests within the Nigerian federation.

According to Adams, Fasoranti’s commitment to democratic values and justice earned him respect beyond the Yoruba nation, across Nigeria’s diverse ethnic groups.

The Aare Ona Kakanfo said the late elder statesman played a pivotal role in shaping Nigeria’s socio-political discourse, particularly through his advocacy for true federalism.

He said Fasoranti believed that Nigeria’s unity could only be sustained through equitable power-sharing and respect for the autonomy of its constituent regions.

Adams also recalled that Fasoranti helped preserve the ideals of the late Chief Obafemi Awolowo’s progressive vision for Nigeria, which emphasised education, social justice and economic development.

He said the late Afenifere leader remained committed to national unity despite his strong advocacy for Yoruba rights.

Adams further described Fasoranti’s leadership style as inclusive and conciliatory, saying he consistently favoured dialogue and peaceful conflict resolution.

He noted that the approach contributed to peace and stability in Yorubaland and Nigeria during turbulent periods.

World.title: Family announces burial plans for late Afenifere leader, Fasoranti
World.content:
Pa Fasoranti

By Dayo Johnson

The family of the late Afenifere Leader, Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti, has announced his burial plans, showing that his remains will be buried on December 17, 2026.

According to the programme of activities signed on behalf of the family by the Secretary to the Ondo State Government and his son, Dr. Taiwo Fasoranti:

“The family of late Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti, CFR, is pleased to announce the burial arrangements of our beloved patriarch, leader of Afenifere and foremost nationalist, who passed away at the age of 100 years.

“Burial arrangements are as follows: Christian Wake Keeping Service: Wednesday, 16th December, 2026

Venue: His residence at Omolere Nursery and Primary School Compound

Time: 4:00 p.m.

“Funeral Service & Interment: Thursday, 17th December, 2026

Venue: St. David’s Cathedral, Ijomu, Akure

Time: 10:00 a.m.

Interment will follow immediately after the service at the Church Cemetery.

“Reception: Guests will be entertained at his residence immediately after the interment.

“Outing & Thanksgiving Service: Sunday, 20th December, 2026

Venue: St. David’s Cathedral, Ijomu, Akure

Time: 10:00 a.m.

“We request your prayers and presence as we honour the memory of a distinguished elder and patriot.”

World.title: Judge gives Trump Dec. 11 deadline to testify in BBC lawsuit
World.content:
WASHINGTON, DC – OCTOBER 22: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to the media o the South Lawn before departing the White House on October 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. President Trump is traveling to Iowa to stump for midterm candidates with 12 days until Election Day. Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images/AFP (Photo by Aaron Schwartz / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP)

A US judge on Thursday issued President Donald Trump a December 11 deadline to testify under oath in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

Judge Enjolique Lett in Miami gave the order in response to complaints by the British broadcaster that Trump has refused to sit for a deposition, including canceling a previously agreed date of October 16.

If Trump fails to attend the deposition by then, he risks sanctions, including dismissal of his lawsuit, the court said.

Trump has accused the BBC of deceptively editing its documentary “Trump: A Second Chance” to make it seem as if he was inciting violence when he told supporters to march on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, after losing the presidential election.

The crowd proceeded to storm Congress in an attempt to stop the formal certification of Democrat Joe Biden’s victory.

While the BBC has apologized for the incident, which prompted the resignation of multiple senior executives, the broadcaster has denied it caused Trump any real injury and moved for the case to be dismissed.

Trump filed his suit against the BBC in December 2025 and is seeking at least $5 billion on each of two counts.

Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, said in court that Trump had no real excuse not to testify and that on October 16, he had only been campaigning, “participating in party politics.”

“No plaintiff is above the law,” Tobin said.

In a court filing Wednesday, Trump’s legal team argued that he was not seeking to avoid a deposition but had been constrained by “matters of national importance.”

The lawyers said Trump would be able to give a deposition between January 11 and 22.

Trump has made attacks on the media a signature of his two presidential terms, insulting reporters who ask questions he doesn’t like and seeking to ban outlets airing critical reports from the White House.

Most recently, the administration has plunged into a legal dispute with CNN, MSNOW and Politico over attempts to bar them from the White House.

With his approval ratings in the low 30 percent range and polls showing his Republican Party likely to lose control of the House of Representatives in the November 3 midterm elections, Trump faces increasing headwinds as he approaches his final years in power.

AFP

World.title: N10bn untouched – APC accuses Atiku of politicising Ebola response
World.content:
Atiku Abubakar

The All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council has accused former Vice-President, Atiku Abubakar, of politicising Nigeria’s Ebola response, insisting that approved emergency funds remain untouched.

The council’s spokesperson, Mr Dele Alake, said this in a statement issued on Thursday in Abuja.

Alake said President Bola Tinubu approved N10 billion for the Ebola emergency in June, but relevant agencies deployed other available resources.

“On accountability, the Atiku camp should note that the N10 billion the President approved for the Ebola emergency in June remains untouched,” he said.

He said the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) and other agencies strengthened surveillance at entry points.

According to him, the surveillance network alerted the government to the index case and facilitated contact tracing for 44 contacts.

The council commended the agencies for their contributions to monitoring the Ebola threat and supporting the public health response.

It also criticised Atiku’s reference linking President Tinubu’s name to Ebola, saying it risked turning a serious health concern into political ridicule.

“We believe linking and rhyming President Bola Tinubu’s name to Ebola only risks turning a serious health concern into a vehicle to ridicule the President,” Alake said.

The council also defended the handling of the infected Nigerian’s detection, citing the virus’s incubation period and the timing of symptoms.

“For anyone infected with the virus, the incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, with symptoms typically appearing eight to 10 days after exposure.

“An infected person cannot spread or transmit Ebola to others until they actively develop symptoms,” he said.

Alake urged opposition politicians to support health authorities rather than criticise the government’s response to the public health threat.

“A responsible opposition will applaud the Task Force for being responsive. But the Atiku camp always goes for cheap shots at the government,” he said.

The council also rejected Atiku’s allegation that a ministerial briefing was intended to discourage Nigerians from attending campaign rallies or voting.

Alake described the allegation as speculative, adding that the briefing instead urged Nigerians to comply with protocols announced by the task force.

He called on Atiku and his supporters to avoid politicising public health concerns, urging Nigerians to shun rumours and follow health authorities’ guidance.

“We advise Atiku Abubakar and his hirelings to avoid politicising public health issues,” he said.

The council said protecting Nigerians from the deadly disease should remain the priority. (NAN)

World.title: Leemon Ikpea: Tinubu Must Resist Pressure, Sustain Bold Reforms
World.content:
FOCUS

Chairman of Lee Engineering Group, Chief Leemon Ikpea, in this piece, maintains that President Bola Tinubu must resist pressure to abandon his bold economic reforms. He insists that the measures are necessary to reposition Nigeria for sustainable growth. For Ikpea, the Tinubu administration’s reform agenda must be assessed not only by the immediate sacrifices it has imposed on Nigerians but also by its potential to correct longstanding economic distortions, strengthen public finances, improve national security and reposition the country in the global investment community, writes Emmanuel Addeh.

Why Tinubu Must Continue with Current Reforms

Ikpea reasons that Nigeria cannot continue to postpone difficult economic decisions and expect a different outcome. For decades, the country operated an economic system that placed enormous pressure on public finances, discouraged investment and limited the resources available for critical infrastructure and social services. The consequences were visible in the persistent challenges of inadequate infrastructure, weak public revenue, foreign exchange pressures and the difficulty of creating sufficient employment opportunities for a growing population.

The removal of petrol subsidy and the reform of the foreign exchange market marked a significant departure from this pattern. Although the consequences have been difficult for households and businesses, the measures, the businessman points out, have created an opportunity to address structural weaknesses and establish a more sustainable foundation for economic growth.

For Ikpea, the important thing is for the government to remain focused on its objectives rather than succumb to pressure to reverse policies whose benefits may take time to materialise.

“President Tinubu has demonstrated the courage to take decisions that previous administrations found difficult to implement. These are not easy decisions, and we must acknowledge that Nigerians are making sacrifices. However, we must look at the bigger picture and ensure that these reforms deliver lasting benefits for the country,” he says.

He argues that consistency is essential to restoring confidence among investors, who need predictable policies to make long-term commitments. According to him, businesses planning investments in manufacturing, energy, infrastructure and other productive sectors require a clear understanding of the economic environment in which they will operate.

For Ikpea, frequent reversals of major policies could increase uncertainty and discourage the very investments Nigeria needs to expand production and create jobs.

Therefore sustaining the reforms must involve more than maintaining existing policies, he points out. It requires improving implementation, strengthening institutions, ensuring transparency and establishing mechanisms through which Nigerians can see tangible benefits from the changes, he adds.

The government, therefore, must continue to pursue policies that expand economic opportunities while providing targeted support for vulnerable Nigerians. Such an approach, he argues, would help preserve public confidence without sacrificing the objectives of the reform programme.

Move for Better Military Welfare

For a country confronting terrorism, banditry, kidnapping and other security threats, the welfare of military personnel remains a critical national priority. The Tinubu administration’s approval of a salary increase for members of the armed forces, according to the Edo-born entrepreneur, represents an important recognition of the sacrifices made by personnel deployed to protect lives and property.

The increase, which took effect on September 1, 2026, provides for adjustments ranging from 30 per cent to 80 per cent across different categories of military personnel. The annual military salary bill is expected to rise from N660 billion to N924 billion, reflecting the government’s decision to commit additional resources to improving the conditions of service.

According to him, the demands of military service extend well beyond the ordinary responsibilities of public employment. Personnel deployed to conflict zones, he argued, often operate in dangerous environments, spend long periods away from their families and face the physical and psychological pressures associated with confronting armed groups.

Ikpea believes that those who risk their lives to defend Nigeria deserve the support and appreciation of the government and citizens.

“Our military personnel are making enormous sacrifices to keep Nigeria safe. Many of them operate in extremely difficult and dangerous conditions, often far away from their families. Improving their welfare is not just a reward for their service; it is an investment in our national security,” he says.

He maintains that better remuneration can strengthen morale and reinforce the recognition that the sacrifices of military personnel matter to the country they have sworn to protect. “A government that prioritises the welfare of its security personnel also sends an important signal about the value it places on national security,” he adds.

He argues that national security and economic development are closely connected. For this reason, he sees the government’s intervention in military welfare as a welcome step that should be sustained alongside other efforts to strengthen the country’s security architecture.

Relief Through Fuel Discount, CNG

The removal of petrol subsidy has increased transportation costs, putting additional pressure on households and businesses. The government’s efforts to expand Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) as an alternative fuel, he emphasises, therefore represent an important component of its response to the economic difficulties associated with the reforms.

Expanding the use of CNG, according to Ikpea, offers an opportunity to diversify the country’s energy mix, reduce dependence on conventional automotive fuels and lower operating costs for transport operators where the infrastructure and economics support its adoption.

“This administration has pursued vehicle conversions, refuelling infrastructure and partnerships with private operators to expand access to alternative-energy transportation. These initiatives are intended to encourage transport businesses and individual vehicle owners to consider cheaper fuel alternatives while creating opportunities for domestic investment. The President needs our support,” Ikpea notes.

Initiatives such as CNG, alongside targeted fuel discounts and other relief measures, he explains, demonstrate the importance of combining structural reforms with practical interventions to cushion their impact.

“Removing the subsidy was a difficult but necessary decision. However, initiatives such as CNG and targeted fuel discounts can help reduce the burden on households and businesses while allowing the country to move towards a more sustainable energy system,” he says.

For him, the value of CNG extends beyond the immediate reduction in transportation expenses. The programme could stimulate investment in gas infrastructure, support local engineering and manufacturing businesses, create technical employment and strengthen the domestic utilisation of Nigeria’s natural resources.

He believes that Nigeria should take advantage of its gas endowment to develop an energy system that supports industrial expansion and reduces the cost of doing business. A more affordable transportation system, he states, would also help businesses move goods more efficiently, with potential benefits for agriculture, manufacturing, distribution and retail trade.

The government, he says, is also working with private investors to expand the infrastructure required to make alternative fuels commercially viable. Fuel discounts have also been recently launched through NNPC stations nationwide.

The ultimate objective of this move, he argues, is to reduce the cost of moving people and goods without recreating the fiscal problems associated with the old subsidy system.

State Police One of Tinubu’s Best Decisions

According to Ikpea, the growing demand for a more effective response to insecurity has spurred the president’s renewed attention to the establishment of state police. The proposal seeks to bring policing closer to communities, strengthen local intelligence gathering and improve responses to threats that vary from one state to another.

He explains that Nigeria’s geographical size, population and complex security environment place considerable demands on the existing police system. Communities facing kidnapping, banditry, communal violence and other criminal activities often require rapid responses informed by detailed local knowledge.

For Ikpea, the establishment of state police represents an opportunity to address the limitations of a highly centralised policing structure and develop a system better equipped to respond to local security challenges.

“Security is fundamental to development. Our farmers must be able to go to their farms without fear, businesses must operate in a safe environment, and communities must have confidence that help will come when they need it. State police can bring security closer to the people if the system is properly designed and implemented, like the president is doing.

“A decentralised policing structure could improve intelligence gathering, strengthen community engagement and enable authorities to respond more quickly to security threats within their jurisdictions. Local knowledge can be particularly valuable in identifying criminal networks, understanding community dynamics and preventing threats before they escalate.

“Don’t forget, the economic implications are equally important. Insecurity disrupts agricultural production, increases business operating costs, discourages investment and prevents communities from participating fully in productive activities. It can also undermine infrastructure development and limit access to essential services.This is what I believe Tinubu is trying to stop,” he maintains.

Ikpea, however, believes that state police must be supported by appropriate constitutional and legal safeguards. Questions concerning funding, recruitment, training, operational standards, accountability and respect for fundamental rights must be addressed to ensure that the system serves the public interest.

He argues that state police will complement federal security institutions rather than create competing structures. “ The president’s priority, I think, is to sustain the political commitment to the reform while ensuring that the resulting framework is practical, accountable and capable of delivering improved security at the grassroots,” he contends.

Not in Nigeria’s Interest to Return Subsidy

Among the most consequential decisions of the Tinubu administration is the removal of petrol subsidy, a policy that has generated considerable public debate because of its immediate impact on the cost of living.

Before its removal, subsidy payments placed a significant burden on public finances, limiting the resources available for infrastructure, healthcare, education, security and other national priorities. The system also created market distortions and opportunities for abuse, while the benefits were not always distributed equitably among Nigerians.

Although the transition has been painful, Ikpea believes that returning to the old arrangement would risk recreating the fiscal challenges the government sought to address.

“We cannot continue to spend enormous public resources sustaining a system that is not economically sustainable. The removal of petrol subsidy was a difficult decision, but reversing it would mean returning to the same problems that held our economy back. What we need now is to make the reforms work for Nigerians,” he says.

“The government’s responsibility is to ensure that the resources freed up by the policy are managed transparently and channelled towards productive investments and interventions that improve citizens’ welfare. And I think that is what the Bola Tinubu government is doing,” he stresses.

He believes that investments in public transportation, road infrastructure, electricity, healthcare and education can help improve living standards while strengthening the productive capacity of the economy, while targeted assistance for vulnerable households is also providing relief without recreating the broad fiscal commitments associated with the former subsidy system.

The private sector, in his view, must play a central role in this transition. A more predictable economic environment, he explains, can encourage businesses to invest, expand operations and create employment.

He also argues that the additional fiscal space created by subsidy removal has produced visible benefits, with more effective use of government resources.

Rising Investor Confidence

Nigeria’s reform programme has attracted renewed attention from international investors and financial institutions, with developments in credit ratings and market classifications providing indications of changing perceptions of the country’s economic outlook.

Chief Ikpea says Nigeria’s improving standing with international credit-rating agencies is another indication of the growing recognition of the Tinubu administration’s economic reforms, listing Moody’s, S&P Global Ratings and Fitch Ratings as having all taken positive rating actions on Nigeria.

Moody’s revised the country’s outlook to positive in August 2026, retaining its B3 rating, while S&P upgraded Nigeria’s rating from B- to B in May 2026. On October 9, Fitch revised Nigeria’s outlook from stable to positive and affirmed its B rating, citing reforms, stronger foreign exchange reserves and improvements in the country’s external financial position. JPMorgan has softened its disposition to the country.

These assessments, according to him, suggest that international observers are beginning to recognise the potential benefits of the government’s policy changes.

For Ikpea, the improved assessments could have important implications for Nigeria’s economic prospects. Stronger credit ratings and positive outlooks can improve investor confidence, help Nigerian governments and companies attract foreign capital and potentially reduce borrowing costs over time, particularly if further rating improvements follow.

Greater confidence, he posits, could also encourage investment in manufacturing, oil and gas, infrastructure and other productive sectors, supporting employment and economic diversification.

“Investors want to see consistency, transparency and a government that is prepared to take the necessary decisions to create a stable business environment. When policies become more predictable and the economy is managed more sustainably, confidence improves and investors are more willing to consider long-term commitments,” he says.

He argues that Nigeria must build on this momentum by improving the business environment, strengthening regulatory institutions and addressing the infrastructure constraints that increase the cost of operating in the country.

For a nation with significant opportunities in oil and gas, manufacturing, agriculture, infrastructure and technology, stronger investor confidence, he argues, could support economic diversification, expand productive capacity and create employment.

Ikpea also believes that domestic businesses are benefiting from the changing economic environment. Nigerian companies require access to financing, reliable infrastructure and a predictable policy framework to expand their operations and compete effectively.

“The ultimate objective is to convert improved perceptions into investment, stronger production, job creation and better living standards, which I feel is ongoing and the president knows and he’s doing everything to achieve,” he opines.

According to him, Nigeria has an opportunity to correct longstanding economic weaknesses, improve its security architecture and build a more competitive economy. Abandoning the reform programme prematurely, he argues, could undermine the progress achieved and restore the distortions that made decisive action necessary.

World.title: Nigeria Decides 2027 and the Burden of Proof
World.content:
Beneath the Surface By Dakuku Peterside

A voter who has spent hours in a queue should not need to understand computer servers to believe that a ballot will be counted. The obligation runs the other way. Those entrusted with conducting an election must demonstrate that its outcome reflects the choices citizens made. As Nigeria approaches 2027, this should be the measure of every technological innovation: does it make electoral power more accountable to the people whose consent gives that power legitimacy?

The attraction of technology is understandable. Where human discretion has attracted suspicion, a machine can seem to promise impartiality. Biometric checks offer firmer identification; digital records offer opportunities for scrutiny. Artificial intelligence could improve logistics and detect inconsistencies. Yet the promise becomes dangerous when people mistake sophistication for integrity. Every system still reflects decisions about procurement, access, oversight and what happens when something goes wrong. Those decisions remain human, even when their consequences appear on a screen.

Nigeria’s 2023 elections exposed the fragility of the relationship between technical capability and public confidence. The Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, BVAS, sought to strengthen voter identification through biometric checks. The INEC Results Viewing Portal, IReV, enabled public access to images of polling unit result sheets. Their functions differed, but their democratic value lay in making key stages of the process more open to verification.

Delays in uploading presidential results undermined that promise. They did not, by themselves, establish that votes had been altered. Equally, the lack of expected information mattered. Citizens were entitled to ask what failed, what remained secure, and how to check the records. A transparency mechanism cannot build confidence through its promised availability and then become irrelevant when people need to consult it. Its failure requires an explanation proportionate to the trust invested in it.

Behind these questions stood people who had paid a price to participate. A trader who closed a stall had surrendered income. A worker who travelled home to vote had committed money and time. When the count became difficult to follow, their uncertainty concerned more than a preferred candidate. It touched the belief that peaceful participation mattered. An election can leave institutions formally intact while making citizens less willing to place their hopes in them again.

This is the democratic cost Nigeria must avoid in 2027. Confidence cannot be repaired by asking people to ask fewer questions. It grows when institutions give better answers and make those answers examinable. Before deploying AI, INEC should explain its intended tasks, the data it will process and the suppliers involved. Responsibility for errors must be identifiable in advance. Public scrutiny belongs before deployment, where it can still influence decisions, and after failure.

Communication during disruption deserves its own preparation. An institution should be able to say what it knows, what remains uncertain, and when it will provide another update. Silence invites speculation; premature certainty can destroy credibility when later evidence contradicts it. Clear communication also protects officials from having every operational problem interpreted as deliberate manipulation. It gives the public a basis for distinguishing an interruption from a breach and a documented correction from an unexplained alteration. The aim is neither automatic suspicion nor automatic acceptance, but judgement informed by records that remain available for independent examination after the immediate political controversy has passed.

Independent testing should therefore produce evidence of readiness under actual operating conditions. The examination must include interrupted power, poor connectivity, heavy demand, and uneven technical support. Publish relevant findings and corrective actions without exposing sensitive information. A successful demonstration is reassuring; a serious attempt to discover failure is more useful. The public needs to know which weaknesses were found, which were corrected and which limitations still require practical safeguards.

Those safeguards must reach the polling unit. Officials need clear, lawful instructions for equipment and network problems, supported by rehearsals and accessible technical assistance. Voters and observers should understand the applicable procedures. Otherwise, discretion exercised under pressure can appear indistinguishable from favouritism. Preparedness also means designing for elderly voters, people with disabilities and people whose biometric details are difficult to capture. Efficiency has little democratic value if its apparent success conceals citizens who could not participate.

Verification must continue through the count. A traceable link must exist between the polling unit record, its published image, and the figures carried through collation. Where discrepancies appear, a functioning process must investigate and explain them. Merely allowing citizens to see a problem is insufficient. Visibility without a route to correction can deepen the sense of powerlessness. Technology should make irregularities harder to conceal and evidence-based challenges easier to pursue.

AI can support this work, but its authority needs firm boundaries. A system that flags a suspicious record raises a question; it does not establish wrongdoing. Decisions affecting registration, eligibility or results must remain subject to authorised human judgement and established procedures. Human oversight must involve someone who can examine the evidence, challenge the output, and explain the decision. A signature beneath an opaque recommendation offers weak protection if the signatory cannot meaningfully assess its basis.

The information environment presents a different danger. A cloned voice could announce a false withdrawal; a fabricated security warning could discourage turnout. Such deception can damage an election without touching a result sheet. Worse, convincing fabrications create an excuse to dismiss authentic evidence as fake. Citizens may increasingly believe whatever confirms their loyalties. When disagreement extends to whether any reliable account of events is possible, democratic argument loses the common ground on which persuasion and accountability depend.

This danger becomes intimate when misinformation arrives through trusted relationships. A relative’s forwarded message carries social authority that its contents may not deserve. Citizens should pause before sharing material designed to provoke fear or fury. But individual caution needs institutional support. Electoral authorities, journalists, platforms and civil society should establish coordinated arrangements for early warning, verification and rapid correction. Reliable information must reach people through radio and in Nigerian languages, with clear channels to check urgent claims.

Political parties must answer for the persuasion they organise. Standards against deceptive impersonation should govern campaign staff, contractors and commissioned content. Candidates should correct false claims produced by their campaigns and repudiate dangerous fabrications circulated in their name. Demanding integrity from electoral officials while rewarding dishonesty among supporters hollows out the principle being defended. The duty to respect voters begins with how their choices are influenced, long before those choices are counted.

Journalists face a related discipline. Reporting that a platform failed differs from explaining why it failed or what happened to the underlying records. Speed should not erase that distinction. Observers and fact-checkers need preparation and access sufficiently to examine evidence. Platforms must strengthen reporting channels and responses to deceptive synthetic content in Nigerian languages. Verification becomes more credible when its methods are transparent, and its standards apply consistently across political interests.

Cybersecurity requires continuous work: controlled access, protected backups and rehearsed recovery plans. Yet security cannot be a universal answer to accountability demands. Nor should combating disinformation justify suppressing legitimate criticism. Citizens must remain free to question electoral authorities, including sharply. The institutional response should distinguish demonstrable deception from unwelcome scrutiny. Protecting the election means preserving the freedom to expose its weaknesses and demand correction.

Suppliers, too, must accept obligations that survive the sales presentation. Electoral systems need dependable support, auditable records and clear contractual responsibility for failures. Commercial confidentiality should not make essential questions unanswerable. Developing African technical expertise and regional cooperation could strengthen independent assessment and reduce reliance on suppliers’ assurances. The lasting investment is institutional knowledge: people who can examine systems, investigate incidents, and retain expertise after a contract ends.

Shared responsibility requires careful language. Voters cannot repair infrastructure they did not procure or disclose records they do not control. Accountability must follow authority. INEC answers for administration, suppliers for their obligations and parties for campaign conduct. Each actor needs duties against which performance can be judged. Otherwise, collective responsibility becomes a comfortable way to distribute concern while detaching the power to prevent failure from the consequences of failing.

Citizens also face a test of consistency. Do we require the same evidence when our candidate wins as when our candidate loses? Excusing an irregularity because it benefits our side weakens a protection we may need tomorrow. Standards that change with the winner cannot sustain trust. Credible elections require the willingness to defend a fair process even when its outcome disappoints, while retaining the right to challenge wrongdoing through evidence and lawful procedures.

Before 2027, Nigeria should demand measurable preparedness: published governance rules, independent audits, trained personnel, tested contingency plans and functioning complaints mechanisms. Each commitment needs a responsible institution, a deadline and public evidence of completion. The question is whether citizens will encounter a process they can understand, scrutinise and challenge. They have already supplied their patience and their choices. Those entrusted with conducting the election must now supply the competence and proof that make those choices count.

•Dr Dakuku Peterside is a turnaround expert in leadership and management.

World.title: Ogunsan @ 50: The ‘Civilian General’s’ Journey of Faith, Family, Leadership and Service
World.content:
For the Executive Secretary and Chief Executive Officer of the Lagos State Security Trust Fund (LSSTF), Dr. Ayodele Ogunsan, turning 50 was not just an opportunity to celebrate another milestone but to reflect on a journey shaped by faith, family, relationships and service. Chiemelie Ezeobi writes that the recent launch of the book Dr. Ayodele Ogunsan: The Civilian General – The Man, His Wits, Passion, Influence brought together political leaders, security chiefs, business executives, traditional rulers and family members whose tributes offered insights into his life, leadership, contributions to public service, security collaboration, business and philanthropy

Tributes to Dr. Ayodele Ogunsan’s humility, leadership and contribution to security collaboration in Lagos recently took centre stage as the Executive Secretary and Chief Executive Officer of the Lagos State Security Trust Fund (LSSTF) celebrated his 50th birthday with the launch of a book documenting his life and influence.

Thus, the unveiling of the book “Dr. Ayodele Ogunsan: The Civilian General – The Man, His Wits, Passion, Influence” afforded family, friends, government officials, business leaders and traditional rulers the opportunity to share their experiences of the celebrant.

The book, authored by Mayor Oki Olatunji Samson and co-authored by Abayomi Oyelami, was jointly unveiled by Chief Ajibola Bankole Adebutu, MON, Chief Executive Officer of JB Farms, and Inspector-General of Police, IGP Olatunji Rilwan Disu.

The occasion brought together Lagos State Governor Babajide Olusola Sanwo-Olu, political leaders, business executives, security chiefs, traditional rulers, Christian ministers, family members and associates, whose tributes highlighted Ogunsan’s humility, dedication, faith and ability to build relationships across institutions.

Sanwo-Olu, Disu Praise His Leadership

Sanwo-Olu, reflecting on a relationship spanning almost a decade, recalled that Ogunsan initially struck him as quiet, humble and unassuming. He said their working relationship revealed a dependable leader with compassion, strength and a commitment to getting results.

“Ogunsan is an Omoluabi personified. He is a committed Lagosian. Ayo, my dear aburo, has worked and touched lives in different ways. That’s why I’m truly proud not just to be identified with him but to wish him well,” the governor said.

Describing his character, he added: “He will appear to you as a gentle dove, which he actually is, but inside him is the full roar of a dependable man who is strong in the Lord.”

The governor also praised Ogunsan’s loyalty, precision and ability to complete assignments while providing feedback and anticipating challenges.

Deputy Governor Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, represented by Mr. Moruf Akinderu Fatai, congratulated Ogunsan and urged him to continue contributing to national security, saying: “I celebrate you, Dr. Ogunsan, on your birthday. Do continue to move in this quest to secure Nigeria.”

Disu described Ogunsan as a wonderful person whose humility had helped bring security agencies together.

“Dr. Ayo Ogunsan is a wonderful human being. I have a lot to learn from him, though I am older than him. He doesn’t mind kneeling down to solve problems. He has been able to merge all security agencies in Nigeria,” the IGP said.

FirstBank Managing Director and CEO, Olusegun Alebiosu, praised Ogunsan’s humility, honesty, amiability and impact, saying he continued to learn from him and considered him a great man.

While LSSTF Board Chairman Kehinde Durosinmi Etti commended Ogunsan’s knowledge of security matters and their professional relationship, another board member and Zenith Bank Executive Director, Akin Ogunranti called him an “indefatigable CEO,” citing his energy and regular updates on security initiatives.

Ubon Udoh, board member and MD/CEO of ASR Foundation, described him as “driven and inspirational,” praising his belief in collective effort.

Faith, Family and Lasting Values

Businessman and philanthropist Chief Olu Okeowo, Chairman of Gibraltar Construction, described Ogunsan as a distinguished gentleman whose Christianity was reflected in his work and family. Comparing him with biblical David, he praised the family’s shared expression of worship.

Adebutu conveyed greetings from his father, Sir Kessington Adebukunola Adebutu, and the Adebutu family, praying for Ogunsan to celebrate 60, 70 and more birthdays as God permits.

Lagos Commissioner for Special Duties Gbenga Oyerinde celebrated five decades of memorable experiences, praying that Ogunsan’s coming years would be more fulfilling and bring him “testimonies that money cannot buy.”

The Alara of Ilara, Oba Olufolarin Ogunsanwo, praised Ogunsan’s diligence and commitment to service and thanked his wife, Dr. Ajoke Ogunsan, for supporting him and keeping the home front.

The Ologba of Ogba, Oba Lateef Egbeyemi, said, “We can see the certificate of your parents in you.” He commended the celebrant’s wife and children and prayed that Ogunsan would live to witness their successes.

Family members Abiodun Ogunsan and Dr. Sunday Alabi, his brother-in-law, also paid tribute. Abiodun described him as a leader, mentor and father figure guided by discipline and spirituality, while Alabi recalled recognising his leadership qualities in 1986/87.

Dignitaries at the Celebration

Political figures present included Lagos Chief of Staff Tayo Ayinde; Deputy Chief of Staff Sam Egube; APC Lagos deputy governorship candidate Princess Damilola Senayon James; campaign Director-General Senator Musiliu Obanikoro; Attorney-General Lawal Pedro, SAN; Commissioner for Information Gbenga Omotoso; Commissioner for Trade and Investment Folashade Ambrose-Medebem; Special Adviser on Tourism Idris Aregbe; Gbenga Abiola; and Seriki Muritala. Retired DIG Agboola Oshodi Glover also attended.

Business leaders included UBA Group Managing Director and CEO Oliver Alawuba; Idowu Oguntona, MD of Lagos Bus Service Limited; and other executives.

Disu led senior police officers including DIG Adegoke Fayoade; retired DIGs Bode Adeleke, Ari Muhammed Ali and David Folawiyo; AIGs Simeon Akpanudom, Olohundare Jimoh and Ronke Nurat Okunade; retired AIGs Johnson Adenola and Lanre Bankole; CPs Fatai Tijani, Toyin Agbaminijo, retired Saadat Ismail, Akin Fakorede and retired Abiodun Alamutu; DCPs Anthony Okon Placid, Bayo Sulaiman, Lawal Adeshina, retired Akinbayo Olasoji and Mary Ayim; ACPs Veronica Ameh-Akpa, Frances Oyin Adegbite, Smith Adeleke and Adegbite; and CSPs Tayo Akerele, Solomon Komolafe, Ayodele Elijah, Shola Jejeloye and Shokunbi Toyosi.

Military representatives included Brig. Gen. Ayokunle Owolabi, Air Commodore M.A. Imam, Commodore Aiwuyor Adams Aliu, Gen. Olumuyiwa Okunowo and Rear Admiral Olugbenga Oladipo, Commander of Operation Delta Safe.

Other security officials were NDLEA Lagos Strategic Commander ACGN Wali Liman Abubakar; NSCDC Commandant Adedotun Keshinro; Immigration Comptroller Chris Olu Onajinrin; FRSC Sector Commander Kehinde Hamzat; LNSA General Manager Prince Dr. Ifalade Oyekan; Man ‘O’ War Commandant MC Ayodele Ajayi; and Vigilante Group of Nigeria Commander Sesan Oguntunde.

Traditional rulers included Ooni of Ife Oba Adeyeye Enitan Ogunwusi, represented by his wife; Oba Olufolarin Ogunsanwo; Oba Lateef Egbeyemi and Olori Kadijat Egbeyemi; Onikoyi of Ikoyi Oba Ibikunle Fafunwa; and Lagos white-cap chiefs.

Christian ministers included Pastor Yemi Akinwande of Deeper Life Church UK, who delivered the exhortation; Pastor Sehindemi Johnson; Professor Albert Oikelome; Pastor Tope Ojemen; Pastor Olaomo; and Pastor Olanipekun.

Worship, praise and thanksgiving marked the celebration, as the book documented Ogunsan’s journey and the values associates said had shaped his life and leadership.

As the celebration drew to a close with worship, praise and thanksgiving, the tributes returned to the themes that had run through the occasion: faith, family, humility and service.

For Ogunsan, the book offers a record of five decades of experiences, while the words of those who gathered in his honour provide a personal account of the relationships and values that have shaped his journey. The milestone also marks the beginning of another chapter, with prayers and expectations for continued fulfilment, greater impact and many more years of service.

World.title: Ebonyi Killings: Fresh Revelations Raise Questions Over Soldiers’ Actions
World.content:
Abdullahi Mohammed

The atmosphere in Ihetutu community, Ivo Local Government Area of Ebonyi State, remains tense and sorrowful following the alleged killing of two young men by a soldier reportedly attached to Palladium Mining Company, in an incident that has raised troubling questions about the conduct of security personnel deployed to protect mining operations in the area.

The victims, identified as 18-year-old Chibuike Elema and 20-year-old Obinna Gideon Akandu, reportedly lost their lives on Sunday after allegedly being shot by military personnel at a location said to be some distance from the company’s mining facility.

While the circumstances surrounding the shooting remain the subject of an ongoing military investigation, accounts obtained from grieving families, community representatives and other sources have raised questions about what transpired before the two young men were killed.

At the centre of the controversy are allegations that the victims were shot following a disagreement over money allegedly demanded by soldiers operating in the area.

However, the precise sequence of events, the motive behind the shooting and the circumstances under which the soldiers encountered the victims have yet to be independently established.

Findings gathered suggest that the incident occurred outside the immediate operational premises of Palladium Mining Company, raising questions about the circumstances surrounding the soldiers’ presence at the location.

Sources familiar with the company’s operations claimed that the soldiers allegedly involved were not carrying out any assignment authorised by the mining company at the time of the incident.

The company had neither deployed the personnel for an undercover operation nor instructed them to undertake any activity outside their designated security responsibilities.

These claims, however, remain subject to independent verification, particularly regarding the soldiers’ official deployment arrangements, operational instructions and chain of command.

The development has consequently raised questions about whether the alleged shooting occurred in the course of authorised military duties or resulted from actions undertaken independently by the personnel involved.

Investigators are also expected to establish whether the soldiers were officially assigned to the location where the shooting occurred and whether any operational instructions were breached.

Since the incident happened last Sunday, there have been several misleading reports, which however, encouraged this investigation to ascertain the real story.

For the families of the deceased, the tragedy represents an unimaginable loss that has thrown their households into mourning.

Mr Donatus Okoro, father of 18-year-old Chibuike Elema, alleged that his son was called from home on Sunday morning to join other workers at the mining site.

According to him, the young man had completed his activities and was returning home when the fatal encounter reportedly occurred.

Okoro alleged that eyewitnesses informed the family that soldiers attached to the mining company demanded money from the youths before opening fire on them.

“But they told the soldiers that they were not with anything. The soldiers raised their guns and shot them in the head,” the grieving father alleged.

His account, although emotionally compelling, has not been independently corroborated by the military authorities.

Nevertheless, the allegation that money was demanded before the shooting has become a major concern among residents, who are calling for investigators to establish whether extortion or any other unlawful activity contributed to the incident.

The second victim, Obinna Gideon Akandu, who was identified as a 20-year-old second-year Economics student of Ebonyi State University, Abakaliki was the son of serving councillor representing Ihetutu community in Ivo Local Government Area Mr Joshua Akandu.

According to his father, the young undergraduate had returned to the community on Friday afternoon following the postponement of his examinations.

What was supposed to be a brief visit home ended in tragedy when he reportedly went to the farm on Sunday and was allegedly shot while returning.

“My son was innocent. He just went to the farm, and while coming back, they shot him on the road,” Akandu said.

The father’s account presents an additional dimension to the incident, particularly regarding the movements of the victims before the shooting.

While one family maintained that its son was returning from work, the other stated that the deceased had gone to the farm.

These accounts underscore the need for investigators to reconstruct the victims’ movements, identify eyewitnesses and determine precisely how the fatal encounter occurred.

For residents, however, the immediate concern remains the loss of two young lives and the need to establish accountability.

The killings generated widespread grief and anger among residents of Ihetutu, with women, youths and community leaders demanding an independent and transparent investigation.

Some residents alleged that the incident reflected broader concerns about the conduct of security personnel.

The community’s demands come amid concerns that unresolved grievances could further strain relations between residents, security agencies and companies operating within the locality.

In the aftermath of the reported shooting, tensions reportedly escalated as aggrieved youths descended on the mining facility, destroying property and disrupting operations.

Accounts of the disturbance indicated that equipment, vehicles, offices and staff accommodation were affected during the unrest. Some vehicles were reportedly set ablaze, while offices and residential facilities were allegedly vandalised and looted.

The destruction further complicated an already volatile situation, raising concerns about the safety of workers, residents and investments in the area.

Although the anger generated by the deaths has been widely acknowledged, government officials and community leaders have appealed against retaliatory violence.

The attacks on the company’s facilities also raise separate questions requiring investigation, including the identity of those responsible, the extent of property damage and whether adequate measures were taken to prevent the escalation.

Meanwhile, it was also gathered that Palladium Mining Company has commenced efforts aimed at reducing tensions and restoring its relationship with the host community.

Sources familiar with the development disclosed that the company was initiating humanitarian and reconciliation measures intended to reach the bereaved families and other affected members of Ihetutu.

The intervention is reportedly designed to demonstrate solidarity with the grieving families, address immediate humanitarian concerns and create an atmosphere conducive to dialogue.

The company’s priority is to ensure that the unfortunate incident does not permanently damage the relationship it has maintained with the community.

The proposed engagement is also expected to involve consultations with traditional authorities, community representatives, youth leaders and relevant government officials.

Although details of the humanitarian measures have not been publicly established, sources indicated that the company recognises the importance of rebuilding confidence and ensuring that peace returns to the area.

The company is said to be particularly concerned about preserving its relationship with the host community while allowing the relevant authorities to conduct an independent investigation.

However, the reconciliation initiative does not diminish the demand for accountability or replace the need for a transparent investigation into the circumstances surrounding the deaths.

Ebonyi Government Intervenes, Seals Mining Company

The Ebonyi State Government has condemned the killings and announced the sealing of the mining facility pending efforts to restore peace and ensure justice.

Governor Francis Nwifuru described the incident as tragic and regrettable, expressing concern over the loss of two young lives.

During a government visit to the community, the governor, represented by the Commissioner for Solid Minerals Development, Chief Chinedum Nkah, appealed to residents, particularly the youths, to remain calm and law-abiding.

He assured the community that the government would work with the relevant authorities to ensure that the circumstances surrounding the incident were properly investigated.

The governor’s representative also disclosed that the soldier allegedly implicated in the shooting had been taken into custody.

According to the state government, an investigation had commenced to establish the facts and determine responsibility.

The decision to seal the mining facility represents a significant intervention by the state government as authorities seek to prevent further violence and restore confidence among residents.

Also on his part, the Chairman of Ivo Local Government Area, Chief Michael Anyim, also condemned the incident, describing the killings as unwarranted and unnecessary.

Speaking on the development, Anyim said the community had previously maintained a peaceful relationship with soldiers deployed to the area.

The council chairman appealed to aggrieved youths to desist from further attacks on the mining facility and other acts capable of worsening the situation.

He assured residents that the local government would collaborate with the Ebonyi State Government and the Nigerian Army to pursue justice for the victims and their families.

Anyim stressed the importance of allowing the relevant authorities to conclude their investigations while maintaining peace within the community.

Military Confirms Investigation Is Ongoing

In an effort to obtain the military’s position on the incident, the Commanding Officer of the 24 Support Engineer Regiment at Nkwagu Military Cantonment, Abakaliki, Lieutenant Colonel Ikenna Emmanuel Chielo was contacted. Speaking through a telephone conversation, he confirmed that authorities had visited the scene and that investigations were ongoing.

“We were at the scene today, investigation is ongoing, let’s be patient to get the full details,” Chielo said.

His response indicates that military authorities are examining the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The outcome of the investigation will be critical in determining whether the incident involved unlawful use of force, misconduct or any other offence under applicable military and civilian laws.

Unanswered Questions Surrounding the Killings

Beyond the grief and destruction, the incident has exposed several issues that require clarification.

One major question concerns the exact location of the shooting and why soldiers reportedly attached to a private mining operation were present there.

Another concerns the allegation that money was demanded from the victims shortly before they were killed.

Investigators will also need to establish whether the soldiers were acting under official instructions, whether any confrontation occurred and what circumstances led to the discharge of firearms.

The reported differences in the families’ accounts of the victims’ movements also make it necessary to obtain independent eyewitness testimony and reconstruct the events leading to the shooting.

Equally important is the need to determine the precise relationship between the mining company and the military personnel deployed to provide security around its operations.

The investigation should clarify the extent of the company’s authority, if any, over the movement and activities of the soldiers, as well as the command structure responsible for supervising their deployment.

These issues are particularly significant because the shooting reportedly occurred outside the company’s operational premises.

Until the relevant authorities release their findings, allegations concerning the motive for the shooting and the responsibility of individuals or institutions must remain unproven.

*Abdullahi Mohammed, writes from Ebonyi

World.title: ALWAYS NEVER HIM
World.content:
The cost of Peter Obi’s politics is often borne by someone else, contends JOSHUA J. OMOJUWA

In Manchester on Sunday 18 October, Peter Obi told a hall of Nigerians living in Britain what to do about their relatives. “You have people at home in Nigeria today who are begging you for money. Tell them no! Let us put somebody who has proven to be productive.”

By Tuesday he had clarified. He said he deeply appreciates Nigerians in the diaspora, that their remittances pay for school fees, hospital bills, rent and feeding, that their sacrifices deserve profound respect, and that he never asked anyone to abandon their loved ones. His message, he said, had been distorted by political opponents.

He did not say he had been misquoted. The video exists and he has not suggested otherwise. What he disputed was the meaning, and we are entitled to examine the meaning for ourselves.

Let us start with the mechanics of his proposal.

A nurse in Manchester sends two hundred pounds to her mother in Lagos for blood pressure medication. Under this instruction she says no, so that her mother feels the full weight of her electoral decision, so that her mother votes differently, so that governance improves, so that one day the transfer becomes unnecessary. Or maybe not, considering the global phenomenon of remittances.

The mother is the instrument. The nurse makes the decision. The candidate collects the benefit.

However, notice what the prescription does. It locates the pain in the poorest participant, the one with no agency in the transaction, and it asks a working nurse to administer that pain to her own mother on the strength of a promise from a man who will not be present for the conversation. It also assumes that voting the beneficiary candidate will improve the outcomes of governance.

It was not only the governing party that recoiled. The Labour Party, the NNPP and the SDP all criticised the remarks. When three opposition parties that have every incentive to stay quiet decide to object, something has gone beyond ordinary partisanship.

And this is the point, because the Manchester remark is not an isolated clumsiness. It is a method. His supporters assume he has the right thing to say, until he says something.

Go back to the Anambra doctors’ strike that ran for thirteen months under his own governorship. The defence, which he has restated across years, is that it did not affect a great many sick people, that no catastrophe occurred. Nobody died en masse, so the harm was not real.

Look at the structure of that argument rather than its content. The suffering is acknowledged and then declared acceptable, because the person declaring it is not the person who bore it. The mother who did not survive childbirth during those thirteen months cannot be produced as a witness. The patient whose treatable illness turned terminal is not in the room. So the absence of a headline becomes the proof of innocence.

It is the same architecture as the Manchester instruction. Somebody else’s hardship, assessed from a comfortable distance, and judged bearable.

Then there is the question of what he actually tells people, which varies by room. In one video, he said he had lived in Nnewi all his life. In another, he said he lived in Lagos. And both statements did not leave room to suggest he stayed at more than one location. He seems to forget his assertions, so he sets up contradictions at will.

On 24 August, at the Nigerian Bar Association conference in Port Harcourt, he reaffirmed his support for the removal of the fuel subsidy and argued that the government’s mishandling of the savings was no reason to bring it back. On 28 September, at a town hall in Sokoto, he assured his audience that subsidy would return once corruption had been dealt with.

Five weeks. Two cities. A yes and a no to a question that requires a simple yes or no. Schrödinger’s subsidy. He will remove it and he will not remove it.

A politician is entitled to change his mind. What is owed when a position changes is an account of what changed it. None has been offered. What we have instead is a policy that stays dead in the south and comes back to life in the north, with a condition attached that has no date on it.

A man who will give two answers to the simplest question in Nigerian politics is a man telling each room what it wants to hear, and the honest word for that is not nuance. This has cost him a lot of ground as Atiku Abubakar has now firmly established himself as President Tinubu’s main challenger.

Consider also the platforms. APGA, then the PDP, then the Labour Party, then the ADC in January of this year, then the NDC in May. Five parties, three of them inside twelve months.

Each departure has an explanation, and in every one the party failed him rather than the reverse. But people joined those parties because he was in them. Volunteers, candidates, donors, young people who put their names and money behind a movement. A platform you can leave three times in a year is what? Maybe a vehicle. And the people left stranded on the platform.

Then the supporters. When people campaigning in his name behave indefensibly, the response is that those people are not really his supporters. It is an unfalsifiable defence. Anybody who embarrasses the movement is by definition outside it, which means the movement can never be held responsible for anything done in its name. This is genius by the way. In a sense at least.

In every case the cost of Peter Obi’s politics is carried by somebody who is not Peter Obi. The nurse and her mother. The patients of Anambra. The volunteers of a party he has since left. The ordinary supporter who is disowned the moment he becomes inconvenient.

Because the question is not whether he believes what he says in any particular hall. It is who pays when he is wrong, and the pattern so far gives a consistent answer.

Never him.

Omojuwa is chief strategist, Alpha Reach/BGX Publishing

World.title: THE ESSENCE OF GOOD NUTRITION
World.content:
Do you have a favourite food? If so, what is it? Do you like beans, rice, vegetable soup, or yam? Or is it some other type of food that you especially enjoy?

Good food is needed for a person to grow well, work hard and stay healthy. In many parts of the world, many common illnesses result from the problem of hunger and poor nutrition. Not having enough nutritious food weakens the body’s ability to resist all kinds of diseases, especially infections. Nutritious food helps prevent disease and also helps the sick body fight disease and become well again. So, when a person is sick, eating enough nutritious food is especially important. Anyone who eats a good mixture of foods, including eggs, vegetables, fruits, and other types of foods, gets all the vitamins he needs. It is always better to eat well than to buy vitamin pills, injections, syrups, or tonics.

According to a very valuable healthcare handbook: “Where There Is No Doctor” authored by David Werner and published by Hesperian Health Guides (www.hesperian.org, “To stay healthy, our bodies need plenty of good food. The food we eat has to fill many needs. First, it should provide energy to keep us active and strong. Also, it must help build , repair , and protect the different parts of our bodies. To do all this we need to eat a combination of foods every day.”

However, it is important to note that there is a difference between not eating enough (undernutrition) and not eating right (malnutrition). A person who is weak or sick because he does not eat enough food of any kind is said to be suffering from general malnutrition or undernutrition, while a person who is weak or sick because he does not eat the right kinds of foods his body needs, is said to be suffering from specific types of malnutrition. There are also people who get sick as a result of eating too much of certain foods, like processed and “junk” foods. People who eat a lot of these foods are more likely to have high blood pressure, heart disease, strokes, gallstones, diabetes, and some cancers.

There are many different reasons for hunger and poor nutrition. One main reason is poverty. In many parts of the world, a few people own most of the wealth and the land. They may grow crops like coffee or tobacco, which they sell to make money, but which have no food value. Or the poor may farm small plots of borrowed land, while the owners take a big share of the harvest. The problem of hunger, food insecurity and poor nutrition will continue to exist until people learn to share with each other fairly.

There are many different ways to approach the problem of hunger and poor nutrition, for many different things join to cause it. Some of the things that people can do to help themselves meet their needs for better nutrition at low cost include: creating family gardens; improving their use of land through the rotation of crops; irrigation of land; use of natural fertilizers; better food storage; fish breeding; choosing to have smaller families through family planning; and so forth. Some actions bring quick results. Others work over a longer period of time.

Also, when money is limited, it is important to use it wisely. This means cooperation and looking ahead. A poor family can usually be better nourished if they grow or buy plant foods like beans, peas, lentils, and groundnuts together with a main food such as maize or rice, rather than buy costly animal foods like meat and fish. It is good to eat a variety of plant foods. Different plants supply the body with different proteins, vitamins, and minerals. For example, beans and maize together meet the body’s needs much better than either beans or maize alone. And if other vegetables or fruits are added, this is even better. However, where family finances and local customs permit, it is wise to eat, when possible, some food that comes from animals. This is because even plants high in protein often do not have all of the different proteins the body needs.

Daniel Ighakpe,

FESTAC Town, Lagos State

World.title: THE LEGACY OF PATRICK DELE COLE
World.content:
Patrick Cole, journalist, administrator and diplomat, dies at 86

The recent passing of Dr. Patrick Dele Cole at 86 deserves to be memorialised as a significant life of accomplishments and impact on many fronts. Cole left his mark as a profound thinker and successful performer within and outside the country. He was an outstanding public servant, technocrat, diplomat, and presidential counsel under military regimes in the mid-1970s and civilian administrations of the 1990s. But of all the roles in this exceptional life, his contributions to the development of the Nigerian print and newspaper industry are arguably the most important.

Born on 4th August 1940 in Abonnema, Rivers State, Cole secured a federal government scholarship in 1962 to further his studies abroad. He attended the University of Otago in New Zealand and later University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom, where he obtained a doctorate and spent three years as a fellow. He also taught at the University of Pennsylvania in the United States.

In 1976, Cole returned to Nigeria at the invitation of the then military administration and was appointed Managing Director of Daily Times at a time when the federal government held majority equity in both the newspaper published in Lagos and the New Nigerian with head office in Kaduna. Cole brought to his leadership of the Daily Times the best benefits of his American training and cultural exposure. He recruited and brought home two leading US-based Nigerian journalists whose contributions helped to usher in an era of robust and thoughtful journalism from the 1980s onwards. The first was the late Dele Giwa who came from the New York Times. Dr. Stanley Macebuh, a part-time New York Times Editorial Board member and adjunct professor at New York University, was the second.

The introduction of the American style Editorial Board transformed the Daily Times from its traditional British orientation to a more robust liberal tradition. The board became the newspaper’s intellectual powerhouse, enabling it to explore and enlarge the confines of perspective and thought while its members authored enlightened and broad-based columns every day. This contrasted with the typical British tradition where the editor and his features desk wrote the editorials and sourced opinions from the reading public. This innovation marked a significant development in the Nigerian newspaper industry with intellectuals and high caliber journalists attracted to the newsroom.

This development came to its full bloom with the founding of The Guardian, a privately owned liberal newspaper under the leadership of both Cole and Macebuh. And with that, those wielding state power came to respect and value newspapers as sources of alternative and reinforcing ideas and perspectives for state affairs. Along also came innovative business ideas for profitability in advertising and circulation. These ground-breaking developments led to the general modernisation of the Nigerian newspaper industry that has persisted till today. As President Bola Tinubu noted in his tribute, Cole’s career reflected the enduring value of dialogue, tact, mutual respect and the pursuit of shared interests in advancing national development and international cooperation: His legacy in journalism and public life remains an enduring part of our national story.”

Cole’s impact was, of course, not limited to his practical and galvanising contributions to the transformation of journalism and media publishing in the country. He was also a respected historian and political scholar who published important books on academic history, socio-political structures, and public policy, including the much-quoted Modern and Traditional Elites in the Politics of Lagos (1975). In the public space, he served as Nigeria’s Ambassador to Brazil and Argentina; Special Adviser on International Relations to President Olusegun Obasanjo (1999–2007) and a key member of the ‘Think Tank’ under the military administration before transitioning to media management.

Dr Patrick Dele Cole’s was indeed a full and remarkable life of multiple impact that should serve as an inspiration to present and future generations.

World.title: FIFA Approves  Normalisation Committee to Run Nigeria football
World.content:
*CAF, FIFA to appoint the committee members to run NFF until May 31 next year

Duro Ikhazuagbe

Federation of International Football Association (FIFA), has approved the appointments of a Normalisation Committee to run the affairs of the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) until fresh elections are conducted into the executive committee of the federation.

The Bureau of the FIFA Council at its meeting in Zurich, Switzerland penultimate Thursday, approved the appointment of a Normalisation Committee for the NFF whose leadership resigned enmass last August.

According to a letter signed by FIFA Secretary General, Mattias Grafström and addressed to the Ag. General Secretary of the NFF, Dr Emmanuel Ikpeme MON, “the normalisation committee shall consist of a suitable number of members, who will be appointed jointly by FIFA and CAF as soon as possible.”

The letter also informed that “the period during which the normalisation committee shall perform its functions shall expire as soon as it has fulfilled all of its tasks, but by no later than 31 May 2027.”

Specifically, the FIFA letter warned that nine of the members of the normalisation committee will be eligible for the positions to be filled during the upcoming NFF elections under any circumstances.

In the meantime, the Secretariat of the NFF will continue with the day-to-day running of the organisation and administration of the country’s football pending the appointment of the Normalisation Committee.

The approval of a Normalisation Committee for the NFF is a major shift towards resolving the crisis that engulfed Nigerian football last August when President Ibrahim Gusau, General Secretary, Mohammed Sanusi and the other 11 members of the board had to resign en-mass.

The resignation of the board followed spate of failures witnessed by Nigeria’s national teams across the spectrum of the game. The inabilities of the Super Falcons to qualify for next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil was the immediate call for the resignation of the Gusau-led board. Super Eagles had earlier missed out of the 2026 World Cup hosted by USA, Canada and Mexico. The team also missed the 2022 edition hosted by Qatar.

However, even with the approval of a Normalisation Committee, Nigeria’s football stakeholders are now awaiting those to be appointed to run the federation until May 31, 2027 when fresh elections must have be held for new gladiators in the corridors of football power.

World.title: Suliman Carrim hit with fresh charges in vehicle theft case
World.content:
Businessman Suliman Carrim faces fresh criminal charges linked to the alleged attempted theft of two vehicles and the use of fraudulent bank documents. His case returns to court on 30 October 2026. Image: X

North West businessman Suliman Carrim faces fresh criminal charges linked to the alleged attempted theft of two vehicles belonging to Absa.

Carrim appeared in the Musina Magistrate’s Court in Limpopo on Thursday, 22 October, in connection with allegations involving fraudulent bank documents and an attempt to move vehicles across the border.

The case was postponed to 30 October for a bail application.



The latest development adds to Carrim’s legal troubles as he awaits a separate bail ruling over his alleged failure to appear before the Madlanga Commission.

CARRIM LINKED TO ALLEGED VEHICLE THEFT

According to police, the latest charges stem from an incident at the Beitbridge border post on 22 July 2026.

Officers intercepted two vehicles that were allegedly being transported from Mahikeng in the North West to Malawi.

Police spokesperson Brigadier Athlenda Mathe said investigators established that arrangements had allegedly been made to obtain bank authorisation documents for the vehicles to leave South Africa.

However, the required authorisation was allegedly not provided.

Investigators believe fraudulent bank documents were subsequently arranged to facilitate the vehicles’ movement across the border.



The vehicles were still under finance and were returned to the bank.

Two suspects were initially arrested in connection with the incident.

The Commission’s Recommendations Task Team added Carrim as an accused in the two cases on Wednesday, 21 October.

The National Prosecuting Authority alleges that Carrim acted with others in an attempt to remove the vehicles from South Africa using fraudulent documentation.

The allegations remain before the courts.

MADLANGA COMMISSION CASE CONTINUES

Carrim’s latest court appearance follows his arrest at OR Tambo International Airport earlier this month.

He was arrested while preparing to travel abroad after allegedly failing to return to the Madlanga Commission despite being directed to appear.

He appeared in the Pretoria Magistrate’s Court, where the State opposed his release on bail.

Prosecutors argued that he posed a flight risk.

Carrim’s legal representatives disputed this and maintained that he intended to return to South Africa.

The Pretoria court postponed its bail ruling to 28 October.

Carrim remains in custody and is expected back in the Musina Magistrate’s Court on 30 October in connection with the vehicle case.

World.title: Bank account costs: How South Africa compares with Botswana
World.content:
Bank customers in South Africa and Botswana face different charges for maintaining transactional accounts, with monthly fees and everyday transaction costs varying between banks.

The differences highlight why consumers need to consider more than just the advertised monthly fee when choosing where to bank.

How much do South African Bank customers pay?

According to its official 2026 pricing guide, Capitec charges customers R7.50 per month to maintain its main account. The fees took effect on 1 March 2026.



The bank also charges R2 for payments to other South African banks, R1 for payments to other Capitec customers and R3 for debit orders.

Customers who withdraw cash at another bank’s ATM pay R10 for every R1 000 withdrawn, according to Capitec’s published tariffs.

Meanwhile, First National Bank (FNB) offers an Easy Zero account with no monthly account fee. However, customers may still incur charges when conducting transactions.

FNB publishes separate pricing guides for its various accounts, meaning customers need to check the charges applicable to their chosen product.

What do Botswana bank customers pay?

In Botswana, Botswana Savings Bank (BSB) lists a monthly maintenance fee of P60 for its transactional account.

The account is designed for working people, young customers, pensioners and self-employed individuals. According to the bank’s official website, customers can deposit and withdraw money at BSB branches and ATMs.



Opening the account costs P100, while its listed features include free monthly statements, transaction notifications and transfers between BSB accounts.

BSB also offers an ordinary savings account with a lower monthly maintenance fee of P12. However, this is a different product, with withdrawal conditions that distinguish it from a standard transactional account.

The bank lists a P3.30 fee for withdrawals at its ATMs and charges P25 for subsequent over-the-counter withdrawals after the first free withdrawal.

Why the fees matter

The published tariffs show that banking costs depend on the account customers choose and how frequently they transact.

In South Africa, Capitec’s R7.50 monthly fee provides a clear baseline, while FNB’s Easy Zero account demonstrates that some products have no monthly maintenance charge.

In Botswana, BSB’s P60 transactional account fee is higher than its P12 ordinary savings account fee, but the two products offer different facilities and conditions.

Customers comparing banking costs across the two countries should therefore consider monthly maintenance, ATM withdrawals, electronic payments and other charges together.

The figures are based on the banks’ published tariffs and should be checked against the latest pricing guides before opening an account.
