World.title: Gonet Academy Taps Youth Minister Kruah to Challenge Graduates on Skills, Innovation and Service
World.content:
Her “Paradigm Shift” agenda offers a framework for connecting professional training with entrepreneurship, employment and national development.

Youth and Sports Minister Atty. Cornelia Wonkerleh Kruah

Gonet Academy has named Youth and Sports Minister Atty. Cornelia Wonkerleh Kruah as keynote speaker for its Cohort 15 graduation, bringing the government’s youth empowerment agenda into an event focused on professional development, leadership and practical skills.



The ceremony is scheduled for Saturday, October 31, 2026, at 10 a.m. at Harvest Intercontinental Cathedral in Congo Town, Monrovia.

Kruah’s selection comes as Liberia continues to confront the challenge of translating its youthful population into a productive workforce through skills development, entrepreneurship and employment opportunities.

The upcoming occasion, for Gonet Academy, reinforces a central principle of professional training that emphasizes that education must extend beyond certificates to equip graduates with the competence, discipline and leadership capacity to contribute meaningfully to their workplaces and communities.

The minister’s “Paradigm Shift” approach to youth development similarly emphasizes moving beyond short-term interventions toward programs that provide practical support, build capacity and deliver measurable results.

The significance of her appearance, however, will ultimately depend on the substance of her message and whether the occasion encourages stronger connections between training institutions, government and employment opportunities.

Gonet Academy Chief Empowerment Officer (CEO), Mohamed Kerkulah, welcomed Minister Kruah’s acceptance to serve as keynote speaker.

Kerkulah said the minister’s acceptance underscores the importance of recognizing efforts to develop professional skills and build the capacity of young Liberians.

“We are deeply honored and grateful to Minister Cornelia Kruah, for graciously accepting our invitation,” he said, adding that the Academy looks forward to welcoming the minister and benefiting from her perspectives on “youth empowerment, leadership, innovation, and national development.”

Minister Kruah has emphasized the need to strengthen youth development through institutional reform, technical and vocational education, entrepreneurship, sports and the creative economy. She has also outlined plans for youth resource centers across the 15 counties and greater use of data to inform policy and programming.

Her approach recognizes that providing assistance is only the first step; beneficiaries also need the skills, guidance and follow-up required to turn opportunities into lasting progress.

At the launch of a small-scale grant initiative for market vendors under the National Youth Pathway Program, Kruah said the government wanted to move beyond providing grants without sustained follow-up.

“We want to shift the paradigm that government grants are simply given and forgotten,” she said.

The initiative announced plans to support 2,000 vendors across all 15 counties, with training in financial literacy, customer service, business management and record-keeping.

The government’s National Cadet Program has also expanded, with reported participation increasing from 235 cadets in the first cohort to 1,100 in the second. Its coverage grew from eight counties to all 15, while the service period increased from three to six months.

These initiatives reflect an emphasis on linking youth interventions with practical experience, accountability and broader access to opportunities. Their long-term impact will depend on implementation, sustained support and evidence of improved outcomes for participants.

Gonet Academy’s professional development model complements this agenda by seeking to equip learners with industry-relevant skills, workplace competence and leadership abilities.

The transition from training to employment or entrepreneurship, however, often requires more than technical knowledge. Graduates may also need mentorship, professional networks, workplace exposure and access to financing or business support.

Training institutions can help prepare young people for these demands, while government agencies and private-sector employers can help create pathways through internships, recruitment, enterprise development and other opportunities.

Neither side can achieve this alone. Training providers must remain responsive to workplace needs, while public policy must support an environment in which acquired skills can translate into productive work and economic participation.

Kruah’s keynote therefore offers an opportunity to connect the achievements of Gonet Academy’s graduating professionals with the wider national conversation about employment, entrepreneurship and youth development.

The country’s youth challenge is not simply demographic; it is also about whether young people can access the education, skills and institutional support needed to participate meaningfully in the economy.

The 2022 Liberia Population and Housing Census thematic report on children, adolescents and youth highlights the importance of understanding young people’s circumstances and development needs. Persistent concerns about unemployment, underemployment and vulnerable work further underscore the need to connect education with practical opportunities.

Kerkulah emphasized that academy’s graduation ceremonies represent more than the awarding of certificates and diplomas, noting that each graduating cohort reflects months of commitment, sacrifice, learning and personal growth.

“Every graduation at Gonet Academy represents more than the awarding of professional certificates and diplomas. It represents months of dedication, sacrifice, learning, and personal transformation,” he said.

He described October 31 as an opportunity to celebrate Cohort 15’s accomplishments while reminding graduates that the real value of education lies in how they apply their knowledge and skills beyond the classroom.

“For Cohort 15, October 31 will be a celebration of professional achievement and a reminder that the true value of education lies not merely in the qualifications we acquire, but in how effectively we apply our knowledge and skills to solve problems, create opportunities, and contribute to society,” Kerkulah stated.

His remarks reflect the Academy’s emphasis on practical learning and the application of professional competencies to workplace challenges, entrepreneurship and community development.

The CEO also stressed that the country’s development depends on deliberate investment in its people, particularly its young population.

“Liberia’s greatest resource is its people, particularly its young population. However, potential alone does not guarantee progress,” Kerkula said.

He called for sustained investment in relevant skills, mentorship, practical experience and entrepreneurship to help young people become productive contributors to the economy.

The next test, for Cohort 15 graduates, will be how effectively they apply their training in workplaces, businesses, public institutions and their communities.

Kruah’s public agenda could reinforce that responsibility by challenging graduates to remain adaptable, demonstrate integrity, solve practical problems and use their professional capabilities to create value for others.

Her selection should not, by itself, be interpreted as evidence of a formal partnership between Gonet Academy and the Ministry of Youth and Sports. Any such collaboration would require deliberate engagement, defined priorities and measurable commitments.

Nevertheless, the graduation provides a platform for exploring how professional training can complement national youth development efforts.

The challenge, for Gonet Academy, is to ensure its graduates translate their qualifications into professional growth and meaningful contributions to society. For the government, the task is to turn youth empowerment priorities into accessible programs and demonstrable results.

As Cohort 15 prepares to graduate on October 31, the shared message is clear that certificates are milestones, but the greater measure of success lies in the skills graduates apply, the opportunities they create and the contributions they make to Liberia’s development.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court Hears Kolubah’s Appeal Against Expulsion Today; Five Other Cases on Docket
World.content:
Monrovia – The full bench of the Supreme Court of Liberia is scheduled to hear arguments today, Thursday, October 22, 2026, in former Montserrado County District #10 Representative Yekeh Y. Kolubah’s appeal against his expulsion from the House of Representatives. The case is one of six on the Court’s 5th Day’s Session assignment for the October Term.

Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay, Sr. and Associate Justices Jamesetta H. Wolokolie, Yussif D. Kaba, Ceaineh D. Clinton Johnson and Boakai N. Kanneh were listed to sit for the 11:00 a.m. session. The assignment was signed by the Clerk of the Supreme Court, Cllr. Sam Mamulu.

Kolubah vs. the House



Kolubah’s case, listed as an appeal from a ruling on a Bill of Information, names the House of Representatives, Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, Deputy Speaker Thomas Fallah, the Chief Clerk and the Sergeant-at-Arms as appellees.

The dispute dates to April. The expulsion process began on April 9, 2026, when Kolubah was accused of gross misconduct, violating his oath of office, repeatedly breaching House rules and damaging the Legislature’s reputation. The House said he violated its rules and undermined Liberia’s national interest through comments on the Liberia-Guinea border dispute.

Justice Kaba, then presiding in Chambers, granted Kolubah’s petition for a writ of prohibition on April 16, 2026, summoning the House leadership to a conference on April 20 and ordering a stay of all further proceedings. The House went ahead anyway. The expulsion was supported by 49 lawmakers who signed a resolution from the Committee on Rules, Order and Administration, but the House Clerk’s Office said it had not received any Supreme Court communication to stop the proceedings.

On May 20, Justice Kaba ruled against Kolubah. He held that the House was not properly served with the writ and stay order, noting that under House procedure only the Sergeant-at-Arms is authorized to accept court documents, and that because the House was not lawfully served it could not be held in contempt. Court records showed the Supreme Court’s Marshal had served the papers on a receptionist and a computer operator in the offices of the Speaker and the Chief Clerk. Kolubah’s lawyer, Cllr. Jonathan Massaquoi, said they had appealed to the full bench.

It is not Kolubah’s first clash with his colleagues in court. In 2021, he twice took the House to the Supreme Court over suspensions, and then-Justice Joseph Nagbe reversed one of those suspensions.

Srimex vs. Eco Fuel

Also on the docket is a Bill of Information filed by Srimex Oil and Gas Company, through its Chairman Musa Hassan Bility and CEO Wadei H. Powell, against Civil Law Court Judge Nelson B. Chineh, Eco Fuel Trading of Geneva, Switzerland, and Srimex Eco Fuel FZE, Inc.

The two companies have fought in court for years. In November 2018, Srimex sued the National Port Authority, LPRC and Eco Fuel at the Civil Law Court seeking a declaratory judgment, and obtained an injunction barring Eco Fuel from the Petroleum Storage Terminal. Eco Fuel claimed it invested about US$25 million to build the terminal, which it accused Srimex of hijacking, and argued Srimex had transferred its NPA lease to Eco Fuel through a novation agreement. Eco Fuel separately filed a debt action against Srimex at the Commercial Court in 2018 over unpaid oil products.

Land and labor cases

The Intestate Estate of Daniel Webster Urey, through administrators Edwin M. Urey and Evan Urey, has filed a Bill of Information against the Intestate Estate of Karboyah of Tartee Town, Careysburg District. The Supreme Court earlier upheld a trial court ruling in favor of the Karboyah Estate, relying on a survey showing the estate’s deed predates the Ureys’ and that the Urey claim of 1,337.4 acres far exceeded what their deeds specified.

Edwin Urey, the Careysburg City Mayor, has accused the courts of bias and said the land has belonged to his family for over a century.

ABC Children’s Aid Liberia, Inc. returns to court in a Bill of Information and Appeal in an ejectment action against Augustine Moore, Aruna Bangura, James F. Kolangbanyan and others of Gbengbah’s Town on the RIA Highway. The Court previously ordered the eviction of more than 100 occupants who built about 70 homes on the organization’s 72.76 acres, purchased in 2005 and 2006 from the administrators of the town.

In a labor matter, Ministry of Labor Hearing Officer H. Nyeswa Davis, Sr. and Kou Dolo are seeking to dismiss an appeal by the management of RLJ Kendeja Resort and Villas, through Managing Director Raderick John Peck. The hotel has previously faced accusations of bad labor practices, with more than 300 staff made redundant after management moved from an American to a Ghanaian team.

The sixth case is a Bill of Information by Samuel B. Borley against Circuit Judge J. Boima Kontoe and the family of the late David C. Wilson, represented by Rachael Nyemah.

World.title: Liberians in Rwanda Back Push for Direct Kigali–Monrovia Flights
World.content:
LIBCOR leaders meet travel agency, RwandAir representatives

KIGALI, Rwanda – Leaders of the Liberian Community in Rwanda (LIBCOR) have pledged to support an initiative to establish a direct air link between Kigali and Monrovia. They gave the pledge after meeting a Liberian travel agency working on the effort with Rwanda’s national carrier, RwandAir.

The LIBCOR delegation met Tuesday evening with Gbomai Bestman, chief executive officer of Easy Continental Travel Agency, and two senior members of her team. Bestman is in Rwanda on a working visit.



According to a statement from LIBCOR, the talks focused on the agency’s ongoing initiative with RwandAir, its objectives, and what it could mean for Liberians living in Rwanda.

Seleke Kromah, LIBCOR’s Vice Chairman for Administration, led the delegation. Other members of the community’s National Administrative Council attended, including the Vice Chairman for International Affairs, the Financial Secretary and the Treasurer.

The statement said the council took part on the instructions of LIBCOR Chairman James Edgar Denia. Members discussed how the community’s leadership could support the initiative.

Speaking for the delegation, Kromah thanked Bestman for what he called her continued cooperation, partnership and support for Liberians in Rwanda. He said LIBCOR would work with her team to explain the initiative’s goals and benefits to community members.

LIBCOR said it would share details of a planned engagement with the wider Liberian community in Rwanda beginning Thursday.

“LIBCOR remains committed to building meaningful partnerships that promote connectivity, strengthen relationships, and create opportunities for Liberians in Rwanda and back home,” the statement said.

The statement did not say when direct flights might begin, what routes or schedules are being considered, or what role RwandAir has formally committed to.

World.title: Liberia: Final Arguments Set in Peter Bon Jallah Case
World.content:
After months of contested proceedings, prosecution and defense are expected to present their closing arguments as Criminal Court ‘E’ prepares to conclude the trial phase.

By Victoria G. Wesseh

MONROVIA — Criminal Court “E” is scheduled to hear final arguments on Thursday, October 22, in the high-profile case involving Peter Bon Jallah, who is facing multiple felony charges, including gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping.



The case has reached a critical stage following months of evidentiary proceedings in which the prosecution and defense presented witnesses and sought to establish their respective positions.

The closing arguments will give both sides an opportunity to summarize the evidence, address disputed facts and advance their legal interpretations before the court determines the next steps toward a verdict.

Prosecution and Defense Rest Cases

According to court records, the trial has been vigorously contested, with both sides presenting witnesses in support of their respective cases.

The Government of Liberia, represented by prosecutors from the Ministry of Justice, presented 13 general witnesses and six rebuttal witnesses before resting its case.

The defense, representing Jallah, called eight general witnesses and three subpoenaed witnesses to challenge the prosecution’s allegations and advance its position.

The testimony presented by both sides is expected to feature prominently in their closing arguments as they seek to persuade the court on the strength of the evidence and the applicable law.

Trial Reaches Critical Stage

The case is being heard under Liberia’s legal framework governing rape and other serious criminal offenses. The charges against Jallah include gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping, each of which carries significant legal consequences if established in accordance with the law.

The final arguments are an important stage of the proceedings, allowing prosecutors to explain why they believe the evidence supports a conviction and enabling the defense to challenge the prosecution’s case.

Presiding Judge Wesseh A. Wesseh will be responsible for considering the evidence and legal arguments presented before the court.

The outcome will depend on the evidence admitted during the trial and the court’s application of the relevant legal standards.

Public Scrutiny and the Fight Against Sexual Violence

The proceedings come amid continued public concern over sexual and gender-based violence in Liberia and calls from civil society organizations and women’s rights advocates for accountability in cases involving sexual offenses.

The administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has pledged to uphold the rule of law and strengthen protections for vulnerable people, including minors.

The handling of high-profile cases such as the one involving Jallah is likely to draw continued public attention to the justice system’s response to allegations of sexual violence and the importance of ensuring that criminal proceedings are conducted fairly and without undue delay.

As the court prepares to hear the final arguments, the prosecution and defense will have the opportunity to make their closing submissions before the matter advances toward a determination.

The defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court to Hear Final Appeal in Dennis Estate’s 200-Acre Property Case
World.content:
After earlier rulings affirmed the estate’s ownership, the Supreme Court is set to review a fresh appeal challenging lower court judgments over land in Paynesville’s 72nd Community, with the timeliness of the appeal emerging as a key issue.

By Victoria G. Wesseh

MONROVIA — The Supreme Court of Liberia is set to hear arguments in a decades-long dispute over approximately 200 acres of land in Paynesville’s 72nd Community, as it considers an appeal challenging judgments affirming ownership by the Estate of the late Wilmot F. Dennis.



The appeal was filed by Mark Dennis, also known as Mack Dennis, and Henry Dennis, who are challenging lower court rulings in favor of Madam Estella Dennis-Turay, administratrix of her late father’s intestate estate.

The dispute dates back to 1963 and has passed through multiple judicial proceedings, including earlier appeals to the Supreme Court. The latest proceedings could determine whether the challenged lower court judgments will stand, although the outcome remains in the hands of the justices.

A Dispute Dating to 1963

According to court records, the dispute began in 1963 when four children of Wilmot F. Dennis—Estella Dennis-Turay, Sam Ford Dennis, Mabel Dennis Mann and Jeannette Dennis-Pratt—filed an action before the Sixth Judicial Circuit seeking to cancel deeds they alleged had been improperly obtained by distant relatives to properties belonging to their father, who died before 1954.

After 16 years of litigation, the Civil Law Court ruled in 1979 in favor of the siblings, voiding the disputed deeds and ordering the approximately 200-acre property restored to them.

Subsequent disputes involving boundaries and alleged encroachment by adjoining landowners led to two separate appeals before the Supreme Court.

In 1988 and 1989, the Supreme Court affirmed the 1979 judgment, according to the case history presented in the court records.

Those rulings form a central part of the estate’s position in the latest proceedings.

Dispute Resurfaces After Civil War

The dispute resurfaced during the period surrounding Liberia’s civil conflicts, when Dennis-Turay was reportedly outside the country.

According to subsequent court findings, the defendants began asserting ownership claims over the property during her absence.

On August 30, 2005, then-Civil Law Court Judge Emery Paye issued a writ of possession placing the defendants in possession of the land. The estate later challenged the writ, arguing that it had been issued without notice to the parties previously adjudged to be the rightful owners.

In a ruling dated August 26, 2025, Judge George W. Smith of the Civil Law Court revisited the matter. The decision was subsequently reaffirmed by then-presiding Judge Boima Kontoe on February 25, 2026.

According to the rulings described in the court records, the lower court found that the defendants had misrepresented their status in the proceedings that led to the 2005 writ.

The court characterized their conduct as involving alleged deception, fraud, perjury and contempt, and described them as impostors in relation to the ownership claims.

Those findings form part of the judicial history now before the Supreme Court.

Estate Relies on Probate and Earlier Judgments

Probate records cited by the estate indicate that between 2005 and 2012, Dennis-Turay petitioned the Probate Court to administer her late father’s estate.

The records reportedly included original deeds and certified copies of the 1979 Civil Law Court judgment and the Supreme Court’s 1988 and 1989 decisions.

In 2012, Dennis-Turay was reportedly deeded the property as the sole surviving heir. The deed was subsequently probated and registered.

The estate is relying on these records, together with the earlier judgments, to support its position that ownership of the property has already been judicially determined.

The defendants’ latest appeal has nevertheless brought the matter back before the country’s highest court.

Timeliness of Appeal Becomes a Key Issue

Following Judge Kontoe’s February 25, 2026 ruling, the defendants filed a Bill of Exceptions on March 23, 2026, challenging the judgment.

The estate contends that the filing was made outside the statutory deadline and has asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the appeal on procedural grounds.

According to the estate’s filing, the Bill of Exceptions was submitted 28 days after the judgment, rather than within the 10-day period it says the law requires.

On March 31, 2026, the estate filed a motion seeking dismissal of the appeal for untimely filing.

The case record has since been transmitted to the Supreme Court for consideration.

The justices will have to determine the procedural issues raised by the parties and consider any substantive questions properly before them. Whether the appeal can proceed will depend on the court’s assessment of the applicable legal requirements and the arguments presented.

Earlier Supreme Court Rulings at the Center of the Case

The estate’s position rests substantially on the Supreme Court’s 1988 and 1989 decisions affirming the 1979 judgment.

The doctrines of res judicata and stare decisis may be relevant to the dispute. Res judicata generally concerns the finality of matters already adjudicated between parties, while stare decisis addresses the authority of judicial precedents.

However, the application of these doctrines depends on the specific facts, parties, issues and procedural circumstances before the court.

The Supreme Court’s earlier decisions and the subsequent probate proceedings are therefore likely to feature prominently in the estate’s arguments as it seeks to preserve the lower court judgments.

The defendants’ appeal, meanwhile, will give the justices an opportunity to consider the challenges raised against the latest ruling.

For Dennis-Turay and the estate, a dismissal of the appeal or a decision affirming the lower court judgment would reinforce the existing rulings in their favor.

After more than six decades of litigation, the Supreme Court’s determination could mark a significant development in the long-running dispute over the 200-acre property in Paynesville’s 72nd Community.

The final outcome, however, will depend on the court’s ruling.

World.title: Liberia’s Billion-Dollar Budget: 0.58% for the Capital’s Public Schools
World.content:
Monrovia — Thousands of students in school uniforms marched on Liberia’s legislature on Tuesday, chanting “We want to learn too.” They were protesting months of disruption in the public schools of the capital, Monrovia, where unpaid teachers have repeatedly walked out of classrooms.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The students’ anger has a paper trail. Liberia’s own 2026 budget documents show that the Monrovia Consolidated School System (MCSS), which runs the city’s public schools, receives US$7.23 million. That is 0.58 percent of a national budget the government celebrates as the largest in the country’s history.



The same documents show that schools in the system get US$65,000 a year for educational materials — less than they get for stationery. They also show that three-quarters of the money recorded as the system’s capital spending last year was booked against an airport, a Finance Ministry headquarters and electoral reform.

A billion-dollar milestone

Liberia, a West African nation of about 5.2 million people, is still rebuilding from 14 years of civil war that ended in 2003. Its national budget crossed US$1 billion for the first time this year. Lawmakers approved US$1.25 billion for 2026, up 41.9 percent from the year before, according to an analysis by the budget-monitoring group BudgIT.

President Joseph Boakai’s development plan, known as the ARREST Agenda, names six priorities. The “E” stands for education. The “A” stands for agriculture, which receives about 1.19 percent of the budget even though the Agriculture Ministry’s own target is 10 percent.

The Monrovia Consolidated School System was created by law in 1964 to run public schools in the capital and surrounding communities. Families who cannot afford private fees depend on it. It is where the gap between budget promises and classroom reality is easiest to see.

“Our patience must not be mistaken for weakness”

Tuesday’s march, organized by the MCSS Students Union, lasted more than two hours. It followed a 24-hour ultimatum that expired the same day. Students gathered between the University of Liberia and the Capitol, the seat of the legislature, and handed lawmakers a petition with four demands.

They want the government to carry out a March 27 agreement with the school system on teachers’ pay and status. They want an investigation into alleged intimidation of student leaders. They want the dismissal of an assistant superintendent, Emmanuel Kyne Robertson, whom they accuse of disrupting classes and threatening students. And they want a bigger school budget and more transparency in how it is spent. The allegations have not been independently verified.

“Our patience must not be mistaken for weakness,” the union wrote, “and our commitment to peace must not be used to justify continued inaction while students’ education remains at risk.”

The House of Representatives read the petition in plenary and gave its education and petitions committees one week to report back.

Hours after the march, the government said it would add the remaining 201 volunteer MCSS teachers to the national payroll from October. That brings the number of verified MCSS volunteers absorbed to 409. Back pay is promised one week after October salaries. Teachers’ demands for higher pay were deferred to a government-wide salary reform, for which no date was given.

Where the money goes instead

Education receives US$136.3 million in 2026, or 10.9 percent of the budget. Security and rule of law receive US$154.9 million, about US$18.6 million more than education. Debt service takes US$230 million, 1.7 times the entire education sector.

Capital spending tells a similar story. Of the US$289.7 million set aside for investment projects, education gets 5.3 percent. Roads and energy together take about 61 percent.

Then there is the legislature. The draft budget gave lawmakers US$51.7 million, up from US$41.3 million in 2024. Their travel, goods and services line alone rose to US$14.6 million.

Put differently: the legislature’s running costs for travel and supplies are 38 times what the capital’s public schools get to run their classrooms for a year.

Stationery over science

The school system’s own pages in the 2026 budget book show how little reaches the classroom.

Salaries take 67 percent of the MCSS budget. Capital projects take 28 percent. Everything needed to actually run schools — books, chalk, cleaning, repairs, fuel — gets 5.3 percent, or US$380,000 for a whole year.

Within that sliver:

• Educational materials: US$65,000, down 35 percent from US$100,000 in 2025. That is less than the US$70,000 budgeted for stationery.

• Laboratory supplies: US$5,000 for every science lab in the system, cut from US$25,000.

• Generator fuel: US$54,500, up from US$2,000 — a 27-fold increase. It now nearly equals the entire budget for learning materials.

• ⁠

The outlook gets worse, not better. The government’s own projections cut the system’s operating budget by another 44 percent in 2027, to US$212,112. Educational materials would fall to US$36,282.

The budget also files every dollar of the school system under a single program: “Administration and Management.” There is no separate line for teaching.

The system’s payroll of US$4.85 million covers 1,088 staff, an average of about US$372 a month. That figure includes non-teaching staff. The budget keeps that headcount frozen through 2028, even as hundreds of volunteer teachers are added to the payroll.

An airport, a ministry and an election law

The most striking entry is on page 294 of the budget book. It lists the school system’s estimated capital spending for 2025 at US$388,691.

Only US$94,320 of that — 24 percent — is labeled as school renovation. The remaining US$294,371 is recorded under projects with no apparent link to schools: electoral legal reform (US$117,865), support for small and medium enterprises (US$84,306), a new Finance Ministry headquarters (US$82,135) and an upgrade of Robert International Airport (US$10,065).

The budget book contradicts itself. Elsewhere it records the system’s 2025 capital spending as US$320,150, all on furniture and fixtures, and none under the investment plan at all.

The entries may reflect a coding error rather than diverted money. But either way, the official record of what Liberia spent on its capital’s schools cannot be trusted as published.

For 2026, the budget promises US$2 million for renovating and furnishing MCSS schools. The system’s own list of 2025 achievements, however, claims only that it completed the procurement process to renovate four campuses — not the renovations themselves.

A school system running on volunteers

In December, Finance Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan returned to his old school in Monrovia and announced a 60 percent increase for the capital’s schools, including a US$2 million fund to fix them. On paper, the promise holds: the MCSS budget rose from US$4.52 million to US$7.23 million. Take out the US$2 million capital line, much of it not yet delivered, and the increase is about 16 percent.

The teacher shortage the students are protesting is national. The Education Ministry says Liberia relies on 6,198 volunteer teachers who work without government salaries. In October, the ministry said it had removed more than 1,000 teachers who had abandoned their classrooms from the payroll. Lawmakers have also pressed officials over the U.S.-dollar portion of teachers’ salaries, unpaid since October 2025.

A mid-year supplementary budget, approved in May, added US$7.25 million for education. About 73 percent of it goes to closing payroll gaps and absorbing volunteers — paying for the past rather than building classrooms. MCSS received US$514,510. That includes US$200,000 for its volunteer teachers, roughly US$995 for each of the 201 now being added.

That money is fragile. About nine of every ten dollars in the supplementary package came from the World Bank, not Liberian revenue. BudgIT warned that moving volunteers onto the payroll creates permanent salary costs a one-off top-up cannot sustain. Meanwhile, the government projects total spending will fall to US$1.02 billion in 2027.

The largest share of that mid-year package — 27.8 percent — went not to schools or clinics but to public administration. It included an ambassador’s residence lease in Accra and Independence Day celebrations.

Who lives on the budget

The students did not cite budget codes on Tuesday. But their demands — pay the teachers, fix the classrooms, show where the money goes — line up closely with what the government’s own figures reveal.

The pattern echoes agriculture. A government that puts farming first in its slogan gives it about 1 percent of the budget. A government that puts education among its pillars gives the capital’s public schools less than 1 percent, and less for learning materials than for stationery.

The House committees have until next Tuesday to report on the students’ petition. The salary reform teachers were promised has no start date. The 2027 budget, now being prepared, is projected to be smaller.

For the students who marched, the question is simpler than any budget table. When a country spends US$1.25 billion in a year, why are they still waiting for a teacher to show up?

World.title: Mining companies urged to translate mineral wealth into tangible benefits
World.content:
Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Permanent Secretary, Hapenga Kabeta, has urged mining companies in the country to ensure that mineral wealth translates into tangible and lasting benefits for Zambians.

Dr Kabeta says increased mineral production must be accompanied by local value addition, skills development, technology transfer and the growth of local enterprises.

He has advised that mining activities should also protect the environment and improve the welfare of citizens, noting that production targets would be meaningless if they resulted in environmental destruction and left communities without benefits.

The Permanent Secretary was speaking in Lusaka last evening when he officiated at the cultural night gala night held on the sidelines of the 2026 Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka.

He said the Insaka also provides an opportunity for face-to-face engagements that can strengthen professional relationships, generate ideas and facilitate business deals.

Dr Kabeta encouraged participants to establish meaningful partnerships, share experiences and develop strategies that would help unlock Zambia’s mineral potential for the benefit of the people.

He said Zambia needs a productive, innovative, inclusive and responsible mining industry that attracts investment, creates decent jobs, supports local businesses and contributes to long-term economic transformation.

Dr Kabeta noted that the mining sector has continued to attract significant investments in various parts of the country, including the Copperbelt and North-Western Provinces which are contributing to national economic development.

Meanwhile, Dr Kabeta presented awards to organisations recognised for their participation and contribution to the 2026 Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka.

Among the recipients were ZESCO, Konkola Copper Mines, First Quantum Minerals, Anglo American Corporation, Zanaco and Indo-Zambia Bank.

Passing a vote of thanks, Buterla Investment Limited Chief Executive Officer, Happy Mbulo, said the Grow Zambia Agenda can be achieved if mining firms apply themselves.

Mr Mbulo implored the private sector to work closely with government to fully realise their potential in enhancing the production of goods and services associated with the value chain system.

World.title: Mwense man jailed 12 months for theft
World.content:
The Mwense Magistrates court has sentenced a 34-year-old man of Mulundu village to 12 months concurrent imprisonment with hard labour for two counts of theft contrary to section 272 of the penal code Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia.

This is in a matter in which Simon Kunda masquerading as a traditional healer operating as Dr Mwiko is alleged to have obtained money amounting to K 1,500 belonging to Jacob Mwape and Ireen Chisha respectively.

This is after he claimed he would heal their sicknesses.

In the first count, Kunda is said to have Charged Mwape K 1000 on the pretext that he would give him treatment for his ailing feet.

In count two the now convict is alleged to have charged Chisha a K 500 as payment to treat her stomach pains.

The two complainants are said to have paid the money in full respectively after Kunda refused the 50 percent down payment claiming that the spirits being consulted demanded full payments before treatment could be given.

Testifying before Magistrate Fred Mwangala, the two complainants said that Kunda however vanished without offering the required services and was only arrested a few months after he was spotted in public.

In mitigation, Kunda prayed for the court’s leniency saying he was a poor man.

“Am a poor man so I ask the court to forgive me otherwise I have nothing more to say,” Kunda begged.

In sentencing, Magistrate Mwangala noted that the victims from whom the now convict had stolen the money were also not rich.

Magistrate Mwangala ruled that Kunda should be given a custodial sentence at a correctional facility for reformation.

Magistrate Mwangala handed Kunda eight months imprisonment on each count to run concurrently.

However, Magistrate Mwangala immediately increased the sentence to 12 months imprisonment after the convict warned the complainants as he stood down from the dock.

World.title: Lufuma calls on youths to engage in productive activities
World.content:
Kabompo East Member of Parliament (MP) Ambrose Lufuma has called on young people to engage in productive activities that will contribute to the attainment of the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Lufuma says youths should be active participants in national development by becoming producers, innovators, entrepreneurs and job creators rather than relying on formal employment.

Contributing to the Motion of Thanks on the President’s address during the official opening of the First Session of the 14th National Assembly, Mr Lufuma, a former Defence Minister, also called for the upgrading of feeder roads leading to productive areas in Kabompo to gravel standard.

He said the government will continue creating opportunities for young people to acquire practical skills, establish businesses and participate in productive sectors such as agriculture and construction.

In his median speech to the House, the former minister of defense cited the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) grants, loans, empowerment programmes and National Service training as important interventions that can help empower young people.

Mr Lufuma stated that agriculture remains the mainstay of the constituency’s economy, with an estimated 95 percent of the population engaged in farming and related activities.

The MP called for improved access to farming inputs, extension services, appropriate technologies, irrigation, storage facilities, satellite depots and reliable markets to enhance agricultural production and food security.

Mr Lufuma has further urged the government to upgrade township roads in Kabompo to improve connectivity and facilitate economic activities.

Meanwhile, Nkombwa East MP Jairos Simbeye has called for a results-oriented public service, saying effective delivery of government programmes requires commitment, discipline and proper time management.

Mr Simbeye says public officers should focus on delivering tangible results rather than merely reporting for work.

He has commended the National Assembly for promoting professionalism and orderly service delivery, citing the conduct of security personnel and staff as an example of the standards that should be upheld across public institutions.

He stressed that all stakeholders must work together to support President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda and ensure the country achieves its development targets.

The MP cautioned against spreading misinformation about government programmes, particularly the school feeding programme, saying such conduct can discourage beneficiaries from accessing essential services.

On housing, Mr Simbeye encouraged residents to take advantage of land available in rural constituencies such as Nkombwa Constituency to support settlement and development, rather than concentrating on limited plots in urban areas.

He said efficient public service delivery at all levels is essential to restoring public confidence and ensuring that government policies and programmes benefit citizens.

He further called for unity of purpose among public officers and other stakeholders, saying collective efforts are necessary for Zambia to achieve its national development aspirations.

World.title: Government hails public support for energy diversification
World.content:
Government has commended the public for complementing its efforts to reduce the country’s dependence on hydropower.

Speaking during an interview with ZANIS, Ministry of Energy Principal Public Relations Officer, Bob Sianjalika, said the ministry has recorded an increase of Independence Power Producers and Independence Power Traders, which has increased the solar electricity generation.

Mr Sianjalika disclosed that the ministry is still receiving applications from individuals and groups showing interest in being in the Independence Power Producer chain, while others have power purchase agreements with ZESCO.

He further highlighted that the energy sector is now at 4,700 megawatts of collective generation across the country, giving them an assurance of meeting the target of 10,000 megawatts by 2026.

Mr Sianjalika added that about 2,600 megawatts of electricity is expected to be generated from thermal and solar plants alone, from the community.

He also disclosed that the government will be commissioning three solar power plants in three areas before the end of the year.

“We will be commissioning one in Shimabala generating 100 megawatts, one in Chipata generating 100 and the other one in Mumbwa with120 megawatts” he added.

Mr Sianjalika has described the current electricity generation state as comfortable if compared to the 2021 state.

He also revealed that the government intends to generate 1,000 megawatts of electricity before the end of the year 2026.

He has urged Zambians and foreign investors to invest in Zambia’s growing energy sector.

World.title: Police arrest suspect in Chasefu well poisoning
World.content:
Police have arrested a male suspect in the poisoning of a community well in Chasefu district, that affected about 38 people.

Yelemiya Zimba, 28, of Chalotwa Village of Chasefu District, was arrested immediately he was discharged from Lundazi District Hospital where he was being treated after ingesting the same suspected weed killer he had used to contaminate the community well.

Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer, Robertson Mweemba said that the suspect is expected to appear in court soon.

And all the 17 victims of the water poisoning have since been discharged.

Yelemiya Zimba, who stands charged with the offence of maliciously administering poisonous substances into drinking water with intent to harm innocent people, is one of the 17 victims that have been discharged.

“All the 17 victims who were admitted to Lundazi District Hospital have been treated and discharged today,” Mr Mweemba said.

He added that the other 21 people who also drank the same poisoned water within Chalotwa Village and complained of diarrhea and abdominal pains were treated at the local health facility within Chasefu district.

World.title: MoE staff urged to make cleanliness an everyday work culture
World.content:
Ministry of Education Permanent Secretary for Administration, Noriana Muneku, has implored the ministry staff to make cleanliness an everyday work culture rather than limiting it to national commemorations.

Ms Muneku says cleanliness should be embraced as a way of life rather than a temporary activity, stressing that everyone has a role to play in keeping the environment clean.

Speaking during a cleaning exercise at the Ministry’s premises in Lusaka today ahead of Zambia’s 62nd Independence Anniversary, Ms Muneku emphasised that the ministry’s surroundings should remain clean and presentable at all times.

Ms Muneku urged the administration department to take the lead in maintaining high standards of cleanliness, stressing that staff must demonstrate their commitment through consistent action.

And Lusaka Mayor, Chitambala Mwewa, called on members of the public to take responsibility for maintaining cleanliness around their premises and trading in designated market places.

Mr Mwewa expressed concern over the disposal of plastic waste into drainage systems, which he attributed to trading activities conducted in undesignated areas.

He said traders should operate from markets to promote proper waste management and ensure that business activities are conducted in appropriate environments.

Mr Mwewa further called for high standards of cleanliness along the road between the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Finance, saying the area should be spotless.

He urged the public to support efforts to relocate traders to designated markets, emphasising that the initiative represents a permanent change in the way trading and environmental cleanliness are managed.

World.title: Govt. recommits to reforming Zambia’s pension system
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its commitment to reforming Zambia’s pension system to expand coverage, strengthen regulatory oversight and improve retirement income security, particularly for workers in the informal sector.

Speaking at the official opening of the 2026 Annual Pension Conference, held under the theme “Building Sustainable Pension Innovation, Governance and Policy Reform,” Ministry of Labour and Social Security Secretary Zachariah Luhanga said pension reforms were essential to safeguarding workers’ contributions, enhancing benefits and positioning pension funds to contribute to national economic development.

Mr Luhanga said government remained committed to building a sustainable pension system that protects members’ savings, provides adequate retirement income and supports families in old age.

“Pension is more than a monthly payment,” the Permanent Secretary said, describing retirement benefits as recognition of workers’ years of service and sacrifice.

Mr Luhanga added that pension funds could also contribute to economic development by directing capital towards productive sectors, including infrastructure, housing and capital markets.

“The true measure of success is when the system protects members, provides adequate retirement benefits and reaches those who need it most,” Mr Luhanga said.

The Permanent Secretary also highlighted government’s ongoing efforts to improve the pension system through legislative reforms.

He further identified digital technology as an important tool for modernising pension administration, reducing operational costs and improving access to information.

Mr Luhanga, however, warned that technological advancement must be accompanied by strong data management, cybersecurity safeguards and adequate protection of members’ personal information.

He reiterated government’s commitment to expanding pension coverage, particularly among workers in the informal sector, many of whom remain outside formal pension arrangements.

Speaking earlier, Pension and Insurance Authority Registrar and Chief Executive Officer, Namakau Ntini, called for stronger governance, greater transparency and expanded pension coverage to ensure a sustainable retirement system capable of protecting contributors and supporting national economic development.

Ms Ntini stressed that pension systems could no longer rely on traditional approaches alone, particularly as demographic changes increase the need for sustainable retirement planning.

On governance, the Registrar emphasised the importance of competence, accountability, effective risk management and transparent investment decisions in protecting contributors’ savings and maintaining public confidence in pension institutions.

She said strengthening governance structures was essential to addressing weaknesses in pension administration and ensuring that the interests of contributors and retirees remained central to industry operations.

And Zambia Association of Pension Funds (ZAPF) Chairperson, Collina Halwampa, urged pension industry to embrace innovation, strengthen member engagement and promote policy dialogue to ensure the long-term sustainability of pension schemes amid changing membership demographics.

Meanwhile, Pan African Fund Managers Association Programme Manager, Oguche Aguda, called for reforms in pension systems to ensure retirement income security, promote sustainable contributions and channel pension funds into investments capable of driving economic growth.

Mr Aguda, said pension administrators and regulators must strike a balance between innovation, investment security and the long-term sustainability of retirement savings.

He also urged stakeholders to pay greater attention to younger workers, saying pension systems must become more relevant and understandable to younger generations to encourage early and consistent contributions.

World.title: Petauke senior citizens, freedom fighters receive hampers
World.content:
Senior citizens and freedom fighters in Petauke District have received assorted hampers from the District National Events Committee (DNEC), with support from Dealer’s Corner Millers. ‎

The gesture, which is part of this year’s Independence celebrations, is an appreciation gesture, also aimed at enabling beneficiaries to share in the country’s Independence celebrations.

The hampers were presented by Petauke District Commissioner Wachepa Phiri, who said the initiative was intended to share the Independence spirit with less privileged members of society.

‎

‎ “To share the Independence celebration with others who are not as privileged as some of us might be,” he said.

‎

Meanwhile, Dealer’s Corner Millers Director Ibrahim Phiri said the donation was part of the company’s Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR).

‎

‎Mr Phiri said he valued the partnership and support from the public, which had contributed to the growth of his business.

‎

‎ “We are a Christian nation, so with the little we have, we thought of sharing,” he said.

‎

‎Meanwhile, 83-year-old Alifat Tembo said the gesture reminded him of the celebrations in the early days of Zambia’s Independence.

‎

‎ “With this parcel you have given me, I am reminded of the old days and reassured that we are still remembered. Government should continue to remember freedom fighters,” he said.

‎

‎Another senior citizen, Esnart Mbewe, thanked the organisers for the gesture and appealed for continued support towards senior citizens and freedom fighters.

‎

‎ “I am grateful that you have helped me during this year’s Independence celebration. As a parent, I feel that you have truly thought of me. The honour and respect you have shown us are greatly appreciated. May this continue,” she said.

The hampers included mealie meal, cooking oil and salt, among other items.
