World.title: First Lady takes Zimbabwe’s child welfare agenda to global summit in Samarkand
World.content:
First Lady Auxillia Mnangagwa has taken Zimbabwe’s work on childhood cancer, vulnerable children and youth drug abuse to the World Summit on Investing in Children’s Well-being, reaffirming the country’s commitment to children’s welfare, protection and development.

She attended at the invitation of Uzbekistan’s First Lady, Ziroat Mirziyoyeva

Hosted by the government of Uzbekistan the summit ran on 21-22 October.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Securitised title deeds to strengthen property ownership protection introduced
World.content:
Zimbabwe is introducing a new generation of securitised title deeds containing multiple layers of security intended to make property records harder to forge, alter or counterfeit.

The initiative is being implemented through the Department of Deeds, Companies and Intellectual Property’s Digital Land Administration Platform (DLAP).

The new documents use security technologies similar to those found on banknotes, passports and other high-security government documents.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Zaka girls take centre stage as inaugural festival kicks off
World.content:
HUNDREDS of Zaka schoolgirls are set to take to the pitch on Saturday for the inaugural LM Auctioneers Girls Soccer Festival, a day organisers say is built to celebrate and develop the girl child through football.

Eight schools from across the district will showcase their skill on two pitches at St Joseph High School in Jerera, in the first edition of the tournament to bring together schools exclusively from Zaka.

LM Auctioneers founder and managing director Lewis Muzhara, who is bankrolling the festival, said it was designed to give rural girls a stage.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Stanbic doubles cancer treatment support
World.content:
STANBIC Bank Zimbabwe has doubled its annual donation to the Cancer Association of Zimbabwe (CAZ) for chemotherapy drugs to US$50 000, strengthening a partnership that has supported cancer patients and their families for more than a decade.

The contribution is expected to help patients access treatment as the country continues to grapple with the burden of cancer.

Stanbic Bank head of brand and marketing Tariro Memo said the Standard Bank Group subsidiary considered it a privilege to sustain a partnership built on compassion and a shared commitment to improving the lives of Zimbabweans affected by cancer.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: WestProp targets retirement market with resort apartments
World.content:
WestProp Holdings is targeting Zimbabwe’s retirement housing market with resort-style apartments at The Hills Luxury Golf Estate, betting on demand for specialised accommodation that combines residential living with healthcare, leisure and social amenities.

The initiative comes as migration and changing family structures put pressure on traditional arrangements in which children and relatives care for older family members.

By combining housing with access to essential services and recreational facilities, WestProp aims to offer an alternative to conventional retirement living, although affordability and the cost of ongoing care will influence its wider appeal.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Zimbabwe must act now to secure vulnerable websites
World.content:
THE recent exposure of serious website vulnerabilities through artificial intelligence (AI) is a serious wake-up call for Zimbabwe. Website security can no longer be taken for granted, and organisations must act before cybercriminals exploit weaknesses in their digital systems.

With vulnerabilities in websites becoming increasingly visible, Zimbabwean businesses, government departments, schools, financial institutions and other organisations must urgently review their online security.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Senegal: General Strike Continues Amid Protests Against New Labour Laws
World.content:
Dakar — Senegal's labour unions have called for a 72-hour general strike, from October 21 to 23, 2026. The government disputes the legality of the strike, saying the notice filed by the unions doesn't comply with the procedures. This standoff comes amid ongoing tensions surrounding the reform of the Labor Code and the Social Security Code.

The confrontation between the government and the trade unions has entered a new phase. At the call of the Trade Union Front for the Defense of Labor (FSDT) and the mobilized trade union federations, workers are invited to observe three days of strike action to protest, in particular, against the conditions under which the new labor and social protection laws were adopted.

For several months, unions have been denouncing a process they deem insufficiently consultative. On July 10, the FSDT had already announced a general strike to express its opposition to the approach taken by the authorities. Despite this protest, the two texts were promulgated on September 3, 2026, under laws no. 2026-18 and no. 2026-19, before their publication in the Official Journal on September 18th.

A disagreement over the legality of the movement



Faced with this new call for mobilization, the Ministry of Public Service, Labor, and Public Service Reform considers the strike order unlawful. According to information reported by PressAfrik, the administration contests the use of a single strike notice to cover the public, semi-public, and private sectors, which are subject to separate procedures.

In the private and semi-public sectors, the Labor Code stipulates that the dispute must be notified to the Labor and Social Security Inspector or the relevant Director General, as applicable. If no agreement is reached, or in the event of partial conciliation, a thirty-day notice period may then be given to the company's management.

For civil servants, the ministry reminds them that written notice must specify the reasons for and duration of the strike, with one month's notice given before the action begins. Local government employees, for their part, must notify the president of the departmental council or the mayor concerned of their strike notice.

The administration warns that failure to comply with these formalities may result in salary deductions for days not worked and disciplinary action. It also mentions potential consequences for the right to compensation and damages in the event of termination of the employment contract.

For more, read the original story in French.

World.title: Ethiopia: Drone Strikes Kill Schoolchildren in Amhara, Civilians in Tigray Regions As Conflicts Show No Sign of Abating
World.content:
Addis Abeba — Drone strikes in Ethiopia's Amhara and Tigray regions killed schoolchildren and other civilians on Tuesday, 20 October, according to eyewitnesses and local residents who spoke to Addis Standard, adding to mounting civilian casualties amid renewed fighting between federal forces and armed opponents in both regions.

In South Gondar Zone of Amhara, a drone strike hit Sana Elementary School in Dera Woreda, killing at least six schoolchildren and injuring more than 20 others, according to preliminary reports.

Separately, a drone strike in Finaruo village, in Saharti Samre Woreda of Tigray's Southeastern Zone, killed four people and injured six others as they loaded livestock onto a truck, local residents said.

The strikes occurred as drone attacks increasingly affect civilian areas and infrastructure in both regions, raising fresh concerns about civilian protection amid expanding aerial warfare.



In Amhara, the strike on Sana Elementary School occurred between 10:00 and 11:00 a.m. on Tuesday, 20 October, in Sana Kebele, according to preliminary accounts. The injured children were taken to a local clinic, although their conditions were not immediately known.

Casualty figures remain uncertain. While initial reports put the death toll at six, other accounts circulating publicly have reported between seven and ten students killed and more than 25 wounded. Addis Standard could not independently verify the total number of fatalities.

An elementary schoolteacher who spoke to Addis Standard disputed claims circulating on social media that the strike targeted a nearby hideout used by Fano armed groups.

"This was a school with more than 150 students attending the morning shift; there was no armed people in the school or nearby," the teacher said. "There was not conflict in nearby areas. Many of our students came back to school after three- or two-years interruptions. We don't know why the school was targeted."

The teacher said more than 20 students had been wounded and that parts of two classrooms had been damaged, adding that the full extent of the destruction had yet to be assessed.

Videos circulating on social media showed parents rushing into the school compound and carrying children away as pupils fled in different directions. Some children appeared disoriented, while teachers attempted to direct them to safety. Others could be heard calling for the wounded to be taken for medical treatment.

Alemtshay, whose name has been changed for security reasons, told Addis Standard that her 11-year-old son, Dagim, had stayed home that morning because he was unwell.

"He was having fever and was down with a terrible cold. I was pushing to go to school because he has already missed two years of school due to the war and school closures," she said.

She recalled hearing screams from the neighborhood around 10:30 a.m., during the school's tea break, before families began rushing their injured children to a local clinic.

"It was a complete chaos; mothers were crying and wailing," she said. "When we heard there was a bomb dropped from a helicopter, some men started to go around shouting for people to not leave their houses because they were afraid there might be another attack."

Reflecting on her son's absence from school, she added: "I was unhappy when my son failed to go to the school but now, I know God was protecting him."

In Tigray, the strike in Finaruo occurred at around 9:00 p.m. on Tuesday, 20 October, while a group of people were loading livestock onto an Isuzu truck, according to residents who spoke to Addis Standard.

Four people were killed, including the livestock owner and three people assisting him, while an unspecified number of animals also died, the residents said.

"What is most distressing is that the three of them were close relatives who were helping the owner," one resident told Addis Standard.

The six injured people were taken to different hospitals for treatment. Three were admitted to Samre Hospital, while the other three, who sustained severe injuries, were taken to Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in Mekelle, according to the residents. Some of the wounded were aged between 13 and 17.

One resident said there had been no military movements involving either federal forces or Tigrayan forces in the area in the days preceding the attack.

"It has been almost days since the town was free of military movements from both sides," the resident said.

The latest attack follows a series of drone strikes in Tigray that have killed and wounded civilians and damaged schools and humanitarian infrastructure. The attacks have continued amid renewed fighting between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan forces, which intensified on 23 September.

Earlier this month, a drone strike reportedly hit a shelter housing internally displaced people (IDPs) in Shiraro, in Tigray's Northwestern Zone, killing nine people and wounding 14 others, including a newborn baby. In Adwa, in the Central Zone, residents reported civilian deaths after drone strikes hit several locations in the city, although the exact toll could not be independently verified.

Other reported drone attacks have damaged residential neighborhoods, hotels, schools and media facilities. In September, a drone strike destroyed a Catholic Relief Services truck carrying more than 41 metric tons of food assistance intended for an IDP camp in northwestern Tigray. The United States condemned the attack and called for a transparent public investigation.

The renewed fighting follows the breakdown of the November 2022 Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, which ended two years of devastating war in Tigray, and a sustained drone attacks . The latest escalation has displaced tens of thousands of people, with humanitarian organizations estimating that at least 150,000 people have been displaced across Tigray and neighboring Afar.

Close 

In Amhara, federal forces have been fighting Fano armed groups since 2023, with drone strikes becoming a recurring feature of the conflict. Previous attacks reported by Addis Standard have hit residential areas, health facilities and religious sites, causing civilian casualties and damaging civilian infrastructure. The army has also targeted fighters on their own side killing at least 40.

In July this year, a drone strike on Saint Kirikos Monastery drew condemnation from the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the World Council of Churches, which called for impartial investigations. Earlier attacks have also killed children and other civilians in residential communities across the region.

The two latest strikes on Tuesday underscore the risks facing civilians as Ethiopia's conflicts increasingly involve aerial attacks by federal forces in populated areas.

Addis Standard could not independently establish the circumstances of either strike, determine the intended targets or obtain an official response from the Ethiopian military.

The casualty figures in both regions remain subject to independent verification.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Searches for Missing Ugandan Contact As Ebola Cases Rise
World.content:
Kenyan authorities are searching for a Ugandan national who came into contact with the country's first Ebola patient in Nairobi, as the number of confirmed cases linked to the initial cluster rises to nine.

Kenya's director general of health, Patrick Amoth, says authorities have been unable to locate the contact case, despite having his passport and telephone numbers.

The man is suspected of having crossed the border using an unofficial route to avoid border checks, Amoth said on Tuesday. Ugandan authorities have been notified.

The current Ebola outbreak was first declared in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in mid-May.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

On Tuesday evening, Kenya announced a ninth case. Nairobi said it was "still linked to the first cluster". The patient is being held in isolation, along with the other 129 people identified as contacts by health authorities.

Earlier this week, the United States State Department advised Americans to reconsider travel to Kenya and raised its travel advisory level for the country because of health risks.

A race against time to prevent an outbreak follows Kenya's first Ebola death

Quarantine centre concerns

The authorities maintain that the situation remains under control, but their handling of the outbreak has come in for criticism.

Opponents accuse the government of a lack of transparency in its response.

"It is clear that quarantine centres are turning into incubation units for the Ebola virus," said David Maraga, a former chief justice and candidate in Kenya's 2027 presidential election.

After days of pressure, the doctors' union was included in the national Ebola response task force on Tuesday.

France earmarks a further €7m to help fight DRC's worst-ever Ebola crisis

Regional threat

Nigeria on Tuesday became the latest country to be affected by the recent Ebola outbreak, when a woman who arrived from Uganda around two weeks ago was diagnosed in the capital Abuja.

Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient and were "doing everything possible to contain this case".

Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment, the outbreak has killed at least 4,600 of the 9,500 people affected in DRC.

However, drug trials suggest there may be "reasons for hope". The first clinical trial of a potential vaccine is expected to begin by the end of October, the World Health Organization said on 13 October.

Close 

Nigeria Ebola case matches DR Congo strain

Uganda recorded 20 cases and two deaths before declaring the outbreak over in its territory in late August.

Jean Kaseya, head of Africa CDC - the African Union's health agency in charge of disease control and prevention - warned on Tuesday of "an extremely serious threat" and called for international mobilisation.

France in June confirmed a positive case of Ebola in a doctor traveling back from DRC, making it the only country outside Africa so far to have recorded a case in the current outbreak.

(with newswires)

World.title: Rwanda: Rwandans in France Decry Unresolved Genocide Case of Ex-French Captain
World.content:
The Rwandan Community of France (CRF) has criticised French justice authorities for failing to bring former French gendarmerie captain Paul Barril to justice over allegations of complicity in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

Barril died on Tuesday, October 21 at the age of 80. The former head of the anti-terrorism unit at the Élysée Palace was accused of maintaining close ties with Rwanda's interim government during the Genocide that claimed more than one million lives. In 2013, French prosecutors launched an investigation into the allegation.

ALSO READ: Ex-French captain faces probe over Genocide

In a statement on Wednesday, the CRF said Barril died without being tried over allegations that he helped sustain the government responsible for the Genocide.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The CRF said his death should not end efforts to establish the facts surrounding his alleged activities and the role of other individuals who may have been involved.

"This outcome constitutes a serious failure in the search for truth and accountability," the statement said.

ALSO READ: Safari Madjaliwa: Who is the Genocide suspect facing trial in France?

The community also called for an examination of the obstacles that hampered investigations into Barril's activities, including difficulties accessing archives that could have shed light on his dealings with Rwandan and French officials.

It further questioned whether Barril had received any form of protection that prevented the allegations against him from being fully examined in court.

"How can we accept that accusations of such gravity were never examined in a trial?" the statement asked.

His death ends the criminal proceedings against him personally, but the CRF insists that efforts to establish the truth must continue.

The community called on French authorities to make relevant archives accessible and ensure that investigations into other possible perpetrators and accomplices are not abandoned.

Complaint filed in 2013

In June 2013, three French human rights organisations, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the French Human Rights League (LDH) and Survie, filed a complaint against Barril over his alleged complicity in the genocide.

The complaint, lodged at the Tribunal de Paris, concerned allegations that Barril had entered into an agreement with Jean Kambanda, then prime minister of Rwanda's interim government, to provide arms, ammunition, military training and supervision.

The organisations sought to establish whether his alleged assistance had contributed to the interim government's efforts to remain in power as the genocide unfolded.

Close 

The complaint led to the opening of a judicial investigation, paving the way for an independent inquiry into the allegations. However, Barril died without the case reaching trial.

In 2013, Rwanda's then National Commission for the Fight against Genocide (CNLG) welcomed the investigation. Its executive secretary at the time, Jean de Dieu Mucyo, and then Ibuka president Jean-Pierre Dusingizemungu described the move as an important step towards justice.

Dusingizemungu, however, said accountability should extend beyond Barril to other French officials who held senior military positions during the Genocide.

Barril's alleged involvement had attracted attention following reports about a military assistance contract signed with Kambanda on May 28, 1994, after the United Nations had imposed an arms embargo on Rwanda.

French media also reported that a letter dated April 27, 1994, from then Rwandan Defence Minister Augustin Bizimana requested weapons and 1,000 mercenaries to help the interim government fight the Rwandese Patriotic Front (RPF).

The allegations concerning the supply of arms, mercenaries and military assistance have remained central to questions about Barril's activities during the genocide.

The CRF said that, more than three decades after the Genocide against the Tutsi, victims and their families were still owed the truth.

"Paul Barril's death must not close the case," the community said, urging French authorities to pursue every available avenue to establish responsibility and ensure accountability.

World.title: Africa: Are Bilateral Ties the Route to Renewed West African Security Cooperation?
World.content:
Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) - Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger. (File photo)

analysis

Pending the outcome of ECOWAS-AES talks, cooperation between neighbouring states offers a starting point for rebuilding regional security ties.

Despite tensions between the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the Confederation of Sahel States (AES), recent advances reflect a broader regional trend. In August, Ghana and Burkina Faso signed a defence agreement, while Mali and Côte d'Ivoire agreed to delimit their shared border.

The withdrawal of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger from ECOWAS in January 2025 deeply fragmented West Africa's institutional architecture, but did not end cooperation between individual states. Instead, relations are being pragmatically reorganised around countries' security priorities, mainly through bilateral deals. This shift has been underway since 2025 and offers a concrete way to manage divisions without waiting for ongoing ECOWAS-AES negotiations to produce a political agreement.

Across several ECOWAS-AES fault lines, states are reactivating or deepening bilateral cooperation frameworks, agreements, joint commissions, or operational mechanisms, some of which predate the current regional crisis.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Joint patrols launched by Senegal and Mali in the Kayes region in 2025 build on a cooperation framework established in 2021. Mali and Guinea's shared military commission met in April 2025 and June 2026, producing a memorandum of understanding that provides for intelligence sharing. And in August 2026, Ghana and Burkina Faso signed a defence pact after relaunching their Permanent Joint Commission for Cooperation and signing seven cross-border cooperation agreements.

These initiatives show that institutional fragmentation has not paralysed security cooperation altogether, even if the effectiveness of agreements is yet to be demonstrated. They also challenge the notion of a standstill, as bilateral mechanisms play an increasingly prominent role, enabling states to maintain or rebuild relations around their immediate security interests.

This window of opportunity should be maximised while ECOWAS and the AES negotiate a framework for future security cooperation. Talks could drag on, or even stall, given how politically and symbolically charged relations between the two blocs remain. Meanwhile, armed groups continue to exploit gaps in cooperation.

Rather than waiting for a new institutional agreement, regional actors and their partners could reverse the sequence. They could encourage states to cooperate where their interests converge, facilitate rapprochement where political tensions stand in the way, and over time, connect bilateral arrangements through flexible regional mechanisms.

Two of West Africa's border areas need priority attention.

The first is northern Benin, where jihadist groups exploit gaps in neighbouring countries' collaboration. Around the W-Arly-Pendjari complex, where Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger meet, violence remains intense. Further east, in the Benin-Niger-Nigeria triangle, weak coordination is enabling armed groups to expand. Discussions between Nigeria and Benin remain incomplete without Niger, and the rapprochement launched by Beninese President Romuald Wadagni during his June visit to Niamey has yet to reopen the border.

The second is the Sikasso-Korhogo-Bobo-Dioulasso (SKBo) cross-border area, where Mali, Côte d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso meet. Political distrust between Abidjan and Ouagadougou continues to hinder cooperation on the ground, and progress between Côte d'Ivoire and Mali has yet to translate into joint security efforts commensurate with the risks.

Other regional actors could help unblock cooperation in these priority border areas. The Conseil de l'Entente, which brings together Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Niger and Togo, with Mali as an observer, already has a dialogue framework on security and border management. It could discreetly facilitate rapprochement among its members, particularly around the W-Arly-Pendjari complex and the SKBo area, in a format less exposed to ECOWAS-AES political tensions.

In the Benin-Niger-Nigeria zone, the African Union (AU) Mission for Mali and the Sahel (MISAHEL) could offer a complementary entry point. Its mandate, which will extend to Benin and Togo from 2027, and its AU affiliation independent of both ECOWAS and AES, make it well placed to facilitate dialogue among the three countries. The aim would be to gradually restore trust and help states identify concrete ways to restart joint security initiatives.

MISAHEL could share lessons from the Nouakchott Process, launched by the AU in 2013 to strengthen security cooperation in the Sahelo-Saharan region, with the priority border areas. Although the process is largely inactive, the mechanisms it promoted - intelligence sharing, cross-border coordination, joint patrols and regular exchanges between security officials - are precisely those that several states want to revive on an ad hoc basis in their bilateral cooperation.

This approach should remain flexible enough to adapt to the needs that states themselves identify. On one border, the main requirement may be restoring contact between military officials; on another, establishing intelligence-sharing protocols. Elsewhere, political conditions might allow states to go further, with more frequent joint patrols or more formal coordination between countries.

Close 

The goal would not be to replicate a regional mechanism, but to tailor these tools to the needs and possibilities specific to each border area. This variable-geometry approach is increasingly taking shape through the 'coalition of the willing' proposed by Ghana. Rather than waiting for a regional consensus that would require countries to progress at the same pace, the approach is moving towards implementation among states ready to move forward.

In the long run, an ECOWAS-AES framework could develop from working relations established on the ground, rather than from the top down through an institutional agreement. The resulting regional architecture may be less orderly than before, but more solid - precisely because it would be anchored in states' concrete security interests and their need to cooperate.

Djiby Sow, Senior Researcher, ISS Regional Office for West Africa and the Sahel

World.title: South Africa: Black Market Weight-Loss Drug Sellers Are Moving Fast. South Africa's Regulators Are Struggling To Keep Up
World.content:
Why is South Africa struggling to stop the sellers of illegal weight-loss injections, and how can consumers tell whether the medicines they're buying are safe?

South African regulators have won an important court battle against a pharmacy making its own versions of popular weight-loss injections. But illegal and experimental drugs are still being sold openly, while new rules to crack down on the trade are months away. Why is the country struggling to stop the sellers — and how can consumers tell whether the medicines they're buying are safe?

South African pharmacies are allowed to make up medicines for patients with specific needs. But some are producing weight-loss injections in large quantities without the licences required to manufacture medicines.

In June, the Gauteng High Court ordered Tshwane-based compounding pharmacy iDexis to stop producing medicines containing semaglutide, the substance that makes Ozempic work.

Yet experimental weight-loss drugs such as retatrutide, which are still being studied and haven't been approved for sale anywhere in the world, are still being sold openly in South Africa.

Regulators say clearer rules for pharmacies that make their own medicines are on the way, but these are only expected by February or March 2027. The pharmaceutical industry warns that the delay gives illegal sellers more time to operate.

Australia has banned pharmacy compounding of weight-loss jabs, citing such drugs as "potentially unsafe and dangerous". So why are South African so-called compounding pharmacies still making their own versions of blockbuster weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro , and selling them to the public?

The reality is that such activity is illegal in South Africa as well, at least in instances where the pharmacies make up copycat weight-loss jabs — which dampen appetite and make people feel full for longer — in large quantities, or use unregistered or illegally imported ingredients to make them.



But as demand has soared, some pharmacies have turned the niche practice of compounding into a lucrative business. In June, the Gauteng High Court ordered iDexis, a compounding pharmacy in Tshwane, to stop producing medicine containing semaglutide — the active ingredient of Ozempic — after large quantities of compounded weight-loss jabs had been confiscated on its premises.

The court order was an important legal victory for the country's regulators, including the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (Sahpra), Stavros Nicolaou , chairperson of the Pharmaceutical Task Group , an umbrella organisation for the pharmaceutical industry in South Africa, said during a panel discussion held in Sandton last week.

But he said the momentum built by the court order could be lost if Sahpra and the South African Pharmacy Council (SAPC) don't follow up on it quickly with clearer guidelines for compounding pharmacies about what they can, and cannot legally do. "You can go and win these court cases, and have people on the back foot, but all of that can unravel because we're just not acting swiftly enough as a country," he said.

Illegal drugs in plain sight

The panel gathered representatives from Sahpra and the SAPC, as well as the police service, border control, revenue service and the pharmaceutical industry, to explain to the public how they are working together to stop the trade in fake drugs.

Sahpra says it has received around 600 complaints so far this financial year relating to illegitimate and fake medicines being sold through informal supply chains, reaching the public via online portals, gyms, or even local hairdressers.

"We are worried that the scourge is getting out of control," said Daphne Fafudi , the body's head of regulatory compliance. And it's the public that can pay the ultimate price, she added. "People do die, and it doesn't even come to our attention," she said.

Some fake or illegitimate drugs are sold covertly. Others are traded in plain sight. One of them is retatrutide , a weight-loss injection that is still being tested in studies and therefore hasn't been licensed for sale by a drug regulatory anywhere in the world. Yet, it is sold "openly and brazenly" around the world, including in South Africa, said Nicolaou.

In the July episode of Bhekisisa 's TV programme, Health Beat, we reported how a Johannesburg woman's doctor sold her retatrutide, telling her it's safe because he "had it tested", while making her sign a waiver to release him of any responsibility for what might go wrong .

Earlier this year, a man reportedly died in the United States after taking injections sold as retatrutide on the black market — although the British Medical Journal said the evidence for the drug causing the fatality was "less clear cut" than media reporting suggested.

Nicolaou urged the police service and the Hawks to make an example of those who sell retatrutide in South Africa, as a deterrent to others. "The public needs to know that our enforcement agencies are actually enforcing the law," he told the meeting last week.

Vincent Tlala , CEO of the SAPC , said revised guidelines for compounding pharmacies were underway, a process Sahpra is leading, with input from the SAPC. However, Tlala said, these were not expected to be ready until February or March next year.

According to Nicolaou, this is too late. "The regulations are taking too long," he says. Regulators in other countries have introduced bans and restrictions on compounding pharmacies specifically for weight-loss jabs, to prevent the kind of products that have flooded South Africa. "Why are we not doing the same thing?"

What South African law says about compounding

Compounding medicines is lawful in South Africa, but only under specific conditions . Compounding requires a healthcare professional's prescription, generally for a formulation that is not available as a registered medicine — for instance, if a patient requires a medication as an oral liquid that is only normally sold as a pill.

As for compounding in bulk, the law says that a pharmacy may prepare stock in advance if they can show that patients regularly need the medicine — such as repeat prescriptions for the same person.

But some pharmacies produce large quantities without that evidence, Sahpra chief executive Boitumelo Semete-Makokotlela told Bhekisisa. This means "you're not compounding, you are manufacturing", which requires a good manufacturing practice licence that compounding pharmacies do not hold.

A good manufacturing practice licence shows that a company has met the safety and quality standards required to manufacture medicines.

A second concern is where ingredients come from. Active pharmaceutical ingredients — the substances in medicines that make them work — must be registered in South Africa and imported by a licensed entity, says Semete-Makokotlela. A pharmacy's operational licence does not authorise it to import unregistered ingredients, she says, yet some have arrived in travellers' luggage.

Another loophole that needs to be closed, Semete-Makokotlela notes, is where people sell experimental drugs (meds still being studied) or medicinal products directly to the public that are authorised for "research purposes" only. This includes some peptide products that are neither registered medicines nor experimental drugs in formal trials (like retatrutide), yet are still widely bought and sold as lifestyle or wellness drugs to do things like lower inflammation and boost energy.

Peptides are short chains of amino acids — small building blocks that the body uses to make proteins. Insulin is a peptide , as is semaglutide , the active ingredient in Ozempic. Both are registered medicines in South Africa.

However, there are other peptides, such as BPC-157 , which are being sold online and in gyms as solutions to specific health problems, such as tissue repair. These peptides aren't technically medicines, nor are they actively being studied in drug trials. Yet, they are sold as healthcare products, without evidence that they are safe or effective at treating humans.

Then there is the battle for public opinion, which is proving to be another hurdle. Semete-Makokotlela admits regulators are "on the back foot" when consumers see people losing weight while official warnings struggle to compete.

Close 

The answer, she believes, includes offering people registered alternatives at different prices — including cheaper generics — and working with healthcare professionals to steer patients towards safe, registered medicines.

South Africa's first generic weight-loss drug, containing semaglutide, hit the shelves in August .

How the public can keep safe

During the panel discussion, South African Revenue Service official Gene Ravele called the lack of coordination between enforcement agencies "the number one problem that organised crime is taking advantage of", and that this is also true for counterfeit and illegitimate drugs.

Border Management Authority head Nakampe Masiapato added that police detectives and prosecutors are often generalists, ill-equipped for specialised pharmaceutical cases. "They have no idea what this is about," he said.

For consumers, the advice from regulators is to use authorised channels and check that medicines are registered. Common signs that a drug is not legitimate is that it has unusual or blank packaging, no printed expiry date on the box or container, or that it doesn't have a normal insert detailing how to take it and the common side effects. Broken or dented packaging is another big 'tell', the Sandton meeting heard last week.

The bottom line is that a product's online availability, or a seller's claim that it is equivalent to a registered medicine, is not proof that it has been assessed or approved, said Fafudi. "If you cannot trust the source, do not trust the medicine."

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 22, 2026
World.content:
Cameroon Train Disaster Survivors Still Await Justice 10 Years Later

Ten years after Cameroon's deadliest rail disaster killed 79 people and injured more than 500, survivors are still dealing with serious injuries, while some victims have not received compensation and legal proceedings remain unresolved. The Camrail train derailed near Eseka on 21 October 2016 while travelling from Yaoundé to Douala. An investigation found that it was travelling at 96km/h in a section with a 40km/h speed limit. Overloading, defective brakes and the addition of extra carriages also contributed to the crash. Survivors continue to suffer from chronic pain and lasting disabilities. In 2018, Camrail and 11 employees were convicted of involuntary manslaughter and causing unintentional injuries. The company's former managing director received a suspended sentence, while other officials were also given suspended sentences. The train driver was sentenced to five years in prison. However, Camrail appealed the ruling, and the appeal has yet to be heard. Victims' lawyers say compensation has been inadequate, with some payments still outstanding.

Burkina Faso Restores Death Penalty Amid Crackdown on Critics



Burkina Faso's unelected parliament has unanimously adopted a new penal code restoring the death penalty for offences including high treason, terrorism, espionage, parricide and importing expired or prohibited products. The death penalty for ordinary crimes was abolished in 2018. Human Rights Watch warns that reinstating capital punishment could further threaten civil liberties under the military junta, which took power in a 2022 coup. Authorities have restricted media outlets, suspended civil society organisations and unions, and targeted critics through arrests and enforced disappearances. The government said that the measure will help combat terrorism. Rights advocates argue that weaknesses in the justice system increase the risk of wrongful convictions and irreversible injustice.

Nearly 200,000 Zimbabweans Returned From South Africa

Nearly 200,000 Zimbabweans have returned home from South Africa amid anti-migrant protests and attacks targeting foreign nationals, according to the government. Cabinet was told that 197,294 people had returned, including 42,553 repatriated through government assistance and 154,741 who returned independently. The government deployed buses to collect stranded nationals, including those in Cape Town. The protests, involving groups such as Operation Dudula and March and March, have targeted Zimbabweans and other African migrants. Authorities said the number of returnees has declined but are continuing to monitor the situation. Zimbabwe is also screening deportees arriving from South Africa, including 700 people received from the Lindela Repatriation Centre.

Gambia to Compensate Victims With Proceeds From Jammeh's US Mansion

The Gambia's Reparations Commission has received more than US$2.57 million from the sale of a Maryland mansion belonging to former president Yahya Jammeh. The funds will be used to compensate victims of abuses committed during his more than two decades in power. US authorities secured the right to sell the property in 2022, arguing that it had been acquired using criminal proceeds and misappropriated public funds. Jammeh seized power in a 1994 coup and was accused of overseeing torture, forced disappearances, rape and extrajudicial killings. He lost the 2016 election to Adama Barrow but initially refused to step down. He eventually left office in 2017 and went into exile in Equatorial Guinea. A national inquiry found that he had amassed hundreds of properties and misappropriated more than US$300 million.

Latin American Drug Cartels Expand Operations Across Africa

Latin American drug trafficking organizations are expanding into Africa, using the continent as a transshipment point for cocaine and as a new production base for methamphetamine. Global demand is rising, and enforcement efforts are harder to maintain in the Americas, so criminal groups have tried to link up with African networks. Methamphetamine labs have been found in South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, and Mozambique. It is still common for cocaine to travel through West Africa on its way to Europe. They generate revenue by engaging in money laundering and drug trafficking. They achieve this by capitalizing on corruption, porous borders, and a scarcity of police officers. Nevertheless, the drug trade is gaining popularity, which is a cause for concern as it undermines government institutions and results in a rise in crime, addiction, and violence. The authorities have increased the number of arrests and seizures. Experts warn that criminal networks will continue to thrive where oversight and law enforcement remain weak.

Close 

Kagame Urges Rwanda's Youth to Put Health Before Ambitions

Rwandan President Paul Kagame has called on the youth to prioritise their health and well-being as they chase their personal and professional aspirations. Speaking at a youth engagement event at BK Arena on October 21, he stressed the importance of developing healthy habits from childhood. Kagame warned against alcohol and drug abuse, saying such behaviours can worsen personal difficulties rather than solve them. He also encouraged young people to exercise, continue learning, work hard and make responsible decisions. He called on them to challenge harmful practices in their communities instead of allowing them to become normalised. Kagame said young people should recognise their potential, distinguish right from wrong and take responsibility for shaping their futures.

World.title: South Africa: Government Investigates Gastrointestinal Illness Cases in the Eastern Cape
World.content:
Government has launched an investigation into reported cases of gastrointestinal illness affecting 111 people at Rhodes University in Makhanda and 23 inmates at St Albans Correctional Centre in Nelson Mandela Bay.

The investigation was announced in a joint statement by the Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS), the Eastern Cape Provincial Government, Makana Local Municipality and Nelson Mandela Bay Metropolitan Municipality.

The investigation follows reports of individuals in the two municipalities receiving treatment at various healthcare facilities for symptoms including severe abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting and dehydration.

The joint statement explained that DWS received a media alert about gastrointestinal illnesses reported by Rhodes University, prompting the activation of a response team involving the provincial Department of Health and the DWS regional offices.



A multi-stakeholder technical team has since been established to investigate the source of the illnesses and contain their spread.

The team comprises the DWS, provincial departments of Health and Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs, Sarah Baartman District Municipality, Makana Local Municipality, Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality, the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD), Amatola Water and Rhodes University.

An intergovernmental meeting was held on Wednesday evening, led by Water and Sanitation Minister Pemmy Majodina and Eastern Cape Premier Oscar Mabuyane, alongside Makana Executive Mayor Yandiswa Vara and Nelson Mandela Bay Executive Mayor Babalwa Lobishe.

"The meeting received reports from the technical team covering information on the number and location of gastrointestinal illness cases, the samples taken by the NICD and water quality tests conducted by the DWS as well as additional urgent measures being implemented to protect communities," the statement read.

The technical team collected water samples from various water sources in Makana, including Rhodes University's internal water storage and distribution system, the municipal distribution network and the water treatment works.

At St Albans Correctional Centre, samples were collected from the elevated water storage tower through which the facility receives potable water from the Nelson Mandela Bay municipal supply system.

"Preliminary findings indicate that the spread is currently concentrated within the university and the Saint Albans Prison. Initial test results indicate that the contamination is within the university's water distribution system and within the prison's water distribution system, and not within the municipal water distribution systems.

Close 

"Laboratory test results of all the samples taken are still pending and will be communicated as soon as they become available," the statement said.

Government has urged residents who develop symptoms of gastrointestinal illness to seek medical attention early and report suspected cases to their nearest healthcare facility or local health authority.

"Early reporting protects not only individuals and families but also enables health authorities to respond quickly and prevent further spread."

Communities have also been urged to observe good hygiene practices, including washing hands after using the toilet and before handling food.

Earlier this week, the DWS Minister announced the establishment of a multi-pronged response team after 408 cases of gastrointestinal illness were reported at Bronkhorstspruit in the City of Tshwane (CoT) Municipality.

World.title: Trump pushback, Biden 'disaster' and gender surprise: 5 key moments from Kansas Senate debate
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton sparred over President Donald Trump, immigration, Iran, transgender athletes, artificial intelligence and personal controversies during a contentious Kansas Senate debate Wednesday night.

The hourlong showdown came less than two weeks before Election Day as Marshall seeks a second term and Hamilton, a longtime pastor, tries to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932.

The race has drawn increased national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate, with Trump traveling to Kansas earlier this week to campaign for Marshall.

Here are five moments that stood out from Wednesday night's debate.

SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Debate opens with candidates confronted over personal controversies

The debate wasted little time getting contentious, opening with questions about controversies that have fueled attacks against both candidates.

Marshall was confronted with a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills.

"Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall responded. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric."

Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp who was accused of sexual abuse.

Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp following an initial investigation.

FROM 'THIRD REICH' TO âNOT THAT INFORMEDâ: SENATE DEBATES DELIVER FIREWORKS BEFORE MIDTERMS

"I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part."

Marshall says 'President Trump is not always right'

Trump became part of the debate after moderators played footage from the president's campaign appearance for Marshall in Kansas earlier in the week.

"And at this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just pretend," Trump told the crowd.

Marshall was then asked whether Trump's support meant Kansans should expect him to back every part of the president's agenda.

"No," Marshall responded, saying there had been "multiple times" when he objected to Trump.

Pressed to identify a specific disagreement, Marshall pointed to recent immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports.

"Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right."

Marshall nevertheless urged Trump voters to turn out for him, arguing that electing Hamilton could help Democrats capture the Senate.

Both candidates say there are 'two genders'

The two rivals found themselves in agreement when the moderator asked each candidate how many genders there are.

"There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "I delivered 5,000 of them and almost half were boys and half were girls."

"There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded.

TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM JD VANCE TOWN HALL: COSTLY GAS, DC CORRUPTION, IMMIGRATION HOT TAKES AND THE WAR

The candidates then turned to the debate over transgender participation in women's sports.

Hamilton said decisions over athletic eligibility should generally be made locally but was unequivocal about whether biological males should compete against females.

"I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her," Hamilton said. "It's not a fair, fair fight."

Marshall argued that by high school, "boys need to be in boys sports, girls in girls sports," while accusing national Democrats of pushing "transgender ideology."

Hamilton later accused Marshall of using the issue to "pick on" and "bully" people.

Hamilton calls AI an 'existential threat' â but can't name regulations he'd support

Hamilton called for greater federal oversight of artificial intelligence and compared the emerging technology to the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons.

"We developed a Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We need to do the same thing with AI," Hamilton said.

But when the moderator pressed him to identify specific federal regulations he would support, Hamilton acknowledged he did not yet have an answer.

"You know what? I'm not sure, to be honest," Hamilton said, arguing that even experts are struggling to understand the technology's potential dangers.

Marshall advocated a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, protecting children and privacy, while slamming a one-size-fits-all global order for artificial intelligence advancement.

Hamilton pushed back sharply.

"This is an existential â potential existential threat to the human race," Hamilton said. "We can't just go with a light touch and hope everybody does their best."

BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH

Hamilton calls Biden's border policies a 'disaster'

Hamilton sought to put distance between himself and former President Joe Biden when moderators challenged the Democrat over his claim that he would "lead from the middle."

The moderator pointed to Hamilton's past donations to Democrats, including Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., before asking him to identify a progressive policy he opposed.

"The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton responded. "I believe in strong and secure borders."

"I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton added. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle."

Hamilton also reiterated during the debate that he would not support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for majority leader if Democrats capture control of the chamber.

World.title: NYC votes to end nearly 170-year-old horse carriage tradition as Trump blasts ban, drivers threaten lawsuit
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The New York City Council voted Thursday to ban horse-drawn carriages by June 2028, moving to end a nearly 170-year tradition after the death of a teenager in Central Park and prompting threats of legal action from carriage drivers.

The council voted 40-7, with two abstentions, to approve Romanch's Law, named after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who died in June after being thrown from a runaway carriage in Central Park.

The legislation would phase out the industry by June 1, 2028, while requiring Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration to develop a transition program for more than 150 active carriage drivers and other workers.

The plan would include job training, career counseling and employment referrals, although financial compensation is not guaranteed.

MAMDANI PRAISED OVER MOVE TO DISMANTLE CONTROVERSIAL NYC INDUSTRY — BUT INSIDERS SAY THERE’S MORE TO THE STORY

President Donald Trump weighed in on the decision Thursday, criticizing the move to eliminate one of New York City's longtime tourist attractions.

"The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience. So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!" he wrote on Truth Social.

The Transport Workers Union (TWU), which represents carriage industry workers, threatened to challenge the ban in federal court and seek a temporary restraining order. Union representatives accused City Council Speaker Julie Menin of failing to adequately consult drivers whose livelihoods are at stake.

MAN KILLED AFTER HORSE-DRAWN CARRIAGE BOLTS AND FLIPS NEAR POPULAR NEW YORK CITY TOURIST DESTINATION

Opponents argued the city had failed to establish a concrete financial plan for drivers and carriage owners. An effort to delay the phaseout until January 2030 failed before the final vote.

Menin defended the legislation Thursday, saying the council had strengthened worker protections and was prepared for a legal fight.

"We're very confident in the legislation. That's why we took the time to work over the summer on the legislation," she said at a news conference.

"We made changes to legislation to beef up worker protection. We are very confident in defending this law and will vigorously defend it. I've already talked to Steve Banks about it and our team, and we will vigorously defend this law."

Animal rights group PETA also celebrated the vote, pledging $50,000 to help carriage horses retire as the industry winds down.

The Central Park Conservancy celebrated the decision, arguing that horse-drawn carriages pose growing safety risks in a park that welcomes roughly 40 million visits annually.

MAMDANI, CITY COUNCIL MOVE TO END ICONIC NYC HORSE-DRAWN CARRIAGE INDUSTRY AS WORKERS FACE UNCERTAIN FUTURE

"In the modern era, carriages pose a serious — and even fatal — safety risk to park visitors, carriage drivers and the horses themselves. Our hearts break for the family of Romanch Mahajan, who stepped into a carriage earlier this summer and never thought he might lose his life," the organization wrote in a press release.

The Conservancy said Mahajan's death was the ninth carriage-related incident in just over a year.

The legislation also includes protections intended to prevent retired carriage horses from being sold for slaughter, while allowing owners to keep their animals.

The bill now heads to Mamdani, who has expressed support for ending the industry. If signed, it would bring an end to a decades-long political battle over one of New York City's most recognizable tourist attractions.

World.title: Erika Kirk rips 'absurd' 2029 trial timeline for Charlie Kirk's alleged assassin
World.content:

Erika Kirk is urging a judge to reject a defense proposal that would push the trial of her husband's accused killer into 2029, asking the court to set a trial date in 2027.

In a new court filing obtained by Fox News, Kirk's legal team blasted the defense's proposed timeline as "grossly out of line" with comparable cases, asking the court to schedule the trial for the earliest practicable date in 2027.

Kirk's team also argued that prolonged delays would deepen the emotional toll on the Kirk family, particularly Charlie Kirk's two young children, and cited a report that Robinson's defense had already cost taxpayers approximately $1.6 million in its first year.

"Every additional day of delay carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his two young children who were just three and one year old when their father was murdered and would be seven and five years old by the time a verdict is handed down under the Defense's proposed schedule," the filing reads.

JUDGE IN ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON'S CASE EXPLAINS WHY DEATH PENALTY REMAINS ON TABLE

Kirk's attorneys cited Utah law guaranteeing crime victims the right to a speedy disposition of charges without unwarranted delay. They also asked the court to require monthly progress reports or status conferences and to consider the family's interests before granting scheduling extensions.

Tyler Robinson's defense team proposed a tentative trial start date in the third quarter of 2029, arguing that setting a firm date now would create "false precision" and could jeopardize Robinson's constitutional rights in a death penalty case, where, as the defense noted, "death is different."

The defense cited pretrial motions it plans to file through 2029, the volume of evidence still awaiting review and the complexities of jury selection as reasons for the proposed timeline.

"From the point of view of defense counsel, appointment to a capital case brings with it a slew of responsibilities that apply in no other context," the defense memorandum states.

JUDGE ALLOWS CAMERAS IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION CASE, DELAYS PRELIMINARY HEARING

Robinson's attorneys argue that they must review evidence related to both guilt and potential sentencing before trial and that additional evidence is still being processed, making it premature to establish a firm trial date.

"It will create unrealistic expectations for the public and the victim's representative, it may cause counsel for both parties to give short shrift to constitutionally required activities, it may rush this Court to deliberate upon and enter rulings on important and complex pretrial motions, and it may jeopardize Mr. Robinson's right to a capital proceeding that has the utmost reliability," the defense states.

While prosecutors expect to be ready for trial by Oct. 4, 2027, Utah County Attorney Jeffrey S. Gray argued that beginning the trial in October would mean proceedings would stretch through the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays.

TYLER ROBINSON ASKS FOR MORE SECRET HEARINGS AFTER LOSING FIGHT OVER CAMERAS IN COURT

"The State therefore proposes that the Court schedule the trial to begin January 31, 2028," the prosecution's memorandum states.

Prosecutors estimate the trial would take approximately 17 weeks, while Robinson's defense team anticipates proceedings lasting six to seven months.

World.title: Supreme Court says New Hampshire student IDs can’t be used to vote in November
World.content:
WASHINGTON — In a win for Republicans, the Supreme Court said Thursday that student IDs cannot be used in New Hampshire for the midterm elections.

The justices granted an emergency request filed by the state, which had the backing of the Republican National Committee.

The ballot in New Hampshire includes a closely watched Senate race that could play a key role in deciding control of the chamber. Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu is pitted against Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas for the seat held by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.

The brief court order said a federal judge should not have ordered a change in voting rules so close to the Nov. 3 election, citing existing precedent on that point.

“Here, the District Court did not point to anything that would justify deviating from that principle,” the unsigned order said.

Liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the sole dissenter.

“I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes,” she wrote.

While a state law restricting use of student IDs as a primary form of identification was already on the books, the decision means potential voters also cannot use them as backups when they seek to establish their identities.

The dispute arises from a state law enacted in April that removed student IDs from the list of forms of identification that election officials would accept when someone requests a ballot.

The measure was challenged by a nonprofit voting rights group called Coalition for Open Democracy, which argued that it unlawfully burdened the right to vote and discriminated against young voters.

U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante declined to block the law, but on Oct. 2 he weighed in again, putting guidance from New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, a Republican, on hold.

Scanlan’s guidance said student IDs could not be used for any purpose when people seek ballots, which Laplante said went further than the law itself, which only barred them as a primary source of ID.

A separate provision of state law allows people to establish their identities using other, unofficial forms of ID. It says people can use “any other evidence that reasonably establishes that it is more likely than not that the person is who they claim to be.”

Under Laplante’s ruling, election officials could still take a student ID into account in trying to determine whether someone is a valid voter.

The Boston-based 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put Laplante’s ruling on hold, prompting the state to ask the Supreme Court to intervene.
