World.title: Albania's student protests are only getting bigger
World.content:
As police try to suppress anti-corruption protests by young Albanians, Prime Minister Edi Rama is claiming that "antifa" is behind the unrest. Few are buying that explanation.

The fallout from the October 13 protests was still visible when students and faculty from the University of Tirana gathered outside the Education Ministry in Albania's capital on Tuesday to express their continued discontent. Smashed windows have yet to be replaced; the walls are still black with soot from fires that broke out during the protests.

Albania has seen nearly five months of peaceful anti-government protests, sparked initially when plans were made public that Jared Kushner — a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump — and associates intended to build a luxury hotel complex within a nature reserve.

Since then, anti-government and anti-corruption protests have escalated. Now, college and high school students clash with police forces almost daily, with the fiercest clashes so far occurring last week.

Why Albania's political crisis is deepening To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Protesters denounce corruption, mismanaged universities and the rising cost of education in Albania — and call for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in office since 2013.

Wearing a black hooded jacket and a scarf across her face to conceal her identity, a woman who asked to be called Sara because she fears repercussions for speaking to the press told DW that protesters "communicate via text messages — that's the only way."

She cut the interview short as some protesters began flinging stones at the Education Ministry. Police pushed demonstrators and journalists out of the way, using water cannons to disperse the crowd.

"Social media is the most important public space today — more so than physical spaces," Besmir Semanaj, a prominent Albanian cybersecurity advocate told DW. "Young Albanians no longer organize through traditional structures such as political parties, associations or public appeals. Instead, they organize themselves where they spend much of their daily lives: on their cellphones."

"The most important communication channels include Instagram, WhatsApp groups for academic-year cohorts, departments and dormitories, Telegram channels for general announcements, and TikTok for sharing videos," Semanaj said. He added that people who are especially concerned with security use the Signal messaging app.

"This is a horizontal organizational structure, without individual 'leaders' and without a central command structure," Semanaj said. "That is exactly why the government is having such a hard time understanding and controlling the situation."

Semanaj said the Telegram messenger app had proven particularly useful for protesters. "Telegram channels allow you to reach tens of thousands of people at once," he said. "Notifications are sent out within seconds, and external control is more difficult to establish than on traditional platforms."

Anti-corruption protester "Sara" says communication occurs online Image: Kristi Çavo/DW

Rama: 'Hybrid war'

Rama has called the youth uprising a "hybrid war." He said protesters thought they could "make Albania a better country through TikTok and without even being able to string together more than seven coherent words." Though not all are terrorists, he said, he believes that "they are hostages to a certain mindset, a new ideology that has only one goal: to destroy, to turn everything upside down, to raze everything to the ground."

Over nearly five months, Rama has accused various "true" masterminds of organizing the anti-government and anti-corruption protests. He has alleged that the governments of Greece, Russia and Iran are stirring up dissent.

Most recently, Rama said it was "antifa" — or a decentralized movement of global antifascists — that had stoked anti-government and anti-corruption sentiments in Albania. "These are young people who have been radicalized and ideologically indoctrinated and who are acting under the pressure or influence of a new, dark force that has emerged in Europe and the United States, a force that the President of the United States has designated as a terrorist organization: Antifa," Rama claimed.

A protester hurls back a tear gas canister fired at students by police Image: Florion Goga/REUTERS

Redion Qirjazi, a security affairs researcher who focuses on violence prevention and conflict resolution, told DW that Rama's claim was not likely to prove true. "That is a serious accusation — one that requires equally compelling evidence," Qirjazi said. "To date, no verifiable evidence has been presented to prove the existence of an organized Antifa structure in Albania, let alone its involvement in coordinating the protests."

Qirjazi said Rama's reference to Trump's calling antifa a terror group was problematic. "Antifa is not a unified international organization with a centralized structure or leadership," he said, "but rather an umbrella term for various movements and groups united by the fact that they are, at their core, anti-fascist."

Sara said she rejected the "terrorist" label that Rama had attempted to slap on her and her fellow protesters. "There are groups that are willing to use violence — that's true — but I have nothing to do with them," she said. "As soon as I see violence, I walk away; I'm against it."

Is Rama deflecting?

Arlind Qori, the chairman of the Together Movement, a social-democratic opposition party with just one seat in Albania's parliament, said youths had taken to the streets out of dissatisfaction with the status quo rather than any particular ideology. "Young Albanians are outraged by the current socioeconomic conditions: the poverty, the fact that many of their parents have emigrated because they couldn't support their families, the decline of the education system, the lack of postgraduation prospects," Qori said. The students' central demand is for Rama to resign, he added "not a socialist revolution."

Arlind Qori says the protesters are voicing legitimate demands Image: Kristi Çavo/DW

"People aren't demanding anything radical," Qori said. "They merely want a corrupt head of government to resign — that's a fundamental and moderate demand. But Edi Rama continues to meet this demand with police violence and arrogance."

Qirjazi said Rama's allegations of foreign interference could be a strategy. "When a government faces protests and public discontent, linking demonstrators to extremism and foreign influence may serve to divert attention away from the actual causes and toward a national security narrative," he said.

"This can serve several political purposes: to delegitimize the protesters, to weaken their support among the public, and to justify a tougher crackdown in the name of law and order," Qirjazi said.

Semanaj said this was a common pattern in governments' efforts to dismiss dissent. "Protests are portrayed as acts of violence," he said. "Young people are cast as manipulated, and their legitimate concerns — conditions at universities, tuition fees, corruption and a lack of prospects — vanish from the news agenda."

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Lina Attalah: Mada Masr journalist sent for trial in Egypt
World.content:
Lina Attalah, who is accused of managing a website without a license, will go to court next week. Mada Masr has published reporting critical of Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's government.

Egypt's Supreme State Security Prosecution sent Mada Masr journalist Lina Attalah to stand for trial, the independent Egyptian news website said Thursday.

One of Madr Masar's co-founders, Attalah serves as the site's editor-in-chief. The website, which publishes in both Arabic and English, frequently features critical reporting related to Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's government.

What do we know so far?

Prosecutors questioned Attalah for six hours on Wednesday in New Cairo, Mada Masr said.

She is accused of running a website without a license and the publication of false news "with the aim of disturbing public peace." Under questioning, the latter allegation was dropped from the charge sheet in the trial referral.

The trial has been referred to a New Cairo misdemeanors court and is slated to begin on October 27.

Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr's legal counsel, said there was "haste" in the trial referral and said the trial beginning next week signals "unjustified urgency."

Al-Azhari said Attalah could face a financial penalty of between 1 million to 3 million Egyptian pounds (around €16,000 to €48,000; $18,000 to $54,000) if convicted.

Mada Masr said the organization has sought a license from the Egyptian government to run its news website since 2018 — the same year Egypt passed and ratified a law to regulate the press.

Egyptian authorities have been unresponsive over the past years to Mada Masr's attempts to procure a license, with Mada Masr later finding out in 2022 that its request was rejected. The site filed a lawsuit in 2022 and found out in 2023 that the rejection was due to missing documents.

The proceedings against Attalah come after Egyptian authorities arrested six journalists last month for independent fact-checking and investigative website Matsadaash (Egyptian Arabic for "don't believe").

Press freedom groups condemn actions against Attalah

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) expressed alarm about Attalah's referral to trial.

"Egypt is weaponizing its media law to punish independent journalism and intensify one of its worst crackdowns in years, which began with the arrest of the six Matsdaash journalists," the CPJ's director for Middle East and North Africa Sara Qudah said. "It is long past time for Egypt to end this campaign and allow independent media to report freely."

Reporters without Borders (RSF) had earlier said it was alarmed by prosecutors' questioning of Attalah.

According to RSF's World Press Freedom Index , Egypt ranks 169 out of 180 countries, with many of the country's biggest news outlets either state-owned or controlled by wealthy businessmen who submit to the will of the government.

Egyptian President el-Sissi came to power in a 2013 military coup against Islamist President Mohamed Morsi. Since then, el-Sissi has cracked down and blocked websites such as Qatar's Al Jazeera and The New Arab on allegations of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood.

World.title: 96% of world's coral reefs face critical risk of collapse, IUCN warns
World.content:
Almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs are at risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change the biggest threat. A new study found that 96% of reef systems are critically endangered.

Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change being the greatest threat, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on Thursday.

In the first systematic survey of the world's 127 tropical and subtropical coral reef systems, the IUCN said 96% were critically endangered, which is its highest risk category.

Shallow-water reefs are colorful coral ecosystems found at depths of up to around 40 meters (131 feet), and are home to a high level of biodiversity.

Among the reefs affected are Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Reef System and the reefs in the Red Sea.

"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said when it presented the study at the United Nations' COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.

Coral reefs are home to a high level of biodiversity Image: Yuddy Cahya Budiman/REUTERS

What are the threats to the reefs?

Worldwide, shallow-water reefs cover around 188,000 square kilometers(73,000 square miles).

Their corals are highly sensitive to temperature changes. This means when the water gets too warm, the corals expel the tiny algae living in their tissues, which provide much of their nourishment.

This then leads to coral bleaching and can ultimately lead to their death.

Overfishing is another major threat. In particular, the overfishing of parrotfish and groupers affects reef ecosystems since these fish help maintain ecological balance.

Coastal development, pollution, tourism and increasingly severe storms also contribute to reef degradation.

When hard corals disappear, their structures are often replaced by algae, rubble and sponges, leaving less diverse ecosystems that do not sustain as many species. Affected animals include reef fish, mussels, sea turtles, and sharks.

Sea turtles are among the animals that depend on coral reefs Image: Great Barrier Reef Foundation/dpa/picture alliance

Can the reefs still be saved?

"The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems," according to Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

The study uses a climate scenario developed by the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which expects global warming of around 2.7 degrees Celsius (4.86 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels by 2100.

Despite the bleak outlook, the IUCN said most reefs had not yet been lost. Without projections of future climate change and based on the changes over the past 50 years, only 24% would qualify as critically endangered.

"This gives us a critical window for action for us to scale up conservation efforts and climate action to prevent the worst outcomes from occurring," Gudka explained.

"The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people," he added.

IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar said it was "not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover."

"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them," she said.

World.title: Canada's Mark Carney visits Turkey to boost trade ties
World.content:
It's the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey. Canada and Turkey upgraded their relations to a "strategic partnership" as Canada seeks to diversify trade beyond the US.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Turkey on Thursday to kick off a two-day visit to the Mediterranean country.

During the visit, Carney met with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the Turkish presidential palace in Ankara.

Erdogan: A 'new era' in Turkey-Canada relations

The two leaders announced that the Canadian-Turkish relationship would be upgraded to a "strategic partnership," covering areas such as trade, energy and people-to-people ties.

"We've planted the seeds of something new: a strategic partnership that will create new opportunities for our workers and businesses, and greater security and prosperity for both of our peoples. With care and commitment, it will grow for generations to come," Carney said alongside Erdogan.

Erdogan said we "are starting a new era between Turkey and Canada," while hailing Carney as a leader with "common-sense and acumen." The Turkish leader said negotiations on a free trade agreement with Canada will begin before the end of 2026.

"We hope to increase our trade volume, which is currently around $3 billion (€2.6 billion), to $5 billion and then $10 billion. We will approximately double direct flights between our countries," Erdogan continued.

Turkey has a bigger military than Canada and is a global leader in drone production Image: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press/PA Images/picture alliance

Canada and Turkey, both members of the NATO military alliance, agreed to deepen their defense relationship during the visit.

Canada seeks to diversify trade relationships amid Trump tariff onslaught

The Canadian prime minister, a former central banker, is expected to meet with Turkish business leaders on Friday in Istanbul.

Carney's visit comes as Canada seeks to broaden its trade relationships with other countries beyond its southern neighbor. Nearly 70% of Canadian exports go to the United States.

Since reentering office in 2025, US President Donald Trump escalated a trade war against Canada and imposed tariffs on many Canadian goods, leading Canada to wean itself off the US.

Turkey has a population of over 86 million people and the world's 16th-largest nominal GDP as of 2026. Canada, meanwhile, has a population of over 41 million people and the 11th-largest GDP.

Amnesty tells Canada: Emphasize human rights in negotiations with Turkey

Carney's visit to Turkey also comes as Erdogan and his conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP) crack down on the opposition and critical media. In addition, the Turkish government has targeted the LGBTQ+ community with mass arrests.

LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ruhat Sena Aksenir, the Turkey director of human rights watchdog Amnesty International, said: "Canada must not treat human rights as secondary in the negotiations."

"Sustainable partnerships depend on accountability and respect for the rule of law," she continued.

The AKP has ruled Turkey since 2002, with the party, and particularly Erdogan, consolidating power.

According to human rights organization Freedom House , Turkey is "not free" and scores low in the areas of political rights and civil liberties. Reporters without Borders ranks Turkey 163 out of 180 on its World Press Freedom Index .

World.title: France's Macron says 'illegitimate' protests will be banned in coming days
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to ban unauthorized protests after France was rocked by violence and looting. As anger over public services and the cost of living grows, authorities are bracing for more protests.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that demonstrations organized by groups without legitimate authority would be banned in the coming days.

Over the past weekend, protests over the education system and the cost of living escalated into violence and looting, which the government blamed on ultra-left groups.

"Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic," Macron said after a special security meeting at the Elysee Palace with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers.

"The general recommendation is not to hold demonstrations in the coming days," he explained. "We want calm to return."

French business owners share harrowing accounts of violent protests To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Macron said the ban on protests aimed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.

"Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law, but alternative routes will be proposed," he added.

Fresh demonstration in Paris

In the wake of the past weekend’s violence, several cities had already implemented curfews for certain parts of town. Protests planned Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were banned from going ahead.

Authorities say a massive security operation was planned for the coming weekend to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s violence.

The historic city hall in Limoges was set on fire and partly collapsed on October 17 Image: Elise Cabane/PHOTOPQR/Populaire du Centre/MAXPPP/IMAGO

Student and university groups as well as unions have said they would continue to mobilize and hold protests. On Thursday, thousands gathered in Paris when a local court was said to have overturned the day's demonstration ban.

France's main student union, UNEF, has called for rallies on Saturday, while the Yellow Vest movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook the country in 2018 and 2019, has filed plans for a march through central Paris.

France: Why students are taking to the streets To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What are the protests about?

The protests started in September at a school near Paris over lack of funding for the education system.

The demonstrations then spread to other Paris suburbs and eventually to other French cities. They have since widened to also address the soaring cost of living and deteriorating public services.

On October 17, the protests escalated into the worst urban unrest in years when masked rioters clashed with police, looted shops and set cars and buildings on fire.

Two people have been arrested over an arson attack on the 19th-century Limoges city hall, French media reported.

Across France, there were around 2,700 arrests last weekend and hundreds of protesters, police and firefighters were injured.

French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said courts jailed 217 people in fast-track trials linked to rioting over the weekend, adding "this figure is continuing to rise a lot."

Macron on Thursday said talks between authorities, student groups, unions, and employers would take place on Monday. He stressed that dialogue over protesters' legitimate demands should continue.

The unrest comes just months before next year's presidential election, in which voters will choose Macron's successor.

World.title: Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
World.content:
As protests continue in France, the French police are under scrutiny after new allegations of police brutality. The force has a bigger arsenal than most in Europe.

Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.

The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups , not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.

France's protests grow

More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.

Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.

The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.

More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.

Some tools used by the French police are banned or rarely used in other countries Image: Manon Cruz/REUTERS

Weapons made for war?

The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.

Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests. In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.

"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."

Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.

What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades.

"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.

Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material ."

France: Why students are taking to the streets To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

French police: the 'most brutal' in the EU?

The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.

"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Roche.

He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.

"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."

Confrontation vs. de-escalation

Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.

Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.

"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."

Police arrested protesters in the German town of Lützerath, but with less force than at similar protests in France Image: Federico Gambarini/dpa/picture alliance

When can police officers use force?

According to international standards set by the United Nations , use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.

French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.

However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."

The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.

DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.

"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."

Experts are critical of the police's actions.

"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."

Less oversight than in the UK and Denmark

The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.

Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.

"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: El PSOE acepta un cara a cara con Feijóo el 16 de noviembre y sigue en el aire la celebración del debate a cuatro
World.content:
El Partido Socialista ha confirmado este jueves que participará en un cara a cara con el principal líder de la oposición el próximo 16 de noviembre, primer lunes de campaña electoral. De esta forma, Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo se volverán a encontrar en un debate organizado por una cadena privada, tal y como ocurrió el 10 de julio de 2023 en Antena 3 (Atresmedia), 13 días antes de las elecciones generales. Desde principios de octubre, el Partido Popular ya había confirmado su disposición para celebrar el cara a cara con el líder socialista en esa misma fecha. Los populares quieren que tenga lugar en la cadena privada Mediaset, aunque el PSOE no lo ha confirmado.

Los socialistas también se han mostrado a favor de participar en un debate a cuatro en RTVE el jueves 26 de noviembre y, aunque los populares coinciden en el día, piden que sea en Atresmedia. En RTVE, en cambio, proponen que se desarrolle un encuentro de los portavoces de los grupos políticos el lunes 23 de noviembre. Fuentes del PP señalan que “no habrá debate a cuatro en RTVE” con los dos candidatos presidenciales y que el partido “no entiende el intento de boicot del PSOE a Atresmedia”. “Los debates serán el 16 [de noviembre] en Mediaset y el 26 en la cadena en la que hace tres años sí le valía debatir a Pedro Sánchez”, insisten, en referencia al cara a cara entre Sánchez y Feijóo en 2023.

El debate a cuatro de la pasada campaña electoral se celebró la noche del 19 de julio de 2023 en RTVE, la cadena pública. Sin embargo, en aquella ocasión, Feijóo decidió no asistir al encuentro televisivo en el que, además de Sánchez, se presentaron los otros dos representantes de los partidos mayoritarios: Yolanda Díaz, de Sumar, y Santiago Abascal, de Vox. El popular explicó su ausencia con que no se había desarrollado en el formato que él quería ―un debate a siete, con las fuerzas minoritarias, que sí se había celebrado una semana antes con los portavoces―. El líder del PP también manifestó entonces que la directiva de la cadena pública se encontraba en una situación “alegal”: unos meses antes había dimitido José Manuel Pérez Tornero, que fue elegido presidente de la corporación gracias a un acuerdo entre PP y PSOE en esa legislatura, y Elena Sánchez Caballero ocupaba el cargo en interinidad.

Ante la ausencia de Feijóo, fue Abascal quien recogió las críticas de Sánchez y Díaz, que escenificaron la sincronía de la izquierda ―que más tarde se tradujo en el Gobierno de coalición―. El representante de Vox habló entonces en nombre de la derecha sin mencionar al PP y no develó si exigiría a los de Feijóo entrar al Gobierno en caso de que tuvieran los votos necesarios para una investidura ―finalmente, la suma de los diputados no fue suficiente para formar el Ejecutivo―. Fue, en general, un debate poco bronco, a diferencia del que habían mantenido Sánchez y Feijóo unos días antes.

Los socialistas ahora se han anticipado a que uno de los atriles del encuentro a cuatro quede vacío como en 2023, cuando, aseguran, se “hurtó” a los ciudadanos “la posibilidad de contrastar su programa [el del Feijóo] con el resto de fuerzas políticas”. Por ello, han aclarado que es “indispensable que ambos encuentros se produzcan”. La negativa del PP a celebrarlo en la cadena pública deja en el aire esta propuesta.

“A lo largo de nuestra historia democrática, los debates electorales siempre se han celebrado cuando ha gobernado el PSOE y únicamente se han obstaculizado o impedido cuando el Partido Popular ha estado en el Gobierno. Debatir no es una concesión partidista, es una obligación democrática con los ciudadanos”, ha señalado el PSOE. Los socialistas consideran que “al menos” deben existir dos encuentros entre los cabezas de lista, incluyendo el debate a cuatro, y han mostrado su disposición para asistir al “mayor número posible de debates electorales en las próximas semanas”.

Aunque no hay aún cadena confirmada para el cara a cara, el PSOE ha acotado que “no va a vetar a ninguna cadena privada de igual forma que no vamos a consentir, bajo ningún concepto, el veto a la televisión pública”. “El Partido Socialista no elegirá ni vetará a ningún grupo mediático. En su lugar, pide a todos los grupos que encuentren un acuerdo entre ellos y que emitan la señal en abierto para todas las cadenas, como ya se ha comprometido a hacer TVE”, añaden.

World.title: Inteligencia artificial y manipulación: nuevas claves para interpretar lo que vemos en internet
World.content:
El avance de la tecnología permite a los estafadores generar fraudes digitales con mayor rapidez y, sobre todo, más convincentes. Frente a esta nueva generación de engaños hay hábitos sencillos que pueden ayudarnos a no caer: parar, pensar y verificar

Si un internauta de 2019 pudiera navegar por las redes sociales de hoy quedaría perplejo ante la dificultad para distinguir algunos vídeos generados por inteligencia artificial (IA) generativa de vídeos reales. En tan poco tiempo la tecnología ha evolucionado tanto, señala Carmen Torrijos, lingüista computacional especializada en este campo, que el ojo humano puede tener grandes dificultades para detectar determinados contenidos creados de manera sintética. Y los estafadores se aprovechan de ello. “Ahora tienen la posibilidad de crear anuncios, webs o de imitar la voz de personas en poco tiempo y con un resultado excelente”, añade.

Ese mismo internauta dudaría ante los sofisticados fraudes que cada día se lanzan a la red, como los anuncios de inversiones en los que se suplanta la identidad de personas conocidas, las tiendas online que venden productos inexistentes o las notas de voz que llegan de repente en forma de mensaje en nombre de un familiar que pide ayuda. “Vivimos un tiempo en el que consumimos contenidos cortos que nos exigen una reacción muy rápida, por eso son el caldo de cultivo perfecto para los engaños digitales”, alerta la experta.

Para luchar contra tanto espejismo existen tecnologías para detectar contenido sintético, pero ninguna ofrece una detección universal y completamente fiable, agrega Torrijos. Solo queda entrenarse en unos hábitos básicos para cambiar nuestra exposición a este tipo de trampas. Siga leyendo.

Anuncios generados con IA, una oferta demasiado buena para ser cierta

En las redes sociales proliferan contenidos creados con IA que utilizan imágenes, sonidos o textos impactantes, a menudo protagonizados por figuras públicas, para difundir contenidos falsos o manipulados y conseguir que el usuario haga clic. Estas son algunas señales para detectarlos:

Suplantan la identidad de personas o entidades conocidas. Recurren a fotos o vídeos generados con IA de famosos, sin su consentimiento, para explotar la confianza que genera un rostro popular. También pueden utilizan la imagen de compañías conocidas o medios de comunicación a través de sus logos y sus colores corporativos.

Prometen un producto o un servicio extraordinario. Lo más común, explica Martín Vigo, fundador de la empresa de ciberseguridad Triskel Security, son las inversiones que ofrecen grandes beneficios en poco tiempo. También se crean anuncios engañosos de videojuegos para el móvil. “Muestran unos gráficos de alta calidad en la publicidad que luego no se corresponden con los reales, mucho más básicos”, agrega el experto.

Crean una falsa sensación de urgencia. Presentan sus ofertas agresivas como una promoción limitada o exclusiva para quien la recibe.

El fraude se produce fuera del anuncio. Llevan al usuario a una página donde se le exige un pago por el supuesto servicio, se le solicitan sus datos personales a través de un formulario de captación, o se le redirecciona a una conversación en una plataforma de mensajería donde se continúa con la estafa.

El mayor engaño tras los anuncios: la estafa de inversión. Las falsas inversiones son uno de los principales usos fraudulentos de los anuncios generados con IA. En este fraude, el delincuente actúa como asesor financiero al frente de una empresa falsa, desde la que promete rentabilidades muy altas si se le confía dinero o criptomonedas. Los estafadores aseguran que la cantidad inicial puede multiplicarse hasta por diez.

Después de realizar el primer pago, el estafador suele mostrar a la víctima los rendimientos a través de una aplicación falseada. Entonces le sugiere una aportación mayor. En el momento en el que el inversor decide recuperar su capital, se le exige más dinero, en concepto de comisión o pago de impuestos. Si paga, la estafa continúa; si no, el estafador se esfuma y con él todo lo invertido.

Comercios ‘online’ falsos, creados al detalle mediante IA

La IA permite a los estafadores dar forma a tiendas digitales con todos los elementos que hoy tienen este tipo de páginas. Ofrece la posibilidad de elaborar textos, imágenes de productos y un diseño coherente, incluso falsas reseñas de usuarios, explica Vigo. “Muchas de las herramientas de IA generativa dan la posibilidad de hacer todo esto en cuestión de horas. También clonar una web de alguna marca conocida”, detalla el experto. “Si, además, se compra un dominio que se parezca mucho al original, pero que no sea exactamente igual, el engaño resulta todavía más difícil de identificar”, completa. Vigo recomienda conocer sus características para estar alerta:

Pueden imitar con gran precisión la apariencia de páginas legítimas. Cuidan al máximo todos los aspectos, como la política de privacidad, las condiciones de compra, entre otros. Incluso pueden disponer de un servicio de atención al cliente mediante un bot de IA.

Ofrecen precios anormalmente bajos. Su principal gancho son los descuentos, especialmente en productos de marcas conocidas, bajo el pretexto de una falsa liquidación, un excedente de existencias o una promoción temporal.

‘Comercializan’ productos atractivos. En muchas ocasiones promocionan artículos con propiedades extraordinarias, como aparatos para eliminar lesiones o cremas antiarrugas que garantizan resultados prodigiosos; también juguetes o electrodomésticos con funcionalidades de ciencia ficción o muebles de formas sorprendentes.

Incorporan sistemas de pago reales. Utilizan plataformas de pago como las de las tiendas legítimas porque su objetivo es obtener el dinero de los compradores; muchas solo aceptan transferencia, Bizum o métodos sin protección al comprador. Existen varios tipos de comercios fraudulentos en línea, describe Vigo: los que no realizan ningún envío una vez se ha realizado el pago, los que despachan un producto de mucha peor calidad que el anunciado y los que su único objetivo es capturar los datos de la tarjeta de la víctima.

Se publicitan en buscadores y en redes sociales. Suelen promocionarse a través de anuncios creados con IA en las principales plataformas.

Aprovechan acontecimientos comerciales. Multiplican sus anuncios en momentos de grandes compras como los periodos de rebajas, Black Friday o Navidad, donde se camuflan entre el aluvión de ofertas.

Tienen una vida muy corta. Suelen desaparecer una vez que han obtenido un determinado número de pedidos o de datos de los usuarios. Lo más habitual es que vuelvan a aparecer con otro dominio y otra identidad.

Pueden fingir la tramitación del pedido. Suelen enviar correos electrónicos falsos sobre el estado del pedido, con órdenes de compra y facturas falsas e incluso información ficticia sobre el seguimiento del envío. Lo hacen para reforzar la apariencia de legitimidad en todos los canales de contacto con el comprador y prolongar el engaño.

Tres segundos para suplantar una voz, el auge del ‘deepfake’

La gran revolución de la IA generativa, señalan los expertos, es la creación de vídeos y audios que imitan la apariencia y la voz de una persona con tal precisión que engañan tanto a algoritmos como a humanos. La palabra deepfake combina los conceptos en inglés deep learning, que significa aprendizaje profundo, y fake, que quiere decir falso.

“Hoy, esta tecnología ha avanzado mucho”, explica Torrijos, lingüista computacional especializada en IA. “Antes se necesitaba hasta una hora de voz para clonar a una persona con garantías. Hoy bastan tres segundos para lograr una reproducción aceptable y 15 para obtener una imitación óptima”. Este es el uso fraudulento más extendido en la actualidad y el que más preocupación genera, añade Torrijos. De esta técnica se valen los estafadores en fraudes tanto en el ámbito familiar como en el empresarial. Y se usa en mensajes cortos, explica la experta, ya que camuflan mejor cualquier fallo de la clonación y no permiten a la víctima pararse a reflexionar.

La estafa del hijo en apuros. El estafador clona la voz de un familiar de la víctima, que suele ser un hijo o un nieto, y le envía, desde un número desconocido, mensajes cortos a través de una plataforma de mensajería instantánea. En esas notas de voz el estafador plantea una emergencia, como que ha perdido el teléfono, y escribe desde el de un amigo, o ha tenido un accidente y se ha quedado sin batería y ha de realizar un pago con urgencia. Se trata de una estafa que con el avance de la IA se produce cada vez más por notas de voz. Los estafadores suelen estudiar a sus víctimas a través de sus redes sociales, en el caso de que no sean privadas, señala el Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad (INCIBE). De esta manera pueden recopilar información sobre los miembros de la familia, así como números de teléfono y audios de voz con los que generar la estafa.

La estafa del CEO. En este tipo de fraude, el delincuente suplanta la identidad de un directivo de una empresa, habitualmente un CEO (siglas en inglés de chief executive officer, puesto equivalente a director ejecutivo). El objetivo es engañar a uno de sus empleados para que revele información privada que puede ser utilizada posteriormente o realice una transferencia a una cuenta ajena a la compañía. La Agencia de la Unión Europea para la Cooperación Policial (Europol) señala que cada vez es más común el uso de la IA en esta modalidad de estafa a través del deepfake. La clonación de voz es el uso más extendido, pero la facilidad para clonar la imagen que permiten los programas de última generación está multiplicando los ataques en los que también se suplanta la apariencia física y los movimientos de directivos.

Ante fraudes perfeccionados con IA, ¿qué se puede hacer? El principal recurso de los usuarios de internet para no caer en estafas generadas con IA es la misma que para el resto de fraudes: pararse un segundo a pensar y verificar por otro canal. Una pausa antes de actuar. Muchos fraudes están diseñados para provocar una reacción inmediata, como una supuesta oportunidad de inversión que termina en unas horas, un producto rebajado temporalmente o un familiar que necesita dinero de manera urgente. Esta premura reduce el tiempo que la víctima puede dedicar a pensar y favorece que actúe instintivamente. Al mismo tiempo, señala Vigo, la exigencia de una respuesta inmediata ha de ser un indicador que haga saltar la alerta de que se puede estar frente a un engaño. Verificar por otro canal. Si un contenido genera dudas sobre si es real o ha sido generado con IA, los expertos recomiendan comprobarlo por otra vía. En el caso de un anuncio generado con IA. No clicar en el anuncio. Si promete una inversión extraordinaria, un producto muy rebajado, ponerlo bajo sospecha. Se debe buscar información por otro canal, como los buscadores, o comprobar si la empresa se encuentra en el registro oficial de la Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores (CNMV), que cuenta con una sección de Advertencias sobre Entidades No Autorizadas. Se actualiza periódicamente, pero que no aparezca ahí no significa que sea fiable, puede deberse a que aún no la haya detectado.

En el caso de una tienda online. Si se ha llegado a la web a través de un anuncio, conviene realizar una búsqueda por otra vía, como los buscadores. Se puede recabar más información añadiendo al nombre términos como estafa, fraude, reclamaciones... Si se trata de una marca conocida, comprobar la URL, si se parece al nombre de la marca pero no es igual, conviene desconfiar.

En el caso de recibir una petición urgente de un familiar o de un directivo. Comprobar la petición por el número habitual de esa persona, nunca devolver la llamada desde “llamadas recientes o perdidas”. Vigo recomienda acordar de antemano una contraseña familiar: una palabra o una pregunta con una respuesta que solo conozcan los miembros de la familia. Si alguien llama o envía una nota de voz pidiendo dinero con urgencia, basta con pedirle esa palabra. Una voz clonada puede imitar el tono y la forma de hablar, pero no puede saber algo que nunca se ha dicho en público. En el caso del superior, contactar por las vías oficiales o incluso, si fuera posible, confirmar la petición en persona.

World.title: La huelga de camioneros en el sur de Italia vacía los supermercados y desabastece de combustible aeropuertos y gasolineras
World.content:
El Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni aprueba ayudas de 550 millones para acabar con los cortes de carreteras y la escasez de suministros

Una oleada de protestas de transportistas por el aumento del precio del carburante sacude desde hace días el sur de Italia, donde los bloqueos en las carreteras están provocando problemas de abastecimiento en supermercados, gasolineras y aeropuertos. La huelga ha llevado al Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni a aprobar de urgencia este jueves, en un consejo de ministros extraordinario, ayudas por valor de 550 millones de euros para poner fin a los cortes de carreteras y la escasez de suministros.

El desabastecimiento afecta a las regiones de Sicilia, Calabria, Campania o Apulia, donde esos bloqueos de la red viaria están dificultando la distribución de mercancías. En Nápoles, una de las ciudades más afectadas, la situación es crítica tras casi una semana de huelga de camioneros: las estanterías de numerosos supermercados están vacías, especialmente las de productos frescos, y muchas gasolineras se han quedado sin combustible.

Las consecuencias de la huelga han llegado incluso a los aeropuertos. Los de Reggio Calabria y Crotone se han quedado sin combustible para los aviones, mientras que el de Nápoles también registra restricciones en el suministro. Las compañías aéreas han recibido instrucciones de comenzar a repostar en otros aeropuertos para garantizar la continuidad de los vuelos. Las universidades han recurrido a la enseñanza a distancia ante las dificultades de movilidad.

Supermercado sin existencias en las baldas, este jueves en Nápoles. Alessandro Garofalo (LaPresse/AP)

Los transportistas reclaman medidas urgentes para compensar el impacto del aumento del precio del gasóleo, mientras el Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni ha prometido movilizar más de 1.000 millones de euros en ayudas al transporte por carretera. De momento, ha aprobado este jueves ese decreto de ayudas por más de 550 millones de euros destinados a refinanciar la deducción fiscal al sector, reforzar la bonificación del precio del gasóleo y suspender las cuotas del leasing de los vehículos de transporte durante cinco meses.

El anuncio de ese descreto ha disminuido ya algo la tensión. Según el diario La Repubblica, la mayor parte de los piquetes en las carreteras del sur de Italia se ha disuelto, pero persisten algunos puntos críticos, sobre todo en el cruce de la autopista A1 con la A30, en la provincia de Caserta, en la región meridional de Campania.

“No se trata de promesas, sino de recursos que ya están llegando al sector. El Ministerio de Transportes ya ha empezado a pagar”, ha dicho Meloni en un vídeo publicado en sus redes sociales, en el que ha pedido que se despejen las carreteras bloqueadas.

El sector del transporte llevaba tiempo acumulando tensiones por el aumento de los costes, especialmente del combustible, pero el malestar estalló la semana pasada con protestas que comenzaron en Apulia y Calabria y se extendieron después a otras regiones del sur, como Sicilia, Campania, Basilicata y Molise. En Sicilia y Calabria los camioneros suspendieron las movilizaciones hace unos días después de que el Gobierno se comprometiera a desbloquear las ayudas económicas pendientes y estableciera una vía de diálogo para negociar nuevas medidas. Sin embargo, el conflicto ha seguido abierto y los bloqueos han continuado en otras zonas, especialmente en Campania. A las protestas se han sumado también los agricultores, afectados por el aumento de los costes de producción.

Varios camioneros durante la huelga en Nápoles, este jueves. Alessandro Garofalo (LAPRESSE)

Ante el agravamiento de la situación, Giorgia Meloni convocó el consejo de ministros extraordinario de esta jornada que se cerró con la aprobación de los 550 millones para apoyar a los transportistas y al sector agrícola. Mientras tanto, las autoridades han puesto en marcha dispositivos especiales de seguridad para garantizar el transporte de productos esenciales y evitar que los bloqueos agraven el desabastecimiento.

El principal motivo de las protestas es la subida del precio del gasóleo, que ha disparado los gastos de los transportistas y reducido sus beneficios. El sector reclama una rebaja de impuestos, ayudas económicas y la posibilidad de cobrar más por sus servicios cuando aumente el precio del combustible.

Actualmente el litro de gasóleo cuesta de media 2,30 euros en las autopistas italianas, mientras que el de gasolina se sitúa en torno a los 2,05 euros.

Según la organización agraria Coldiretti, el precio del gasóleo agrícola prácticamente se ha duplicado desde el inicio de la guerra en Irán, y ha pasado de 0,85 a 1,62 euros por litro. La organización también denuncia los elevados costes del transporte de mercancías en Italia, de 1,12 euros por kilómetro, superiores a los 1,08 euros por kilómetro de Francia y a los los 1,04 euros de Alemania, según sus estudios.

Ante la creciente tensión provocada por las protestas, el Gobierno ha endurecido su respuesta frente a los bloqueos y ha recordado que la Policía identificará a los camioneros que bloquean las carreteras del sur de Italia para retirar los piquetes y permitir de nuevo la circulación. Según el Ministerio del Interior, hasta el miércoles la Policía había identificado a 1.339 personas, denunciado a 71 y multado a otras 242. Además, las fuerzas de seguridad han escoltado a unos 500 camiones para garantizar el transporte de mercancías. El Ejecutivo insiste en que las protestas no pueden impedir la circulación ni perjudicar el abastecimiento de la población.

Mafia

A este panorama se suma la preocupación por posibles infiltraciones mafiosas. El ministro de Justicia, Carlo Nordio, ha asegurado este jueves que es “muy probable” que las organizaciones criminales estén aprovechando las protestas para sus propios intereses. El ministro del Interior, Matteo Piantedosi, también ha pedido a las fuerzas de seguridad que extremen la vigilancia ante el riesgo de infiltraciones de los clanes.

Aunque la subida del precio del combustible afecta a los transportistas de toda Italia, las protestas se han concentrado en el sur, donde hay una mayor presencia de pequeñas empresas y camioneros autónomos, que tienen más dificultades para afrontar el aumento de los costes. A ello se suman problemas específicos de algunas regiones, como Sicilia, donde los transportistas también deben pagar los ferris para trasladar sus mercancías a la península.

A las protestas de transportistas y agricultores se ha sumado este jueves la movilización de los pescadores, que han dejado sus barcos amarrados en numerosos puertos italianos, especialmente en el Adriático. El sector denuncia el encarecimiento del gasóleo, que en algunos casos supone más del 60 % de sus gastos, y las restricciones europeas que limitan los días de pesca. Las asociaciones reclaman medidas urgentes al Gobierno para afrontar la crisis.

Desde que comenzó la guerra de Irán el pasado febrero, que ha disparado los precios de los combustibles, el Gobierno italiano es consciente de que el encarecimiento de la energía es uno de sus principales problemas. Para intentar contener las subidas, ha recurrido en varias ocasiones a rebajas temporales de los impuestos sobre los carburantes, pero estas medidas no han sido suficientes para evitar una crisis que ha acabado por estallar y que ahora está afectando también a la distribución de alimentos y otros productos esenciales.

World.title: Unions call off bus and regional train strikes for two weeks
World.content:

Unions FNV and CNV have suspended their weekly strikes in regional public transport for two weeks after employers made new commitments on a collective labour agreement, broadcaster NOS reported on Wednesday.

The suspension means Thursday’s planned strike did not go ahead, the unions said in a press release.

The unions announced in early October they would strike one day a week after talks broke down. Staff at operators including Arriva, Keolis and Qbuzz walked out for the first time last week, cancelling many buses and regional trains across the country.

The unions are demanding a 9.5% pay rise over two years and better conditions for older staff.

World.title: Gambling regulator hits illegal casino with record €37m fine
World.content:
The Dutch gambling regulator KSA has issued a record fine of €37 million on a company for running a dozen unlicensed online casinos.

EOD Code SRL, which says it is registered in Costa Rica, offered games to players in the Netherlands through sites including Instantcasino and Skyhills without a Dutch licence, KSA said on Thursday.

KSA inspectors were able to register and gamble on the sites with no measures in place to stop people in the Netherlands using them. Several of the sites had no visible age checks and accepted cryptocurrency and other anonymous payment methods.

The investigation began with Instantcasino and later uncovered 11 more sites run by the same company. The KSA based the fine on an estimate of the company’s Dutch revenue.

Online gambling was legalised in October 2021, with the government arguing a regulated market would draw players away from illegal sites. But the KSA estimated last year that more money goes to unlicensed sites than to legal ones.

In August, radio station BNR found that illegal operators were targeting Facebook and Instagram ads at people on Cruks, the national register that bars them from gambling. The cabinet set out plans in June to ban online gambling advertising and bonuses.

If you are concerned about your own or someone else’s use of alcohol, drugs, or gambling, the Jellinek addiction helpline can be reached on 088 505 1220 or at jellinek.nl. The line is staffed in Dutch and English on weekdays, 1pm to 5pm.

World.title: Airbnb to hosts: no more asking guests to wash the dishes
World.content:
In addition to increasingly strict rules for hosts renting out their homes on Airbnb – including limits on the number of nights, guest caps and permit fees – there are now new rules to abide by: they can’t ask their guests to do the dishes or remove bed sheets.

Airbnb introduced a new policy on house rules earlier this week that will go into effect on November 20, 2026. Among them are what the company considers “reasonable requests”, which Airbnb defines per chore.

“You may not ask guests to wash everything and store the dishes, but you may ask them to put the dishes in the sink,” says the site.

“You may not ask guests to pick up the bed linen or put the laundry in the washing machine, but you may ask them to collect used towels.”

And: “You may not ask guests to take the garbage and dispose of it elsewhere, but you may ask them to separate their residual waste and recyclable waste in the designated waste bins in the accommodation.”

But “reasonable” appears to be a relative term. Airbnb will let hosts, for example, ask guests to put their garbage in animal-resistant containers if there are bears in the area.

“It’s ridiculous,” said one former Airbnb host who doesn’t want to be named. “The rules were changing all the time, getting more restrictive, which made it increasingly hard to make any money at all. I’m glad I got out of it before I can’t tell my guests to clean up after themselves. What’s next? Will we have to provide sunbeds for them?”

According to the booking website, the world’s largest for private stays, landlords already charge their guests a cleaning fee. Making them clean more is unfair, says Airbnb, and leads to guest dissatisfaction.

Airbnb has faced criticism for years in many cities where it operates, with detractors saying it leads to higher rents, less housing for locals and less livable neighbourhoods, especially in smaller cities with huge tourist populations like Amsterdam and Barcelona.

World.title: Get help with careers, homes and more at IamExpat Fair The Hague
World.content:
The IamExpat Fair is returning to the Grote Kerk in The Hague on Saturday November 7 with more exhibitors than ever, three international centres from across South Holland and large sections for families and health.

The IamExpat Fair, now in its 24th edition, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, from housing and careers to schooling and leisure, including special offers only available for attendees. Tickets go for €6 online, or €10 at the door.

“We have an exciting lineup of exhibitors and workshops this year in The Hague,” says events manager Claire Leunissen.

“From exhibitors specialised in preparing newcomers for the inburgering exams, to career coaches experienced in advising expats, and stocking the health & leisure section with physical and mental resources, we’re confident that services at the IamExpat Fair will help internationals thrive. ”

Workshops, presentations and centres

Experts will run workshops throughout the day on topics including buying a house and securing a mortgage, job hunting and help with lifestyle and health. Places are limited, so make sure to book your chosen sessions in advance – you can sign up here.

The Hague International Centre will have a large stand, joined by representatives from across the province, including Leiden International Centre and the Rotterdam International Center, to answer practical questions about settling in the region.

Learning Dutch and finding work

For newcomers working toward the inburgering exams, there are resources from Inburgering Online and Easy Dutch, alongside language schools including Language Institute Regina Coeli, and Bart de Pau.

Career stands and coaches include recruitment agency Undutchables and Work & Worth Coaching, while Work in South Holland will explain the state of the labour market across the region’s main industries.

Families and health

The Family & Kids section brings together several international schools, including the International School of The Hague, The British School in the Netherlands, International School Delft and Optimist International School. There is also kids’ area where families can play games together.

The Health & Leisure section is one of the largest at the fair, with exhibitors ranging from mental health services to dentists and chiropractors.

The IamExpat Fair The Hague takes place in the Grote Kerk on Saturday November 7 from 10am to 5pm. Free tickets are available online while they last; after that, entry costs €6 in advance or €10 at the door. The first 1,000 visitors receive a free tote bag.

World.title: Police shut 30 webshops linked to counterfeit pill deaths
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Thirty websites were taken offline and three men arrested earlier this week in connection to sites that sold counterfeit pills that led to the deaths of three people.

The suspects – a 35-year-old man from Kwintsheul, a 39-year-old man from Rotterdam and a 66-year-old male from The Hague – are suspected of “offering, selling and supplying illegal drugs”, including sedatives, sleeping pills and painkillers like oxycodone, which contained extremely potent synthetic opioids known as nitazenes.

Nitazenes can be many times stronger than morphine and more lethal than fentanyl.

Police say the victims bought the prescription-only pills on websites Slaappillen.net or regionapp.net shortly before they died, and are holding the suspects responsible for running them.

Whack-a-mole

Even though Slaappillen.net was taken down last year, police say the men continued to sell the counterfeit drugs through other websites, which kept popping up as soon as others were taken down.

But according to police, this time they not only took the web shops offline, but confiscated the servers they ran on.

“We have taken down the entire technology behind the websites,” Ron van Brussel told NOS. He is responsible for tackling serious organized crime at the National Investigation and Interventions Unit. “This makes it more difficult to make a restart.”

Both the servers and data have been seized for investigation, and more arrests have not been ruled out.

The police searches were carried out in five locations, including homes and a storage box in The Hague. Crypto wallets, cash and valuables were seized.

With this week’s arrests, police say the main players from the group are now in custody. But, they add, the sale of illegal drugs is far from over.

“There are several criminal groups that keep these types of sites online,” said Van Brussel.

World.title: Are you financially fit for your life in the Netherlands?
World.content:
New to the Netherlands or a longer-term resident looking to get your finances organised to make the most of your Dutch life? A little planning, a few local habits and some expert coaching will soon have you in the best financial shape.

The foundation of any fitness plan is the basics, so first of all you need to establish what your monthly costs are likely to be. Alongside your rent or mortgage repayments, you’ll have to pay for health insurance, council taxes, public transport, gas and electricity, and perhaps a gym membership.

“If you are financially fit, you are able to meet all your monthly and annual payments, save some money and live the life you would like to have at that moment,” says Ame Pots, a financial health coach with ABN Amro who helps expats make the most of their money.

What costs can you expect?

ABN Amro is hosting a free webinar on October 28 to explain how to get financially fit in the Netherlands.

You will have to pay for insurance. Health insurance, for example, will cost you upwards of €160 a month from next year, and you will have to pay the first €400 of insured treatment. You can cut the monthly premium by around €25 if you raise your voluntary deductible by €500, but that means you’ll need to increase your savings so you can pay if you do fall ill. If you want supplementary insurance, such as dental coverage or extra physiotherapy, you will pay more.

By the way, the six-week window for changing health insurer kicks off in mid-November, so now might be a good time to start shopping around for a better deal.

You’ll also have to pay your local authority for waste collection and the water board for water usage. How much you pay depends on the size of your home and how many people live there, but between €250 and €450 a year is the norm in most places. If you are a homeowner, you will pay slightly more. These bills often arrive at the same time of year, in the spring, so you’ll need to make sure you have enough savings to cover them as well.

“We rarely use credit cards, and this surprises a lot of people,” Ame says.

Some bills are monthly, others come once a year

If you live in rented accommodation, you may have to pay service costs, which can range from around €50 to over €250 a month if you live in a building with a lift and lots of amenities such as co-working spaces or a gym. The monthly service fee is an estimate, and you will get a final invoice once a year. Rents also go up once a year, usually in July, by a percentage set by the government. For 2027, the increase in the non-rent-controlled sector, where most expats live, will be 4.4%.

You can keep an eye on your gas and electricity bills if you have a smart meter. If you pay too little to cover your usage, you will be invoiced for the extra costs and your monthly payment is likely to increase. If you pay too much, you’ll get the difference back.

“All this means that you need to really plan out your spending over the year,” says ABN Amro expert Ame. “For example, if you have the 30% ruling, will you still be able to meet your payments when it ends in five years’ time?”

Once you understand the costs you face, create a budget that includes fixed spending, savings and fun stuff. Remember to adjust it if your financial situation changes.

Why is banking in the Netherlands different?

“It’s important to explain to new arrivals how the financial system works in the Netherlands, because it may be very different to back home,” says Ame. “For example, we rarely use credit cards, and this surprises a lot of people from countries where they use a credit card as part of their regular spending.”

You’ll need a Dutch bank account for your salary, your rent and pretty much everything else. The Netherlands runs on digital payments, with debit cards, internet payments and payment request apps dominating how the Dutch spend their money.

“If I ask people how much they spend on rent or groceries, they often give a round number – €100 or €200 – but in practice it is more than that,” says Ame. “Once you are aware of what is really happening in your finances, you will understand how much you can actually spend each month.”

How can you improve your financial fitness?

What to know more about how to stay financially fit in the Netherlands. Join ABN Amro’s free webinar on Wednesday, 28 October, 12:00–13:00 CET. Register now

World.title: Afghans washed up on Texel were human smuggling victims
World.content:
Two Afghan men whose body parts washed ashore on Texel in 2023 were victims of a vast human smuggling network led by infamous migrant smuggler Idriss Ghazi Kareem, according to an investigation by regional broadcaster NH and investigative TV programme Zembla.

The Afghan refugees, Samiullah (20) and Ahmad Jan (27), were only identified this summer. They had boarded a rubber dinghy on the night of August 12, 2023, along with 66 others just north of Calais, in an attempt to cross the English Channel. The boat’s engine failed and, after an explosion, the vessel tore apart.

Although 60 men survived, six were declared dead when found. Samiullah and Ahmad Jan, though, had gone missing.

Two months later, a single foot still in a shoe and a torso washed up on Texel. Dutch detective Fetze Venema worked with the Red Cross to identify the remains, including tracking down the relatives of the missing men in Afghanistan for DNA testing.

Idriss Ghazi Kareem

Following the incident, French authorities dismantled a huge human-trafficking network led by Idriss Ghazi Kareem. He was tried with eight others in Paris last year and sentenced to 15 years in prison for, among other things, procuring boats and other equipment for migrants to cross the English Channel.

The court found he earned hundreds of thousands of euros a year from his people-smuggling operations, which he continued to organise from prison.

Kareem had visited the Netherlands several times, including just three days before the fatal accident. The Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border control, says the country plays a key role in people-smuggling.

“It involves the import, transit, and storage of nautical equipment that is transported to the French coast, where it is then used to ferry migrants across to Great Britain.”

The Marechaussee has not commented on the latest media investigation, saying it “may be part of an ongoing investigation”.

Additional research by NH and Zembla found that at least 26 people, including eight women and two children, have died this year attempting to cross the English Channel in unseaworthy boats.

“Floating coffins”

Much of the equipment – from the rubber boat to its motor and life vests – was substandard. “These rubber boats are not seaworthy and generally originate from China,” national public prosecutor for migration-related crime Petra Hoekstra told Zembla. “They are imported into the Netherlands via Turkey.”

And, he said, the smugglers knew that. “For us, that is an aggravating circumstance. They believe that the money outweighs a human life. And that means they are deliberately placing people in floating coffins.”

World.title: Rotterdam police arrest AI scammers over €400k thefts
World.content:
Police in Rotterdam have rounded up a gang who ran a sophisticated phishing scam using a fake banking app that stole nearly €400,000 from 170 victims.

The gang set up a bogus bank helpdesk service that targeted customers by phone and asked them to download an app that could read the NFC chip on their bank card.

Police arrested the two men behind the operation, a 23-year-old man from Vaassen, and a 25-year-old man from Ede, on October 4. On Tuesday they appeared in court, where a magistrate extended their detention for 90 days.

The fraudsters made the scam more plausible by using AI-generated voices to read out messages telling their victims to check if Google Pay had been installed on their phones by their bank.

When they saw it had not, they were told to press 1, which connected them straight to the fake helpdesk.

The victims were told to install the app and hold their card to their phone, allowing the criminals to download their details. At the same time accomplices would try to hack into the account using the card’s PIN.

Ruben van Well, head of the Rotterdam cybercrime team, said the victims ranged in age from their twenties to their eighties. “We found a lot of young people had been defrauded,” he said. “The victims also came from all over the country.”

Police confiscated hundreds of thousands of euros in cryptocurrency following the arrests and took the fake app and server offline. “We are not ruling out further arrests,” said Van Well.

Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin. He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons. After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused. On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then. Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week. "Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway. The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban. Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN. The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”. Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty. A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”. However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026 The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”. In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations. Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia. Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states.
