World.title: Kazakhstan, ICAO Pledge to Strengthen Civil Aviation Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov met with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar in Astana on Oct. 21 to discuss strengthening cooperation on aviation safety, infrastructure development and the country’s transit potential.

During the meeting, Bektenov highlighted the strategic importance of cooperation with ICAO as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its transport and logistics potential, develop aviation hubs and expand its role as a regional transit center.

Salazar praised Kazakhstan’s progress in aviation safety. According to him, the country ranks among the world’s top 20 states under ICAO’s aviation safety assessment, with a score of 95.7%. He also noted Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop airport and air navigation infrastructure, while domestic airlines are modernizing their fleets and expanding international routes.

Kazakhstan’s civil aviation sector has recorded significant growth in recent years. Over the past five years, the industry’s gross output increased 6.5 times to $2.9 billion. In 2025, the country’s airports handled 31.8 million passengers, while the international route network expanded to 161 destinations.

The officials attributed these results to the consistent implementation of international standards and the expertise of Kazakh aviation professionals. They also highlighted the importance of the Civil Aviation Development Master Plan through 2050, which is currently being developed. The document is expected to set strategic priorities for modernizing the sector, establishing aviation hubs and strengthening Kazakhstan’s international competitiveness.

Bektenov and Salazar reaffirmed their commitment to closer cooperation between Kazakhstan and ICAO to further improve aviation safety and support the sustainable development of civil aviation.

Salazar arrived in Kazakhstan to attend Aviation Safety Week 2026. His visit marks the first official visit by an ICAO secretary general to a Central Asian country, according to the prime minister’s press service.

World.title: Kazakhstan Approves Military Reform Plan to Modernize Armed Forces
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Security Council has approved a military reform plan aimed at modernizing the Armed Forces, restructuring military management and training, and establishing a new Unmanned Forces branch, according to the presidential press service.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev chaired an Oct. 21 Security Council meeting, where he called for the creation of a modern, mobile and technologically advanced army in the shortest possible time.

“Special attention is required for service security, command culture, and the efficient use of public resources. The interaction between the army and society also needs to be changed. This is a matter of comprehensive reform. Half‑hearted solutions will not yield the necessary results,” Tokayev said.

Deputy Security Council Chair Aida Balayeva presented the main provisions of the plan, which was developed with consideration of international military experience, modern warfare and proposals from domestic specialists. Defense Minister Aidos Myrzakhmetov reported on the planned modernization of the Armed Forces.

The plan introduces a two-stage model of compulsory military service. Recruits will spend the first six months training at military training centers and the next six months serving in military units, focusing on combat training and carrying out tasks as part of their units.

The reform also includes measures to strengthen servicemen’s safety and protect their rights. Kazakhstan plans to establish military adviser positions and an authorized body for servicemen’s affairs to reinforce military discipline. Other initiatives include expanding the unified military-patriotic training system, increasing the number of specialized military schools and improving initial military training.

The Armed Forces will also adopt a new information and communications strategy and improve educational work based on the constitutional principle of Law and Order. Organizational measures under the plan are scheduled for completion by the end of 2026, while the main conceptual reforms are expected to be implemented in 2027.

Tokayev also instructed officials to complete by the end of the year the work of a commission conducting a comprehensive review of the Defense Ministry.

He stressed that military security is a national priority requiring coordinated efforts across relevant government bodies. The government and the Security Council will coordinate implementation of the reform plan.

World.title: Deer born at Tbilisi Zoo continue to return to wild – video
World.content:
Nine red deer born at Tbilisi Zoo have returned to the wild — or, more precisely, to a semi-wild environment. They have moved to Algeti National Park, near Tbilisi.

Life at the Tbilisi Zoo: video

Deer born at Tbilisi Zoo were first moved to Algeti National Park in the summer of 2025. It was the first attempt to reintroduce the species into the wild in Georgia.

The process will continue in the coming years until the park has enough deer to restore the population.

The idea of restoring Georgia’s deer population emerged in the 1990s, when their numbers in the country fell sharply. Poaching and uncontrolled hunting contributed to the decline. Today, the red deer features on Georgia’s Red List of threatened species. In 2023, at the initiative of the Ministry of Environmental Protection and with funding from the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency, authorities drew up a national plan to restore endangered species.

Zurab Gurielidze, a professor at Ilia State University and director of Tbilisi Zoo, led the development of the plan. As part of the project, authorities established an enclosed area of around 60 hectares in Algeti National Park, providing the deer with a suitable habitat and the conditions they need.

The process will take time and require continuous monitoring, adequate protection and cooperation between various agencies. Once the deer population in the park reaches a sufficient level, authorities will release the animals fully into the wild, where they will be able to live independently.

World.title: ‘Another attempt is being prepared to deprive Armenia of its independence’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on threats to Armenia’s independence

“For the first time in our history, the ‘metropolis’ is not drawing us towards it. Instead, it seems to be saying, ‘We will push you away’,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said, commenting on a report on the possibility of suspending Armenia’s participation in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).

Speaking at his weekly briefing, he stressed that the documents governing the EAEU do not give member states the authority to expel another member. The report makes the same point.

However, he drew a parallel with another organisation operating under Russia’s auspices: the Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO).

“The CSTO allows for such a possibility. Since the EAEU and CSTO have essentially the same member states, the question arises: why don’t they expel Armenia from the CSTO?” Pashinyan asked.

According to the prime minister, the restrictions Russia has imposed on Armenia in recent months have failed to achieve the results that certain circles, both inside and outside the country, had hoped for. The measures include a ban on exporting most Armenian food products and other goods to Russia. Pashinyan said the move had failed to achieve either its economic or political objectives.

The prime minister sees Russia’s economic pressure as an attempt to trigger domestic political instability and deprive Armenia of its independence.

Journalists asked him to clarify whether Russia itself was destabilising Armenia.

“I said very specifically: certain circles in the Russian Federation — yes. Is that news to you?” he replied.

Nevertheless, Pashinyan said he was confident that Armenia was “resilient enough and would overcome this situation too”.

“Time will tell”: on the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council’s report

Armenian journalists asked Pashinyan what he thought about the risk of a catastrophic economic downturn if Armenia left the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), as experts from the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council have forecast.

“Time will tell. Our main priority is Armenia’s continued development and the protection of our independence and sovereignty, as well as diversifying our relations. We will follow this path,” the prime minister replied.

In his view, forces both inside and outside Armenia are trying to exploit the current situation and problems in Armenia-Russia relations. Their aim, he said, is not only to trigger political instability in the country but also to effectively abolish Armenia’s independence.

The prime minister did not specify which forces he meant. However, he noted that several such attempts had taken place over the past three years. First, he recalled the events in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023, particularly the exodus of the entire Armenian population from their homeland while Russian peacekeepers were present.

“The aim was to channel the flow of people into Armenia, while calls for a change of political power were coming from well-known quarters,” he said.

Pashinyan considers the situation surrounding the 2026 parliamentary elections to be a second attempt. He appears to be referring to hybrid attacks on Armenia and an alleged attempt to bring Armenians living in Russia to the polls to vote for pro-Russian forces.

“A third attempt is now being prepared. It is part of a certain ‘secret plan’ that is currently the subject of widespread discussion,” he concluded.

Samvel Karapetyan, leader of the pro-Russian opposition party Strong Armenia, has recently spoken openly about a “secret plan” to change the government. He has invoked the plan when asked what steps the opposition intends to take to overthrow the authorities after losing the election.

The prime minister believes the struggle is political rather than economic:

“The aim is to provoke domestic political instability in Armenia. As a consequence, they intend to take control of the Armenian state. In other words, they want to deprive Armenia of its independence — first de facto, and then de jure.”

He added that events over the past several decades had also been directed towards achieving this goal.

“There will be no apocalypse”: on a possible rise in Russian gas prices

Pashinyan stressed that there was no guarantee that gas prices would remain unchanged. He also said that prices had risen at least twice over the past eight years.

“Gas prices have gone up before. You simply didn’t know about it. They rose in 2019 and then — I can’t remember exactly whether it was in 2022 or 2023. The point is that, thanks to citizens who work in Armenia, create added value and pay the taxes required by law, the Armenian government managed to ensure that the public did not notice these increases.”

The prime minister is convinced that even if gas prices rise by 69%, as the EAEU has warned, the Armenian economy will not face an “apocalypse”.

“Those who talk about an apocalypse simply don’t understand economics. I say that quite plainly.”

As the prime minister noted, people also predicted an “apocalypse” in 2018, 2019 and 2020. Yet Armenia’s economy grew throughout those years, Pashinyan said.

“You cannot erase history”: on relations with Russia

Speaking about his communications with Putin and Armenian-Russian relations, Pashinyan stressed that the relationship had always been positive and would remain so. However, he said this did not mean Armenia could simply erase the events of 2020, 2021 and 2023 from its history.

“That does not mean our history will no longer record the weapons we paid for but never received. Nor will it erase September 2022. That month, when Azerbaijani forces invaded Armenia’s sovereign territory, the CSTO failed to fulfil its treaty obligations to Armenia. This had extremely serious consequences.”

The prime minister’s conclusion was clear: dependence on a single country for weapons, gas and even apricots poses a threat to the state.

“We must address this threat. We are increasing Armenia’s level of independence. Are we doing so deliberately? Let’s put it this way — yes. We are consciously, you could even say relentlessly, strengthening the independence and sovereignty of the Republic of Armenia.”

Pashinyan concluded the discussion by saying that “the current situation is much more serious than many people think”. He said Armenia’s independence and statehood were at stake.

“We must learn the lessons of history,” he added.

Pashinyan on threats to Armenia’s independence

World.title: Georgia appoints new special envoy for relations with Russia: what does it mean?
World.content:
On 21 October, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze appointed Giorgi Zurabashvili, the first deputy foreign minister, as his special representative for relations with Russia. The post had remained vacant since December 2025.

The announcement came on the same day that the Constitutional Court began hearing on the merits a lawsuit by the ruling party seeking to ban five opposition parties.

Opposition figures have interpreted the timing as a signal to Moscow. Kobakhidze, for his part, insists that the appointment does not mark a new phase in relations with Russia.

What Kobakhidze said

The prime minister announced the appointment at a briefing in the government administration. Asked by a journalist whether this marked the beginning of a new phase in efforts to reset relations with Russia, he said it did not.

Kobakhidze said the Georgian Interests Section at the Swiss embassy in Moscow had been working actively. However, the government had decided that it needed an additional channel alongside the section to “resolve the conflict peacefully, maintain humanitarian ties and develop trade and economic relations”.

The prime minister also denied that the decision was linked to recent restrictions Russia had imposed on products from Georgian companies.

“Of course, work on these issues is a priority overall, but this was certainly not the basis for the decision,” Kobakhidze said.

Asked about restoring diplomatic relations between Georgia and Russia, Kobakhidze said an obstacle remained: “This situation has not changed, and neither has our position.”

Regarding Russia’s demand that Tbilisi provide Sukhumi and Tskhinvali (the capitals of Abkhazia and South Ossetia) with guarantees of non-use of force, the prime minister said Georgia could not sign an agreement with them because it could not recognise them as independent states in any form.

Giorgi Zurabashvili

Giorgi Zurabashvili will also retain his post as first deputy foreign minister, which he has held since July 2025. He previously served as Georgia’s ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to Ireland from 2019 to 2024.

The special envoy role

Since 2012, diplomat Zurab Abashidze had served as Georgia’s special representative for relations with Russia. He held regular meetings with Grigory Karasin, a Russian deputy foreign minister. This channel of talks became known as the “Abashidze–Karasin format”.

Zurab Abashidze and Grigory Karasin, 2019. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

In March 2024, Irakli Kobakhidze moved Abashidze to the post of his adviser and appointed Giorgi Kajaya as his replacement. However, the government administration told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that Kajaya left the post on 1 December 2025.

The public learned that the position had remained vacant only in August 2026, when Kobakhidze answered a question from journalists.

Meanwhile, on 6 October 2026, Zurab Abashidze became Georgia’s non-resident ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia and Albania.

“A cynical signal”: opposition reaction

Grigol Gegelia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia–Lelo opposition coalition, whose party the government is seeking to ban, believes that:

“This is a direct, cynical signal that the parties are being banned at Russia’s behest, and that on the very same day, in a synchronised move, a person is appointed to pursue warmer relations with Russia.”

According to Lasha Parulava, a member of the governing council of another opposition party, the United National Movement, the appointment serves no economic purpose and is a symbolic gesture.

“Here, at the Constitutional Court, they are dismantling the pro-Western opposition while, at the same time, appointing a special representative to Russia.”

The founder of the United National Movement and Georgia’s third president, Mikheil Saakashvili, wrote on social media that “the rapid restoration of diplomatic relations with Russia is being prepared without de-occupation, which amounts to formally endorsing capitulation”.

Moscow welcomed the appointment. Konstantin Zatulin, first deputy chairman of the Russian State Duma’s Committee on CIS Affairs, called the decision a step in the right direction.

“The decision to appoint a special representative is a step in the right direction. Relations between Russia and Georgia must develop,” Zatulin said.

Relations with Russia under Georgian Dream

Restoring relations with Russia was one of the main campaign promises of the current ruling party, Georgian Dream. The special representative post was established shortly after it came to power, on 1 November 2012. Following the August 2008 war, Tbilisi and Moscow had communicated directly only through the Geneva International Discussions.

The Abashidze–Karasin format helped restore exports of Georgian wine, mineral water, fruit and vegetables to the Russian market in 2013. The authorities also softened their rhetoric towards Russia.

On 20 June 2019, mass protests broke out in Tbilisi after Russian MP Sergei Gavrilov addressed the Georgian parliament. Russia subsequently suspended direct flights to Georgia. In May 2023, Russian President Vladimir Putin lifted visa requirements for Georgian citizens and restored direct flights.

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgian Dream declined to join international sanctions against Russia, saying it wanted to protect Georgia’s economy.

From January to August 2026, Russia accounted for around 62.5% of the value of Georgia’s wine exports.

On 9 October, Russia’s food safety watchdog suspended imports of products from seven Georgian companies. On the same day, Russia’s Foreign Ministry again demanded that Tbilisi provide Sukhumi and Tskhinvali with guarantees of non-use of force and begin delimiting the so-called state borders.

Georgia’s special representative for relations with Russia

World.title: Court begins hearing case to ban opposition parties in Georgia: first-day developments
World.content:
On 21 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court in Batumi began hearing on the merits a lawsuit brought by the ruling Georgian Dream party, which seeks to ban five opposition parties: the United National Movement, the Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists.

Below are the main events and statements from the first day of hearings. The court rejected all the opposition’s motions. The session ended at 19:00.

The hearings continue today, 22 October, and will also take place on 23 October. The court has until 24 June 2027 to deliver its ruling. Four of the seven judges must vote in favour for the court to uphold the claim.

Opening of the hearing

● The court hearing began at 12:00. Georgian Dream is represented in court by MPs Archil Gorduladze, Giorgi Kakhiani, Tengiz Sharmanashvili and Tornike Cheishvili.

● The United National Movement was represented by Ana Tsitlidze, Khatia Dekanoidze and lawyer Zaza Bibilashvili; the Coalition for Change by Nika Gvaramia; Lelo by Badri Japaridze, Giorgi Sioridze and lawyers; and Gakharia for Georgia by Berdia Sichinava.

● The Federalists did not attend the hearing, as the party believes there is no point in taking part in the proceedings.

● Two leaders of the Coalition for Change, Nika Melia and Elene Khoshtaria, are following the proceedings from prison. Melia was arrested for failing to appear before a parliamentary commission whose findings now form the main basis of the lawsuit seeking to ban the parties.

● Only journalists from Georgia’s Public Broadcaster were allowed to bring cameras into the courtroom. Other media outlets followed the hearing on the court’s YouTube channel. Until now, the Constitutional Court had been the only court exempt from the ban on filming that applies in courts of general jurisdiction.

Calls for judges to recuse themselves

● The hearing began with a motion to disqualify the judges. Ana Tsitlidze, leader of the United National Movement, called for all seven members of the court’s plenary session to recuse themselves. She read out each judge’s biography and argued that the panel could not act freely and fairly.

● Tsitlidze described the proposed ban on the parties as “a decision taken by the Kremlin against Georgia’s sovereignty and freedom”.

Presiding judge Revaz Nadaraya responded: “Make your political assessments elsewhere. This is a courtroom, where rules, procedures and the law apply. You are free to make assessments, but somewhere else.”

● Tsitlidze then called Nadaraya himself a member of the “judicial clan”.

Nadaraya replied: “You must present your position with legal justification. When you use such insulting language, the court will not accept it. I will have to issue a warning and may have to order you to leave the courtroom.”

Tsitlidze then replaced the word “clan” with other terms.

● Tsitlidze also called judge Eva Gotsiridze a “member of the clan”. Regarding judge Vasil Roinishvili, she highlighted the fact that he had served as deputy chief prosecutor in 2008–09, during the United National Movement’s time in power.

● Lelo also called for three judges to recuse themselves. The Coalition for Change joined its motion. Gakharia for Georgia did not state its position.

● The plenary session rejected all the motions for recusal. Nadaraya explained that a judge’s biography or past career, if someone dislikes it, does not constitute legal grounds for disqualification. He also recalled that the plenary session had rejected a request for judge Manana Kobakhidze to recuse herself, describing that decision as “a high-standard ruling”.

On 9 October, the plenary session refused to let Kobakhidze, one of the founders of Georgian Dream, recuse herself. She subsequently left the court.

“One party, one proceeding”

● The court also rejected a motion by Gakharia for Georgia to hear its case separately from those against the other four parties. The party’s representative, Berdia Sichinava, called for the principle of “one political party — one proceeding” to be upheld.

The party put forward two arguments, both of which Sichinava outlined at a briefing on 20 October, the day before the hearing. First, the court must assess each party’s constitutionality individually. Sichinava called this “a minimum legal obligation and standard” that the court should meet, at least formally.

Second, Gakharia for Georgia is the only opposition party that took up its seats in parliament rather than surrendering its mandates. Sichinava argued that including it in the lawsuit undermines Georgian Dream’s narrative that it seeks to ban only so-called “boycott parties” that reject the authorities’ legitimacy. He also described the ruling party’s approach as unconstitutional.

Nadaraya explained that the court would base its decision on each defendant solely on the facts relating to that party. He added that the law would not allow the court to issue an adverse ruling if the evidence proved insufficient.

Witnesses: from Saakashvili to Ivanishvili

● The United National Movement asked the court to summon the party’s founder, Georgia’s third president Mikheil Saakashvili, and former party chairman Levan Khabeishvili as witnesses. The court rejected the motion.

● The United National Movement also sought to summon Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder and honorary chairman of Georgian Dream, along with current and former senior officials who had previously served under the United National Movement government. Tsitlidze argued that if the court wanted to ban the party for “systemic crime”, these people should answer questions about whether the alleged crimes were indeed systemic.

Nadaraya replied: “The plenary session has not seen a specific connection to the case or the lawsuit, or any indication of what exactly these witnesses would confirm.”

● The court ordered Khatia Dekanoidze to leave the courtroom while she was arguing in favour of summoning Ivanishvili. She said Ivanishvili ran the country single-handedly and was steering Georgia closer to Russia.

Nadaraya warned her several times, saying she was making political statements rather than explaining the legal grounds for calling Ivanishvili as a witness. The judge then instructed a court usher to remove Dekanoidze from the courtroom.

The Tsulukiani commission’s findings: the main basis for the lawsuit

● The second half of the day focused on the findings of a parliamentary commission led by Tea Tsulukiani. Parliament established the commission on 5 February 2025 to investigate the United National Movement’s time in power from 2003 to 2012.

The opposition considers the commission, like parliament itself, illegitimate. Several opposition leaders have been arrested for failing to appear before it. Georgian Dream filed its lawsuit on the basis of the commission’s findings, which also form part of the case documents.

● The Coalition for Change asked the court to exclude the commission’s findings from the evidence. Nika Gvaramia said the findings underpinned 95% of the lawsuit. He argued that the commission itself had been established in breach of the Constitution, which requires the opposition to make up half its membership. In his view, the commission could not legally operate without meeting this requirement.

● Gvaramia and Nadaraya clashed while he presented the motion. Nadaraya reprimanded Gvaramia for making political assessments.

● Georgian Dream representative Archil Gorduladze argued that the commission had been established lawfully because all parliamentary groups had the opportunity to join it. “The defendant’s problem lies with the facts cited in the findings, not with the content of the findings themselves, which cover all those facts,” he said.

● After several hours of debate, the plenary session refused to exclude Tsulukiani’s commission findings from the evidence.

What happened outside the courthouse

● A protest took place outside the courthouse while the hearing was under way. Police deployed around the perimeter of the building.

● Nineteen non-governmental organisations issued a joint statement describing the hearing as a particularly grave stage in Georgia’s autocratisation. They also noted that, according to the Central Election Commission’s official results, the parties Georgian Dream wants to ban received 784,830 votes in the 2024 parliamentary election — almost 38% of the total.

● German Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Kathrin Deschauer said in Berlin: “This is another step in this trend, which is increasingly distancing Georgia from the European Union and weakening domestic democracy.” She added that Germany would convey its concerns to the Georgian side.

● The European liberal party ALDE called on the European Union to impose tougher sanctions on those responsible within Georgian Dream.

● Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, released a video statement saying: “Today is a shameful day for Georgia and Georgian statehood.” She also criticised Gakharia for Georgia for seeking a separate hearing. According to Zourabichvili, the party was “somehow trying to ingratiate itself and present itself as saying: ‘Look, I’m good, I’m a good slave, and I’ll serve you even more.’”

● Georgian Dream MP Giga Parulava advised Zourabichvili to improve her vocabulary and “come down to earth”.

Reactions after the hearing

● Georgian Dream representative Tengiz Sharmanashvili said the discussion was beginning to focus on legal issues and that he felt more optimistic.

● Archil Gorduladze said the opposition’s motions to disqualify the judges were an attempt to turn the proceedings into a political debate.

“We will not allow you to politicise this case,” judges also told the opposition several times yesterday.

● Ana Tsitlidze said the first day had exposed the proceedings as a formality and that the decision had already been made. Giorgi Sioridze, representing Lelo, said the judges appeared “disorganised” and that their refusal seemed “helpless”. Nika Gvaramia said the opposition needed the allegations to be set out individually, as it could not respond to a “collective phantom”.

Ban on the opposition in Georgia

World.title: Another Azerbaijani citizen found in Armenia after illegally crossing the border, reportedly a shepherd who got lost
World.content:
Azerbaijani shepherd crosses into Armenia

A new incident has occurred on the Armenia–Azerbaijan border after an Azerbaijani citizen entered Armenian territory illegally. Armenia’s National Security Service confirmed the incident on 22 October.

Yashar Ali Gasimov, born in 1968, reportedly lost his way on 19 October. “Appropriate steps are being taken to return the Azerbaijani citizen,” the National Security Service said.

Armenian media had been reporting since 19 October that an Azerbaijani shepherd had crossed the border illegally and been taken to military police. Some reports claimed he was carrying a white flag.

On 21 October, Azerbaijan’s State Border Service responded to a query from Azerbaijani media, saying that “no such incidents have occurred in the territory under its control”.

The incident has caused concern in both countries following another recent border incident. On 1 October, Azerbaijani serviceman Nasimi Musayev was detained in Armenia. According to Armenian investigators, he illegally crossed the border, entered a house in the village of Shaki in Syunik province, opened fire and wounded a woman. Criminal proceedings have been launched against Musayev. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said he would stand trial in Armenia. He also said Azerbaijan had not requested his transfer and stressed that Yerevan and Baku had agreed to handle cases involving servicemen separately from other matters.

Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan, responding to a question about the incident, said shepherds can get lost and accidentally cross the border in either direction. He stressed the importance of resolving such situations constructively.

World.title: Russian-led EAEU bloc warns Armenia of possible ‘serious blows’ to its economy
World.content:
Report on suspension of Armenia’s membership of EAEU

Four countries in the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) may discuss suspending Armenia’s membership of the bloc. A report prepared by experts from the intergovernmental council of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan says so.

The report’s main argument is that Armenia would face serious economic difficulties if it left the Eurasian Economic Union. These would include a 15.6% contraction in GDP.

“All the figures in this report are exaggerated by around 50%,” Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan said in response.

He assured journalists that the impact on the country’s economy would be negligible, at around -0.61%. Papoyan cited figures from a study conducted in Armenia. The country set up a working group to assess the potential consequences of leaving the EAEU. It included representatives of the Central Bank and two ministries: the economy and finance ministries.

Unlike members of the ruling party, the parliamentary opposition considers the figures in the report alarming. Arthur Khachatryan, an MP from the Armenia bloc, said that even if the forecast proved only half accurate, the consequences would be “apocalyptic”.

Moscow has yet to comment on the document. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the presidential administration had not yet reviewed the report.

Context

At a meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council in Astana on 29 May 2026, the presidents of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan issued a joint statement. They expressed concern about Armenia’s moves to strengthen ties with the European Union. In their view, European integration by an EAEU member could pose risks to the economic security of the bloc’s other countries.

They urged the Armenian authorities to hold a nationwide referendum as soon as possible on whether to choose the EAEU or the EU.

“We are working within the Eurasian Economic Union and will continue to do so until a choice between the European Union and the EAEU becomes unavoidable,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan replied at the time. He stressed that the people would make the decision in a referendum. However, he said he currently saw no grounds for a nationwide vote on the issue. He explained that Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make such a choice: “Until Armenia officially applies for EU membership or comes close to obtaining candidate status, holding any referendum would make no sense.”

The heads of state also instructed their representatives to prepare a report by December 2026 on “the possible consequences of suspending the Treaty on the Eurasian Economic Union in respect of the Republic of Armenia”.

A closer look at the report

According to the report, Armenia’s actions contradict an obligation set out in Article 3 of the EAEU Treaty. The article requires member states to help create favourable conditions for the union to fulfil its functions and to refrain from actions that threaten its objectives.

The authors apparently mean a law adopted by Armenia’s parliament to launch the process of joining the EU. The EAEU may also have taken note of Armenia’s more active political dialogue and growing economic ties with the European Union.

The report again calls for a referendum in Armenia on “the EAEU or the EU”. The authors note that if the decision to suspend Armenia’s EAEU membership goes ahead, the suspension could remain in force until the referendum takes place.

However, the authors themselves acknowledge that the EAEU Treaty contains no explicit mechanism allowing member states to unilaterally suspend another country’s membership.

Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan nevertheless invoke the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. The report says the four countries could consider adopting a joint decision to suspend Armenia’s membership under the convention’s provisions.

The document specifically warns that suspending Armenia’s membership would reduce the total volume of trade with other EAEU member states by 55.6%. The EAEU report also warns of the following consequences:

the reintroduction of customs controls and duties, comprehensive sanitary inspections and taxation of goods;

a 30–50% decline in exports of Armenian-made goods and a reduction of more than 90% in the re-export of goods;

a 15.6% contraction in the country’s GDP, a 14.9 percentage-point rise in inflation and a 14.6% fall in consumption;

an increase in the price of gas for Armenia from $177.50 to $300 per 1,000 cubic metres, a rise of 69%;

tighter restrictions on labour migration for Armenian citizens.

How Yerevan has responded to the report

“Armenia has always honoured its obligations to the EAEU in good faith”

Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan said Armenia had always honoured its obligations to the EAEU in good faith.

“There are no obligations that we have failed to fulfil. We see this as an economic dispute, one that also concerns economic restrictions.”

Papoyan said Yerevan had lodged a complaint with the Eurasian Economic Commission and was awaiting a meeting on the issue, scheduled for 3 November.

“What do the EAEU rules say? They say that if you believe you have been treated unfairly — for example, if someone has imposed unjustified restrictions on you — you have the right to file a complaint.”

The dispute concerns economic restrictions that Russia imposed on imports of Armenian products. They have been in force since May and remain in place. Other EAEU member states have also backed them.

Although Armenia has already filed a complaint, the minister doubts it will secure a favourable ruling. He noted that the commission requires consensus, meaning all member states — including Russia — must agree.

As for the threat of higher gas prices, Papoyan expects a negative impact.

“A change in gas prices can have varying effects: one scenario could see a 5% impact, another 7% or more. Even a 1% increase in the price would be highly undesirable.”

However, the minister said that even a rise in gas prices would not have consequences so severe that Armenia’s economy could not cope with them.

“In principle, I find this acceptable, even normal. Everything should be paid for at market prices. If we do not pay the market price for something, we ultimately pay for it in some other way.”

Amid debate over a possible increase in the price of Russian gas, some Armenian experts and residents say that “Armenia has spent decades paying for cheap gas with its sovereignty”.

“They cannot expel Armenia from the EAEU”

Hasmik Hakobyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, is not worried about Armenia being expelled from the EAEU because no such procedure exists.

“They cannot expel Armenia from the EAEU, even if every other member state wants to.”

She stressed that Armenia is not leaving the union and has expressed no intention of doing so. Under EAEU rules, the only way to end membership is for the country itself to decide to withdraw.

“We want to continue cooperating in the same spirit and, where possible, discuss all issues and challenges at the negotiating table,” she said.

Commentary

According to analyst Vahe Davtyan, the most interesting part of the document concerns the potential losses for other EAEU member states. It says that suspending Armenia’s membership would not cause them serious economic problems. In Russia’s case, for example, the projected decline in the total volume of imports and exports of goods and services would not exceed 1%.

“The report’s political message is crystal clear. Economic pressure on Armenia could prove virtually painless for the other EAEU countries, while dealing a heavy blow to Armenia itself,” he argues.

He warns that if Armenia leaves the EAEU, the sectors hardest hit would include agriculture, food processing, alcoholic beverage production and light industry.

“These are industries for which the Russian market has been one of the main destinations for sales for many years.”

On the possibility of higher prices for Russian gas, the analyst notes:

“Suspending membership of the EAEU does not automatically mean that gas prices will be revised. The inclusion of this scenario in the document can therefore be seen as a political signal.”

In Davtyan’s view, the report’s authors have overlooked an important detail: bilateral agreements between Armenia and Russia also govern gas supplies. Nevertheless, he stresses that any change in gas prices would inevitably affect electricity generation costs and the competitiveness of Armenian industry.

World.title: German foundations leave Georgia: what the crisis in Berlin-Tbilisi relations means
World.content:
Two German foundations, the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, have ceased operations in Georgia, where they had worked for more than two decades.

The move follows the adoption of a law on grants that requires foreign foundations to obtain government permission to operate in Georgia. The two foundations failed to secure approval and announced their withdrawal from the country.

Two other German foundations, the Heinrich Böll Foundation and the Friedrich Ebert Foundation, have resumed operations after a pause — at least for now.

The problems facing German foundations in Georgia are not viewed in isolation. Instead, they are seen as another consequence of repressive legislation and a clear sign that relations between Tbilisi and Berlin have reached an impasse.

Germany was among the first countries to support Georgia and express solidarity with it in the early years after independence. However, relations between Georgia and Germany have deteriorated over the past several years.

The crisis deepened in 2024, when the Georgian government’s decision to suspend European integration, its adoption of repressive laws and its crackdown on protests drew sharp criticism from the German government.

The Georgian authorities responded by launching a campaign to discredit Germany’s ambassador and the country as a whole. Germany, in turn, imposed visa restrictions on some members of the ruling Georgian Dream party. It also suspended planned development projects worth €237 million with the Georgian government.

Germany is more than just a partner country for Georgia. It is one of the European Union’s most influential political players, while Georgia remains a candidate for EU membership. The deterioration in Georgian-German relations therefore goes beyond diplomatic disagreements.

What German foundations did in Georgia

All four German foundations had operated in Georgia since the early 2000s. Their aim was to support the country’s democratic development and strengthen civil society. They worked with government agencies, civil society organisations, young people, researchers, women and minority groups. Their activities covered a wide range of areas, and they implemented dozens of projects across the country that benefited hundreds of people.

Dea Metreveli, who holds a doctorate in philology, headed the state-run Book Centre for many years. She says it would have been very difficult for the centre to attend prestigious events such as the Frankfurt Book Fair without support from the German foundations. Georgia’s participation, which also brought Georgian authors to the fair, had been a major achievement.

“When we prepared for the fair in 2018, the foundations had already laid the groundwork for our participation. They helped us organise various events. Much of this tremendous success came from our cooperation with them,” Metreveli recalls.

Giorgi Butikashvili, a lecturer at Ilia State University, worked for 12 years as a programme manager at the South Caucasus office of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation.

He recalls, among other things, joint Georgian-Abkhaz projects and dialogue between religious communities. The foundation’s support made these initiatives possible. He says Georgian government agencies took part in all these projects.

“When projects involving Abkhaz participants began, for example, everything was coordinated with the Ministry of Reconciliation. We planned everything in line with the government’s strategy. Germany was not pursuing its own interests; it was helping Georgia pursue its national interests. The German government provided resources that the Georgian state itself lacked.”

Metreveli also remembers a specific project involving Abkhaz participants: a joint collection of works by contemporary Georgian and Abkhaz women writers, published in Georgian and Abkhaz. It was one of the last projects the Konrad Adenauer Foundation helped implement.

“Imagine a single book featuring four contemporary Georgian women writers alongside four Abkhaz women writers living in Sukhumi. They worked together for a year, discussed the concept of the publication together and became friends.”

The Soviet Past Research Laboratory (SOVLAB) also worked with all four German foundations at various times over many years. Irakli Khvadagiani, a historian and researcher at the organisation, says their support enabled SOVLAB to publish a range of works on the Soviet and Russian occupation, state terror and the stories of countless individuals.

“From 2012 onwards, the state effectively pursued a passive-aggressive approach. It had no agenda for memory politics. On the contrary, it left the door wide open to Russian disinformation. Then, from the late 2010s, the authorities moved into a more aggressive phase: attacks on us and civil society, and the closure of archives. Under these conditions, we were able to keep working largely thanks to these foundations.”

Khvadagiani says the foundations helped fill the vacuum that the Russian regime was creating in the fields of historical memory, research and the teaching of contemporary history. None of this work would have been possible without the support of Germany’s partners.

Beyond the foundations’ work in Georgia itself, the German government also supported hundreds of young Georgians in pursuing higher education in Germany. One of them is Mamuka Andguladze, chair of the Media Advocacy Coalition. Funding from Germany’s DAAD programme enabled him to earn a doctorate in media law in Germany.

“It was very important to me to have the opportunity to study in Germany. Hundreds of young people had the same opportunity. And what happened to the knowledge they gained? They brought it back to our country. You get an education and return home to help build better institutions, a better court system and better elections.”

Why the problem facing the foundations is about more than the foundations themselves

Tina Khidasheli, Georgia’s former defence minister and now head of the organisation Civic IDEA, believes the problems facing German foundations should not be viewed solely as a consequence of repressive legislation.

In her view, this is the first clear sign of deteriorating relations between Georgia and Germany. She says Germany has historically played a key role in the development of the Georgian state, dating back to the early 20th century. Georgia’s state institutions are rooted in German legislation, law and institutional structures. Politicians from successive generations have attached particular importance to relations with Germany, making the current situation unprecedented.

For Giorgi Butikashvili, the situation clearly confirms an attempt to consolidate autocratic rule in Georgia.

“The closure of foreign foundations was the final stage in Russia, Belarus and Azerbaijan, when the authorities decided to consolidate autocracy once and for all. This is a symptom of autocratic regimes,” Butikashvili stresses.

What does the tension with Berlin mean for Tbilisi?

According to Irakli Khvadagiani, the crisis in relations with Germany means that Georgia remains behind an Iron Curtain.

“This is a continuation of the imperialist and aggressive policy Russia pursued, including during the Soviet era. Its sphere of influence — the territory it claims, which it sees as encompassing much of Eurasia — must remain behind an Iron Curtain. No outside influence, no ties, no cooperation.”

Tina Khidasheli, meanwhile, does not believe the Georgian Dream government singled out Germany in particular. She points out that its representatives have used similar rhetoric against other European countries. Nevertheless, she sees this as a dangerous sign.

“We are talking about a country that belongs to the G7. A country that is the strongest economically, or by any other measure. Moreover, since Brexit, Germany has become the most important player in the European Union. It carries the greatest weight internationally when it comes to European policy,” Khidasheli says.

She recalls that Germany blocked Georgia’s path towards NATO membership in 2008. It is therefore logical and natural that Georgia’s state policy has always aimed to establish and maintain good relations with Berlin.

“Germany’s veto, Germany’s opposition, mean that we have no chance not only of joining any future round of enlargement, but even of establishing serious relations with either the European Union or NATO.”

Meanwhile, relations between Georgia and Germany have reached an impasse despite the fact that several senior Georgian officials built their professional careers in Germany.

From 2003 to 2020, Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili worked for the German Agency for Technical Cooperation (GTZ) and the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ), including as head of the Georgian team.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze earned a doctorate in law at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf.

Another Georgian Dream member, Nikoloz Samkharadze, who chairs parliament’s Foreign Relations Committee, also studied in Germany on a Konrad Adenauer Foundation scholarship. In 2003, the foundation funded his master’s degree in European studies at the University of Hanover.

For Tina Khidasheli, the Georgian government members’ ties to Germany are the main reason for the current problems.

“[Georgian Dream founder] Bidzina Ivanishvili demanded that they ‘sort things out’ with Germany, but they failed to do so. This subsequently gave way to aggressive rhetoric,” Khidasheli believes.

She adds that if Georgia wants to make progress towards joining the European Union or NATO, it is crucial for Berlin to support Tbilisi. Otherwise, such progress is impossible. In her view, however, this is precisely what Georgian Dream wants to prevent.

“That is their goal: to squander the opportunity for European integration and then make it look as though they are not to blame.”

World.title: Old enemies in same cell: crime boss beaten, codes and politics. What is happening in Georgia’s prisons?
World.content:
The beating of crime boss Peikrishvili in Georgia

A scandal has erupted at Gldani Prison No. 8 in Tbilisi. Davit Peikrishvili, a well-known crime boss, was taken to hospital twice in two days with multiple injuries.

According to his lawyer, on 16 October, prison authorities placed five inmates whom Peikrishvili considers his “underworld enemies” in his cell. They included Vato Kipiani and Avtandil Bilanishvili, known as Katsro. Authorities had arrested them the previous day over a fight at a restaurant.

The lawyer says the men beat Peikrishvili for several days and demanded the codes to his phone.

Background: Crime bosses Davit and Giorgi Peikrishvili were arrested on 22 September 2026 on charges of violence and extortion. Authorities arrested Kipiani and Bilanishvili on 15 October on charges of group violence. Georgian media often describe Bilanishvili as a friend of Bera Ivanishvili, the son of billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, who is widely regarded as the country’s power behind the scenes. The alleged links between those involved and Georgia’s elite have long attracted intense discussion in the media and on social networks. Their arrests have caused a major public stir.

In January 2020, law enforcement agencies in Georgia and Ukraine announced that they had foiled a plot to kill brothers Davit and Giorgi Peikrishvili. According to investigators, the perpetrators planned to use a remotely detonated explosive device. Vato Kipiani was charged in connection with the case.

Now, six years later, Peikrishvili’s lawyer says Kipiani and Davit Peikrishvili ended up in the same prison cell.

The Special Penitentiary Service, however, insists that nobody mistreated Peikrishvili. Kipiani’s lawyer says the two men were never held in the same cell.

The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into the case.

Davit Peikrishvili (left), Vato Kipiani (right)

This is not the first such incident at Gldani Prison No. 8

Financier Giorgi Bachiashvili was beaten there in suspicious circumstances in 2025. Bachiashvili formerly served as executive director of an investment fund belonging to billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party, whom many regard as the country’s “power behind the scenes”.

Bachiashvili said at the time that, before the beating, the prison governor had advised him to hand over his financial data to Bidzina Ivanishvili as quickly as possible. The State Security Service later claimed that Bachiashvili had staged the beating.

Opposition politicians are now linking the Peikrishvili case to cryptocurrency wallets, fraudulent call centres and the Ivanishvili family. Peikrishvili’s lawyer rules out a political motive.

A cell without cameras

The Peikrishvili brothers’ lawyer, Paata Gogiashvili, described the incident in an interview with Formula TV.

He said that after their arrest, both brothers had stayed in cells equipped with CCTV. Prison staff then moved them to different cells and placed Davit Peikrishvili alone in a cell that, according to the lawyer, had no camera.

At 20:00 on 16 October, five more inmates joined him in the cell: Vato Kipiani, Shota Kipiani, Avtandil Bilanishvili, Kacharava and Gotsiridze. Earlier that day, on Friday, Gogiashvili had visited his clients, the Peikrishvili brothers. The lawyer…

On 17 October, journalist Keta Tsitskishvili wrote on Facebook, citing a source, that someone had beaten Peikrishvili in prison. The Penitentiary Service press office denied the report in an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

On 19 October, Davit Peikrishvili called his mother and told her he was fine. However, she continued to insist that someone had beaten her son, although she admitted that she had not witnessed the incident herself and that his lawyer had not confirmed it to her.

That same day, lawyer Gogiashvili went to the prison.

He said he found Peikrishvili badly beaten. The prisoner had four broken ribs, fractures to his skull and facial bones, and bruises.

His mother says he had five broken ribs and a double jaw fracture. Based on Peikrishvili’s account, the lawyer alleges that all five cellmates took part in the beating.

According to the lawyer, the cellmates told Peikrishvili that he and his brother had landed them in prison. They demanded access to the brothers’ phones. The lawyer does not know what information the phones contained. He says investigators seized the brothers’ phones and laptops during a search.

The lawyer alleges that prison officials knew about the conflict between the inmates.

At 16:31 on 19 October, the Public Defender’s hotline received a report of alleged ill-treatment of Peikrishvili. According to the ombudsman’s office, its representative arrived at the prison that day, but Peikrishvili declined to meet them.

The lawyer gives a different account. He says prison officials showed the ombudsman’s representative a brightly lit cell, but Peikrishvili could not speak because two of his five cellmates were in the room with him.

That night, according to the lawyer, Giorgi Peikrishvili, who was held in another cell at the same prison, cut his wrists “to demand that authorities save his brother’s life”. At 21:00, staff took Davit Peikrishvili to Vivamedi clinic. The clinic’s medical director, Zurab Chkhaidze, said Peikrishvili had multiple injuries.

20 October: Broken glass during a meeting with his lawyer

A second incident occurred the following day, on 20 October, during a meeting with his lawyer.

According to the Penitentiary Service, Davit Peikrishvili suddenly left the meeting room, smashed a corridor window and threatened to hurt himself with the broken glass. The service also said he urged other inmates to disrupt prison operations and demanded a meeting with his brother. The law prohibits such meetings because the brothers face charges in the same case.

Gogiashvili confirms that Peikrishvili injured himself in his presence. Davit jumped up from his chair, smashed the glass with his hand and injured his arms. According to the lawyer, Peikrishvili had already sustained the injuries from the alleged beating in his cell before this incident.

Staff took Peikrishvili back to Vivamedi. Doctors said he had injuries to his upper limbs that he had not sustained the previous day and needed surgery. The clinic’s director said the injuries were not serious and that Peikrishvili’s condition was stable.

Prison authorities: “There was no violence”

In a statement on 20 October, the prison administration again denied the lawyer’s allegations.

The administration cited statements from the prisoner’s mother and his lawyer. “On 19 October, his mother said that her son had confirmed he was fine. The lawyer also denied that any beating had taken place when speaking to the mother,” the administration said. It described the events as a “provocation” and a “deliberate campaign to discredit the prison leadership”.

However, the statement did not explain how Peikrishvili sustained the multiple injuries that clinic staff recorded the day before his meeting with the lawyer.

On 20 October, the investigative department of the Ministry of Justice’s General Inspectorate launched an investigation into the alleged infliction of bodily harm on Peikrishvili. The department acted on information reported in the media and opened the case under the article on violence.

Lawyer Gogiashvili holds the prison leadership responsible. He has urged the prosecutor’s office to obtain CCTV footage from the prison corridor urgently, “before it is lost”.

Background: What are the people involved accused of?

On 22 September 2026, authorities arrested 40-year-old twin brothers Davit and Giorgi Peikrishvili in two separate cases.

Prosecutors accuse Giorgi of extorting a large sum of money from businessman Rati Gurgenishvili. They accuse Davit of group hooliganism in connection with an attack on a taxi driver on 2 October 2025.

On 2 October 2026, authorities also charged both brothers with laundering 10 million lari (about $4 million) between 2020 and 2026. The brothers deny the allegations.

In 2023, authorities arrested Davit Peikrishvili on suspicion of attacking a cryptocurrency exchange and carrying out a robbery worth more than 1 million lari (about $380,000).

Both brothers face up to 12 years in prison.

Old enemies in the same cell

On 30 January 2020, law enforcement agencies in Georgia announced that they had uncovered a plot to kill the Peikrishvili brothers. Authorities detained six people in Tbilisi and Batumi, while Ukraine’s security service arrested another suspect in Kharkiv.

According to investigators, the plot originated in Ukraine. On 25 June 2021, authorities detained 47-year-old Vakhtang (Vato) Kipiani at Tbilisi airport after Ukraine deported him. Kipiani has numerous previous convictions. Prosecutors charged him with preparing a premeditated murder under aggravating circumstances.

Avtandil Bilanishvili, known as “Katsro”, is the son of 75-year-old Kako Bilanishvili, a well-known crime boss. Katsro first attracted public attention in 2019, when investigators questioned him in connection with the death of 19-year-old footballer Giorgi Shakarashvili. The Interior Ministry later said that video footage did not show Bilanishvili.

Authorities arrested Kipiani, Bilanishvili and Shota Kipiani in Tbilisi on 14 October. They accuse the three men of beating a 65-year-old man at a restaurant in the Vake district. Group violence carries a prison sentence of up to two years. A court ordered all three to remain in pre-trial detention.

Kipiani’s lawyer, Marika Phaladze, told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that her client categorically denies sharing a cell with Peikrishvili or having any conflict with him. “Vato Kipiani’s position is that the investigation will establish all the facts, and everything will become clear,” Phaladze said.

“They let them in to take the money”: theories about the beating in the cell

The Peikrishvili brothers’ mother is convinced that authorities staged Kipiani and Bilanishvili’s arrests over the fight. She believes they did so to get the men into Davit Peikrishvili’s cell and show him that “thieves run everything in Georgia’s prisons”.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the opposition United National Movement, has put forward an even more elaborate theory.

He suggests that officials let Kipiani and Bilanishvili into the prison to seize money linked to call centres. According to Parulava, they wanted the codes Peikrishvili used for cryptocurrency transactions. Parulava believes that the entire incident may be linked to Bidzina Ivanishvili’s financial operations, but he has offered no evidence to support his theory.

Peikrishvili’s lawyer rejects this explanation. He rules out political motives and sees the incident as an old feud between two rival underworld groups.

Call centres have already come up in the Peikrishvili case. On 3 October, when prosecutors charged the brothers with money laundering, journalists asked the prosecutor handling their case, Mariam Berdzenishvili, whether the charges had any links to illegal call centres. She neither confirmed nor denied such a connection.

Fraudulent call centres have become one of the biggest crime stories in Georgia in recent years

In March 2025, OCCRP, Studio Monitor and more than 30 media partners published an investigation titled “The Scam Empire”.

According to the journalists, a Tbilisi call centre located just metres from the headquarters of Georgia’s State Security Service had defrauded more than 6,100 people worldwide out of $35.3m since May 2022.

In December 2025, authorities arrested Grigol Liluashvili, the former head of the State Security Service. Prosecutors accuse him, among other things, of taking bribes to protect call centres operating in the country.

In July 2026, his relative, Andria Liluashvili, received a 12-year prison sentence for transferring bribes from call centres and laundering money.

According to an investigation by Georgia’s Studio Monitor, the network exposed in 2025 may still be operating from a new location.

The Bachiashvili case: the same prison, a similar incident and two conflicting accounts

In July 2025, Giorgi Bachiashvili, the former head of a co-investment fund he established with Bidzina Ivanishvili, suffered a brutal beating at Gldani Prison No. 8. He was serving an 11-year sentence for allegedly embezzling about $39m in cryptocurrency belonging to Ivanishvili.

Bachiashvili said that three days before the beating, on 8 July, prison governor David Gogoberishvili had summoned him and demanded that he give Ivanishvili access to all his bank accounts and cryptocurrency transactions.

What followed was tragic.

On 21 August, Gogoberishvili and Giorgi Kemoklidze, deputy head of the penitentiary department, resigned. On 7 October 2025, authorities found Gogoberishvili dead with gunshot wounds. Investigators opened a case on suspicion of incitement to suicide.

Two days later, the State Security Service arrested Kemoklidze but offered a completely different account of events. According to the service, Kemoklidze conspired with Bachiashvili to bring carefully selected inmates into his cell and stage a beating. The service claimed that someone had switched off the cameras in the cell and that Kemoklidze had ordered the deletion of all footage from that day.

Bachiashvili’s lawyer called the allegations absurd and said his client did not even know Kemoklidze.

In February 2026, authorities released Bachiashvili from prison under a plea deal.

The role of Bera Ivanishvili, son of the billionaire often described as Georgia’s “power behind the scenes”

Bidzina Ivanishvili’s son, Bera Ivanishvili, also features in this story.

According to reports by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Georgian service and the Pirveli and Formula TV channels, Avtandil Bilanishvili, known as Katsro, has been friends with Bera Ivanishvili for many years. Social media contains numerous photographs of the two together.

On 10 October, the Pirveli TV programme Saturday with Nodar Meladze reported that the Peikrishvili brothers had sent a letter from prison to Amiko Janelidze, Bera Ivanishvili’s best man and a long-time friend of Bilanishvili.

According to the channel, the brothers thanked Janelidze for helping them in the past and expressed regret that they had been unable to contact him. Janelidze denied receiving any messages from the brothers when a reporter approached him.

Tamar Chergoleishvili, one of the leaders of the opposition Federalists party, wrote on Facebook about the prison incident: “Bera Ivanishvili’s own father has landed him in trouble.” She said neither the arrests of Kipiani and Bilanishvili nor the beating of Peikrishvili would help resolve the problem. Chergoleishvili also called for the release of the prison footage.

During an interview with lawyer Gogiashvili on Formula TV, the presenter asked why he so categorically ruled out a political motive for the beating, given the numerous social media posts showing crime bosses Kipiani and Bilanishvili alongside Bera Ivanishvili.

The lawyer replied that he could not comment on Kipiani’s connections because he had no information about them.

Bera Ivanishvili has not publicly commented on the prison incident. Earlier, on 30 September, he said that he and his family had faced a smear campaign for many years. Among other things, he said, people had accused him of protecting call centres and ordering the arrests of individuals.

“I want the defamatory attacks against me to be addressed through the courts,” Bera Ivanishvili wrote. According to his lawyer, David Asatiani, the lawsuit will target several Georgian media outlets and specific individuals.

The beating of crime boss Peikrishvili in Georgia

World.title: Kyrgyzstan’s foreign trade rises 13.3% to $12B in eight months of 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. Kyrgyzstan’s foreign and mutual trade in goods totaled $12 billion from January through August 2026, up 13.3% from a year earlier, the National Statistical Committee said in preliminary data.

Mutual trade with other members of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) reached $4.3 billion, up 5.5%. Trade with countries outside the union totaled $7.7 billion, or about 64% of the total.

Within the EAEU, exports and imports moved in opposite directions: Kyrgyz exports to union countries fell 9.1%, while imports from them rose 9.3%.

Russia accounted for 64.5% of Kyrgyzstan’s mutual trade within the union and Kazakhstan for 32.7%, together 97.2%. The other members, Armenia and Belarus, made up the remaining 2.8%.

Trend estimates that Kyrgyzstan’s foreign trade turnover is likely to continue expanding through the end of 2026, supported by growing trade with countries outside the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and sustained import demand.

However, trade growth with EAEU partners may remain more moderate unless Kyrgyz exports to the bloc recover. In January–August 2026, trade with countries outside the union increased by 18.2% year on year, compared with 5.5% growth in mutual trade with EAEU members. The divergence suggests that markets beyond the bloc are becoming an increasingly important contributor to Kyrgyzstan’s trade expansion.

World.title: Azerbaijan protests against UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. Azerbaijan has voiced its protest against a report by the UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief during a session of the Third Committee of the UN General Assembly.

Shahriyar Hajiyev, First Secretary of the Permanent Mission of Azerbaijan to the UN, delivered a statement to this effect during an interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur.

He emphasized that the effective safeguarding of freedom of religion or belief is a fundamental prerequisite for stable societies characterized by mutual understanding, tolerance, and respect.

Mr. Hajiyev pointed out that the report (A/81/376), presented by the Special Rapporteur, contains unsubstantiated claims. He argued that, instead, the report should have addressed the damage inflicted upon religious heritage—including monuments of Islamic culture that hold universal human value—during the 30-year occupation of Azerbaijani territories.

It was noted that, throughout the occupation, at least 65 mosques were completely destroyed, while cemeteries were subjected to widespread desecration and looting.

The diplomat highlighted that the Special Rapporteur’s silence regarding these documented violations, coupled with the inclusion of unverified information in the report, raises serious questions concerning the impartiality and objectivity of his work.

He further noted that, as of 2025, there are 994 registered religious communities in Azerbaijan; of these, 956 are Islamic, while the remainder consist of Christian, Jewish, Baha’i, and Krishnaite communities. Currently, there are 2,387 mosques, 16 churches, 23 prayer houses, 7 synagogues, one Baha'i place of worship, and one Krishnaite place of worship operating in the country.

"In accordance with the 'Code of Conduct for Special Procedures Mandate-holders,' adopted by UN Human Rights Council resolution 5/2 on June 18, 2007, mandate-holders must perform their functions objectively and impartially, free from any external interference," stated Shahriyar Hajiyev.

World.title: Azerbaijan's banks ranked by loan portfolio in Q3 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. The loan portfolios of banks operating in Azerbaijan in the third quarter of 2026 have been disclosed, according to the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA).

The International Bank of Azerbaijan (ABB) ranked first, with a loan portfolio of $4.62 billion.

Kapital Bank ranked second, with $3.76 billion, followed by Pasha Bank in third place, with $2.35 billion.

World.title: Uzbekistan’s microfinance assets more than double to about $1.7B
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. Uzbekistan’s microfinance sector more than doubled its total assets year over year, reaching 20.8 trillion soums (about $1.7 billion) as of September 1, 2026, compared with 9.7 trillion soums (around $807.5 million) in the same period last year.

This was reflected in the statement by Central Bank of Uzbekistan.

Loans and microleasing remained the largest component of the sector’s assets, with their net balance increasing by 106% year over year to 18.1 trillion soums (approx. $1.5 billion) from 8.8 trillion soums (about $732.6 million). However, their share of total assets declined to 87.1% from 90.6%, a decrease of 3.5 percentage points.

Funds held with banks also increased significantly, rising more than fourfold to 1.31 trillion soums (around $108.2 million) from 304.1 billion soums (approx. $25.3 million) a year earlier. This represents an increase of approximately 327.2%, or nearly 1 trillion soums (about $83.2 million).

The sector’s capital base continued to expand, with total capital rising 56.6% year over year to 4.4 trillion soums (around $366.3 million) from 2.8 trillion soums (around $233.1 million). Retained earnings increased by 80.5%, while current-year profit rose by 133.4%, reflecting stronger earnings growth.

Meanwhile, total liabilities increased by 138.1% year over year to 16.3 trillion soums (about $1.36 billion) from 6.9 trillion soums (about $574.4 million). Loans, borrowings and lease obligations accounted for 80.1% of total liabilities, amounting to 13.1 trillion soums (around $1.09 billion).

According to Trend’s calculations, the increase in total assets amounted to 11.1 trillion soums (approx. $924.1 million), while total liabilities grew by 9.4 trillion soums (about $782.6 million). Liabilities therefore expanded at a faster pace than capital, which increased by 1.6 trillion soums (around $133.2 million) over the same period, based on the rounded figures provided.

The data point to continued expansion in Uzbekistan’s microfinance sector, supported by rising lending volumes, stronger profitability and an expanding capital base. At the same time, the faster growth in liabilities highlights the increasing role of external financing in supporting the sector’s development.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 23, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 27-th day of the second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev shared a publication on Twitter about the liberation of Zilanli, Kurd Mahrizli, Muganli and Alagurshag villages of Gubadli district.

- President Ilham Aliyev shared a publication on Twitter about the liberation of Dolanar and Bunyadli villages of Khojavend district, Dag Tumas, Nusus, Xelefli, Minbashili and Veyselli villages of Jabrayil district, Venedli and Mirzehasanli villages of Zengilan district.

- President Ilham Aliyev had a phone conversation with the father of the National Hero Shukur Hamidov, who became a martyr.

- The Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense disseminated information about the latest situation at the front. Important territories and heights were liberated. The Armenian armed forces, leaving the positions, deserted.

- Territories of Tartar, Aghdam and Aghjabadi districts were subjected to intensive shelling, and four UAVs of Armenian armed forces were neutralized.

- Video of the destruction of Armenian personnel and armored vehicles was published.

- Video from the Minbashili village of Jabrayil district, liberated from the Armenian occupation, was published.

- Video of the destruction of Armenian volunteer detachments in the Khojavend and Fuzuli directions published.

- Video of the destruction of artillery units and the command post of the Armenian armed forces as a result of air strikes was published.

World.title: Turkish MP condemns statements directed against Azerbaijan (VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Turkish-Azerbaijani relations are too deep and ancient to be used as a tool for day-to-day politics.

This was stated today by Şamil Ayrım, a Member of Parliament and head of the Türkiye-Azerbaijan Inter-Parliamentary Friendship Group, during his address to the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye (GNAT).

He noted that these relations go far beyond the standard ties between two sovereign states.

"I strongly condemn the statements directed against Azerbaijan. Criticism is one thing; demeaning rhetoric is quite another. The position of the Justice and Development Party and our government is firm. We do not accept any approach that goes beyond the parameters set by the President of Türkiye, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

Türkiye is strong, and Azerbaijan is strong. One nation, two states—together, we are stronger," said Şamil Ayrım.
