World.title: Azerbaijan raises issue of landmine threat at UN
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. During the UNGA81 First Committee thematic discussions on conventionalweapons, Azerbaijan informed the Committee that for nearly three decades, parts of its territory that were under occupation served as a “grey zone”, creating conditions conducive to illicit activity, including the trafficking of conventional arms, ammunition and related material. It was emphasised that, following the restoration of its sovereignty, Azerbaijan strengthened border controls in these areas, thereby reducing the risk of such illicit trafficking.

This is stated on the X page of the Permanent Mission of Azerbaijan to the United Nations.

"Particular attention was drawn to the landmine threat in Azerbaijan. Over the past three decades, more than 3,500 people have fallen victim to landmines and explosive remnants of war. Since November 2020 alone, 443 Azerbaijani citizens, including women and children, have been killed or injured, with the number continuing to rise.

The statement underscored that, beyond the immediate threat to human life, extensive landmine contamination continues to impede reconstruction and rehabilitation efforts, restrict the use of agricultural land, and hinder the safe and dignified return of internally displaced persons to their places of origin.

Addressing the persistent landmine threat in Azerbaijan requires sustained international solidarity, stronger partnerships and enhanced assistance for humanitarian mine action," the statement said.

World.title: ABC staff targeted in sophisticated cyber attack
World.content:
The ABC has wiped staff devices that were exposed to a new, sophisticated cyber-attack carried out as part of a broader campaign to track and even hack into networks of some of Australia's most high-profile and sensitive organisations.

It can be revealed the ABC is among more than two dozen Australian government, critical infrastructure, universities and media organisations that researchers claim were targeted by an Israel-based company abusing the online advertising system.

The public broadcaster confirmed a "small number" of devices had been exposed but said so far it had not identified any impact from the attack discovered by researchers at The Citizen Lab.

"The ABC is aware of the Citizen Lab report that describes exposure to advertising that may contain spyware. There is no evidence of a resulting compromise," a spokesperson said.

Know more about this story? Email Cam Wilson on wilson.cameron@abc.net.au or his secure email cmwlsn@protonmail.com

'No evidence' ABC impacted by cyber-attack

The ABC attack was part of a bigger campaign, dubbed "Adfection", revealed by Citizen researchers last week.

The Canadian-based group found evidence that company Discover-Tech exploited digital advertising technology from major platforms like those run by Google to deliver spyware that could infect devices merely by viewing an online  and without clicking.

Cyber attack infected millions of devices via online ad Australia's nuclear science agency and other highly sensitive government organisations have been targeted by a sophisticated, foreign bad actor that secretly weaponised online ads to install spyware.

Researchers were able to confirm Discover-Tech's technique was used to infect devices at international news network Al Jazeera with spyware from another Israeli company, Candiru.

A spokesperson for the ABC confirmed that this had included the public broadcaster but had found no evidence so far of any adverse impact.

"Our review found that ads from this network were shown on a small number of ABC devices. We have found no evidence that any staff member has been identified or tracked," they said.

"For the small number of ABC devices identified, we have found no signs of compromise, and are wiping any still in service as a precaution. We take the privacy of staff and the protection of journalists' sources seriously."

New method of cyber-attack exploits known risks of online advertising

Even if this infection is unsuccessful, researchers said, the same method also allowed the attackers to profile tens of millions of devices that were shown these malicious s — measured by "impressions" — potentially giving information about their identities and online habits.

University of Queensland Professor Nicholas Carah, whose research focuses on digital advertising, said the attack was proof of the well-known risks about online advertising technology.

"On one level, it's horrifically surprisingly, but on another level it's like, well, yeah of course, online advertising is really useful infrastructure for doing something like this," he said.

Professor Nicholas Carah says the attack is proof of the risks about online advertising technology. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Professor Carah said the report showed how bad actors could exploit existing characteristics of online advertising technology to thwart protections that were supposed to stop tracking for nefarious purposes.

"You can get an [internet protocol] address, or a mobile, then, hey, presto, you're able to identify those individuals," he said.

Greens leader and digital rights spokesperson David Shoebridge said the report's contents were alarming.

"When foreign zero-click adtech is aimed at our public broadcaster, and other sensitive government agencies, that of course raises serious questions about foreign interference," he said, adding that this shows the need for privacy reform and to include advertising in the government's proposed digital duty of care.

Australian government, critical infrastructure and media organisations targeted

While there were devices targeted across the world using Discover-Tech's techniques, Citizen Lab researchers noted a "substantial cluster of impressions in Australia, including on government and private-sector networks associated with critical infrastructure".

The researchers did not know who Discover-Lab or Candiru were carrying out the attacks on behalf of, if anyone.

Telstra-owned network likely exploited by spies Digicel Pacific's network resources are likely being used by private spy firms to track unsuspecting people on the other side of the world and steal their call, message and location data, according to an expert cybersecurity analysis.

The report singled out Australia's nuclear science agency, ANSTO, as being a hot spot in their data for the number of malicious ads shown. It did not specify the other organisations.

An ANSTO spokesperson told the ABC earlier this week it had not identified any impacts.

Australia's cybersecurity agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, declined to comment.

Researchers also claimed three Australian media organisations had seemingly been targets.

Media organisations and journalists are common targets for commercial spyware operations, alongside politicians, dissidents and human rights groups.

"The use of spyware against journalists is on the rise," international group Reporters Without Borders wrote late last year.

"Digital attacks often go unnoticed, so it is vital that journalists regularly check if their devices are compromised."

World.title: The high-rise housing battleground that has wide political consequences
World.content:
Residents of a leafy Melbourne street are getting a glimpse of what the future could hold for their neighbourhood, and it's a dramatic departure from the low-rise streetscape they know.

In Armadale, in the Liberal-held electorate of Malvern, plans have been lodged with council for a six-storey development on Mercer Road, about 900 metres away from the train station.

The developer intends to demolish five single-storey units and build a six-storey block of apartments. If approved, there would be 29 two-three bedroom apartments and two levels of underground parking.

A render of an apartment development that is proposed for Armadale. (Supplied)

Dave Corrigan lives in an apartment across the road and described the plan as outrageous.

"[It's] enough to almost make me consider moving, to be honest," he told 7.30.

"I could probably understand on a main road and High Street … but in the middle of Mercer Road, that's just ridiculous."

Under Labor's new "deemed to comply" planning rules, Mr Corrigan's objections carry limited weight and his right to appeal has been stripped away.

Dave Corrigan opposes the plan and the government regulations. (ABC News)

"Deemed to comply" means that if a development meets a series of standards set out by the government, it can be approved without the usual scope for objections or appeals.

The rules took effect in April, with Labor arguing it would reduce red tape, speed up housing approvals and give developers greater certainty.

With the state election approaching, Labor's high-rise housing plans are becoming a political test: as residents push back against towers in their neighbourhoods and the Coalition pledges to scrap the activity centres and return planning powers to councils.

Labor's plan to build up

Under the Victorian Labor government's activity centres plan, designated areas around major train and tram routes are being opened to more intensive housing development, including buildings of up to 20 storeys or higher in some locations.

Armadale, in the City of Stonnington, is among 60 designated activity centres.

Some residents in Armadale aren't happy about the new six-storey development. (ABC News: Kathleen O'Connor)

Labor says Victoria needs an estimated 2.24 million additional homes by 2051, with at least 70 per cent targeted for established areas.

The federal government has targeted building 1.2 million new homes nationally by 2030.

State Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny says the existing planning system failed to provide enough housing in areas where people want to live.

"We've acted to say that the status quo is no longer an option," Ms Kilkenny told 7.30.

"We cannot continue to have a planning system that continues to lock out Victorians from living in places where they want to live."

The policy has drawn fierce opposition from residents and councils who argue the changes will alter the character of established suburbs, while limiting their ability to influence what gets built.

Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr said residents often assumed taller buildings would be concentrated around railway stations and major roads, but that was no longer the case and that councils have been stripped of meaningful influence over decisions that would fundamentally change their communities.

"Council's involvement is minimal because if they tick the government's planning boxes now, residents have no right to object, they have no appeal rights and council has very limited ability to make changes to those proposed developments," Mayor Sehr said.

Box Hill: The future of high-rise Melbourne?

East of Melbourne's CBD, Box Hill offers an example of what a shift towards high-density housing could look like.

Danny Todica lives in a 30-storey apartment block, in Box Hill. (ABC News)

Danny Todica lives there with his partner in a two-bedroom apartment in a 30-storey tower.

The 52-year-old said the convenience of apartment living is hard to beat.

"We have the highway just there, we have the shopping centre just around the corner here, so it's in walking distance of everything and the tram stop is just out there," Mr Todica said.

" People still need to live somewhere. What you can do is give people opportunity to live in a great spot. "

Phil Ward has lived in Box Hill for 47 years. He once campaigned against high-rise development but in 2016 bought an apartment in the 36-storey Sky One tower he had opposed.

"If you can't beat them, join them," he said.

Phil Ward has lived in Box Hill for 47 years. (ABC News)

Mr Ward enjoys the convenience of being able to reach shops and public transport within minutes, but he said the transformation had come at a cost.

He said traffic congestion was now a major concern, while green space was increasingly under pressure from development.

"It only takes a little glitch and all of a sudden gridlock," Mr Ward said.

Box Hill is a major transport hub with the busy Whitehorse Road cutting through the centre, linking to the Maroondah Highway and the eastern suburbs.

But its congestion problem extends beyond one busy road. A 2025 government report found several major roads in the suburb were nearing capacity.

Now, construction work for Labor's multi-billion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop is bringing lane closures and pedestrian detours to the busy centre.

Box Hill illustrates the challenge facing governments trying to accommodate a growing population and how to provide more homes while maintaining liveability and updating infrastructure.

Ms Kilkenny said new developments in activity centres would attract infrastructure contributions to help fund parks, schools, road upgrades and community facilities as populations grow.

Who gets the final say?

For residents and councils opposed to Labor's plan, the issue is not simply how tall new buildings should be. It is whether local communities still have a meaningful say in what happens around them.

Ms Kilkenny rejected the suggestion that councils had lost their influence.

Victorian Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny rejects the claim that council's have lost their influence. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"Our deemed to comply planning applications will mean that if the development meets those various standards, there is no capacity to object to that and they will be approved," she said.

Mayor Sehr said that left residents with little choice when a proposal met the new state rules.

"They either sell or just put up with it," she said.

Dr Stephen Glackin, Senior Research Fellow in urban planning at Swinburne University of Technology said the Labor government is trying to use the existing infrastructure.

"The more we expand, it's just more expensive and it's leaving the people who are on the fringes of the city open to travel poverty. They might have an affordable house, but getting into the jobs is going to be really difficult," he said.

"If there's already train lines there, why not build around them? If there's already plumbing and electricity there, build around them. Sure you're going to have to upgrade some stuff, but it's largely there already."

The Coalition has promised to scrap Labor's activity centres policy if elected, return third-party appeal rights to residents and give councils a greater role in planning their communities.

There are a number of apartment towers in Box Hill. (ABC News)

"We believe that local communities should have a say in how their community grows," Opposition Leader Jess Wilson told 7.30.

Ms Wilson said a Coalition government would shift the focus of high-rise development to Melbourne's CBD and inner city, rather than impose Labor's density targets on established suburban neighbourhoods.

"We all know the need to build more homes right across this state, but what we want to do is make sure that we actually deliver more homes and more choice," she said.

She then attacked Labor's record on regional development.

"We want to see a mix of homes right across this state," Ms Wilson said.

"We''ve seen in Geelong, for example, precincts that have been designated for new homes sit there idle for years under this Labor government because they have not acted."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Man United legend lashes current players for behaving 'like babies'
World.content:
Manchester United's all-time leading scorer Wayne Rooney has labelled the club's current players selfish, lashing them for behaving "like babies" after captain Bruno Fernandes questioned the coaching staff's tactics following their Champions League thrashing by Como.

Fernandes said United failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a "mood of defeat" after conceding in the second minute, as Thursday morning's 4-1 loss intensified scrutiny of manager Michael Carrick.

United's collapse at Como left them staring at another damaging result, with only a stoppage-time goal from Joshua Zirkzee reducing the margin of defeat.

Man United captain branded 'disgrace' for comments following latest loss Bruno Fernandes takes aim at Michael Carrick as Manchester United's horrible start to the season goes from bad to worse in the Champions League.

The criticism follows signs of growing frustration within the squad. Earlier this month, defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club's hierarchy after a 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid, saying he expected greater investment to help the team compete at the highest level.

"When Martinez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart," Rooney told the United Stand podcast on Thursday.

"That was the start. We've seen it now with Bruno, and you're going to see it with more players because they don't want to take responsibility.

"You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said, but you have to take responsibility on the pitch. You have to take responsibility as a group of players.

Wayne Rooney (right) was a long-time teammate of current United boss Michael Carrick (left). (Getty Images)

"These players, they're selfish. They don't care about their teammates, don't care about the manager, the staff or the fans, they care about themselves.

"If they're not getting what's right for them, they're like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves."

Carrick, a former United midfielder who played alongside Rooney at Old Trafford, was appointed on an interim basis following Ruben Amorim's dismissal in January before earning a contract through 2028 after overseeing a dramatic improvement in results.

Carrick is under growing pressure with United winless in seven matches across all competitions. They are 20th in the Champions League standings and 13th in the Premier League.

Reuters

World.title: Mayor told staff member to 'lose some weight', misconduct probe finds
World.content:
A regional South Australian mayor said a staff member "needs to go back to netball and lose some weight", an investigation into alleged breaches of behavioural standards has found.

District Council of Robe Mayor Lisa Ruffell has led the council, located about 350 kilometres south-east of Adelaide on the state's Limestone Coast, since 2023.

In June, the council ordered an independent investigation into allegations she had undermined the professional reputation of council employees, contributed to distress, created governance instability and contributed to psychosocial risks for staff.

On Wednesday, the council published an investigation summary report as part of papers for a special meeting scheduled for Monday.

The Kelledy Jones Lawyers investigation outlined its findings across seven pages, including that Ms Ruffell said a staff member "needs to go back to netball and lose some weight" while at a community photo shoot for council grant recipients.

It identified multiple instances of Ms Ruffell allegedly criticising council staff in public settings, including telling one employee an asset could be fixed "if it wasn't for your big fat salary" while at a meeting with state government representatives unrelated to that asset.

District Council of Robe CEO Nat Traeger with Lisa Ruffell. (Supplied: District Council of Robe)

Ms Ruffell was also found to have discussed council business and employee matters with community members, including describing employees as "lazy" and saying "they don't do anything".

This was in addition to multiple instances where the investigation described Ms Ruffell as "dismissive" in meetings and would "roll her eyes" while staff spoke.

Investigators also reviewed "rude, undermining and disrespectful" emails sent by Ms Ruffell to employees.

The investigation stated Ms Ruffell was first made aware of the allegations in February, before she responded a month later.

The matter was referred to the local government Behavioural Standards Board, which recommended the council contract independent lawyers to conduct the investigation.

Mayor denies findings

The investigation will be tabled to a council meeting on Monday night, where Ms Ruffell will be absent from discussion due to conflict of interest protocols.

There, elected members will vote on whether to censure Ms Ruffell.

The investigation noted the mayor disputed the findings in full and stated she submitted "the report does not adequately identify the evidence relied on" and "that adverse witness material was not provided to her in full".

Ms Ruffell told the ABC she would wait until Monday's meeting to comment further, but she "strongly" disputed the investigation's findings and had concerns about its process.

"I am also disappointed that the publicly available meeting papers contain only the investigator's summary, rather than the full report," she said.

" I believe the community deserves a fuller understanding of the material being relied upon. "

The investigation noted a failure to come to a private resolution over the complaints necessitated them being discussed at a public council meeting.

Ms Ruffell said she had sought informal resolution and mediation "from the outset" and the decision to pursue a formal investigation "was not mine".

World.title: Dozens arrested over illegal casino operations, drug trafficking
World.content:
Police have arrested 29 people after uncovering two illegal casinos operating in Melbourne's eastern suburbs, as part of a wider investigation into alleged drug manufacturing.

Detectives also uncovered weapons, including firearms, machetes, swords and daggers, $600,000 in cash, illegal tobacco and vapes, seven kilograms of methylamphetamine and five kilograms of ketamine, when they executed search warrants in Carnegie, Box Hill, Balwyn North and South Melbourne.

During the initial stages of the investigation in July, police arrested nine people allegedly linked to a crime syndicate at a property in Bundoora, in Melbourne's north.

Those arrested included two Malaysian nationals, a Chinese national and a woman from Thailand.

The 38-year-old Malaysian national was charged with possessing substances, equipment or material for trafficking, and handling stolen goods.

The 29-year-old Malaysian national was charged with trafficking methamphetamine, possessing an imitation firearm, negligently dealing proceeds of crime and using false documents.

A 27-year-old man from China was charged with possessing methylamphetamine, possessing prohibited weapons and trafficking tobacco and vapes.

The 25-year-old woman from Thailand was charged with possessing methylamphetamine and being in possession of a stolen police uniform.

All four remain in custody, while the other five people arrested at the property are expected to be charged on summons with a range of drug offences.

Then in August, detectives from the clandestine laboratory squad uncovered a suspected illegal casino operating in Carnegie.

Police allege multiple gambling rooms had been set up, and 15 people, including two working at the venue, were playing illegal casino games.

All 15 people were interviewed and released, with police expecting to charge them on summons with knowingly dealing with proceeds of crime and being in a place providing unauthorised gambling.

As part of the investigation, another search warrant was executed at a property in South Melbourne on October 15.

Police arrested a 40-year-old South Melbourne woman and charged her with numerous offences including trafficking a large commercial quantity of methylamphetamine, possessing cocaine and possessing a prohibited weapon.

Second casino uncovered, Chinese national arrested

Five days later, they searched a property in Box Hill, where a second illegal casino was discovered.

Two people allegedly operating the casino were arrested at the scene.

A 43-year-old Chinese national was charged with dealing with property suspected to be proceeds of crime and being in a place provided for unauthorised gambling.

Police seize a casino table at an illegal casino operating at Box Hill, in Melbourne's east. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

Police said he remains in custody.

They also expect to charge the second man, a 49-year-old from Balwyn North on summons with similar charges.

That same day detectives also searched an address on Whitehorse Road in Box Hill, where they alleged found cash and handwritten ledgers showing large-scale gambling occurring at the venue.

They arrested a 59-year-old Box Hill woman, who was allegedly a staff member, at the property.

Officers searching a property in Balwyn North uncovered more cash and casino chips, as well as four firearms, other weapons, and a large quantity of tobacco and drug manufacturing equipment.

A 45-year-old Balwyn North woman was arrested and is expected to be charged on summons with dealing property believed to be proceeds of crime and firearms offences.

In a statement, Detective Inspector Carlie Kohler from Victoria Police's clandestine laboratory squad, said the arrests would help dismantle drug syndicates operating in the community.

"Uncovering these casinos and putting an end to the illegal activities taking place inside them helps get drugs and weapons off the streets," she said.

"These arrests are a crucial part of our commitment to dismantle organised crime on every level.

"We need anyone with information on illicit drugs being imported, manufactured or trafficked to come forward."

World.title: Grenades caused deadly fire at Canadian military base
World.content:
A fast-moving grass fire that killed at least four soldiers at a western Canadian military base was sparked by an exercise using live grenades, a senior defence official has said.

High winds propelled the blaze across the army base in Wainwright, overwhelming dozens of soldiers.

The incident was one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's military.

"The fire initiated on the automatic grenade launcher range ... [it] initiated as a result of routine military training that was happening on that range at the time," Brigadier-General Vanessa Hanrahan said.

Loading...

Officials said 27 people remained hospitalised, with several in a critical condition. The soldiers and reserve members were preparing to deploy to Latvia, where Canadian forces have their largest international military operation.

Winds up to 96km/h fed the blaze, but they were below 50km/h leading up to the fire, Major-General Wade Rutland has previously said.

He described the sudden high winds and resulting spread of the fire as an "uncommon, rapid" event in which the flames advanced 1km in 30 to 60 seconds.

"I’ve certainly never seen anything like it," said Major-General Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, which is based in Edmonton, about 210km west of the military site.

A satellite image shows the extent of the blaze. (Reuters: Planet Labs PBC)

Officials identified the dead as Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark.

"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost," Prime Minister Mark Carney said, adding that he had ordered flags on federal buildings across the country to be lowered to half-staff to honour the victims.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said many of the injured would require weeks and months of specialised, intensive medical care.

When the fire began, Major-General Rutland said, 85 soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, were in "high intensity" combat training using live munitions at the base, which is located in a prairie setting.

Canadian Forces Base Wainwright had 1,310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data.

Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. (Reuters: Camden Scott/Canadian Forces/File photo)

The base houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which runs training scenarios and exercises for the army.

Mr Carney said those affected in the fire came from military bases across the country.

Military and civilian firefighters fought the fire through the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable", Mr Carney said.

Twenty-two ground ambulances and eight air ambulances responded to the scene.

Patients are being treated in Edmonton, Wainwright, Calgary and Red Deer.

Alberta voters reject move to separate from Canada A group of separatists in Alberta say they will pursue a second referendum despite most people voting to remain part of Canada.

Military search and rescue technicians also parachuted into the site.

Health staff in Edmonton said a "code orange", or mass-casualty event, was declared to coordinate the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright.

The town of Wainwright, with a population of about 6,600, is just north of the base.

Reuters

World.title: Family rift among lines of inquiry for police investigating Brendan Nugent
World.content:
A reported rift between Brendan Nugent and his family is one line of inquiry for Victoria Police as they investigate the attack on federal MP Helen Haines.

Asked by ABC Mildura this morning if one line of inquiry was that Mr Nugent's alleged attack against Ms Haines was a "proxy" for attacking his family, Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush said "yes it is".

"It sounds like a cliche, but every line of inquiry is open ... Every action is under review," he said.

Commissioner Bush said the 43-year-old's father Rod Nugent, and the father's partner Christine Cunningham, had been "very, very helpful" to the police investigation.

The couple released a statement earlier this week in which they said they had been friends with Ms Haines for two decades, and described Monday's events as "devastating and unfathomable".

"We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can," they said.

Independent federal MP for Indi Helen Haines remains in a critical condition. (Facebook)

Commissioner Bush said the couple were "absolutely cooperating".

"They've been very, very helpful," he said.

" It's an absolute tragic circumstance. As we know, Helen was loved in the community, still is loved and cherished. "

Commissioner Bush said Mr Nugent's interactions with neighbours were also being looked at and that the actions of local police who received those neighbour complaints would be examined.

"They are wonderful people, our police in Wangaratta, they come to work every day and every night to do the best," he said.

Commissioner Bush said the force was supporting officers in the Wangaratta region in the wake of the week's events and that Ms Haines had showed great support to his staff after two officers were killed in the line of duty in nearby Porepunkah last year.

Ms Haines, 65, remains in a critical condition at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne, with the staff to provide another update on her condition this afternoon.

'Proactive' approach to security for Victorian election

The attack on Ms Haines has this week drawn attention to the safety of MPs and other officials.

Ahead of Victoria's state election on November 28, Commissioner Bush said police were taking a "proactive" approach to the security of politicians and to address any threats that may arise.

Mike Bush praised the work of Victoria Police officers in Wangaratta. (ABC News: Sarah Buchecker)

He said establishment of a central command centre last year, operating 24 hours a day, would enable police to respond effectively.

"What we're going to do is extend the remit of the [State Commanding Coordination Centre] to be a one-stop-shop for anyone, any politician, any electioneer, if they have threats," he said.

" We will triage them there and we will respond and deploy accordingly. "

Victoria's Electoral Commissioner Sven Bluemmel yesterday assured the community that the election would be run safely.

Former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan worried MP would be killed More than a dozen Victorian MPs tell the ABC they have concerns over their safety.

"We have done quite a lot of additional work since 2022 to make sure we can continue our strong tradition of a really healthy, participatory democracy," he said.

Mr Bluemmel said he was in "absolute lockstep" with Commissioner Bush and that he met Premier Ben Carroll on Wednesday to discuss safety and security at voting centres.

Commissioner Bush said this morning that Victoria Police had "very good, trained analysts" working around the clock.

"We'll take a proactive approach …. with social media scrapings, intelligence briefings, to try and get ahead of any threat that might be out there," he said.

Victoria Police officers had been advised to be "highly visible in the communities", he said.

World.title: Trump calls LeBron 'total disgrace' over perceived anthem disrespect
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has accused LeBron James of disrespecting the United States after the NBA star appeared to continue his warm-ups while the national anthem was performed before Philadelphia's season opener on Wednesday AEDT.

"I said right from the beginning that he's no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE," Trump said of James in a social media post sharing the video.

"LeBron James should apologise to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!"

James appeared to practice a golf swing and jump shot as The Star-Spangled Banner was performed at New York's Madison Square Garden.

James, starting his first season with Philadelphia, was lined up alongside teammates who mostly stood still during the anthem.

Trump and James have been critical of each other for years, occasionally trading public swipes.

James had not made a public comment or a social media post as of Thursday afternoon about Trump's gripe.

Coach Nick Nurse had talked at length since training camp opened about the Sixers' need to tune out outside distractions. Hours before their home opener, the Sixers had to deal with one from the president.

"I think that goes right in with other outside noise we've already had," Nurse said before Friday's game against the Cleveland Cavaliers.

"I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor. The focus that they've had and the intent and all the stuff like that has been outstanding."

AP

World.title: Woman accessed key to apartment building before being found dead with five-year-old girl
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Woman accessed key to apartment building before being found dead with five-year-old girl Robert Sharp Alexander Darling and Updated October 23, 2026 — 12:40pm ,first published October 22, 2026 — 11:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A woman used her work in the real estate industry to gain access to a Box Hill apartment building where she and a child fell to their deaths. Police are investigating after the body of a 38-year-old woman and five-year-old girl, from Blackburn South, were found outside the Prospect Street building about 6.20pm on Thursday night. The scene of a double fatality in Box Hill. AAP Emergency services attended, but the pair could not be revived. The 29-storey complex was cordoned off late Thursday but had been reopened by Friday morning. Police remain at the woman’s home, but said in a statement they are not looking for anyone else in relation to the incident.



A man who works nearby, but asked not to be identified because of the nature of the incident, said the woman had collected the key to a vacant apartment upstairs, saying she was showing it to a client. Loading The young girl was with her at the time and the pair were seen entering the building. Residents leaving for work and school at the apartments on Friday said they knew very little about what had happened. Michael said the residents inside were a tight-knit community.



“The whole building is in mourning, crying,” he said. One resident spoke to the press when leaving the building on Friday morning, tearing up when she heard the news the woman and child had died. The Age One young woman, who didn’t want to be named, said people in a residents group chat had been praying for the woman and child before learning they had died. “I think everyone will feel sad,” she said. “We don’t know what will happen.” Another resident said she arrived home late on Thursday to find police and paramedics at the front of her building. She said she only found out on the news on Friday why they were there.



“I just feel a little terrified that it happened in my building,” she said. Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: Embattled Queensland minister resigns from cabinet
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandQueensland government Embattled Queensland minister resigns from cabinet Cameron Atfield and Catherine Strohfeldt Updated October 23, 2026 — 12:40pm ,first published October 23, 2026 — 9:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Under-fire Queensland Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm has resigned from the frontbench. The Whitsunday MP insisted the decision to step down was due to her health, but it followed a spate of highly publicised incidents including her relationship with fellow cabinet member Tim Mander and disturbing reports of children in state care. Amanda Camm says her decision to step down from cabinet was her decision, and she was not pushed. Brisbane Times / Cameron Atfield Premier David Crisafulli said Camm would be replaced, but he had so far resisted the opportunity to trigger a wider reshuffle of cabinet at the halfway mark of the election cycle. Along with the Child Safety and the Prevention of Domestic and Family Violence portfolio, Camm also served as Families, Seniors and Disability Services Minister.



Related Article Analysis

Queensland Government Inside the alliances, rivalries and machinations of Queensland’s LNP Camm said she informed Crisafulli of her resignation late on Thursday and the decision was “mine and mine alone”. The attack on Helen Haines affected her decision, Camm said, as did her recovery from recent surgery. “The devastating incident involving Helen Haines has reinforced the importance of taking concerns about personal health, safety and well-being of people in public life very seriously,” she said. “Public scrutiny and accountability are essential to democracy and to our institutions. Harassment, threats, bullying and personal vilification are not – and, for the past year, this has been my experience.” Asked if she would recontest the seat of Whitsunday, Camm was non-committal, saying only she would focus on her health.



“It became apparent to me coming back – maybe I came back a little bit early – that physically, I don’t get second chances with my health and I’m prioritising that,” she said. Camm had been under mounting pressure to step down. Earlier this year, she defended the state government’s decision to cut millions in funding from the domestic violence sector, following the alleged murder of a mother west of Brisbane. Questions swirled over children in need of emergency shelter sleeping on the floor of government facilities, a $38.5 million cut to the domestic and family violence services budget, and a bungled IT system roll-out compromising responses to time-sensitive child safety matters. Camm came under more scrutiny in August amid revelations that statements made during estimates might have been flawed.



And in September, reports revealed the group said to have taken up the work of a dumped domestic violence reform oversight office had not given Camm any progress update in the 16 months since it was set up. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli confirmed Camm would step down from cabinet. Cameron Atfield Later in the month, child safety workers walked off the job alongside employees from the Department of Youth Justice. The minister was also caught in a public grilling when her undeclared romantic relationship with Sports Minister Mander was brought to light earlier this year. Questions centred on whether the pair had fulfilled their obligations to report any conflicts of interest and adhere to the parliamentary code of conduct.



Related Article LNP Crisafulli under fire over ministers’ extramarital affair The extramarital affair was again scrutinised when the Australian Federal Police investigated reports Mander had not been living at his declared address – which had been the home he shared with his wife Gayle, before their marriage ended in April 2025. On Friday, Crisafulli said Camm had come in to a broken system. “I constantly saw her put the concerns of vulnerable women and children above all else and above her own health,” he said. Camm said she would not concede mistakes had been made in her two years in charge of a sensitive and scrutinised portfolio.



“I have delivered the biggest reform to these portfolios in the last two years than any minister before me in 20 years,” she said. Crisafulli said there would be no wider reshuffle and an announcement of Camm’s replacement would be made shortly. “I want today to be about Amanda,” he said. “She’s standing here before you, explaining her personal situation, and that takes a lot of ticker,” he said. “The question [of Camm’s successor] is very valid, and it’s an important one – it’s an important role – and there’ll be someone in the role very, very soon.”



Crisafulli said Camm’s departure was not performance related, but Opposition Leader Steven Miles was not so sure. Opposition Leader Steven Miles says Camm must be replaced by an experienced minister. Cameron Atfield “It shouldn’t have taken this long for David Crisafulli to act,” he said. “He kept her in that role for far too long when she was clearly unable to do it. He ignored the warnings from advocates, from children in care, from whistleblowers within his own government. “He should have acted sooner.”



As for Camm’s replacement, Miles said Crisafulli should resist the temptation to appoint from the backbench and appoint an experienced senior minister to the role. “If he refuses to do so for the sake of stability or not upsetting anyone on his front bench, then the result will be signalling to Queenslanders that it’s not enough of a priority for him to take that step and use that political capital,” he said. Miles also rejected any suggestion Labor had crossed any lines in criticising Camm’s performance. “All we have consistently done is raise concerns that have been brought to us by advocates, by whistleblowers, by child safety officers, and highlight the performance of the government when it comes to child safety,” he said. World.title: ‘You can work out how many decades!’ Ann Peacock on famous parents, racing, the Liberal Party – and her stalker
World.content:
From catching flying fruit on the campaign trail to board level racecourse politics, the PR powerhouse holds back little over lunch.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ann Peacock – with the same disarming directness she deploys to talk about horseracing, the Liberal Party, her famous mother Lady Susan Renouf, her children, her fun Braccialini handbag with its teddy bear clasp, the time she stopped mouldy fruit being pelted at her politician dad Andrew – is telling me about her stalker. This is not where I expected to land interviewing a Victoria Racing Club board member ahead of Melbourne Cup Week. But life has been rich and varied and brimming with ups and downs for this former TV weather presenter, charity fundraiser, ex-Crown Casino executive, and Liberal Party blue blood who was once denied membership of the party’s blue ribbon Kooyong branch during a party spat, gallingly, as it was her father’s own electorate. Political violence against women could not be more topical this week given the shocking events in Wangaratta, but Peacock, 61, raises the incident because I ask about a fragment in The Age archive reporting a 1999 police investigation. “It was a shocking thing to have to go through,” says Peacock. “Michael [Kroger, her second husband and Liberal Party powerbroker] and I were engaged. And I was receiving dirty letters and threatening letters.” They demanded Kroger end a political dispute with then premier Jeff Kennett. Her house was broken into and – Peacock says deliberately and pointedly – “all the female clothing was touched”. “I don’t know if the police record says this, but the man had ejaculated on my car. And he stole lots of things. So it really became very personal and dirty.”



Police questioned a man, but the case was judged hard to prove for various reasons and no one was ever charged. How does she reflect on it now? Peacock responds that she doesn’t. And she won’t link it to the attack this week on Helen Haines, which caused the independent MP’s legs to be amputated. “I don’t correlate the two. ” Ann Peacock is disarmingly direct when discussing a range of topics over lunch. Penny Stephens I am on time for lunch with Peacock at Grill Americano, the Manhattan meets Melbourne Italo-steak joint on Flinders Lane in the heart of the city. To be on time for the 61-year-old, who is practically a Melbourne institution in her own right (she has 3513 contacts in her phone), is to be late. For Peacock, as is her habit, is always early. It is a warm sunny day and Peacock is all stylish fun dressed in a Versace ruffled top, Pucci print trousers of many colours, shimmery silver Trussardi ankle boots and an armful of bangles. She has already spotted and paid her respects to restaurant proprietor Chris Lucas (Society, Chin Chin), who is power lunching slap bang in the middle of the restaurant with federal Liberal MP and shadow treasurer Tim Wilson. Peacock orders a non-alcoholic XPA, popular in Europe she says, reveals she doesn’t have a partner, talks about the importance of a career – “I’ve worked hard since I was 17, I enjoy the stimulation greatly” – but also embracing the home for her sons – “I love my children more than anything”. Edward, “Woody”, who has just graduated with honours from law at Monash, is still ensconced at home while his elder brother Andrew is a doctor in neurology at The Alfred.



When Edward gets a job will you kick him out, I wonder. “Absolutely not,” says Peacock, who left the family home during year 6 for boarding school in the late ’70s. Her darling mother Susan, a journalist and model who had caused outrage by advertising Sheridan sheets while Peacock’s father was minister for the army in the 1960s, fell in love with horse trainer Robert Sangster and moved to the Isle of Man and married him. During school holidays, Ann would fly with her sisters Caroline and Jane around the world to visit. At Flemington in 1983 with her mother Susan Sangster. Ross Anthony Willis/Fairfax Media Racing has been part of her life since 1974, when Leilani, part-owned by her parents, won the Turnbull Stakes, Toorak Handicap, and the Caulfield Cup before taking a close second in the Melbourne Cup. “I’ve had this link to the VRC for decades. You can work out how many decades! To actually be there now, representing, the members and people that are not yet members, is an honour that I hold the highest esteem.” It is a big year for the VRC. For the first time, the famous Cox Plate will run at Flemington on Saturday while its Mooney Valley racecourse is reconstructed. Ever the PR, Peacock says young people are coming back to racing to experience a whole day’s entertainment. Robbie Williams will perform on Cup Day, while the Gold Coast DJ Fisher, who has 2.6 million Instagram followers, will return after performing at Stakes Day last year. Laughing like a 13-year-old, she admits she didn’t know who the global DJ phenomenon was. “But, of course, I got up to speed. And he was a phenomenal success.”



Related Article Victorian racing Profits prompt Wilson’s departure from VRC as he downplays talk of board rift She waves away the big news that VRC chairman Neil Wilson is stepping down, to be replaced by board member Vin Cox, as simply normal change, despite reports of board level machinations. Peacock herself was re-elected to the board without a ballot in December for a second three-year term. Peacock and her sister, British horse trainer Jane Chapple-Hyam, have two horses, Military Academy and Ambassadorial, both set to run on Cup Day in different races. But she laughs off press reports her sister, who trains more than 50 horses in the UK, is planning to relocate to Australia. Like racing, politics threads through her life. Her “loving, caring” father Andrew was Liberal Party leader twice before he became ambassador to Washington. “He would get a bit agitated when he was cooking the chops on the grill. He didn’t want to be disturbed because he wanted them to turn out perfectly. We baked the potato and had to align with the timing of the chops. He was a great father. I was very fortunate to have him.” She accompanied him on campaigns. The two-time Liberal Party leader performed well in two federal elections but failed to unseat the hugely popular Bob Hawke’s Labor government. Campaigning with her father in 1984. Joanna Bailey/Fairfax Media



During the 1993 federal election campaign launch in Sydney I sat as a university student with a row of Liberal Party dowagers as I was on a work placement with advertising agency George Patterson Bates, which was producing ads for the ill-fated leader, John Hewson. Peacock was the star, judging by the applause when he entered the auditorium. But the dowagers expressed consternation at the youth of the woman accompanying Peacock, until one finally said in relief. “It’s his daughter.” One time Peacock travelled with her father to Perth, where a radio broadcaster had urged locals to throw rotten fruit at the Liberal leader. At a campaign rally organisers set up mesh in front of the stage. “And so having been warned about it, he got on and did his work. And my eyes were on the fruit coming towards us. And I actually caught out of the side of my eye someone climbing over the mesh. And just in time, I was able to let the security know.” Flying back over east, the politician told her daughter to enjoy the ride in the government jet because it would be their last. He knew he had lost. We are here at Grill Americano partly because Peacock has staged fondly remembered family dinners here, the mixed grill a family favourite. But that is now off the menu.

World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Golden Dragon drills for gold beneath 3km WA anomaly Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 23, 2026 — 12:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Golden Dragon Mining has fired up the drill rigs at its Cue Gold project in Western Australia’s Murchison region, launching a major aircore drilling campaign to test two sizeable anomalies in a corridor stretching more than three kilometres. The 6000m to 9000m program will probe gold-in-soil targets at the Coodardy/Behring Bore area, where recent surface work has suggested the company’s known gold footprint could be considerably larger than previously thought. Golden Dragon Mining has kicked off drilling at its Cue gold project in Western Australia’s prolific Murchison region. The project sits 60km north of the township of Cue (pictured). The results have effectively linked Golden Dragon’s Curtis Find, Behring Bore, Coodardy and Piston prospects, pointing to the potential for a single, big mineralised system rather than a series of isolated targets. An extensive auger campaign revealed a broad northeast-trending geochemical trend, with gold strongly associated with arsenic and antimony, two key pathfinder elements that can help explorers track concealed gold mineralisation.



‘Our recent auger program has identified a significant, coherent northeast-trending gold anomaly extending over more than three kilometres.’ Golden Dragon Mining managing director Simon Buswell-Smith The mineral signature, including a peak gold-in-soil value of 720 parts per billion, has defined the primary exploration target for the new campaign. The drilling will systematically test the regional-scale surface anomalies and determine whether they are associated with underlying bedrock mineralisation, helping prioritise targets for follow-up reverse circulation (RC) drilling. Golden Dragon Mining managing director Simon Buswell-Smith said: “The commencement of this extensive AC drilling program marks an important step forward for the Coodardy gold system. We are particularly encouraged by the potential to better understand the relationship between these known prospects and determine whether they form part of a broader mineralised corridor.” Additionally, the company is awaiting assay results from 2833m of RC drilling recently completed at its priority Coodardy and Behring Bore prospects. That program targeted extensions to high-grade mineralisation at Coodardy, where previous drilling delivered some cracking results, including a headline hit of 12m assaying 6.5 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 44m, featuring a richer core of 4m at an impressive 17.6g/t gold.



Other notable intercepts from earlier campaigns assayed 8m grading 10.82g/t gold from a shallow 25m, including a four-metre slice grading a whopping 21.37g/t gold. Re-assaying of previous 4-metre composite samples also returned spectacular results, with one 11-metre interval at 6.42g/t gold from 45m containing a one-metre section going an eye-watering 59.2g/t gold. The campaign comes as exploration activity remains strong across the Murchison province, where explorers are successfully combining modern geophysics, geochemistry and drilling to chase major gold discoveries along the region’s extensive mineralised structures. Golden Dragon has also been building its acreage in the prolific gold district, a strategy that recently attracted a significant vote of confidence from Shanghai-listed heavyweight Chengtun Mining Group. The major player tipped in $2.2 million for a cornerstone 19.89 per cent stake in the junior explorer at a premium to its share price at the time. Once all of its new applications are granted, the company will control a dominant landholding of roughly 619 square kilometres in a region that hosts Westgold’s 2.3-million-ounce Big Bell gold mine. The expanded project area contains over 50km of mineralised shear zones. While immediate focus remains on the Cue project in the Murchison, Golden Dragon is also advancing its Stella Range project near Laverton, where recent auger drilling has mapped out a substantial 2.2-kilometre-long gold-in-soil anomaly, yet to see a drill bit.



With an aircore rig now turning to test a compelling three-kilometre-long target and a batch of RC assays from deeper drilling already at the lab, Golden Dragon appears to have set itself up for a period of strong newsflow. If the aircore program can confirm surface anomalism is leaching from a continuous bedrock source, the company may potentially have a significant gold system on its hands in one of WA’s most revered gold-producing postcodes. World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Albanese granted Greens 15 staff just before party blocked inquiry into PM’s powers Nick Newling October 23, 2026 — 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Anthony Albanese signed off on a letter providing 15 advisers to the Greens three days before the minor party voted against an inquiry into his power to allocate staff to federal politicians. The prime minister’s control over the number of staff each MP can employ has come under increased scrutiny, as One Nation leader Pauline Hanson joins independent senators to ramp up their demands for higher staffing levels. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s control over the number of staff each MP can employ is under increased scrutiny. Dominic Lorrimer Under federal legislation each MP is entitled to five electorate officers, but the provision of extra highly paid “personal staff” remains entirely under the prime minister’s discretion. Albanese has been criticised for the way he grants extra hires following revelations in this masthead that he allowed former independent senator Tammy Tyrrell to retain additional staff when she joined Labor, and offered former opposition leader Sussan Ley additional staff for support of the government’s friendless attempt to change freedom of information laws.





In her most recent letter sent in August – seen by this masthead – Hanson requested proportional staffing to the Greens, who also have minor party status. Proportional staffing would more than double One Nation’s staff, from four to nine, and raise salaries so the party could attract more experienced employees. The letter has not yet had a response. Related Article NACC Corruption watchdog’s interest ‘piqued’ by Labor’s invite-only grants “One Nation has six MPs and just five personal staff. Yet, Labor, the Liberals and the Greens joined forces to block an inquiry into fair staffing for independents and minor parties,” Hanson told this masthead. “Our request to the prime minister includes advance staff to plan visits, coordinate security and liaise with the AFP so our MPs and staff can work safely in the community. These are basic responsibilities. The safety of our people should never be subject to political games.” Several crossbench MPs and their staff have told this masthead, under condition of anonymity to protect their safety, that understaffing directly impacts their ability to manage threats from the public.



On October 15, three days after the Greens’ renewed staffing allocation came into effect, Hanson put forward a motion in the Senate to have a “safe staffing guarantee” bill put before a Senate inquiry for reporting by the end of the year. The bill would establish mandatory minimum staffing levels for independent, minor party and opposition MPs, outside the remit of the prime minister’s discretion. Labor, Greens and Coalition senators voted the motion down. The Greens have been contacted for comment. Independent senator David Pocock, who voted for the motion, said: “Staffing allocation shouldn’t be able to be used as a bargaining chip or to reward or punish parliamentarians. The current process needs reform”. Many independent MPs have relied on private fundraising to cover additional staffing costs in their offices. Pocock currently fundraises to pay the equivalent of 2.1 full-time staff responsible for casework and correspondence with constituents.



MPs must petition the prime minister for additional staffing. Payman has repeatedly pleaded for additional staff since she left Labor last term over the party’s stance on the Israel-Gaza war, but her requests have never received a formal response. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Albanese’s staffing double standard props up Lambie defector after joining Labor Payman, Le and One Nation MPs David Farley and Tyron Whitten are the only crossbench representatives without additional staff. Dr Catherine Williams, executive director of the Centre for Public Integrity, said the current system is “clearly open to abuse” and needed immediate reform. “The leader of the government may perceive it to be useful to hobble the ability of other members of parliament to hold the government to account. It is for this reason that the UK, Canada and New Zealand use robust systems to determine allocations,” Williams said.



The Remuneration Tribunal, which sets MP salaries, has been proposed as a better decision maker on staffing. Beyond the capacity to select the number of staff each MP has, the prime minister also has the discretion to select which salary bands staff receive. In the renewed Greens staffing agreement, Albanese provided for two senior advisers to be paid up-to $190,231 and $205,808 respectively. The five electorate officers each MP is entitled to currently earn between $77,071 and $102,681. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Haines pursues a political experiment – that decent people can disagree. Has this attack changed that?
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cathy McGowan knows better than most how hard it is to build a democracy from the ground up. For more than a decade, the former independent MP has helped the people of north-east Victoria do something remarkable. They took politics away from the major parties, put it back into the hands of their communities and helped inspire a movement that changed the face of federal parliament. On Wednesday evening, standing before hundreds of shaken residents in Wodonga, McGowan confronted the possibility that everything they had built was now under threat. Not from a political opponent nor an election defeat, but from violence. “There is another level of grief, different and deeper from the actual violence, from the sorrow, the shame and the hurt,” she told the crowd. “It’s about Helen in her role as our elected representative – in attacking her, we intuit that this is an attack on our political system, on our democracy.” For McGowan, the horror was personal. Helen Haines was not simply her successor in the federal seat of Indi, she was a friend and torchbearer of a political experiment built on the proposition that decent people could disagree without despising one another. Former independent member for Indi Cathy McGowan embraces a community member on Wednesday. Eddie Jim Floral tributes at Helen Haines’ office in Wangaratta. Jason South



Now Haines was fighting for her life in a Melbourne hospital, both legs amputated following an allegedly deliberate attack outside her Wangaratta electorate office when she was rammed by a LandCruiser as she stood behind her car. McGowan pondered what sort of nation attacks its politicians. And what sort of democracy emerges from the aftermath. Australia has arrived at a moment that now feels like a turning point. Whether it becomes one may depend on what happens next. Related Article Analysis

Haines attack Helen Haines once said she had no mortal enemies. That remark hangs heavily over this town Late on Monday afternoon, as the horrific details emerged from Wangaratta, private messaging groups used by federal MPs from across the political divide lit up with disbelief. Politicians accustomed to trading insults across the parliamentary chamber were suddenly exchanging messages of anguish. Haines, 65, was among the least polarising figures in federal politics. A former nurse and midwife, she had built a reputation for patient negotiation, integrity and finding common ground. If someone like Helen Haines could be attacked, who was safe? As the severity of her injuries became clear, the mood in Canberra shifted from shock to something darker.





Police have charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee, over the attack. He made no application for bail when he appeared before Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday. His alleged motivation has not been established. Related Article Haines attack The split-second decision that put Ricky in danger to save Helen Haines But that uncertainty does not erase the broader problem confronting Australian democracy. The attack occurred against a backdrop of escalating threats and harassment directed at public officials at every level of government. Lydia Khalil, a political extremism expert at the Lowy Institute, said violence against an Australian politician had long seemed a matter of “when, not if”. She warns that conspiracy theories, social media and growing anti-institutional sentiment have turned political figures into lightning rods for public anger. “I’ve been very surprised at how mainstream some of these anti-elite, anti-institutional conspiracy theories have gone,” she said. Politicians, she argues, are increasingly portrayed not as ordinary Australians entering public life, but as a corrupt, self-serving class divorced from the communities they represent. That the victim was Haines, “probably the least controversial political figure that you could get”, makes the attack particularly confronting.



Khalil sees hope, however, in the stories of those who rushed to Haines’ aid and the communities rallying around her family: the barber who tackled the driver, the shop assistant who rendered aid, the staff who reassured her. Australia has known political violence before. In June 1966, then-opposition leader Arthur Calwell was leaving an anti-conscription rally at Sydney’s Mosman Town Hall when a young man approached his car. His facial injuries covered by a bandage, Arthur Calwell is wheeled on a stretcher into Sydney’s Royal North Shore Hospital after he was shot on the night of June 21, 1966. Fairfax Media Assuming he was a well-wisher, Calwell began winding down his window. Instead, 19-year-old factory hand Peter Raymond Kocan raised a sawn-off .22 rifle, aimed at his jugular and fired. The bullet shattered the window, showering Calwell with glass and fragments. Kocan fled but was quickly caught. An isolated young man who wanted to be remembered for killing somebody important, he chose Calwell “because I don’t like his politics”. Calwell survived, forgave his would-be assassin and sought to have his sentence reduced. Kocan spent a decade in prison before becoming an acclaimed poet. In 1994, NSW Labor MP John Newman was gunned down outside his Cabramatta home in a killing orchestrated by political rival Phuong Ngo.

Caramelised carrots, pillowy whipped feta and hot honey come together in this vibrant side dish that steals the spotlight.

Roast vegetables often play second fiddle on a spread. Not these Dutch carrots. Deeply caramelised and nestled atop a pillow of creamy whipped feta, this is a side that steals the show.

The secret sauce is, well, the sauce: a hot honey glaze infused with Angostura Bitters.

Gently warmed with butter, chilli flakes and a squeeze of fresh lemon juice, just a few dashes of bitters make the honey sing and add a decidedly moreish botanical depth.

Loading

It’s also one of those brilliant sides that’s easy to assemble yet packs a serious visual punch. The carrots are sticky and scrumptious, and their golden colour pops against the feta and once topped with chopped pistachios, fresh green herbs and lemon zest.

World.title: Woman accessed key to apartment building before being found dead with five-year-old girl
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Woman accessed key to apartment building before being found dead with five-year-old girl Robert Sharp Alexander Darling and Updated October 23, 2026 — 12:40pm ,first published October 22, 2026 — 11:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A woman used her work in the real estate industry to gain access to a Box Hill apartment building where she and a child fell to their deaths. Police are investigating after the body of a 38-year-old woman and five-year-old girl, from Blackburn South, were found outside the Prospect Street building about 6.20pm on Thursday night. The scene of a double fatality in Box Hill. AAP Emergency services attended, but the pair could not be revived. The 29-storey complex was cordoned off late Thursday but had been reopened by Friday morning. Police remain at the woman’s home, but said in a statement they are not looking for anyone else in relation to the incident.



A man who works nearby, but asked not to be identified because of the nature of the incident, said the woman had collected the key to a vacant apartment upstairs, saying she was showing it to a client. Loading The young girl was with her at the time and the pair were seen entering the building. Residents leaving for work and school at the apartments on Friday said they knew very little about what had happened. Michael said the residents inside were a tight-knit community.



“The whole building is in mourning, crying,” he said. One resident spoke to the press when leaving the building on Friday morning, tearing up when she heard the news the woman and child had died. The Age One young woman, who didn’t want to be named, said people in a residents group chat had been praying for the woman and child before learning they had died. “I think everyone will feel sad,” she said. “We don’t know what will happen.” Another resident said she arrived home late on Thursday to find police and paramedics at the front of her building. She said she only found out on the news on Friday why they were there.



“I just feel a little terrified that it happened in my building,” she said. Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: Embattled Queensland minister resigns from cabinet
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandQueensland government Embattled Queensland minister resigns from cabinet Cameron Atfield and Catherine Strohfeldt Updated October 23, 2026 — 12:40pm ,first published October 23, 2026 — 9:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Under-fire Queensland Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm has resigned from the frontbench. The Whitsunday MP insisted the decision to step down was due to her health, but it followed a spate of highly publicised incidents including her relationship with fellow cabinet member Tim Mander and disturbing reports of children in state care. Amanda Camm says her decision to step down from cabinet was her decision, and she was not pushed. Brisbane Times / Cameron Atfield Premier David Crisafulli said Camm would be replaced, but he had so far resisted the opportunity to trigger a wider reshuffle of cabinet at the halfway mark of the election cycle. Along with the Child Safety and the Prevention of Domestic and Family Violence portfolio, Camm also served as Families, Seniors and Disability Services Minister.



Related Article Analysis

Queensland Government Inside the alliances, rivalries and machinations of Queensland’s LNP Camm said she informed Crisafulli of her resignation late on Thursday and the decision was “mine and mine alone”. The attack on Helen Haines affected her decision, Camm said, as did her recovery from recent surgery. “The devastating incident involving Helen Haines has reinforced the importance of taking concerns about personal health, safety and well-being of people in public life very seriously,” she said. “Public scrutiny and accountability are essential to democracy and to our institutions. Harassment, threats, bullying and personal vilification are not – and, for the past year, this has been my experience.” Asked if she would recontest the seat of Whitsunday, Camm was non-committal, saying only she would focus on her health.



“It became apparent to me coming back – maybe I came back a little bit early – that physically, I don’t get second chances with my health and I’m prioritising that,” she said. Camm had been under mounting pressure to step down. Earlier this year, she defended the state government’s decision to cut millions in funding from the domestic violence sector, following the alleged murder of a mother west of Brisbane. Questions swirled over children in need of emergency shelter sleeping on the floor of government facilities, a $38.5 million cut to the domestic and family violence services budget, and a bungled IT system roll-out compromising responses to time-sensitive child safety matters. Camm came under more scrutiny in August amid revelations that statements made during estimates might have been flawed.



And in September, reports revealed the group said to have taken up the work of a dumped domestic violence reform oversight office had not given Camm any progress update in the 16 months since it was set up. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli confirmed Camm would step down from cabinet. Cameron Atfield Later in the month, child safety workers walked off the job alongside employees from the Department of Youth Justice. The minister was also caught in a public grilling when her undeclared romantic relationship with Sports Minister Mander was brought to light earlier this year. Questions centred on whether the pair had fulfilled their obligations to report any conflicts of interest and adhere to the parliamentary code of conduct.



Related Article LNP Crisafulli under fire over ministers’ extramarital affair The extramarital affair was again scrutinised when the Australian Federal Police investigated reports Mander had not been living at his declared address – which had been the home he shared with his wife Gayle, before their marriage ended in April 2025. On Friday, Crisafulli said Camm had come in to a broken system. “I constantly saw her put the concerns of vulnerable women and children above all else and above her own health,” he said. Camm said she would not concede mistakes had been made in her two years in charge of a sensitive and scrutinised portfolio.



“I have delivered the biggest reform to these portfolios in the last two years than any minister before me in 20 years,” she said. Crisafulli said there would be no wider reshuffle and an announcement of Camm’s replacement would be made shortly. “I want today to be about Amanda,” he said. “She’s standing here before you, explaining her personal situation, and that takes a lot of ticker,” he said. “The question [of Camm’s successor] is very valid, and it’s an important one – it’s an important role – and there’ll be someone in the role very, very soon.”



Crisafulli said Camm’s departure was not performance related, but Opposition Leader Steven Miles was not so sure. Opposition Leader Steven Miles says Camm must be replaced by an experienced minister. Cameron Atfield “It shouldn’t have taken this long for David Crisafulli to act,” he said. “He kept her in that role for far too long when she was clearly unable to do it. He ignored the warnings from advocates, from children in care, from whistleblowers within his own government. “He should have acted sooner.”



As for Camm’s replacement, Miles said Crisafulli should resist the temptation to appoint from the backbench and appoint an experienced senior minister to the role. “If he refuses to do so for the sake of stability or not upsetting anyone on his front bench, then the result will be signalling to Queenslanders that it’s not enough of a priority for him to take that step and use that political capital,” he said. Miles also rejected any suggestion Labor had crossed any lines in criticising Camm’s performance. “All we have consistently done is raise concerns that have been brought to us by advocates, by whistleblowers, by child safety officers, and highlight the performance of the government when it comes to child safety,” he said.
