World.title: ‘You can work out how many decades!’ Ann Peacock on famous parents, racing, the Liberal Party – and her stalker
World.content:
From catching flying fruit on the campaign trail to board level racecourse politics, the PR powerhouse holds back little over lunch.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ann Peacock – with the same disarming directness she deploys to talk about horseracing, the Liberal Party, her famous mother Lady Susan Renouf, her children, her fun Braccialini handbag with its teddy bear clasp, the time she stopped mouldy fruit being pelted at her politician dad Andrew – is telling me about her stalker. This is not where I expected to land interviewing a Victoria Racing Club board member ahead of Melbourne Cup Week. But life has been rich and varied and brimming with ups and downs for this former TV weather presenter, charity fundraiser, ex-Crown Casino executive, and Liberal Party blue blood who was once denied membership of the party’s blue ribbon Kooyong branch during a party spat, gallingly, as it was her father’s own electorate. Political violence against women could not be more topical this week given the shocking events in Wangaratta, but Peacock, 61, raises the incident because I ask about a fragment in The Age archive reporting a 1999 police investigation. “It was a shocking thing to have to go through,” says Peacock. “Michael [Kroger, her second husband and Liberal Party powerbroker] and I were engaged. And I was receiving dirty letters and threatening letters.” They demanded Kroger end a political dispute with then premier Jeff Kennett. Her house was broken into and – Peacock says deliberately and pointedly – “all the female clothing was touched”. “I don’t know if the police record says this, but the man had ejaculated on my car. And he stole lots of things. So it really became very personal and dirty.”



Police questioned a man, but the case was judged hard to prove for various reasons and no one was ever charged. How does she reflect on it now? Peacock responds that she doesn’t. And she won’t link it to the attack this week on Helen Haines, which caused the independent MP’s legs to be amputated. “I don’t correlate the two. ” Ann Peacock is disarmingly direct when discussing a range of topics over lunch. Penny Stephens I am on time for lunch with Peacock at Grill Americano, the Manhattan meets Melbourne Italo-steak joint on Flinders Lane in the heart of the city. To be on time for the 61-year-old, who is practically a Melbourne institution in her own right (she has 3513 contacts in her phone), is to be late. For Peacock, as is her habit, is always early. It is a warm sunny day and Peacock is all stylish fun dressed in a Versace ruffled top, Pucci print trousers of many colours, shimmery silver Trussardi ankle boots and an armful of bangles. She has already spotted and paid her respects to restaurant proprietor Chris Lucas (Society, Chin Chin), who is power lunching slap bang in the middle of the restaurant with federal Liberal MP and shadow treasurer Tim Wilson. Peacock orders a non-alcoholic XPA, popular in Europe she says, reveals she doesn’t have a partner, talks about the importance of a career – “I’ve worked hard since I was 17, I enjoy the stimulation greatly” – but also embracing the home for her sons – “I love my children more than anything”. Edward, “Woody”, who has just graduated with honours from law at Monash, is still ensconced at home while his elder brother Andrew is a doctor in neurology at The Alfred.



When Edward gets a job will you kick him out, I wonder. “Absolutely not,” says Peacock, who left the family home during year 6 for boarding school in the late ’70s. Her darling mother Susan, a journalist and model who had caused outrage by advertising Sheridan sheets while Peacock’s father was minister for the army in the 1960s, fell in love with horse trainer Robert Sangster and moved to the Isle of Man and married him. During school holidays, Ann would fly with her sisters Caroline and Jane around the world to visit. At Flemington in 1983 with her mother Susan Sangster. Ross Anthony Willis/Fairfax Media Racing has been part of her life since 1974, when Leilani, part-owned by her parents, won the Turnbull Stakes, Toorak Handicap, and the Caulfield Cup before taking a close second in the Melbourne Cup. “I’ve had this link to the VRC for decades. You can work out how many decades! To actually be there now, representing, the members and people that are not yet members, is an honour that I hold the highest esteem.” It is a big year for the VRC. For the first time, the famous Cox Plate will run at Flemington on Saturday while its Mooney Valley racecourse is reconstructed. Ever the PR, Peacock says young people are coming back to racing to experience a whole day’s entertainment. Robbie Williams will perform on Cup Day, while the Gold Coast DJ Fisher, who has 2.6 million Instagram followers, will return after performing at Stakes Day last year. Laughing like a 13-year-old, she admits she didn’t know who the global DJ phenomenon was. “But, of course, I got up to speed. And he was a phenomenal success.”



Related Article Victorian racing Profits prompt Wilson’s departure from VRC as he downplays talk of board rift She waves away the big news that VRC chairman Neil Wilson is stepping down, to be replaced by board member Vin Cox, as simply normal change, despite reports of board level machinations. Peacock herself was re-elected to the board without a ballot in December for a second three-year term. Peacock and her sister, British horse trainer Jane Chapple-Hyam, have two horses, Military Academy and Ambassadorial, both set to run on Cup Day in different races. But she laughs off press reports her sister, who trains more than 50 horses in the UK, is planning to relocate to Australia. Like racing, politics threads through her life. Her “loving, caring” father Andrew was Liberal Party leader twice before he became ambassador to Washington. “He would get a bit agitated when he was cooking the chops on the grill. He didn’t want to be disturbed because he wanted them to turn out perfectly. We baked the potato and had to align with the timing of the chops. He was a great father. I was very fortunate to have him.” She accompanied him on campaigns. The two-time Liberal Party leader performed well in two federal elections but failed to unseat the hugely popular Bob Hawke’s Labor government. Campaigning with her father in 1984. Joanna Bailey/Fairfax Media



During the 1993 federal election campaign launch in Sydney I sat as a university student with a row of Liberal Party dowagers as I was on a work placement with advertising agency George Patterson Bates, which was producing ads for the ill-fated leader, John Hewson. Peacock was the star, judging by the applause when he entered the auditorium. But the dowagers expressed consternation at the youth of the woman accompanying Peacock, until one finally said in relief. “It’s his daughter.” One time Peacock travelled with her father to Perth, where a radio broadcaster had urged locals to throw rotten fruit at the Liberal leader. At a campaign rally organisers set up mesh in front of the stage. “And so having been warned about it, he got on and did his work. And my eyes were on the fruit coming towards us. And I actually caught out of the side of my eye someone climbing over the mesh. And just in time, I was able to let the security know.” Flying back over east, the politician told her daughter to enjoy the ride in the government jet because it would be their last. He knew he had lost. We are here at Grill Americano partly because Peacock has staged fondly remembered family dinners here, the mixed grill a family favourite. But that is now off the menu.

World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Golden Dragon drills for gold beneath 3km WA anomaly Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 23, 2026 — 12:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Golden Dragon Mining has fired up the drill rigs at its Cue Gold project in Western Australia’s Murchison region, launching a major aircore drilling campaign to test two sizeable anomalies in a corridor stretching more than three kilometres. The 6000m to 9000m program will probe gold-in-soil targets at the Coodardy/Behring Bore area, where recent surface work has suggested the company’s known gold footprint could be considerably larger than previously thought. Golden Dragon Mining has kicked off drilling at its Cue gold project in Western Australia’s prolific Murchison region. The project sits 60km north of the township of Cue (pictured). The results have effectively linked Golden Dragon’s Curtis Find, Behring Bore, Coodardy and Piston prospects, pointing to the potential for a single, big mineralised system rather than a series of isolated targets. An extensive auger campaign revealed a broad northeast-trending geochemical trend, with gold strongly associated with arsenic and antimony, two key pathfinder elements that can help explorers track concealed gold mineralisation.



‘Our recent auger program has identified a significant, coherent northeast-trending gold anomaly extending over more than three kilometres.’ Golden Dragon Mining managing director Simon Buswell-Smith The mineral signature, including a peak gold-in-soil value of 720 parts per billion, has defined the primary exploration target for the new campaign. The drilling will systematically test the regional-scale surface anomalies and determine whether they are associated with underlying bedrock mineralisation, helping prioritise targets for follow-up reverse circulation (RC) drilling. Golden Dragon Mining managing director Simon Buswell-Smith said: “The commencement of this extensive AC drilling program marks an important step forward for the Coodardy gold system. We are particularly encouraged by the potential to better understand the relationship between these known prospects and determine whether they form part of a broader mineralised corridor.” Additionally, the company is awaiting assay results from 2833m of RC drilling recently completed at its priority Coodardy and Behring Bore prospects. That program targeted extensions to high-grade mineralisation at Coodardy, where previous drilling delivered some cracking results, including a headline hit of 12m assaying 6.5 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 44m, featuring a richer core of 4m at an impressive 17.6g/t gold.



Other notable intercepts from earlier campaigns assayed 8m grading 10.82g/t gold from a shallow 25m, including a four-metre slice grading a whopping 21.37g/t gold. Re-assaying of previous 4-metre composite samples also returned spectacular results, with one 11-metre interval at 6.42g/t gold from 45m containing a one-metre section going an eye-watering 59.2g/t gold. The campaign comes as exploration activity remains strong across the Murchison province, where explorers are successfully combining modern geophysics, geochemistry and drilling to chase major gold discoveries along the region’s extensive mineralised structures. Golden Dragon has also been building its acreage in the prolific gold district, a strategy that recently attracted a significant vote of confidence from Shanghai-listed heavyweight Chengtun Mining Group. The major player tipped in $2.2 million for a cornerstone 19.89 per cent stake in the junior explorer at a premium to its share price at the time. Once all of its new applications are granted, the company will control a dominant landholding of roughly 619 square kilometres in a region that hosts Westgold’s 2.3-million-ounce Big Bell gold mine. The expanded project area contains over 50km of mineralised shear zones. While immediate focus remains on the Cue project in the Murchison, Golden Dragon is also advancing its Stella Range project near Laverton, where recent auger drilling has mapped out a substantial 2.2-kilometre-long gold-in-soil anomaly, yet to see a drill bit.



With an aircore rig now turning to test a compelling three-kilometre-long target and a batch of RC assays from deeper drilling already at the lab, Golden Dragon appears to have set itself up for a period of strong newsflow. If the aircore program can confirm surface anomalism is leaching from a continuous bedrock source, the company may potentially have a significant gold system on its hands in one of WA’s most revered gold-producing postcodes. World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Albanese granted Greens 15 staff just before party blocked inquiry into PM’s powers Nick Newling October 23, 2026 — 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthony Albanese signed off on a letter providing 15 advisers to the Greens three days before the minor party voted against an inquiry into his power to allocate staff to federal politicians. The prime minister’s control over the number of staff each MP can employ has come under increased scrutiny, as One Nation leader Pauline Hanson joins independent senators to ramp up their demands for higher staffing levels. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s control over the number of staff each MP can employ is under increased scrutiny. Dominic Lorrimer Under federal legislation each MP is entitled to five electorate officers, but the provision of extra highly paid “personal staff” remains entirely under the prime minister’s discretion. Albanese has been criticised for the way he grants extra hires following revelations in this masthead that he allowed former independent senator Tammy Tyrrell to retain additional staff when she joined Labor, and offered former opposition leader Sussan Ley additional staff for support of the government’s friendless attempt to change freedom of information laws.





In her most recent letter sent in August – seen by this masthead – Hanson requested proportional staffing to the Greens, who also have minor party status. Proportional staffing would more than double One Nation’s staff, from four to nine, and raise salaries so the party could attract more experienced employees. The letter has not yet had a response. Related Article NACC Corruption watchdog’s interest ‘piqued’ by Labor’s invite-only grants “One Nation has six MPs and just five personal staff. Yet, Labor, the Liberals and the Greens joined forces to block an inquiry into fair staffing for independents and minor parties,” Hanson told this masthead. “Our request to the prime minister includes advance staff to plan visits, coordinate security and liaise with the AFP so our MPs and staff can work safely in the community. These are basic responsibilities. The safety of our people should never be subject to political games.” Several crossbench MPs and their staff have told this masthead, under condition of anonymity to protect their safety, that understaffing directly impacts their ability to manage threats from the public.



On October 15, three days after the Greens’ renewed staffing allocation came into effect, Hanson put forward a motion in the Senate to have a “safe staffing guarantee” bill put before a Senate inquiry for reporting by the end of the year. The bill would establish mandatory minimum staffing levels for independent, minor party and opposition MPs, outside the remit of the prime minister’s discretion. Labor, Greens and Coalition senators voted the motion down. The Greens have been contacted for comment. Independent senator David Pocock, who voted for the motion, said: “Staffing allocation shouldn’t be able to be used as a bargaining chip or to reward or punish parliamentarians. The current process needs reform”. Many independent MPs have relied on private fundraising to cover additional staffing costs in their offices. Pocock currently fundraises to pay the equivalent of 2.1 full-time staff responsible for casework and correspondence with constituents.



MPs must petition the prime minister for additional staffing. Payman has repeatedly pleaded for additional staff since she left Labor last term over the party’s stance on the Israel-Gaza war, but her requests have never received a formal response. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Albanese’s staffing double standard props up Lambie defector after joining Labor Payman, Le and One Nation MPs David Farley and Tyron Whitten are the only crossbench representatives without additional staff. Dr Catherine Williams, executive director of the Centre for Public Integrity, said the current system is “clearly open to abuse” and needed immediate reform. “The leader of the government may perceive it to be useful to hobble the ability of other members of parliament to hold the government to account. It is for this reason that the UK, Canada and New Zealand use robust systems to determine allocations,” Williams said.



The Remuneration Tribunal, which sets MP salaries, has been proposed as a better decision maker on staffing. Beyond the capacity to select the number of staff each MP has, the prime minister also has the discretion to select which salary bands staff receive. In the renewed Greens staffing agreement, Albanese provided for two senior advisers to be paid up-to $190,231 and $205,808 respectively. The five electorate officers each MP is entitled to currently earn between $77,071 and $102,681. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Haines pursues a political experiment – that decent people can disagree. Has this attack changed that?
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cathy McGowan knows better than most how hard it is to build a democracy from the ground up. For more than a decade, the former independent MP has helped the people of north-east Victoria do something remarkable. They took politics away from the major parties, put it back into the hands of their communities and helped inspire a movement that changed the face of federal parliament. On Wednesday evening, standing before hundreds of shaken residents in Wodonga, McGowan confronted the possibility that everything they had built was now under threat. Not from a political opponent nor an election defeat, but from violence. “There is another level of grief, different and deeper from the actual violence, from the sorrow, the shame and the hurt,” she told the crowd. “It’s about Helen in her role as our elected representative – in attacking her, we intuit that this is an attack on our political system, on our democracy.” For McGowan, the horror was personal. Helen Haines was not simply her successor in the federal seat of Indi, she was a friend and torchbearer of a political experiment built on the proposition that decent people could disagree without despising one another. Former independent member for Indi Cathy McGowan embraces a community member on Wednesday. Eddie Jim Floral tributes at Helen Haines’ office in Wangaratta. Jason South



Now Haines was fighting for her life in a Melbourne hospital, both legs amputated following an allegedly deliberate attack outside her Wangaratta electorate office when she was rammed by a LandCruiser as she stood behind her car. McGowan pondered what sort of nation attacks its politicians. And what sort of democracy emerges from the aftermath. Australia has arrived at a moment that now feels like a turning point. Whether it becomes one may depend on what happens next. Related Article Analysis

Haines attack Helen Haines once said she had no mortal enemies. That remark hangs heavily over this town Late on Monday afternoon, as the horrific details emerged from Wangaratta, private messaging groups used by federal MPs from across the political divide lit up with disbelief. Politicians accustomed to trading insults across the parliamentary chamber were suddenly exchanging messages of anguish. Haines, 65, was among the least polarising figures in federal politics. A former nurse and midwife, she had built a reputation for patient negotiation, integrity and finding common ground. If someone like Helen Haines could be attacked, who was safe? As the severity of her injuries became clear, the mood in Canberra shifted from shock to something darker.





Police have charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee, over the attack. He made no application for bail when he appeared before Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday. His alleged motivation has not been established. Related Article Haines attack The split-second decision that put Ricky in danger to save Helen Haines But that uncertainty does not erase the broader problem confronting Australian democracy. The attack occurred against a backdrop of escalating threats and harassment directed at public officials at every level of government. Lydia Khalil, a political extremism expert at the Lowy Institute, said violence against an Australian politician had long seemed a matter of “when, not if”. She warns that conspiracy theories, social media and growing anti-institutional sentiment have turned political figures into lightning rods for public anger. “I’ve been very surprised at how mainstream some of these anti-elite, anti-institutional conspiracy theories have gone,” she said. Politicians, she argues, are increasingly portrayed not as ordinary Australians entering public life, but as a corrupt, self-serving class divorced from the communities they represent. That the victim was Haines, “probably the least controversial political figure that you could get”, makes the attack particularly confronting.



Khalil sees hope, however, in the stories of those who rushed to Haines’ aid and the communities rallying around her family: the barber who tackled the driver, the shop assistant who rendered aid, the staff who reassured her. Australia has known political violence before. In June 1966, then-opposition leader Arthur Calwell was leaving an anti-conscription rally at Sydney’s Mosman Town Hall when a young man approached his car. His facial injuries covered by a bandage, Arthur Calwell is wheeled on a stretcher into Sydney’s Royal North Shore Hospital after he was shot on the night of June 21, 1966. Fairfax Media Assuming he was a well-wisher, Calwell began winding down his window. Instead, 19-year-old factory hand Peter Raymond Kocan raised a sawn-off .22 rifle, aimed at his jugular and fired. The bullet shattered the window, showering Calwell with glass and fragments. Kocan fled but was quickly caught. An isolated young man who wanted to be remembered for killing somebody important, he chose Calwell “because I don’t like his politics”. Calwell survived, forgave his would-be assassin and sought to have his sentence reduced. Kocan spent a decade in prison before becoming an acclaimed poet. In 1994, NSW Labor MP John Newman was gunned down outside his Cabramatta home in a killing orchestrated by political rival Phuong Ngo.

Caramelised carrots, pillowy whipped feta and hot honey come together in this vibrant side dish that steals the spotlight.

Roast vegetables often play second fiddle on a spread. Not these Dutch carrots. Deeply caramelised and nestled atop a pillow of creamy whipped feta, this is a side that steals the show.

The secret sauce is, well, the sauce: a hot honey glaze infused with Angostura Bitters.

Gently warmed with butter, chilli flakes and a squeeze of fresh lemon juice, just a few dashes of bitters make the honey sing and add a decidedly moreish botanical depth.

Loading

It’s also one of those brilliant sides that’s easy to assemble yet packs a serious visual punch. The carrots are sticky and scrumptious, and their golden colour pops against the feta and once topped with chopped pistachios, fresh green herbs and lemon zest.

Labour's Tāmaki Makaurau candidate Kerrin Leoni has resigned after a video emerged of her campaigning alongside Mongrel Mob members.

The footage showed Leoni, wearing a Labour Party jacket, talking to gang members about enrolling to vote and changing the government.

A photo from the same event - published by Newsroom - showed the former Auckland councillor posing with a group of people including some in Mongrel Mob regalia pulling hand gestures associated with the gang.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the footage was "inconsistent" with the standards he expected from his candidates.

"I have made it very clear that campaigning alongside gangs is unacceptable," he said in a statement released on Friday.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407256721112

Speaking to reporters later that morning, Hipkins said Leoni had displayed "very very bad judgement" and had paid a "very high price" for that.

"It is a clear violation of the very clear standards that I have set out for our MPs and candidates," he said. "Her position had become untenable."

Hipkins said he had a brief conversation with Leoni on Friday morning, in which she apologised and conceded she had not handled the situation well.

"Clearly, this has been very, very difficult for her. This is her family who we're talking about."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins. RNZ/Baz Macdonald

Hipkins said Leoni had not given the party the "full information" about the gathering and had not managed the conflict appropriately.

But he said he bore her no "ill will" for the mistake and became emotional while expressing his frustration at the "unfortunate" circumstance.

"All of us navigate family situations in politics, and it's bloody hard," he said.

"In her case, she should be really proud of what she has been able to achieve. She has grown up in an environment where she's been surrounded by gang members. She is not a gang member herself. She has made a good life for herself.

"She has made a mistake here, and she has paid a high price."

Hipkins said he also believed there was an element of "racism" to the reaction and chided National for "crowing" and "salivating" over the candidate's mistake.

"Our Māori MPs get held to a very different standard to others."

Hipkins said he was "very disappointed" in the situation and acknowledged it was "not helpful at all" to the prospects of a centre-left coalition.

He said he was not aware of any other Labour candidates visiting gang pads during this election campaign.

Hipkins had earlier condemned Green and Te Pāti Māori candidates for taking photos with gang members at a Mongrel Mob pad during the campaign.

He ruled out giving law-and-order portfolios to MPs from either party, saying it was unacceptable for politicians to "go out and celebrate with gangs".

Leoni herself criticised Te Pāti Māori rival Oriini Kaipara for the visit during an electorate debate on Wednesday. Kaipara hit back, accusing Leoni of having visited a gang pad the week before her, which Leoni denied.

Te Pāti Māori candidate for Tāmaki Makaurau Oriini Kaipara. VNP/Phil Smith

On Friday, Leoni said she stepped down as a candidate because she did not want the controversy surrounding her whānau to help National return to government.

She said she could handle media scrutiny and attacks from National, but the intense focus on her family and community had become "increasingly difficult".

"A whānau function attended by mokopuna, kaumātua, gang members and non-gang members has been turned into a political weapon, used for political gain and media clicks."

Leoni said she would never turn her back on her whānau, arguing family connections could help people leave gangs.

"Change is possible and I believe we should be encouraging it rather than making it harder."

She stood by her apology to Hipkins and said she was proud to have represented the party.

"Finally, I want everyone to know that I am okay. I will be back."

In a Facebook post on Thursday, Leoni said she had not visited a gang pad during the campaign but admitted attending a "whānau function" in early October where some close relatives who were gang members were present.

"I will not turn my back on them or pretend they are not my whānau because of their associations," she wrote. "I've always tried to be a role model for my whānau."

With nominations already closed, Leoni's name will remain on the ballot paper, despite Hipkins saying she no longer represents Labour.

The video - first reported by Whakaata Māori but also independently obtained by RNZ - showed a patched Mongrel Mob member advocating for the gangs to stop fighting each other and to instead turn their attention to the government.

The footage then cut to Leoni, addressing those present: "Some of them you might know that aren't enrolled to vote and they can have the power to change this government."

The Post reported that the event had been advertised online as a "fundraiser for the Mongrel Mob's Rogue Chapter". But Hipkins told reporters he had been reassured that the function was not a fundraising event.

Labour MP Priyanca Radhakrishnan. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Speaking earlier on Friday on NZ Herald's Ryan Bridge Today, Labour MP Priyanca Radhakrishnan defended Leoni, saying she had been visiting family.

She said she was willing to accept Leoni's version of events: "She was there at a whānau event, and that's the information that I have."

Hipkins also initially stood by Leoni on Thursday - before further footage emerged - saying she was entitled to interact with her own family.

World.title: Tax Traders and Taxi named country's best places to work
World.content:
Tax Traders and Taxi have been named the country's best place to work.

The Best Places to Work programme evaluates employers and workplace culture through confidential employee feedback and surveys.

Tax Traders and Taxi, founded by Josh and Nicola Taylor, took the overall award and the small workplace category on Thursday night.

The businesses combine provisional tax solutions through Tax Traders with access to working capital through Taxi.

Staff are offered support with childcare and school holiday programmes, and help with getting to work. The business also distributes 20 percent of net profits equally among staff regardless of their role. Pay decisions are made through one-to-one conversations and personalised letters outlining contributions to the business. It invests 9.5 percent of its total budget in staff wellbeing.

Audio player for " Should you buy a house from your mother-in-law? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2100786%2Ftax-traders-and-taxi-named-country-s-best-places-to-work

Best Places to Work chief executive Julie Gill said the business had been through a difficult commercial period but had remained transparent with employees, involved them in decisions about what should happen next and continued investing in wellbeing, development and culture.

"When conditions get tough, the choices leaders make tell people whether the organisation's values hold up under pressure," Gill said.

"It's not about the perks or programmes or policies, it's actually about what people experience every day … also it's about the values that show up in the decisions and leaders who build that trust and feedback, and they want to see that lead to action."

Other category winners included Auckland civil engineering company March Cato, Presbyterian Support East Coast's social services across Hawke's Bay and Gisborne, and GO Rentals.

She said the programme's research had found people wanted recognition at work and openness from leadership.

"When people found their feedback was valued and actually led to change, 81 percent said they would recommend their organisation as a place to work. Simple things can be quite powerful at the same time."

The 2026 employee experience survey results showed 62 percent of employees selected work-life balance among their top three priorities, while 84 percent rated flexibility favourably.

"The results also ask employers to look closely at whether their actions match their values," Gill said.

"Do leaders follow through? Do those values guide difficult decisions? Those experiences shape whether people trust an organisation and feel confident recommending it."

But just 48 percent of employees surveyed said their employer had prepared them for the changes AI would bring. Preparedness was associated with a different view of the employer: 70 percent of employees who felt prepared for AI would recommend their organisation.

Gill said the programme was about continuous improvement.

"The heart of the Best Places to Work programme is the employee experience survey, so companies get involved in the programme and they do the independent survey, and they work with us and say, 'look, it could take us two, three years, maybe four years to become a Best Places to Work', so a lot of them start on the journey, but they want to have an independent way to understand how their people feel and experience work, and it's fully confidential."

World.title: EDS patients in limbo as Hamilton surgeon Chris Holdaway stops seeing patients
World.content:
Correction: This story has been updated. Dr Holdaway was not subject to Medical Council restrictions preventing him from seeing patients, as previously reported. Instead, a recommendation he works in a multidisciplinary team on these cases made it impractical for him to continue seeing EDS patients seeking treatment for vascular conditions.

Hundreds of patients seeking treatment for a controversial group of vascular conditions have been left in limbo after a Hamilton surgeon was asked by the Medical Council to do further training.

Hamilton vascular surgeon Chris Holdaway is no longer consulting patients with the connective tissue disorder Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDS) who are also suspected of having abdominal vascular compression syndromes.

The 71-year-old has become one of the country's most prominent advocates for patients with EDS and suspected vascular compression syndromes. He has seen around 200 EDS patients with the condition, which can cause chronic pain, gastrointestinal symptoms and often an inability to tolerate food.

Holdaway, who was interviewed for the RNZ podcast All In Her Head - which examines the debate around EDS and vascular compressions - believes many patients have been misdiagnosed or dismissed before reaching him. His advocacy has attracted strong support from some patients who say they have struggled to obtain diagnoses, but criticism from some medical colleagues.

While individual abdominal vascular compression syndromes are recognised conditions, there is no medical consensus about whether it is possible to have more than one at a time. Yet EDS patients are being diagnosed with multiple abdominal compression syndromes - sometimes up to four - at once.

Medical Council's intervention

The Medical Council told RNZ it could not comment on the circumstances of any individual doctor but it could impose conditions on a doctor's scope of practice where necessary to protect public safety.

"The Medical Council's role is to protect the health and safety of the public by ensuring doctors are competent and fit to practise," council chair Dr Kenneth Clark said in a statement to RNZ.

Dr Holdaway declined to comment on the decision or its impact but a note circulated to patients from advocates Rachel McKenna and Zalie Doyle said the situation preventing him from consulting EDS patients with abdominal vascular compression syndromes was temporary.

He could still see EDS patients for other conditions, including thoracic outlet syndrome and Eagle Syndrome. Patients already undergoing investigations may be eligible for a follow up appointment to review scan results, the letter said.

'Desperate' patients

Holdaway was an advocate for patients seeking surgical treatment overseas, despite Health New Zealand warning these operations were experimental and risked death. Despite the warnings, dozens of New Zealand patients had undergone surgical treatment for multiple compressions in Germany, and more recently in Australia.

Whakatāne woman Rachel Weatherly, a former patient of Dr Holdaway, believed the current situation would leave patients without anywhere else to go.

"I think it will eventually cost lives. My inbox is already full of parents reaching out desperate to know if there's someone else that they can take their child to see, and I just don't have the answer for them," she said.

Weatherly had surgery in Australia with vascular surgeon Gert Frahm-Jensen in September 2025 which resolved many of her symptoms.

Holdaway diagnosed her vascular compressions, which had been dismissed by Health New Zealand specialists, and gave her hope she could find someone to help her.

"I think that hope's now been stripped away for others, which is not going to be really good for families."

In their note to patients, McKenna and Doyle said it was understandable people would feel frightened, angry or disappointed by the situation.

"But how we respond to this situation matters. How we conduct ourselves as a patient community is particularly important right now."

World.title: Green Party releases fiscal plan, promises to increase health spending by $3 billion each year
World.content:
The Green Party would hike taxes, take on more debt and delay balancing the government's books to put billions more into hospitals and healthcare.

The party's just-released financial plan promises a fresh $3 billion increase in health funding at each of the next four Budgets, at a cost of $30b over the full period.

The government would start collecting more than it spends in 2029/30, a year later than Treasury currently forecast. By 2030/31, debt would be $26.6 billion higher than Treasury expects under current plans.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407256033112

Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick released the plan at Parliament this morning.

She said it was irresponsible for parties to chase a surplus without thinking of the real-world economic ramifications.

"Children in poverty cannot eat a surplus. A surplus that this government is chasing is not going to deliver the nurses and the frontline healthcare workers who are desperately needed."

Swarbrick said New Zealand could afford the extra borrowing, with public debt low compared with other countries.

The plan relies on nearly $29 billion in extra revenue over four years from tax changes targeting wealthy people, large companies, banks and landlords.

These include the party's proposed wealth tax, a tax on large gifts and inheritances, and higher company taxes for big businesses.

The package also includes income tax cuts for most workers.

Swarbrick said the Greens would increase future operating allowances - essentially new funding for new initiatives - to between $4.5b and $4.7b across the forecast period. The coalition government has set its planned operating allowances at about $2.4b.

She said the government's efforts to cut spending had come at the expense of essential services: "Cutting public spending deepens economic downturns and inequality, pushes up unemployment and reduces output."

The plan commited to using future Budget funding to buy overseas carbon credits, paying for emissions cuts elsewhere to help meet New Zealand's climate targets.

Treasury estimated that bill could reach $5 billion, although the Greens say cutting more emissions at home would reduce the cost.

Economic consultancy Infometrics has reviewed the plan's direct effects on government finances.

Swarbrick said every one of its election policies had been fully costed, but the Greens remained committed to a Parliamentary Budget Office that could evaluate all parties' proposals on the same basis.

She also took a dig at the government, pointing out that she had featured 13 times on National's Instagram in the past week, compared to its own finance spokesperson Nicola Willis, who appeared just twice.

Swarbrick challenged Willis to a face-to-face debate on their respective fiscal plans, in front of a live audience.

"Come on Nicola, let's get our credentials and credibility and put them to the test," she said. "If you've got anything to say about our plan, which I'm sure you will, come and say it to my face."

National's campaign chair Simeon Brown said the Greens fiscal plan would undo all the government's progress over the past three years.

He said the party had focused on Swarbrick given what a threat she posed to the country.

"The reality is the Greens' plan has nine new taxes on the table... which will take our economy backwards, and which will make New Zealand and New Zealanders poorer," he said.

He warned the Greens would have "real leverage" in a Labour government, with recent polling showing they would not just be a "minor partner".

ACT leader David Seymour said the Greens' plan offered a clear binary for voters: "It is a choice between financial security or financial ruin."

World.title: Wellington social housing sale: Living there 'changed my life' councillor says
World.content:
A Wellington councillor says living in a block of social houses at the centre of a controversial sale changed the course of his life.

Labour's Paekawakawa/Southern Ward councillor Nureddin Abdurahman said Kāinga Ora's decision to sell the sites on 6,8,4 Nuku Street in Strathmore was personal for him, after he and his family lived in one of the units between 2010 and 2017.

"It was crucial because I had nothing.

"It changed my life."

Having arrived in New Zealand from Ethiopia in 2008 to join his wife who had a refugee background, Abdurahman said he was driving taxis at night and studying during the day at Victoria University when he lived in the Strathmore flats.

He said he couldn't afford to rent on the private market at the time, and it gave him the chance to "navigate through and get to my potential".

"I had my kids there, so it gave me an opportunity to spend more on food instead of going to the private market."

Abdurahman said he contested the idea that people got trapped in social housing, and that it had helped him gain a higher tertiary education with a master's degree, going onto his career in national and local politics.

He said he forged strong friends there, recounting a former neighbour called Chris who he had shared food and money with when times were tight, and who had tracked him down during Covid, asking if his family had enough to get by.

"Those people are my family."

Protest signs erected by Strathmore Housing Action on the Nuku Street public housing blocks. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He was among 11 Labour/Green members of Wellington City Council, including Mayor Andrew Little and Deputy mayor Ben McNulty, who signed a letter to the minister and associate minister of housing Chris Bishop and Tama Potaka, as well as Kāinga Ora chief executive Tracey Taylor.

"Why [is Kāinga Ora] selling when there are hundreds of people sleeping on our streets? For me it doesn't make sense," Abdurahman said.

But not all city councillors agree on the issue.

Wharangi/Onslow-Western Ward councillor Diane Calvert said she did not sign the open letter, because she wanted the council to focus on its own housing portfolio.

The council needed to make sure it could meet its own commitments under the Deed of Grant with government, she said.

"We have tenants living in our own substandard housing and I think our efforts are better directed to ensuring council housing upgrades occur as quickly as possible and at a minimum cost to ratepayers."

The council had recently reached an agreement with Kainga Ora regarding a scaled back development in Arlington Street in Mount Cook, she said.

Housing minister Chris Bishop has declined to comment on the sale, saying it was "an operational decision for Kāinga Ora".

The deadline sale - which was for 21 October - sparked community and political backlash - including from Wellington City Mission, Downtown Community Ministry, Pōneke Public Housing Futures, Strathmore Housing Action. Residents protested and sat in at the site earlier this week.

RNZ earlier walked inside the properties, where mould flaked from the ceilings, paint was peeling, and puddles of rainwater collected on the floor.

On Friday, fences had been put up outside the blocks.

Kāinga Ora regional director for Greater Wellington Sarah Willson said earlier this week the agency had no plans to review the sale at Nuku Street.

"We understand the strength of feeling in the Strathmore community about the Nuku Street site and recognise how important public housing is to Wellington," Willson said.

Willson had earlier said that developing the site into social housing was not financially viable, but that other buyers may see potential in it.

She said a scaled back plan for 37 homes on the nearby Ngatiapa Street would still go ahead, and that any money from Nuku Street would go back into the homes.

Willson would not reveal how many offers the site had, saying that could jeaopardise the sale process, and saying the next step in the sale process could take several weeks.

World.title: Police have confirmed Rakesh Naidoo is not under investigation, Labour says
World.content:
Labour says police have confirmed that top cop candidate Rakesh Naidoo is not under investigation.

However, Police Minister Mark Mitchell says it's an "ongoing matter for police and it would be inappropriate for me to comment".

It comes after Mitchell said last month there was an "ongoing matter" in relation to Naidoo, but would not say what it was.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said in response at the time he had "absolute confidence in Rakesh Naidoo".

"He has behaved with absolute integrity throughout this process."

Hipkins said Mitchell "should not be using his position as minister of police to make unsubstantiated insinuations against the character of a rival political candidate".

"Neither Mr Naidoo nor the Labour Party have any idea what is actually being alleged.

"The police need to front up here and explain what is going on."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins has said he has "absolute confidence in Rakesh Naidoo". RNZ/Baz Macdonald

This week, a Labour spokesperson told RNZ that they had spoken to police and could confirm Naidoo "is not under investigation".

"Rakesh has handled himself with dignity and integrity over the past few months and is focused on campaigning for Labour."

On Friday, Mitchell told RNZ it was an "ongoing matter for police…"

"As I have previously said, this does not relate to the Labour Party, and they should not be commenting on matters that do not involve them."

Asked for comment, a spokesperson said "police do not comment on employment matters".

Naidoo's candidacy - announced in June - prompted public criticism from police Commissioner Richard Chambers and minister Mark Mitchell, both claiming the superintendent should have declared his intentions earlier.

An internal review later concluded that Naidoo had complied with police policy, though noted it would have been "prudent" for him to have given his superiors more advance warning.

In response to media questions last month Mitchell said there were "two or three different facets to this situation".

"And they have dealt with one of them."

Rakesh Naidoo RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

After the review's findings were announced, Mitchell confirmed to RNZ he had two phone calls with Chambers on 8 and 9 June.

"[The calls] were to discuss the situation, including the response to media queries, concerns the minister held in relation to the disclosure timeline, including pre-existing concerns regarding a sensitive briefing Mr Naidoo had attended with the minister prior to Mr Naidoo advising anyone at police of his political intentions."

Mitchell declined to release information in relation to the sensitive briefing under section 6 (c) of the Official Information Act.

Section 6 (c) relates to prejudicing the maintenance of the law, including the prevention, investigation, and detection of offences, and the right to a fair trial.

Mitchell's office earlier told RNZ the grounds for withholding under Section 6c of the OIA still applied.

Mitchell referred to the OIA again last month nd said "the OIA is very clear it says there's matters that can't be disclosed because there's an ongoing matter".

He said he was unable to comment further.

In response, Hipkins said Mitchell had "crossed a line here".

"He is the minister of police, and he is using that office to spread claims about a Labour candidate who doesn't even know what the specific accusation against him is. You cannot use the power of the police portfolio to invent allegations against political opponents.

World.title: Awkward questions linger as creaky Australia receives South African hiding
World.content:
That Australia slowly folded and lost the Gqeberha Test by an innings and 31 runs late on day five was hardly surprising in light of its batting calamities of 24 hours earlier. That Kagiso Rabada and Marco Jansen ran through the tail to finish things off even less so.

But it remains startling to consider the reversal of fortunes this quite disastrous loss represented for Australia. On day two, they were 1-0 up in the series, had South Africa on the ropes at 5-97, on a greenish pitch, and fancied a rout of their own.

Bavuma hides from Smith catch as Boland outdoes batters in loss Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha. Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test.

Instead, in a game that lost 145 overs to rain and associated delays, the annihilation took place in reverse and a series some considered Australia's stepping stone to more difficult engagements ahead is now set for an enticing decider. For Australia, the task ahead is now daunting on multiple levels — not just to find form and the right combination of players to defeat an ascendant and cohesive opponent, but how to do so in Cape Town, with all the extra heat that will entail.

First the few positives. Travis Head, whose role as opener will continue to be endlessly scrutinised, laboured unselfishly for five hours to make 121. Nightwatchman Scott Boland, who was Australia's best all-round performer of the game, absorbed 187 deliveries for his rearguard 40.

Scott Boland's vigil at the crease on day five was one of the few positives for Australia. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

The negatives? Australia's next-best batsman was Mother Nature, who wiped out the first session of play and briefly raised hopes that Australia would force a draw. It didn't, for neither did Boland's patient hand inspire his better credentialed batting partners to hang around and save the day.

It is pointless to analyse the tail. Most culpable this time was Steve Smith, who in his short and strange stay at the crease was given a reprieve by Proteas keeper Ryan Rickelton but failed to make South Africa pay, falling soon after to an objectionably unserious dismissal in a game that was, from Australia's perspective, a little too full of them.

Australia was 5-219 at the time of this pivot point, not entirely written off. Rabada had just taken the second new ball. Boland, batting steadily, had just driven him to the long-off boundary with a beautifully straight bat. Smith? Convention be damned. Rabada sent down a length ball on a fourth-stump line. Smith, for reasons known only to him, decided he should launch over the fence at deep mid-wicket. Instead he skied it and Matthew Breetzke juggled a catch. Therein lay the death of the contest.

Steve Smith's nightmare shot in the second session opened the door to a South African win. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Much has been made of Marnus Labuschagne's battle against morality, but Smith is now a fairly pressing problem too. For a long time, he has been Australia's Mr Dependable — not simply a better batsmen than younger alternatives, but an undroppable ornament, encouraged to play how he likes, to bat where he wants and indulge his obsessions however he sees fit.

Yet that greatness is suddenly fading fast, the numbers dwindling, Smith's insularity intensifying into less pardonable distractions. It is hard to shake the feeling that he and Labuschagne's overall effect on Australia's flaky batting group is a net negative on a psychological level as much as a statistical one.

A subtle but remarkable insight into this dynamic — ignored at the time — was glimpsed during the Bangladesh series in August, when Cameron Green used a post-match interview to explain the genesis of his own breakthrough first Test century on home soil.

South Africa has the momentum going into the final Test, something that seemed inconceivable two days into this match. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

"I was able to go back to Shield cricket … kind of a good little reminder about how I want to go about it," Green told ABC Sport at the time. "I think when you're playing in a pretty good Australian Test team, you bat behind some pretty good players in front of you and I think I probably got caught up in how they go about it. So, I think the beautiful thing about going back to state cricket is to remind myself how I want to go about it."

In other words, Australia's most gifted player of the generation to come was admitting that in order to get himself firing as a middle-order batsmen in this Test side, first he had to get himself far away from the influence of his teammates.

Green, of course, will be pushing his case for selection in Cape Town after injury ruled him out of the first two Tests. Should he be declared fit, the Beau Webster dilemma need not be as emotive as Australian coach Andrew McDonald made it in his press conference on day four.

Beau Webster (right) is likely to make way for Cam Green for the series finale, provided Green is fit to play. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

But it is puzzling to consider the reasoning for even selecting Webster in this match, in which he was never likely to bowl many of his seamers in an attack featuring four frontline quicks, was not asked for his off-spin, nor deemed top-six material with the bat.

McDonald was right to say the issue is not as straightforward as armchair selectors would have it. Like Mitch Marsh before him, Webster is clearly a much-loved team man. Over the English summer just gone, Warwickshire teammate Sam Hain spoke with genuine emotion of the mutual respect and pride Webster had created from the minute he arrived. Warwickshire duly won the championship trophy. But Webster's numbers told a less compelling story: 403 runs at 33, 12 wickets at 40. At Test level, same goes.

The most sensible scenario at the top of the order is that Nic Maddinson, a walking wicket against Rabada, will drop out and Matt Renshaw slide up. Cooper Connolly, who at ODI level recently justified the hype around him, must surely be in line to enter a team crying out for fresh blood.

Australia selector George Bailey's refusal to infuse the Test side with youth is providing diminishing results. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Looking beyond this result and this series, one wonders whether Australian cricket can find a clarity of purpose and be as ruthless as it needs to be to avoid toppling over a cliff when Smith, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon are finally gone.

On that note, here is a quote to consider, from Australia's chairman of selectors: "Part of our charter is obviously to provide for the future," he said. "We are very aware that some of these blokes are getting on in age, and that's why it's very, very important for them to continue to perform."

Unfortunately, that was not George Bailey referring to this current Australian team, average age 34, which in Durban was the oldest XI since the 1920s and the first in Test history to not feature a single player under the age of 30.

No, it was Trevor Hohns, late in 2000, referring to arguably Australia's greatest combination ever. Its average age? Erm, 30.

Time, perhaps, for a new charter.

World.title: England stunned as Sri Lanka chases 430 after Brook's record ODI knock
World.content:
Sri Lanka has chased down 430 in a thrilling one-day clash against England despite Harry Brook scoring the fastest double-century in ODI history.

Brook's double-century helped England post a mammoth score of 4-429 before Sri Lanka chased down the target with two wickets and one ball to spare.

Sri Lanka's chase is the second-highest of all time in ODI cricket, trailing only South Africa's chase of 435 against Australia in 2006.

The 27-year-old captain rewrote the record books by racing to his double hundred in 114 balls, surpassing the previous mark of 117 deliveries set by India's Shubman Gill.

Brook's double-century was the fastest of all time and he also eclipsed England's highest individual ODI score of 182, previously held by Ben Stokes.

He made 202 from 116 deliveries, peppering the Sri Lanka attack with 21 fours and 10 sixes before departing to warm applause from the crowd.

The defeat leaves England bottom of the standings after losing both their matches, with Brook saying they need to win their next two games to reach the final in Lahore.

Harry Brook's record-breaking double-century was ultimately in vain as Sri Lanka chased down the target of 430 with a ball to spare. (Getty Images: Sameer Ali)

"Unfortunately, it [the record] doesn't matter now. I thought we were going to be in a good position but, unfortunately, it doesn't even count," Brook said after the game.

"Heartbreaking. I think you've hit the nail on the head there. It's very disappointing that we haven't been able to defend 430, but that's life, that's cricket," he added.

"You don't see many teams chase down 430 and hats off to Sri Lanka. They've played exceptionally well. We couldn't execute our skills enough with the ball and, again, they've just played an absolute blinder there.

"We'll have a good chat about it now and over the next couple of days. We've got a good opportunity in the next couple of games to really try and get to that final in Lahore."

Pavan Rathnayake top-scored for Sri Lanka with 130 from 106 deliveries, while opener Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka both fell three runs short of centuries.

Needing six runs from the final two deliveries, Sri Lanka sealed victory when Janith Liyanage launched Josh Tongue over long-off for six, leaving Brook's record-breaking innings all in vain.

Tongue was England's most successful bowler with 3-79.

England lost by 87 runs at the same venue in Rawalpindi on Tuesday to Pakistan, who lead the table with two wins from two.

Reuters

World.title: Wallaroos great inspired by mantra 'you can't be what you can't see'
World.content:
As Emily Chancellor runs out for her final Test, she will know she has fulfilled one of her ambitions as a Wallaroos representative.

Upon making her Test debut in 2018, Chancellor wanted to help increase the visibility of the Wallaroos among young fans.

Even though she followed rugby growing up, the Wallaroos were not on her radar as the women's game lacked adequate support and promotion.

Chancellor only began playing as a 21-year-old university student, admitting earlier this week "rugby wasn't an option" during her childhood.

At Canberra Stadium this evening, there will be young girls among the spectators eagerly watching the Wallaroos play Scotland.

They will be cheering on their heroes and dreaming of playing for the national women's rugby team, proving Chancellor has taken giant steps in accomplishing her mission.

Inspiring young fans has been at the forefront of Emily Chancellor's mind. (Getty Images: Robbie Stephenson)

"You can't be what you can't see," Chancellor told ABC Sport on the eve of her Test farewell.

"I feel like that is something that has driven me so hard; to want to keep playing and pushing the image of the Wallaroos to a wider audience.

"I feel like I've had a positive impact on that over the last eight years. I love seeing the kids in the crowd, with their parents, excited.

"What excites me is that there has been so much growth when I look back over the last eight years, considering where I was when I was a kid and the visibility of the game in the women's world [at the time].

"It's come so far. I'm really proud of where we've got to and how many young girls are turning up to games."

Tight bond

After 42 Tests, Chancellor will leave the game as a Wallaroos great.

The 35-year-old appeared in two World Cups and captained the team during the 2025 season.

A stellar domestic career with the NSW Waratahs and stints playing club rugby in the UK and Japan are also among her most cherished experiences.

Emily Chancellor captained the Wallaroos in 2025. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Aside from her on-field achievements, nothing means more to Chancellor than the tight bond she enjoys with her Wallaroos teammates.

She describes the close-knit squad as a "sisterhood".

"We're all struggling or thriving with the challenges rugby faces, particularly in the women's space," said Chancellor, who will start at openside flanker against Scotland.

"Be it pay, the lack of professionalism, or the striving for both of those things, I think that bonds you together massively."

'Limitless' future

The Wallaroos's semi-professional status has made it difficult for the squad to compete with the likes of England and New Zealand, both of which benefit from having full-time programs.

The Wallaroos are in the process of becoming full-time in the build-up to the 2029 World Cup, which will be hosted by Australia.

Emily Chancellor made her Test debut against New Zealand in 2018. (Getty Images)

Chancellor believes the team's opportunities will be "limitless" when this is finally achieved.

"You see how much natural ability the girls have, how much we do with so little in terms of game time at the moment," she said.

"I get excited by what Rugby Australia did with the Aussie women's sevens team when they went full-time.

"A bit more hard work and time together … wow, I think it will be exciting."

Chancellor will be enjoying retirement once the next World Cup rolls around, but her commitment to the Wallaroos's cause shows no signs of diminishing.

The drive to increase visibility of the Wallaroos and women's rugby will remain.

"We've still got a long way to go, and I don't plan on letting up on that goal of making it as visible as possible when I step away from playing," she said.

World.title: Quick hits: Bavuma hides from Smith implosion as Boland outdoes batters
World.content:
Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while nightwatchman Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha.

Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Head passes 100 but can't go on

Travis Head began day five needing 13 runs for a gritty, fighting century.

And after a two-hour rain delay, the punchy southpaw reached three figures with relative ease, bringing up the milestone with two leg-side boundaries against South African destroyer Marco Jansen in the sixth over of the day.

Travis Head scored his 13th Test century. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

His celebrations were understandably muted given the state of the game, with his helmet staying in place as he raised his bat and a grin not even threatening to peek through his grill.

It was just Head's second overseas ton after his effort in the 2023 World Test Championship final at the Oval against India, and first against a team on its home patch.

But Head was unable to set up for the long haul his team so craved, with the Australian departing just after the first drinks break, chopping on while attempting a cut shot that was never there.

Head was out for 121 and Australia was 5-209.

2. Boland shows batters how it's done

By now, Australian cricket fans should know better than to doubt Scott Boland.

But even the most optimistic of those watching back home surely wouldn't have expected the nightwatchman to outlast both Head and Steve Smith, take his innings deep into the day and soak up a staggering 166 deliveries.

Boland found the middle of the bat more often than not during his heroic vigil. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

There were a couple of streaky moments, sure, but Boland made his luck more than he rode it, defending with the kind of authority and simplicity his more celebrated batting teammates were so desperately lacking throughout the Test.

He even played a few memorable shots, including an immaculate straight drive back past South Africa spearhead Kagiso Rabada.

But finally, in the second over after tea, Boland's marathon vigil was over, with Wiaan Mulder producing a jagging peach to have the brave nightwatchman bowled through the gate for a new Test best of 40.

3. Bavuma can't watch as Smith throws it away

It was the moment — and didn't Temba Bavuma know it.

The South Africa captain just couldn't watch as Steve Smith top-edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer high into the blue Gqeberha sky, turning his back completely as Matthew Breetzke raced back and settled under the ball.

Bavuma couldn't watch as Breetzke took a dramatic juggling catch. (Fox Cricket)

It was a rash, ugly shot from Smith, and certainly not one befitting of a man tasked with saving a Test match.

But for a moment, it looked like he was going to get away with it.

Having just-about settled underneath the ball, Breetzke juggled once and then twice before securing the wicket that was destined to end the Australian resistance.

Smith, perhaps still struggling with his neck issue from day four, was out for 3 and Australia was 6-255.

4. Mulder does damage after tea

With four wickets still in reserve, Australia reached tea still with a sniff of pulling off one of the great escapes.

But in removing Australia's best two batters, the Proteas had already done the hard part, and there would have been no panic as they readied themselves for the game's final stanza.

And in the opening exchanges of what was being sold as a marathon, 44-over evening session, all-rounder Mulder struck not once, but twice.

First, he ended Boland with that divine off-cutter; then he produced something similarly inspired to send the newly-arrived Pat Cummins packing for 4.

At 8-262, it was all beginning to unravel.

There was only one thing that could save the Aussies now ...

5. South Africa beats descending gloom

All of a sudden, things were beginning to darken in Gqeberha.

With ominous clouds gathering on the outskirts of the oval and ground staff poised to pounce at the boundary rope, the South Africans were in a race with the elements.

Clouds were gathering ominously with the Proteas in search of their final two wickets. (Fox Cricket)

Two wickets were needed.

Well aware of the descending gloom, Bavuma threw the ball to his premier spearhead.

And Rabada delivered in the first over of his spell, bowling Mitchell Starc with the tailender attempting an ugly and wholly unnecessary slog.

But with the skies continuing to intimidate, we were treated to surely one of the most farcical drinks breaks in Test history.

Those five lost minutes, however, were not enough to save the Australians.

The heavens never did open, and number 11 Josh Hazlewood was promptly caught behind the wicket, confirming a chastening innings and 31-run defeat for Australia and a richly deserved series-levelling triumph for the South Africans.

World.title: Cummins admits Australia 'long way from our best' as South Africa levels series
World.content:
Australia has fallen to defeat by an innings and 31 runs against South Africa in the second Test at St George's Park in Gqeberha.

Brave innings from Travis Head (121) and night watchman Scott Boland (40) were not enough for Australia, as the Proteas levelled the series at 1-1.

"We were a long way away from our best," Pat Cummins said at the presentation.

"Across the board just not enough of us contributed.

"Ideally we'd be scoring more runs. The pitch was pretty good out there."

The two teams will now head to Newlands in Cape Town for the final Test on Tuesday with the series on the line.

The hosts came into the final day needing just six wickets for victory, but were made to wait to get on the field after the first session was washed out by rain.

The persistent drizzle, interspersed by heavier squalls, may have given Australia hope that they may be able to orchestrate a great escape.

Even once play eventually resumed, every over that Head and Boland successfully negotiated raised hopes even further.

Head's 13th Test century was the first by an Australian batter in a follow-on innings since the 1980s and added to the pressure South Africa must have been feeling, with Anrich Nortje's injury leaving the Proteas a bowler down.

"I thought there was some good fight today," Cummins said.

"Scotty Boland and Trav [Head] both played their roles really well, but it was a fair way to come back from and it wasn't quite enough."

Travis Head scored his 13th Test century. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Once Head chopped on to Wiaan Mulder just before the second new ball was due, the writing may have been on the wall.

Steve Smith, batting at seven after being hampered by a sore neck on day four, initially looked sprightly, before he top edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer to Matthew Breetzke when on 3.

Boland's brave, 166-ball vigil came to an end soon after, a brilliant off cutter from Mulder taking the top of his off stump.

Pat Cummins followed in the same way for just 4 to leave South Africa just two wickets from victory.

Still, Australia had hope as clouds gathered and threatened yet more rain to rescue an unlikely draw.

But then Rabada returned, bowling Mitch Starc for 11, before Marco Jansen extracted an edge from Josh Hazlewood for a duck.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Schutt banned for two matches after prescription medication failure
World.content:
Australian women's fast bowler Megan Schutt has been banned for two matches for failing to meet guidelines on the use of prescription medication.

Cricket Australia confirmed Schutt's suspension in a release on Thursday afternoon.

"The breach was a failure to adhere to requirements under the Sports Science and Sports Medicine guidelines with regard to prescription medication," Cricket Australia said.



"This relates to a single incidence which occurred while out of competition and was not for performance-enhancing purposes."



The two-match ban applies to all international and domestic cricket.

Schutt starred in the recent three-match ODI series against Bangladesh. She had series figures of 10-71.

She has not played in a three-match T20 international series against New Zealand, which wraps up tonight at North Sydney.

Schutt released a statement acknowledging the breach and accepting the penalty.

"I fully accept the penalty handed down and apologise for failing to meet the standards expected of me," Schutt said in her statement.

"I'm sorry for the attention this has caused and appreciate the support I've received.

"While this occurred out of competition and was not performance related, I understand that I am responsible for following the Sports Science and Sports Medicine Guidelines, which players receive regular education on, and I should have adhered to these guidelines."



Cricket Australia said it would continue to provide "appropriate support" to Schutt and to reinforce standards and responsibilities expected of all involved in the game.

World.title: Aussie Borlase on winning side as Atlanta Dream leads WNBA Finals
World.content:
Angel Reese recorded 21 points and 12 rebounds to help the Atlanta Dream secure a 97-71 home victory over the Golden State Valkyries, giving the Dream a 2-1 lead in the WNBA Finals after Game 3.

Rhyne Howard added 16 points, and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who also host Game 4 on Sunday (AEDT).

Australian guard Izzy Borlase played a solid role for the Dream on Wednesday night, local time. She played 26 minutes, finishing with 12 points, including one three-pointer, plus five rebounds, two assists and a block.

Another Australian Opals star, Miela Sowah, sat on the bench for the Valkyries and will remain there throughout the finals due to her restricted status as a development player.

The Dream highlighted one of Borlase's drives to the basket on its social media.

It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for its first-ever victory in the Finals. She now has a double-double in each game of the Finals.

"It feels good when you're in the finals. It's a long season, and you play against everybody and go through and push through, but when you can do it at the highest level, this is what you live for, this is what the off-season is for," Reese said.

"I put the work in for this moment, and I'm just happy I could lead the team to a win. We're feeling good going into Saturday."

With the game tied at 49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes's lay-up, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter, scoring 12 of the final 14 points.

With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who got fouled.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Golden State could never recover. Gabby Williams scored 15 points, and Hayes added 14 for the Valkyries.

"Protect home court," Howard said of the team's focus. "Giving our fans a show. We fought for this arena so we had to protect it. It's big. We went and stole one, but we can't let them come in and do the same thing."

The game was moved from the Dream's home Gateway Center Arena to the NBA's Atlanta Hawks home arena. Wednesday night's game was sold out, with more than 17,000 fans attending, as is Game 4 on Saturday at the same venue.

The game got off to a slow start as Atlanta led 9-1 after the first five minutes. Golden State missed its first eight shots before Aminata Gueye scored the first basket with 4:39 left.

They got within 13-10 before Naz Hillmon hit consecutive 3-pointers and then Reese hit one. The Dream led 23-15 after the opening quarter.

Atlanta built its lead to 37-26 midway through the period. Golden State was able to hang around and only trailed 46-40 at the break as the teams combined to shoot 15-for-31 (48 per cent) from behind the arc.

That was more completed 3-pointers in the first 20 minutes than in either Game 1 or Game 2.

Game 1 and 2 had huge ratings, with the opener on NBC averaging 2.1 million, the most ever for a first game of the Finals. Game 2, which was broadcast on USA Network, averaged 1.33 million viewers.

AP/ABC

World.title: Amid the hunt for World Cup glory one of Tonga's greats is not done yet
World.content:
As Tonga's World Cup campaign prepares to hit fever pitch, Tui Lolohea cannot stop smiling even when the young bulls give him stick.

After a training session in the lead-up to Friday's match against Lebanon it is rising prop Demetric Vaimauga, who is the kind of guy you hear before you see, that gees Lolohea up.

"Awwww yeah, it's Mr I Ain't Done Yet!" Vaimauga crows as he grabs Lolohea by the shoulders.

That's what they called Lolohea in an Instagram post after he came off the bench for an injured Latu Fainu to set up a try in Tonga's 30-12 win over England last week and he's been copping it ever since.

It was a cameo Lolohea, at 31 and with Tonga enjoying more depth and talent in the halves than ever before, thought would never come.

But once it did it added to an already sterling legacy in the red jersey, tacking an extra chapter on a story that, against all odds, is still being written.

Lolohea has already played for Tonga more times than any other player in history and against the Cedars he'll extend his own record with his 23rd cap.

Along with Jason Taumalolo, Lolohea is the only player to have appeared in each of Tonga's five wins over Tier 1 nations, making them the only two constant faces in every image of Tonga's greatest days.

Loading Instagram content

Lolohea has been wearing these colours when those days were still just a dream. When he debuted for Tonga back in 2015, Fainu, the man he replaced last week and will partner in the halves on Friday, was only nine years old.

Vaimauga himself had just turned 11 and as the giant youngster runs away cackling, Lolohea fires back in Tongan through a grin and shakes his head.

"I knew I'd get stick for this. Mr I Ain't Done Yet — they're always taking the piss out of me," Lolohea said.

"I hope he gets banged next time he goes off the back fence, so I can go laugh at him.

"They joke around, but I am one of the oldest in the team and it's good to show you can run around with the young bucks."

Jason Taumalolo and Tui Lolohea have played in every one of Tonga's wins over Tier 1 nations. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yueng)

Lolohea and Taumalolo are the elders this time around as the two longest-serving players in the team by a mile and while Taumalolo dragged Tonga into a new world, Lolohea is very much a product of the old.

Watching his debut from 11 years ago against Samoa on the Gold Coast is a measure of how far things have come.

When the two meet again next week it will be in front of a sold-out crowd at Parramatta Stadium, which they probably could have filled twice over, and both sides will boast some of the best players in the world.

Back on Lolohea's first day, a little over 12,000 came through the gates and both nations had to choose between grey beards, who wanted to give back to their community, journeymen who knew this would be as good as it got, or youngsters before their big futures came for them.

International rugby league has come a long way since Tui Lolohea's Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Lolohea was one of the latter and at the time he was counted as one of rugby league's brightest prospects, with feet so fast tackling him was like trying to grab a handful of smoke.

So much has transformed since those times but according to Lolohea, the most important things have stayed the same.

"Why you're doing it, what you're representing, that never changes," Lolohea said.

"We're a little dot on the map and there's always talk about financial stuff but the pride of our island nation, the proud culture we put out to the people, we've built that over the years and the support from the people is massive.

Why Jason Taumalolo is still more than just a man for Tonga In the NRL, we only talk about what Jason Taumalolo can't do anymore. But when he pulls on the red of Tonga it's a reminder of what he still is and always will be for the island nation and for Test rugby league.
